final.content:
Maternal mortality and prenatal-care access among Rohingya refugees in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, versus Karen refugees in Mae La camp, Thailand, 2017–2023

Executive summary

The available evidence supports a clear but qualified comparison:

• Mae La generally achieved stronger routine maternity-care coverage than Cox’s Bazar, particularly in the early comparable years. UNHCR’s Health Information System (HIS) recorded antenatal-care coverage of 89% in Mae La in 2017 and 91% in 2018, skilled attendance at 96% and 95% of births, and neonatal mortality of 20 and 6 per 1,000 live births, respectively. The Mae La indicator is “antenatal-care coverage,” however, not explicitly completion of four or more visits.

• Cox’s Bazar began from much lower and more heterogeneous access after the 2017 influx. In 2018, UNHCR camp/site reports ranged from 45% to 94% antenatal coverage, 83% to 101% skilled birth attendance, and neonatal mortality of 17–22 per 1,000 live births in sites for which results are retrievable. Values over 100% reveal denominator and cross-camp attendance problems and should not be read literally as population coverage.

• Survey evidence gives a less favorable picture than facility reporting in Cox’s Bazar. Among women surveyed in one camp in September 2019–January 2020, 71.6% reported four or more antenatal visits and 69.4% reported skilled attendance at their last delivery. By April 2023, a Kutupalong survey found that approximately 47% of women had received no antenatal care in their most recent pregnancy. These estimates differ in population, period and definition, so they indicate severe geographic and social inequality rather than a simple time trend.

• Mae La’s favorable coverage is associated with a mature, community-staffed camp clinic and a referral relationship with Thai public hospitals roughly one hour away. This is not full Thai Ministry of Public Health (MoPH) absorption of refugee primary care: camp-level services remained NGO-operated, while MoPH hospitals supplied surgery, blood-bank-supported care and specialist services.

• Cox’s Bazar used a much larger, fragmented humanitarian network of NGO/UN field hospitals, primary health centres, health posts, midwife-led centres and ambulances. Basic emergency obstetric and newborn care was available in camp, but comprehensive emergency obstetric care depended on referral. Congestion, hills, monsoon damage, insecurity, weak telephone coverage, language barriers and consent/referral delays made nominal two-hour access less reliable.

• Obstetric haemorrhage remained Cox’s Bazar’s dominant documented maternal-death mechanism: 28% of pregnancy-related deaths in 2017–2018, 26.7% of maternal deaths in 2020, 44% in 2022, and roughly 35–46% in 2023 depending on classification. These are proportions of deaths, not postpartum-haemorrhage incidence among deliveries. No defensible 2017–2023 PPH-incidence series was found for either population.

• The premise that a “2021 UNFPA funding reduction” directly interrupted both sites is only partly supported. The documented event was the UK’s approximately 85% reduction in its expected 2021 contribution to UNFPA Supplies—from £154 million to about £23 million—plus a £12 million core-resource cut. Cox’s Bazar nevertheless received a new US$38.8 million World Bank–UNFPA agreement and maintained supported facilities, outreach and ambulances. Mae La’s core maternity services were not shown to be UNFPA-financed in 2021; they were principally NGO-delivered with Thai-hospital referrals. Therefore, a causal service discontinuity in both locations cannot be inferred from the evidence.

1. Scope and comparability

The study period begins with the mass Rohingya arrival in Bangladesh in August 2017 and ends in 2023. Mae La, by contrast, was already a mature, protracted refugee settlement with a long-established reproductive-health programme.

The indicators are not perfectly harmonized:

1. UNHCR HIS “antenatal-care coverage” is not necessarily ANC4+, and may count registration or at least one visit.
2. Skilled birth attendance is sometimes represented by facility delivery, but the concepts are not identical: a skilled attendant may attend outside a facility, and a facility birth is not automatically proof of an appropriately skilled attendant.
3. Neonatal mortality is deaths before 28 completed days per 1,000 live births. UNHCR’s indicator guide confirms this definition (https://medref.unhcr.org/ressources/footer/Standards_and_Indicators_Guide_2019.pdf).
4. PPH incidence means PPH cases divided by deliveries. Most Cox’s Bazar sources instead report the share of maternal deaths caused by obstetric haemorrhage; those quantities cannot be substituted.
5. Later Cox’s Bazar surveillance used WHO EWARS, community-based surveillance supported by UNHCR and facility reporting, rather than a single UNHCR HIS site report. Improved case finding can raise reported mortality without a true deterioration.

These limitations make precise pooled 2017–2023 rates inappropriate. The strongest conclusions concern levels, direction, service architecture and documented barriers.

2. Comparative indicator evidence

2.1 Antenatal-care completion: four or more visits

Mae La

UNHCR HIS reported:

• 2017 antenatal-care coverage: 89%.
• 2018 antenatal-care coverage: 91%.

The corresponding site reports are available at:
https://reliefweb.int/attachments/39ea9ee8-f0f1-3911-a9c5-b75ce55bc944/Thailand_2017_Maela.pdf
and
https://his.unhcr.org/ar2018/files/TH/Thailand_2018_Maela.pdf

These are not explicitly ANC4+ measures. Evidence from other long-term Karen refugee camps on the Thai–Myanmar border found that more than 90% of pregnant women attended four or more visits, but that study covered Mae La Oon and Mae Ra Ma Luang—not Mae La—and should be treated as contextual rather than camp-specific evidence (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11091483/).

The defensible conclusion is that Mae La had near-universal contact with antenatal services and probably high continuity, but a precise Mae La ANC4+ percentage for every year through 2023 is not documented in the retrieved evidence.

Cox’s Bazar

UNHCR HIS showed wide 2018 variation:

• Kutupalong: 75% antenatal coverage.
• Kutupalong New: 94%.
• Kutupalong Extension: 45%.
• Nayapara: 79%.

Sources:
https://his.unhcr.org/ar2018/files/BD/Bangladesh_2018_Kutupalong.pdf
https://his.unhcr.org/ar2018/files/BD/Bangladesh_2018_Kutupalong_New.pdf
https://his.unhcr.org/ar2018/files/BD/Bangladesh_2018_Kutupalong_Extension.pdf
https://his.unhcr.org/ar2018/files/BD/Bangladesh_2018_Nayapara.pdf

The range is 94 − 45 = 49 percentage points, demonstrating major site inequality.

A January–February 2018 demographic assessment found that only 53.5% of 370 currently pregnant women had received at least one ANC visit. That equals approximately:

370 × 0.535 = 198 women,

which matches the report’s stated 198 attendees (http://dspace.icddrb.org/jspui/bitstream/123456789/9067/2/Special%20Report%20153.pdf).

A Camp 4 survey conducted from September 2019 to January 2020 found:

• 297 of 415 women had ANC4+.
• 297 ÷ 415 × 100 = 71.57%.

The same survey found strong associations between maternal-health information and service uptake, emphasizing that cultural and informational mediation mattered (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41225600/).

Administrative activity increased later. In 2022, partners reported 394,357 ANC contacts, of which 160,279 were first visits and 234,078 repeat visits; 74.3% of all contacts were for Rohingya women. Repeat contacts therefore comprised:

234,078 ÷ 394,357 × 100 = 59.4%.

This is workload, not ANC4+ population coverage, because one woman can generate multiple contacts (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/sexual_and_reproductive_health_working_annual_bulletin_2022.pdf).

In contrast, an April 2023 survey of 708 women in Kutupalong found approximately 47% had received no antenatal service in their most recent pregnancy, implying approximately:

708 × 0.47 ≈ 333 women with no ANC,
708 × 0.53 ≈ 375 with at least one contact.

The survey did not establish a comparable ANC4+ rate (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10835278/).

Interpretation

Mae La’s stable, long-running clinic appears to have produced more consistent continuity than Cox’s Bazar’s geographically variable emergency response. Cox’s Bazar did achieve substantial improvement in some camps, but administrative visit totals conceal women who never entered care. The 2019–2020 ANC4+ estimate of 71.6% should not be extrapolated to all 33–34 camps.

2.2 Skilled birth attendance

Mae La

UNHCR HIS recorded:

• 2017: 96% of births attended by skilled personnel.
• 2018: 95%.

Thus, the decline was one percentage point, while both years remained above UNHCR’s then-reported 90% standard. Mae La’s mature reproductive-health programme had provided ANC, delivery, postpartum and neonatal care for many years, historically through the Shoklo Malaria Research Unit and subsequently through other NGO arrangements.

Cox’s Bazar

UNHCR’s 2018 site results included:

• Kutupalong: 99%.
• Kutupalong New: 83%.
• Kutupalong Extension: 101%.
• Nayapara: 100%.

The 101% result is impossible as true individual coverage and indicates denominator mismatch, cross-site service use, population movement or reporting error. Consequently, HIS numerators should not be aggregated as a clean camp-wide estimate.

Population and sector evidence was much less favorable:

• Early analyses indicated that only about one in five Rohingya mothers delivered in a camp health facility (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0230732).
• In the third quarter of 2019, 3,998 facility births were reported across 32 primary health-care facilities, averaging 47% of expected births; camp rates ranged from 12% to 100% (https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/searo/bangladesh/bangladesh---rohingya-crisis---pdf-reports/health-sector-cxb-bangladesh-no-11.pdf).
• In the 2019–2020 Camp 4 survey, 288 of 415 women reported skilled attendance:

288 ÷ 415 × 100 = 69.4%.

• In 2022, monthly facility-delivery coverage rose from 69–76% through much of the year to 81% in October–December; annual progress was reported as 75% (https://reliefweb.int/attachments/781cd052-99b4-4eba-8eb9-160e25c04b8b/coxs_bazar_health_sector_bulletin_nov_dec_2022.pdf).

Because facility delivery is a proxy rather than exactly SBA, the safest comparison is:

• Mae La: approximately 95–96% documented SBA in 2017–2018.
• Cox’s Bazar: initially around 20–47% facility delivery at response-wide level, approximately 69% self-reported SBA in one camp in 2019–2020, and approximately 75% facility delivery in 2022.

The trajectory in Cox’s Bazar was positive, but remained uneven and generally below Mae La’s early HIS performance.

2.3 Maternal mortality

Cox’s Bazar

The strongest baseline is the retrospective reproductive-age mortality study covering September 2017–August 2018:

• 82 pregnancy-related deaths.
• 52 confirmed maternal deaths.
• Pregnancy-related death ratio: 282 per 100,000 live births, 95% CI 221–343.
• Maternal mortality ratio: 179 per 100,000 live births, 95% CI 130–228.

Source:
https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/Final%20RAMOS%20Summary%20Report%20for%20circulation_0.pdf

The implied live-birth denominator is approximately:

52 ÷ 179 × 100,000 = 29,050 live births.

That denominator also approximately reconciles with pregnancy-related mortality:

82 ÷ 29,050 × 100,000 = 282 per 100,000.

Prospective surveillance subsequently recorded:

• 2020: 45 confirmed maternal deaths among 144 deaths of women of reproductive age.
• 2022: 83 maternal deaths.
• 2023: 57 maternal deaths, of which 43 occurred in facilities or during referral and 14 in the community.

Sources:
https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/annual_report_of_mpmsr_2020_03_august_2021.pdf
https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/mpmsr_annual_report_2022.pdf.pdf
https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/2024-09/MPMSR%20Annual%20Report%202023%20Final.docx.pdf

These counts should not be converted to annual MMRs without reliable live-birth denominators and complete ascertainment. The increase from 45 reported deaths in 2020 to 83 in 2022 may reflect changing surveillance completeness as well as risk. In 2022, facility event-based reporting completeness was only 56%, compared with 95% for community surveillance.

Mae La

UNHCR HIS recorded one maternal death in 2017 and none in 2018. With few births, annual ratios are statistically unstable; one death can produce a large apparent rate. Historical SMRU data for women with at least one ANC consultation gave an average MMR of 133 per 100,000 live births in 2002–2007, but this predates the requested period and is not a 2017–2023 estimate.

The broader Thai-border cohort reported maternal mortality of 176 per 100,000 live births over 94,645 pregnancies extending from 1986 to 2024, but it combines periods, refugees and migrants and cannot be assigned to Mae La in 2017–2023.

Conclusion on mortality

The evidence does not support a precise 2017–2023 camp-to-camp MMR ratio. Cox’s Bazar has a credible 2017–2018 MMR of 179 per 100,000 and persistent annual maternal-death counts thereafter. Mae La recorded 1 and 0 deaths in 2017 and 2018, but small numbers prevent concluding that its underlying MMR was zero or necessarily below Cox’s Bazar’s with statistical confidence.

2.4 Postpartum haemorrhage

Cox’s Bazar

Available data concern cause-specific mortality, not PPH incidence:

• 2017–2018: obstetric haemorrhage caused 28% of 82 pregnancy-related deaths, approximately 23 deaths:
82 × 0.28 = 22.96.
• 2020: haemorrhage caused 12 of 45 maternal deaths, or 26.7%; eight were PPH and four antepartum haemorrhage.
• PPH alone therefore represented:
8 ÷ 45 × 100 = 17.8% of maternal deaths in 2020.
• 2022: haemorrhage caused 44% of 83 maternal deaths, approximately 37 deaths:
83 × 0.44 = 36.5.
• 2023: the report’s headline classification attributes 20 of 57 deaths to obstetric haemorrhage:
20 ÷ 57 × 100 = 35.1%.
A later cross-year table uses a broader 46%/22-death classification, illustrating evolving audit definitions.

Obstetric haemorrhage was consistently a leading lethal complication. It would nevertheless be incorrect to label 17.8%, 35% or 44% as “PPH incidence,” because the denominator is maternal deaths rather than deliveries.

Mae La

A clinical quality assessment found PPH was the most common observed intrapartum complication; skilled attendants followed protocol but were sometimes slow to recognize severity and act (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12884-015-0444-0). The study predates 2017 and does not provide a 2017–2023 incidence rate.

Historical border-program evidence suggests training mattered: after Advanced Life Support in Obstetrics training, PPH-related mortality among women delivering at SMRU fell from 59.3 per 100,000 live births in 2000–2007 to zero in 2008–2015, although this is historical and not equivalent to PPH incidence.

No source gathered supplies a defensible PPH cases-per-100-deliveries series for Mae La or Cox’s Bazar during 2017–2023. Any exact comparative claim would be unsupported.

2.5 Neonatal mortality within 28 days

Mae La

UNHCR HIS reported:

• 2017: 20 deaths per 1,000 live births.
• 2018: 6 per 1,000.

Absolute reduction:

20 − 6 = 14 deaths per 1,000.

Relative reduction:

(20 − 6) ÷ 20 × 100 = 70%.

With small annual birth cohorts, this large swing is likely affected by random variation and possibly reporting changes. Nonetheless, it demonstrates that Mae La had neonatal outcomes at or below the then-used HIS threshold by 2018.

Cox’s Bazar

UNHCR’s 2018 results included:

• Kutupalong: 17 per 1,000.
• Kutupalong New: 22 per 1,000.
• Nayapara: 20 per 1,000.

The simple unweighted mean is:

(17 + 22 + 20) ÷ 3 = 19.7 per 1,000,

but this is not a population-weighted Cox’s Bazar rate and excludes sites without a usable value.

Later surveillance reported 51 neonatal deaths during weeks 30–44 of 2019, but no live-birth denominator was supplied, so an NNMR cannot be calculated. In 2023, perinatal surveillance began only in August and reported 304 perinatal deaths through year-end. Perinatal deaths combine stillbirths and early neonatal deaths and therefore are not equivalent to 28-day neonatal mortality.

Comparison

In 2017–2018, Mae La moved from approximately the same neonatal-mortality level as Cox’s Bazar sites to a substantially lower reported level. For 2019–2023, available Cox’s Bazar counts and Mae La evidence do not permit a harmonized NNMR comparison.

3. Healthcare delivery models

3.1 Cox’s Bazar: humanitarian field-hospital network

The Rohingya response was a large, decentralized partnership under Bangladesh government leadership, with UN agencies and many national and international NGOs. MSF’s initial operational model illustrates the emergency-field structure: by November 2017 it had opened six health posts and expanded inpatient capacity from 50 to 120 beds across Kutupalong and Balukhali, while treating more than 67,000 patients and over 1,500 inpatients (https://www.msf.org/sites/default/files/coxsbazar_healthsurveyreport_dec2017_final1.pdf).

By 2022, UNHCR supported 28 health facilities, alongside nutrition, stabilization and psychosocial services. Facilities offered 24-hour basic emergency obstetric and neonatal care, with referral for more complex emergencies (https://data.unhcr.org/en/documents/download/100119).

Strengths:

• rapid scale-up across a population approaching one million;
• many geographically dispersed entry points;
• 24/7 basic emergency obstetric and newborn functions;
• dedicated field hospitals and ambulances;
• midwife-led birthing centres;
• UNFPA-led coordination and mortality review;
• community surveillance and community-health-worker outreach.

Weaknesses:

• fragmented operators and reporting systems;
• inconsistent quality and catchment denominators;
• difficult interfacility referral;
• service disruption from monsoon flooding, fires and access restrictions;
• limited comprehensive EmONC and surgery inside many camps;
• language, trust, gender and consent barriers;
• high turnover and dependence on short-cycle humanitarian funding.

One documented midwife-led centre served approximately 8,500 people, managed 267 births in 2022 and referred 70 complicated cases:

70 ÷ 267 × 100 = 26.2 referrals per 100 births.

This high transfer burden demonstrates the centre’s triage role and dependence on higher-level care. Reported challenges included night transport, security, weak mobile coverage and the need for a closer referral hospital (https://journals.plos.org/globalpublichealth/article?id=10.1371/journal.pgph.0004033).

3.2 Mae La: NGO camp care linked to Thai public hospitals

Mae La’s model is better described as NGO-operated primary/maternity care integrated by referral with Thailand’s MoPH system—not as full MoPH operation of the camp service.

Historically, NGO-run facilities provided outpatient, inpatient, laboratory, pharmacy and maternity services using trained refugee medics, nurses and birth attendants, supervised by a small number of expatriate or Thai clinicians. Complicated cases were sent to Mae Sot General Hospital, about one hour by vehicle, for surgery, imaging and specialist care (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6620057/).

In 2018, preventive and curative services were transferred to a single NGO, while changes in financing improved access to tertiary hospital care for obstetric complications. The Special Care Baby Unit and longstanding SMRU systems provided a continuity of maternal and newborn expertise uncommon in newer emergency settlements (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2023.1144642/full).

Strengths:

• one established camp population and clearer catchment;
• mature reproductive-health records;
• high ANC and skilled-delivery uptake;
• refugee/community health workers who shared language and culture;
• referral to Thai district/provincial hospitals for comprehensive care;
• established neonatal special-care capability.

Weaknesses:

• camp itself lacked caesarean, advanced anaesthesia and stored blood capacity;
• public-hospital access depended on authorization, transport and external payment;
• legal restrictions prevented normal inclusion in universal Thai services;
• recurrent donor dependence and provider transitions;
• “integration” stopped short of equal public-system entitlement.

Thus, the contrast is not “NGO hospitals in Bangladesh versus government care in Thailand.” Both relied heavily on NGOs. The meaningful distinction is a vast, fragmented emergency network in Cox’s Bazar versus a mature camp clinic with an established MoPH referral interface in Mae La.

4. Midwife staffing and outcome correlation

Cox’s Bazar had 341 midwives among approximately 3,500 health workers in April 2020. Using a Rohingya population of approximately 889,704 in 2021 as the nearest documented denominator:

889,704 ÷ 341 = 2,609 people per midwife,

or:

341 ÷ 889,704 × 10,000 = 3.83 midwives per 10,000 population.

Sources:
https://www.who.int/bangladesh/news/detail/17-12-2020-celebrating-the-work-of-nurses-and-midwives-in-cox-s-bazar-leading-the-way-with-the-right-care-at-the-right-times
and
https://healthcluster.who.int/docs/librariesprovider16/meeting-reports/bangladesh-health-sector-bulletin-apr-june-2021.pdf

This is an approximate ratio because some staff served host communities, staff categories may overlap, and population and workforce dates differ.

Mae La’s 2018 HIS listed 72 qualified nurses for 39,061 residents:

39,061 ÷ 72 = 543 residents per qualified nurse,
or 18.4 nurses per 10,000.

However, the report does not separate midwives from nurses, so a midwife-to-population ratio cannot be calculated. Comparing Cox’s 3.83 midwives per 10,000 with Mae La’s 18.4 nurses per 10,000 would be an invalid occupational comparison.

The data therefore support only a qualitative correlation: Mae La had denser documented qualified clinical staffing and much higher skilled-delivery coverage, while Cox’s Bazar had a larger absolute midwifery workforce but an enormous, dispersed catchment and lower continuity. Causation cannot be isolated from camp maturity, transport, trust, facility distribution and referral access.

5. Emergency obstetric care within a two-hour radius

Mae La

Mae Sot General Hospital was approximately one hour away by car, placing comprehensive emergency services nominally inside a two-hour transport radius under normal conditions. The camp itself lacked caesarean capacity, advanced airway/anaesthetic support, long-term blood storage and neonatal ventilation. Therefore, effective EmONC depended on:

recognition time + authorization/dispatch + road travel + hospital reception.

Even a one-hour road distance could exceed two hours from onset to definitive treatment.

Cox’s Bazar

Camp facilities generally offered basic EmONC, while comprehensive care required ambulance transfer to field hospitals or government referral hospitals. During 2021 floods, UNFPA deployed five ambulances across ten camps and eight affected host-community unions, illustrating both active referral support and the scale of transport vulnerability (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/external_hsc_sitrep_jul-sep_2021_october_2021_final.pdf).

No gathered source provides the percentage of either population living within two hours of comprehensive EmONC. Consequently:

• Mae La can be classified as nominally within a one-hour vehicular referral radius of Thai hospital care.
• Cox’s Bazar had multiple closer basic-EmONC points but variable time to comprehensive care.
• A formal two-hour coverage percentage cannot be reported.

Outcome correlation is plausible but not causal: Mae La’s reliable referral axis aligns with high SBA and low 2018 NNMR; Cox’s Bazar mortality audits repeatedly identified referral difficulty, delayed surgical consent, equipment/medicine gaps and incomplete referral documentation. The Cox’s Bazar 2023 finding that 75% of maternal deaths occurred in facilities or during referral also shows that physical arrival alone did not ensure timely definitive treatment.

6. Cultural mediation and traditional birth attendants

Cox’s Bazar

Rohingya women’s barriers included distrust of facilities, restrictions imposed by family members, preference for informal providers, language differences, concerns about respectful care, night-time security and transport. Traditional birth attendants—often called dai or dai ma—remained culturally influential.

The response increasingly used:

• Rohingya community health workers and volunteers;
• women-friendly spaces;
• midwife-led centres;
• counseling and birth preparedness;
• outreach linking pregnant women to facilities;
• respectful maternity care;
• engagement of influential community and family members.

The 2019–2020 survey’s association between exposure to maternal/SRH information and ANC4+/SBA supports the importance of mediation. The midwife-led centre study likewise found that women attended because of kind, respectful midwives and recommendations from volunteers and relatives.

Nevertheless, the gathered evidence does not document a standardized, camp-wide dai accreditation or formal co-practice system. Traditional attendants appear mainly as trusted intermediaries or informal providers to be engaged for referral, rather than substitutes for skilled attendants.

Mae La

Mae La’s model relied heavily on trained refugees and local Karen/Burmese-speaking personnel. This embedded workforce reduced language and trust barriers and transformed community members into skilled or semi-professional health workers. Women could retain a support person during labour, and clinical protocols were delivered by staff familiar with local customs.

This represents deeper institutional cultural mediation than a parallel external NGO service: community personnel were inside the clinic workforce. However, available sources do not quantify the proportion of traditional birth attendants formally transitioned into skilled roles during 2017–2023.

Comparison

Cox’s Bazar used outreach to bridge a relatively new humanitarian system and a distrustful displaced population; Mae La had decades to institutionalize refugee staff within clinical care. That difference plausibly contributed to Mae La’s stronger continuity and SBA coverage. The evidence supports association, not a numerical effect size.

7. The 2021 UNFPA funding reduction

7.1 What was actually cut

In April 2021, the UK informed UNFPA that its expected contribution to UNFPA Supplies would fall from £154 million to approximately £23 million:

Reduction = £154m − £23m = £131m.

Percentage reduction:

£131m ÷ £154m × 100 = 85.1%.

The UK also planned a £12 million cut to UNFPA core operating funds (https://aa.unfpa.org/press/statement-uk-government-funding-cuts).

UNFPA’s 2021 Supplies report states that spending plans were reduced by 30%, although other donors partly mitigated the shock and US$84 million in reproductive-health commodities was still delivered globally (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/UNFPA%20Supplies%20Partnership%20Annual%20Report%202021.pdf).

7.2 Cox’s Bazar effect

The cut created a credible risk to contraceptive commodities, partner continuity, outreach and flexible emergency capacity. Yet the available evidence does not show wholesale interruption of maternal care:

• UNFPA supported 22 facilities providing family planning, ANC, facility delivery and PNC in July–September 2021.
• It deployed midwife-led mobile teams, community workers and ambulances during monsoon flooding.
• Those facilities reported 21,417 ANC visits and 2,151 facility births during the reporting period, including 10,546 ANC visits and 1,136 births among Rohingya.
• A separate US$38.8 million World Bank-financed agreement strengthened SRHR and gender services across Cox’s Bazar over three years (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/en/news/strengthening-health-and-gender-services-coxs-bazar-district-us388-million-through-world-bank).

Therefore, the most evidence-consistent assessment is that the UK/UNFPA shock increased fragility and forced reprioritization, but earmarked and multilateral financing buffered frontline continuity. No gathered source quantifies missed ANC visits, midwife layoffs, facility closures or excess deaths attributable specifically to the cut.

7.3 Mae La effect

The claimed direct impact is even less supportable in Mae La:

• Mae La’s principal maternal-health providers were NGOs and community-based staff.
• Comprehensive emergency care was accessed through Thai public hospitals.
• UNFPA Thailand’s 2017–2021 programme focused largely on adolescent SRHR, population issues and national/subnational cooperation; the retrieved documentation does not identify Mae La maternity care as a major UNFPA-funded service line.
• Earlier UNFPA border programming explicitly named Mae La Oon and Mae La Ma Luang, which are different camps from Mae La.

Accordingly, there is no evidence that the 2021 UNFPA reduction caused a measurable discontinuity in Mae La’s ANC, delivery or newborn services. Any effect would have been indirect—through regional commodities, family planning, partner grants or broader donor pressure—and cannot be quantified.

7.4 Comparative conclusion on funding

The funding shock was more directly relevant to Cox’s Bazar because UNFPA led the SRH working group and financed facilities, midwifery, ambulances and commodities. Mae La’s maternity platform was structurally less dependent on UNFPA. The proposition that the same cut materially interrupted both settings is not supported.

8. Role of UNHCR HIS and MSF evidence

UNHCR HIS provides the clearest standardized early comparison:

• Mae La 2017–2018: ANC coverage 89–91%, SBA 95–96%, NNMR 20 declining to 6.
• Cox’s Bazar 2018 sites: ANC 45–94%, SBA 83–101%, NNMR approximately 17–22.

Its limitations are important: site catchments were porous, denominators changed rapidly, and rates above 100% show that service data and population estimates were not always aligned.

MSF’s operational evidence is most informative for Cox’s Bazar’s delivery model and emergency scale-up. It confirms rapid construction of health posts and inpatient capacity in 2017, but does not provide a complete 2017–2023 maternal-indicator series.

For Mae La, MSF should not be presented as the 2017–2023 maternity operator. MSF had handed general camp care to AMI in 2005; obstetric care was historically managed by SMRU, and later provider transitions occurred. Thus, MSF operational reporting cannot validly supply a contemporary Mae La trend where it was no longer the responsible maternity provider.

9. Overall assessment

On the indicators that can be compared, Mae La performed better in access and probably in neonatal outcome:

• ANC: Mae La had 89–91% HIS coverage in 2017–2018; Cox’s Bazar ranged from 45% to 94% in 2018, with only 53.5% receiving even one visit in one early survey. Cox’s ANC4+ reached 71.6% in one 2019–2020 camp survey, but a 2023 Kutupalong survey still found 47% with no ANC.
• Skilled attendance: Mae La recorded 95–96%; Cox’s response-wide facility delivery rose from about 20–47% early in the response to approximately 75% in 2022.
• PPH: Cox’s data establish haemorrhage as a persistent leading cause of maternal death, but neither setting has a comparable PPH-incidence rate for 2017–2023.
• Neonatal mortality: Mae La reported 20 per 1,000 in 2017 and 6 in 2018; Cox’s 2018 sites clustered around 17–22 per 1,000. Comparable later rates are unavailable.
• Maternal mortality: Cox’s best estimate was 179 per 100,000 live births in 2017–2018. Mae La’s annual death counts were one in 2017 and zero in 2018, but denominators were too small to establish a stable MMR.

The most plausible system explanation is not simply national income or government versus NGO provision. It is the interaction of:

1. Mae La’s decades-old, culturally embedded clinic and trained refugee workforce;
2. high continuity from ANC to delivery;
3. a relatively clear referral route to a Thai hospital approximately one hour away;
4. Cox’s Bazar’s much greater scale, density, terrain and provider fragmentation;
5. uneven trust and cultural mediation following recent mass displacement;
6. variable access to comprehensive EmONC despite wide availability of basic services.

Confidence is high that Mae La had higher routine coverage in 2017–2018 and that Cox’s Bazar improved facility delivery over time. Confidence is moderate that Mae La’s model produced better neonatal outcomes because later harmonized data are absent. Confidence is low for any precise comparison of PPH incidence, 2019–2023 Mae La outcomes, midwife-specific ratios, two-hour comprehensive-EmONC coverage, or mortality effects attributable to the 2021 UNFPA funding reduction.

final.content:
MEDICAL-GRADE VACCINE REFRIGERATION ASSESSMENT  
Eight rural clinics in Montana and Wyoming | 10-year planning horizon

EXECUTIVE RECOMMENDATION

Select the Thermo Scientific TSX pharmacy refrigerator—such as the 11.5-cu.-ft. TSX1205PA—paired with:

1. A calibrated, independent Thermo Smart-Vue Pro buffered temperature logger at each clinic;
2. An Ethernet/4G-LTE Smart-Vue gateway with automatic communications failover;
3. A properly engineered external UPS providing at least 12 hours of compressor operation, not merely alarm/display backup;
4. Generator connection where available, plus a written vaccine-relocation agreement with a second compliant facility; and
5. A network-wide service contract that explicitly includes travel, annual calibration, preventive maintenance, loaner equipment, and response-time commitments for Montana and Wyoming.

The TSX is the best overall fit because it is purpose-built for 2–8°C vaccine storage, NSF/ANSI 456 certified, has documented rapid recovery, and offers the strongest documented cellular monitoring architecture. Its estimated 10-year network cost is approximately $331,000–$499,000 for eight locations, including assumed remote-geography service contracts, monitoring, UPS systems, battery replacement, and electricity.

The Helmer iPR113-GX is a very close alternative and may become the preferred choice if Helmer provides a materially stronger regional service guarantee or lower bundled bid. It has excellent documented stability, NSF/ANSI 456 certification, lower energy consumption, rich onboard records, and a 20-hour alarm/display battery. Its principal disadvantage is that the documented native connection is Ethernet—not cellular—and the 20-hour battery does not operate the refrigeration compressor.

Do not procure the Panasonic/PHCbi MDF-DU702VH-PA as a replacement for an ordinary vaccine refrigerator. It is a 729-liter, −40°C to −86°C ultra-low-temperature freezer, not a 2–8°C refrigerator. It may be appropriate only for a separate, centralized ultra-low-temperature vaccine or biologic requirement. Its estimated 10-year cost is also substantially higher, approximately $534,000–$854,000 for eight sites.

COMPARISON AT A GLANCE

| Criterion | Helmer GX: iPR113-GX | Thermo TSX: TSX1205PA class | Panasonic/PHCbi MDF-DU702VH-PA |
|---|---|---|---|
| Intended temperature | 2–10°C; 5°C set point | 2–8°C pharmacy/vaccine storage; 5°C set point | −40°C to −86°C ultra-low storage |
| Suitable for routine refrigerated vaccines | Yes | Yes | No |
| NSF/ANSI 456 | Yes, for identified pharmacy model | Yes, TSX pharmacy series | No documented NSF/ANSI 456 certification |
| Internal battery runs compressor | No | No documented capability | No; standard battery supports alarms/logging, not compressors |
| Documented alarm/display backup | 20 hours | Battery-backed alarm, but no runtime documented in evidence reviewed | Battery-backed alarm/logging; runtime not documented |
| External backup needed for 6–12-hour outage | Yes | Yes | Yes, or optional liquid-CO₂ system for only “a few hours” |
| Door-opening recovery evidence | 15 min to 8°C after a 3-min opening | 3 min to 5°C after a 1-min opening | 8 min to within ±5°C after a 15-sec opening |
| Stability/uniformity evidence | Stability 0.64°C; uniformity ±1.0°C | Stability 2.3°C and unloaded peak variation ±1.6°C in available 12-cu.-ft. sheet | ±5°C uniformity; 17-point empty-cabinet data |
| Native connectivity | Ethernet/API, Modbus-compatible integration, USB and remote contacts | Remote contacts; strongest option is Smart-Vue Pro LoRaWAN plus Ethernet/4G gateway | USB; optional RS-232/RS-485 or Ethernet |
| Cellular resilience | Requires third-party cellular router/gateway | Documented 4G-LTE gateway and Ethernet/cellular failover; logger stores 4,000 offline readings/channel | Requires third-party cellular gateway |
| Published normal energy | 2.69 kWh/day | 3.2 kWh/day in available 12-cu.-ft. technical sheet | 9.0 kWh/day at −80°C with six openings |
| Indicative 10-year cost, eight sites | $313,000–$521,000 | $331,000–$499,000 | $534,000–$854,000 |
| Overall assessment | Strong alternative; best onboard controls and lowest energy | Recommended; best documented cellular/offline monitoring package | Reject for routine vaccine refrigeration |

1. OUTAGE PERFORMANCE AND BATTERY BACKUP

A. Important distinction: alarm batteries versus refrigeration backup

None of the three evaluated units has a documented standard internal battery that operates its compressor for a 6–12-hour outage.

The manufacturers’ internal batteries preserve alarms, displays, clocks, or records. They must not be interpreted as preserving vaccine temperature. Actual refrigeration through a prolonged outage requires one of the following:

- A generator-backed dedicated circuit;
- An external online/double-conversion UPS or battery energy-storage system sized for compressor startup and continuous operation;
- Relocation to a compliant alternate facility; or
- For the Panasonic ULT freezer only, an optional liquid-CO₂ injection system, subject to ventilation and occupational-safety controls.

Helmer iPR113-GX

The Helmer technical sheet documents a rechargeable 12-V lead-acid battery providing 20 hours of i.C3 touchscreen display and alarm backup. It does not claim 20 hours of compressor operation. The refrigerator therefore warms during an extended outage unless connected to an external UPS or generator. The sheet also specifies USB, remote alarm contacts, Ethernet, buffered monitoring bottles, and power-failure alarms (https://www.helmerinc.com/sites/default/files/2022-02/iLR125GX-Technical-Data-Sheet-380436-1.pdf).

Thermo TSX

The TSX manual describes a battery-backed alarm system and recommends a redundant, independent monitoring system, but the reviewed documentation does not give an alarm-battery runtime or claim compressor operation from that battery (https://documents.thermofisher.com/TFS-Assets/LED/manuals/TSX%20Laboratory%20Refrigerator%20User%20Manual%20327929H01_RevG_English.pdf).

Panasonic/PHCbi MDF-DU702VH-PA

During a power failure, the standard battery keeps the clock, alarm, remote alarm, and operational/alarm logging active; the LCD normally turns off except when touched. The refrigeration system itself does not operate from that battery. After power returns, settings are recovered from nonvolatile memory.

An optional MDF-UB7 liquid-CO₂ kit can suppress temperature rise for “a few hours,” but the manufacturer does not document a guaranteed 6- or 12-hour duration because runtime depends on cylinder size, fill, set point, ambient temperature, freezer load, and leakage. The system also creates an oxygen-depletion risk and requires a ventilation assessment and potentially oxygen monitoring (https://www.easymanua.ls/phcbi/mdf-du702vha/manual?p=56).

B. Approximate UPS energy requirement

Using published daily consumption as an average operating load:

Helmer:

- 2.69 kWh/day ÷ 24 = 0.112 kW average
- Six hours: 0.112 × 6 = 0.67 kWh
- Twelve hours: 0.112 × 12 = 1.35 kWh
- At 85% battery/inverter efficiency: 1.35 ÷ 0.85 = 1.58 kWh usable battery requirement

Thermo:

- 3.2 kWh/day ÷ 24 = 0.133 kW average
- Six hours: 0.80 kWh
- Twelve hours: 1.60 kWh
- At 85% efficiency: 1.60 ÷ 0.85 = 1.88 kWh

Panasonic:

- 9.0 kWh/day ÷ 24 = 0.375 kW average
- Six hours: 2.25 kWh
- Twelve hours: 4.50 kWh
- At 85% efficiency: 4.50 ÷ 0.85 = 5.29 kWh

These are minimum energy calculations, not final UPS specifications. A qualified vendor must account for compressor inrush, 115-V versus 220-V requirements, winter and summer ambient conditions, battery degradation, inverter losses, attached monitoring equipment, and a safety margin. A practical procurement specification would require:

- 12 hours of verified runtime at site ambient conditions;
- At least 25% end-of-life energy reserve;
- Pure-sine-wave output;
- Automatic transfer without compressor interruption;
- Generator compatibility;
- Remote battery-health alarms; and
- A witnessed runtime test before vaccine loading.

For the refrigerators, this likely means a nominal system larger than the calculated 1.6–1.9 kWh—approximately 2.5–4 kWh after reserve and aging. The Panasonic would likely require at least 7–10 kWh and a 220-V inverter.

2. TEMPERATURE RECOVERY AFTER POWER RESTORATION

No manufacturer evidence reviewed provides an exact, directly comparable “recovery after a 6- or 12-hour outage” test. Door-opening and pull-down tests are the best available proxies, but they must not be presented as equivalent to outage recovery.

Helmer

For the iPR113-GX, documented performance is:

- Stability: 0.64°C;
- Uniformity: ±1.0°C;
- Recovery to 8°C after a three-minute door opening: 15 minutes;
- Pull-down to 4°C: 63 minutes;
- Energy consumption: 2.69 kWh/day.

These values are reported in the model’s technical data (https://www.laboratory-equipment.com/media/asset-library/h/e/helmer-scientific-iseries-pharmacy-upright-refrigerator-iPR113GX-Data-Sheet.pdf).

The 63-minute pull-down result is not necessarily the recovery time following a closed-door outage because starting temperature and test loading are not fully stated in the search evidence. It should be treated as a conservative commissioning indicator, not a guaranteed outage-recovery result.

Thermo TSX

The available 12-cu.-ft. TSX pharmacy technical sheet reports:

- Three minutes to recover to 5°C after a one-minute door opening;
- Nine-minute pull-down to 5°C;
- 171 minutes to warm from 5°C to 15°C;
- Stability of 2.3°C;
- Unloaded peak variation of +1.6/−1.6°C; and
- Energy consumption of 3.2 kWh/day.

Source: https://www.scientificlabs.com/handlers/libraryFiles.ashx?filename=Technical_Data_Sheets_T_TSX1205PV.pdf

The 171-minute warm-up result indicates that, without compressor backup, the cabinet would exceed the 2–8°C refrigerated-vaccine range well before a six-hour outage ended under the test conditions. A closed door alone is therefore not an adequate outage strategy.

Panasonic/PHCbi

The MDF-DU702VH-PA is documented to recover to within ±5°C of set point in approximately eight minutes after a 15-second inner-door opening at either −70°C or −80°C. The test is much less severe than a prolonged outage and is not comparable to either refrigerator’s test (https://device.report/m/e4cc1b0208d7929cf08f1d354491a05062df7d5404a4115ea44676b0ac634a6e.pdf).

After power restoration, the freezer automatically resumes its stored settings. The manual warns that simultaneous restart of multiple units can cause a temporary voltage drop and provides a compressor-delay setting. This is relevant if several freezers or refrigerators share generator capacity.

Operational conclusion

Following any outage:

- Keep doors closed;
- Read the independent DDL rather than opening the unit;
- Quarantine, do not discard, vaccine exposed to an excursion;
- Download the complete temperature record;
- Contact the applicable immunization program/manufacturer; and
- Do not resume normal use until temperatures stabilize and vaccine viability is resolved.

CDC outage guidance similarly says to keep units closed, continue monitoring, document duration and maximum temperature, and consider transfer to a facility with reliable power (https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/62107/cdc_62107_DS1.pdf).

3. CDC, MONTANA, AND WYOMING COMPLIANCE

A. CDC requirements

CDC prefers purpose-built or pharmaceutical-grade vaccine storage. Refrigerated vaccines generally require 2–8°C storage. Every storage unit needs a reliable temperature-monitoring device; CDC recommends, and VFC requires, a continuous DDL recording at least every 30 minutes, preferably with a buffered probe. Recommended uncertainty is ±0.5°C or better (https://www.cdc.gov/pinkbook/hcp/table-of-contents/chapter-5-vaccine-storage-and-handling.html).

CDC also expects an emergency plan and an alternate vaccine-storage arrangement even where a generator exists. Equipment certification does not replace those requirements.

Helmer compliance

The iPR113-GX:

- Is purpose-built/pharmaceutical-grade;
- Is ETL certified to NSF/ANSI 456;
- Uses forced-air cooling and microprocessor control;
- Includes product-simulation ballast bottles;
- Has continuous temperature/event logging and min/max display;
- Exports PDF and CSV records; and
- Provides power-failure, high/low-temperature, door, probe, condenser, and low-battery alarms.

Its 2–10°C configurable range means the operational set point and alarms must be locked down to maintain vaccine between 2°C and 8°C. The refrigerator’s own sensor and logs are helpful, but the network should still deploy a separate calibrated DDL to eliminate ambiguity with state VFC inspectors and provide redundancy.

Thermo compliance

The TSX pharmacy series is purpose-built and NSF/ANSI 456 certified. Thermo states that the certified line maintains 5°C ±3°C and remains stable with routine door openings (https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/thermo-fisher-scientific-earns-nsfansi-456-vaccine-storage-certification-for-its-high-performance-refrigerators-and-freezers-301467411.html).

The TSX manual itself recommends redundant independent monitoring and directs users to use the probe in a glycerin bottle for calibration/validation reference. With a calibrated Smart-Vue buffered probe set to intervals of 30 minutes or less, it can meet the CDC monitoring framework.

Panasonic compliance

The MDF-DU702VH-PA does not comply as a routine refrigerated-vaccine unit because it cannot operate at 2–8°C. Its −40°C to −86°C range is intended for ultra-low biological storage (https://www.phchd.com/us/biomedical/preservation/ultra-low-freezers/mdf-du702vhpa).

It can be used only where a vaccine or biologic’s manufacturer specifically requires ultra-low storage. No NSF/ANSI 456 certification was found in the reviewed evidence. Its controller logging is not, by itself, a substitute for a calibrated external DDL and state approval.

B. Montana-specific requirements

Montana requires public-vaccine units to:

- Be stable enough year-round;
- Hold the largest expected inventory;
- Use a CDC-recommended appliance type;
- Have a DDL reading at least every 30 minutes;
- Use a buffered probe;
- Display current, minimum, and maximum temperatures, except for qualifying centralized systems; and
- Generate reviewable and archivable data retained for three years.

Source: https://dphhs.mt.gov/assets/publichealth/Immunization/203a-StorageUnitDataloggerRequirements.pdf

Montana’s VFC handbook also requires an emergency plan and identifies at least one alternate compliant storage facility with backup power; two locations and an MOU are recommended. If backup power is present, the facility should have a written electrical-loss-prevention policy (https://dphhs.mt.gov/assets/publichealth/Immunization/VFCProviderHandbook.pdf).

C. Wyoming-specific requirements

Wyoming’s public-vaccine guidance is stricter for refrigerators: they must be stand-alone pharmaceutical or medical-grade units and maintain vaccine temperatures year-round between 4°C and 6°C. Units must have a calibrated DDL with the buffered probe centrally located. New or moved units cannot hold public vaccine until temperature records have been reviewed and the unit approved (https://health.wyo.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/QRG_-Vaccine-Storage-Units-.pdf).

Wyoming also requires temperature records twice daily, monthly submission for public-vaccine programs, and at least three years of retention. During relocation or emergency storage, a calibrated DDL must continuously accompany the vaccine (https://health.wyo.gov/publichealth/immunization/immunization-provider-resources/vaccine-storage-and-handling/).

For Wyoming clinics, configure refrigerator set points at 5°C and use conservative alarms around the state’s 4–6°C operating target, while still recognizing that federal vaccine excursion limits are generally 2–8°C.

4. REMOTE MONITORING IN SPOTTY CELLULAR AREAS

Thermo Smart-Vue Pro: strongest documented option

Smart-Vue Pro provides:

- LoRaWAN communication between the refrigerator logger and local gateway;
- Ethernet, Wi-Fi, and/or 4G-LTE gateway options;
- Configurable Ethernet-to-cellular communications failover;
- Cloud or on-premises software;
- Remote alarms and audit trails;
- Rural open-area LoRa range reported up to approximately 10 km; and
- Storage of 4,000 offline measurements per channel.

Sources:

- Gateway and failover: https://assets.fishersci.com/TFS-Assets/LPD/manuals/MTCAP_331676H02_RevB_EN.pdf
- Offline storage and system capabilities: https://www.thermofisher.com/au/en/home/life-science/lab-equipment/connected-solutions/regulatory-validation.html
- Gateway product details: https://www.fishersci.com/shop/products/smart-vue-pro-receivers-2/11731063

At a 30-minute interval, 4,000 measurements represent:

4,000 × 0.5 hours = 2,000 hours = 83.3 days of offline storage per channel.

Thus, a cellular outage delays remote notification but should not erase the temperature record. The gateway itself, network modem, and logger should be connected to the clinic UPS.

However, cellular failover is useful only where a compatible carrier signal exists. Clinics should conduct a site survey of at least two carriers. Where neither is reliable, use:

- Primary wired broadband;
- Secondary cellular from a different carrier;
- A high-gain external antenna where lawful and supported;
- Satellite internet as tertiary backhaul at the most isolated sites; and
- Local audible alarms plus an automated telephone dialer or building alarm contact independent of the cloud.

Helmer connectivity

The Helmer i.C3 offers Ethernet, USB, remote alarm contacts, and an API; it can supply temperature, door status, alarms, and refrigeration-system data to compatible monitoring or building-automation platforms (https://www.helmerinc.com/connectivity).

This is rich device-level information, and local records continue even when connectivity is unavailable. Nevertheless, the reviewed Helmer material does not identify an integrated cellular modem. Cellular operation therefore requires a third-party industrial router or a separate system such as Smart-Vue. That adds integration and support responsibility.

Panasonic connectivity

The MDF-DU702VH-PA provides USB export and optional RS-232/RS-485 or Ethernet hardware (https://www.phchd.com/global/-/media/biomedical/global/catalogues/MDF-ULT/MDF_DU702VH_DataSheet_E_0414.pdf). No native cellular capability or documented store-and-forward cellular platform was identified. A third-party logger and gateway are therefore required.

Recommended communications design

Do not depend on the refrigerator’s internet connection as the sole alarm path. At each clinic use:

- Independent buffered DDL;
- Local display and audible alarm;
- Local storage sufficient for at least 30 days;
- Ethernet primary communications;
- 4G-LTE secondary communications using the strongest local carrier;
- UPS power for DDL, gateway, modem, and switch;
- Escalation to at least two on-call staff; and
- Weekly review/download even when no alarm occurs.

5. DOCUMENTED TEMPERATURE STABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION EVIDENCE

A. Controlled performance data

Helmer iPR113-GX

- Stability: 0.64°C
- Uniformity: ±1.0°C
- Recovery: 15 minutes to 8°C after a three-minute opening
- Energy: 2.69 kWh/day

Source: https://www.laboratory-equipment.com/media/asset-library/h/e/helmer-scientific-iseries-pharmacy-upright-refrigerator-iPR113GX-Data-Sheet.pdf

Thermo TSX 12-cu.-ft. pharmacy unit

- Unloaded average: 5.2°C
- Peak deviation: +1.6/−1.6°C
- Stability: 2.3°C
- Recovery: three minutes after a one-minute door opening
- Warm-up from 5°C to 15°C: 171 minutes

Source: https://www.scientificlabs.com/handlers/libraryFiles.ashx?filename=Technical_Data_Sheets_T_TSX1205PV.pdf

Panasonic/PHCbi MDF-DU702VH-PA

At an −80°C set point, 23°C ambient, 230 V/50 Hz, and no load, the published 17-point measurements show a middle-of-cycle average of −79.2°C. Individual middle-cycle readings run approximately −77.7°C to −80.2°C. Published overall uniformity is ±5°C. These are empty-cabinet laboratory data, not vaccine-product temperatures under rural outage conditions (https://www.phchd.com/global/-/media/biomedical/global/catalogues/MDF-ULT/MDF_DU702VH_DataSheet_E_0414.pdf).

B. Rural implementation evidence limitation

No independently documented Montana- or Wyoming-rural implementation was found for any of the three exact products, and no source reviewed reported field temperature traces from clinics experiencing repeated 6–12-hour outages. It would therefore be misleading to claim that any vendor has demonstrated 6–12-hour rural outage protection without external power.

The closest implementation evidence is manufacturer-sponsored rather than independent:

- A large research hospital standardized more than 85 cold-storage units and reported fewer excursions and improved remote-monitoring visibility after adopting Helmer GX equipment, but the hospital was not rural and no numerical before/after temperature dataset was published (https://info.helmerinc.com/research-hospital-testimonial).
- Thermo reports TSX units deployed globally in clinics, pharmacies, and vaccination sites, with NSF/ANSI 456 validation across loads and routine door openings, but the evidence does not isolate rural Montana/Wyoming performance.
- Panasonic reports controlled 17-point uniformity and ENERGY STAR tests, but no comparable rural healthcare deployment data.

Before network-wide acceptance, require a 30-day pilot at the clinic with the worst outage and communications history. Acceptance criteria should include:

- No product-simulation reading below 2°C or above 8°C for refrigerated vaccine;
- Wyoming operating target of 4–6°C;
- Demonstrated 12-hour UPS runtime;
- Successful Ethernet-to-cellular failover;
- Complete backfill after a 48-hour communications outage;
- Recovery without nuisance alarms after normal door openings;
- Documented generator transfer where applicable; and
- Temperature mapping at both normal and maximum anticipated inventory.

6. MONTANA/WYOMING ELECTRICITY AND BACKUP-POWER COST

A. Utility-rate framework

For planning, 2025 commercial average prices were approximately:

- Montana: 13.16 cents/kWh;
- Wyoming: 9.79 cents/kWh.

Source: U.S. Energy Information Administration state commercial-price table (https://www.eia.gov/electricity/monthly/epm_table_grapher.php?t=table_5_06_a&stream=top).

Assuming four clinics in each state, the unweighted planning average is:

($0.1316 + $0.0979) ÷ 2 = $0.11475/kWh.

Actual bills must be modeled by clinic because rural sites may be served by NorthWestern Energy, Rocky Mountain Power, or a cooperative.

Rocky Mountain Power’s Wyoming General Service Schedule 28 applies to certain nonresidential customers exceeding 20.5 kW or 5,000 kWh in more than six months. Its November 2025 secondary-voltage charges include:

- Demand: $17.83/kW;
- Base energy: 2.541 cents/kWh before applicable riders and adjustments.

Source: https://www.rockymountainpower.net/content/dam/pcorp/documents/en/rockymountainpower/rates-regulation/wyoming/rates/028_General_Service.pdf

Consequently, electricity cost is not determined by kWh alone. If rapid UPS recharging establishes a new monthly 15-minute peak, the demand charge can exceed the value of the recharge energy. Configure battery charging to be delayed or rate-limited after generator/grid restoration where clinical risk permits.

B. Ten-year normal operating electricity

Using $0.11475/kWh and no escalation:

Helmer:

2.69 kWh/day × 365 days × 10 years = 9,818.5 kWh/unit

9,818.5 × $0.11475 = $1,127/unit

Eight units: $1,127 × 8 = $9,016

Thermo:

3.2 × 365 × 10 = 11,680 kWh/unit

11,680 × $0.11475 = $1,340/unit

Eight units: $10,720

Panasonic:

9.0 × 365 × 10 = 32,850 kWh/unit

32,850 × $0.11475 = $3,770/unit

Eight units: $30,160

These figures exclude rate escalation and demand charges.

C. Incremental UPS recharge energy after outages

Illustrative scenario: twelve nine-hour outages per year at each of eight clinics, 85% round-trip efficiency.

Helmer:

(2.69 ÷ 24) × 9 × 12 × 10 × 8 ÷ 0.85  
= approximately 1,139 kWh network-wide

Cost: 1,139 × $0.11475 = approximately $131 over ten years

Thermo:

(3.2 ÷ 24) × 9 × 12 × 10 × 8 ÷ 0.85  
= approximately 1,355 kWh

Cost: approximately $155

Panasonic:

(9 ÷ 24) × 9 × 12 × 10 × 8 ÷ 0.85  
= approximately 3,812 kWh

Cost: approximately $437

The incremental kWh cost of battery backup is therefore negligible relative to capital, maintenance, batteries, communications, and possible demand charges. Reliability—not energy price—should drive the backup-power decision.

7. TEN-YEAR TOTAL COST OF OWNERSHIP

Publicly available contract pricing is incomplete. Helmer service agreements are quote-based, and no directly comparable Montana/Wyoming travel-inclusive maintenance prices were identified. The following is therefore a planning estimate, not a vendor quotation.

The model assumes one unit at each of eight clinics and includes:

- Equipment acquisition;
- 12-hour external UPS;
- UPS battery replacements around years four and eight;
- Remote-monitoring hardware and subscriptions;
- Annual preventive maintenance and calibration;
- Remote-geography technician travel allowance; and
- Normal electricity.

It excludes building wiring, generator purchase, taxes, vaccine loss, emergency transport, major facility HVAC changes, and rate escalation.

Helmer iPR113-GX: per location

- Refrigerator: $12,000–$18,000 planning allowance
- UPS and installation: $5,000–$8,000
- Monitoring hardware/integration: $1,000–$2,000
- Ten-year service/calibration including rural travel: $15,000–$25,000
- Ten-year monitoring subscription: $3,000–$7,000
- Two battery replacement cycles: $2,000–$4,000
- Electricity: approximately $1,127

Total per site: approximately $39,100–$65,100  
Eight sites: approximately $313,000–$521,000

Thermo TSX1205PA class: per location

A public institutional listing for TSX1205PD showed $10,050 per unit, providing a useful but nonbinding acquisition benchmark (https://www.govsci.com/product-detail/Thermo--Laboratory--Equipment--Division/TSX1205PD/EA/).

- Refrigerator: approximately $10,050
- UPS and installation: $5,000–$8,000
- Smart-Vue hardware/gateway allocation: $2,000–$4,000
- Ten-year service/calibration including rural travel: $17,000–$27,000
- Ten-year Smart-Vue/data service: $4,000–$8,000
- Two battery replacement cycles: $2,000–$4,000
- Electricity: approximately $1,340

Total per site: approximately $41,400–$62,400  
Eight sites: approximately $331,000–$499,000

Panasonic/PHCbi MDF-DU702VH-PA: per location

A used 2018 unit was listed at $6,995, but that is not a valid benchmark for a new, warranted clinical procurement (https://banebio.com/product/phcbi-mdf-du702vh-pa-ultra-low-80c-lab-freezer/). A new-unit planning allowance is used instead.

- New ULT freezer allowance: $18,000–$25,000
- 220-V, 12-hour UPS and installation: $10,000–$18,000
- Monitoring hardware/integration: $2,000–$4,000

The promotion was Red Rooster’s “$5 Lunchbox” — also advertised simply as the “$5 Lunch.”

The match is strong:

- Red Rooster began in Kelmscott, a Perth suburb, in 1972; sources associate its founding with Greek-Australian brothers Peter and Theo Kailis (https://australianfoodtimeline.com.au/red-rooster-founded/).
- A July 2015 listing reproduces Red Rooster’s wording: “Let us introduce you to your $5 lunch,” consisting of a quarter roast chicken and small chips for $5, available daily from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. (https://www.ozbargain.com.au/node/202131).
- A contemporary September 2015 report independently confirms the same contents, price, and hours (https://www.frugalfeeds.com.au/2015/deal-red-rooster-quarter-chicken-small-chips-for-5/).
- By February 2016, Red Rooster’s promotional wording explicitly called it the “$5 Lunchbox”: “quarter chicken and chips, with our $5 Lunchbox” (https://www.ozbargain.com.au/node/233802).

So, for the circa-2015 promotion you remember, the best-supported name is **the $5 Lunch**, subsequently/also styled **the $5 Lunchbox**. The gathered evidence confirms the deal in 2015, but does not establish that this exact promotion name had continuously existed since the 1990s.

Nature’s Castles: The Treehouse Reimagined — Design and Construction Credits

Conclusion

The three Longwood Gardens treehouses were a collaborative project rather than the work of one designer:

- Canopy Cathedral and Birdhouse: designed and constructed by Peter “Pete” Nelson and Jake Jacob of TreeHouse Workshop, Inc., Seattle.
- Lookout Loft: designed and built by Forever Young Treehouses of Burlington, Vermont, the organization co-founded by Bill Allen and Phil Trabulsy.
- Architect of record for the overall project: Matthew Millan of Matthew Millan Architects.

This division of credit is important: contemporary reporting identifies the specialist treehouse firms as the individual structures’ designers/builders, while a later 2008 Washington Post account identifies Millan as architect of record.

Evidence for attribution

The clearest opening-day source is Bette Alburger’s April 24, 2008 Delco Times article. It identifies:

- Lookout Loft as designed by Forever Young Treehouses;
- Canopy Cathedral as designed by Peter Nelson and Jake Jacob of TreeHouse Workshop; and
- Birdhouse as also designed by Nelson.

The article was published as the exhibition opened and is available at:
https://www.delcotimes.com/2008/04/24/treehouses-are-looking-up-at-longwood-gardens/

A second report from the same day similarly credits Canopy Cathedral to “Peter Nelson and Jake Jacob of Treehouse Workshop Inc.” and Lookout Loft to Forever Young Treehouses:
https://www.dailylocal.com/2008/04/24/longwood-builds-natures-castles-in-the-gardens-trees/

The Washington Post’s October 2008 follow-up makes the roles especially explicit: Forever Young “designed and built” Lookout Loft; TreeHouse Workshop “designed and constructed” Birdhouse and Canopy Cathedral; and Matthew Millan was “the architect of record” who worked with engineers on code and structural-load requirements:
https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/2008/10/02/artisan-treehouses-extend-their-lease-at-longwood-gardens/0872cd19-1d4a-445c-a2f0-d7206d80de84/

This is consistent with Matthew Millan Architects’ present portfolio, which says it worked with Longwood and the two specialist treehouse companies and designed the structures to respond to their individual sites:
https://millanarchitects.com/portfolio/institutional/natures-castles-the-treehouses-at-longwood-gardens-the-lookout-loft/

Contemporaneous description of the concept and construction

The strongest single contemporaneous source is Brian Bingaman’s “The sky’s the limit at treehouse exhibit,” published April 24, 2008:
https://www.thereporteronline.com/2008/04/24/the-skys-the-limit-at-treehouse-exhibit/

It describes both the design ideas and the construction strategy:

1. Overall concept

The project was “two years in the making.” Longwood director Paul Redman explained that environmental responsibility was central because of the Gardens’ history. The treehouses were intended to provide new views of the landscape while celebrating trees without damaging them.

Longwood’s stated interpretive purpose is quoted more directly in the Daily Local report: “Nature’s Castles is designed to celebrate trees and engage our guests in an exciting and unique way about the beauty and importance of trees.”
https://www.dailylocal.com/2008/04/24/longwood-builds-natures-castles-in-the-gardens-trees/

2. Canopy Cathedral

TreeHouse Workshop conceived Canopy Cathedral as an ornate, two-story structure inspired by a Norwegian stave church. Contemporary accounts describe a colorful or intricate glass façade, a balcony overlooking the Italian Water Garden, cedar materials, and hand-carved fantastical creatures.

Reported dimensions vary: The Reporter gave 589 square feet, while the Daily Local and Delco Times gave approximately 400 square feet. This discrepancy probably reflects differing definitions of enclosed floor area, balcony/deck area, or preliminary versus completed measurements; the contemporary sources do not reconcile it.

3. Birdhouse

Also attributed to Nelson/TreeHouse Workshop, Birdhouse was the tallest and smallest of the three, rising approximately 20 feet above the ground. Its concept was to provide a literal bird’s- or squirrel’s-eye view of the woodland.

Construction details included salvaged wood from a Washington dairy barn, floorboards from a dismantled Toronto toothpaste factory, reclaimed warehouse rafters, and Douglas fir recovered after landslides or storms. A copper cable served as a lightning rod. The structure was also arranged around a decaying tree trunk so visitors could look inside and observe the habitat.

Again, reported area differs: The Reporter says 255 square feet, while the Daily Local and Delco Times say roughly 320 square feet—a difference of 65 square feet, or 25.5% relative to the lower figure:

(320 − 255) ÷ 255 × 100 = 25.5%

The sources do not explain the difference.

4. Lookout Loft

Forever Young Treehouses conceived Lookout Loft as a rustic Adirondack-style, universally accessible treehouse. It comprised two viewing platforms linked by a walkway, with one roofed and the other covered by an open trellis intended to fill naturally with the forest canopy. A substantial ramp made the experience accessible to wheelchair users.

Contemporary size estimates range from 720 to 900 square feet. That is a 180-square-foot spread, or 25% of the lower estimate:

(900 − 720) ÷ 720 × 100 = 25%

The Daily Local described 13,000 pounds of salvaged steel supporting the structure; the Delco Times printed 1,300 pounds. Because the reports differ by exactly a factor of ten and the Daily Local supplies the more detailed construction description, one figure is likely a typographical error, but the available evidence does not conclusively establish which.

5. Foundation and environmental construction method

The most distinctive engineering decision was not to rely on the living trees for structural support. According to The Reporter, all three structures stood on sets of five-foot steel pipes forming “pin foundations,” rather than being bolted to trees or placed on conventional poured foundations. The pins were positioned to avoid disturbing root systems:
https://www.thereporteronline.com/2008/04/24/the-skys-the-limit-at-treehouse-exhibit/

The Daily Local adds that the pin system used concrete footings with extended steel rods threaded between roots, while Lookout Loft’s salvaged-steel framework remained visually unobtrusive:
https://www.dailylocal.com/2008/04/24/longwood-builds-natures-castles-in-the-gardens-trees/

The Washington Post reported that architect of record Matthew Millan and the engineers designed for public “live loads” of 100 pounds per square foot, stated as 2.5 times the private-residential requirement. The implied residential benchmark is:

100 ÷ 2.5 = 40 pounds per square foot.

That confirms these were engineered public structures, not conventional backyard treehouses.

Final identification

Accordingly, the most precise answer is:

- Architectural oversight/architect of record: Matthew Millan, Matthew Millan Architects.
- Treehouse designers and builders:
  - Peter Nelson and Jake Jacob, TreeHouse Workshop, Inc. — Canopy Cathedral and Birdhouse.
  - Forever Young Treehouses, associated with Bill Allen and Phil Trabulsy — Lookout Loft.

For a contemporaneous account that covers both concept and construction, the April 24, 2008 Reporter article is the best compact source, supplemented by the same-day Daily Local and Delco Times reports and the October 2008 Washington Post engineering account.
