final.content:
EDGE COMPUTING’S TRANSFORMATION OF INDUSTRIAL IoT ARCHITECTURES AS OF 2024

Executive summary

By 2024, industrial IoT had largely moved from a binary “device-to-cloud” model toward a hierarchical architecture:

Sensors/actuators → machine or field edge → site/regional edge → cloud

The edge now performs time-critical filtering, inference, coordination and control, while the cloud remains responsible for fleet-wide analytics, model training, historical storage and centralized management. This changes failure domains as much as performance: loss of a WAN connection no longer necessarily stops maintenance alerts, robot navigation or feeder protection.

The appropriate performance targets differ substantially by use case:

| Use case | Practical edge latency target | Representative upstream-data reduction | Availability objective |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Manufacturing predictive maintenance | 50–100 ms for anomaly detection; slower cloud analysis remains acceptable | About 60–90% | Local alerts continue during WAN loss; approximately 99.99% or better for monitoring services |
| Autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) | 1–50 ms for command/coordination; approximately 10–100 ms for remote video control | Roughly 80–91% where semantic features or selected regions replace raw video/LiDAR | More than 99.9999% communication-service availability for critical robot links |
| Energy distribution | Under 5 ms for protection/automated switching communication; hundreds of milliseconds for complete fault isolation/restoration | Up to 99% where raw waveforms remain in substations and only events/metadata go upstream | Approximately 99.9999% for distributed switching; local protection must survive control-center or WAN outages |

These are targets and representative results, not universal guarantees. Published industrial case studies often report business outcomes without disclosing end-to-end latency distributions, bandwidth baselines or audited SLA attainment. Accordingly, the report distinguishes standards-based targets, measured experiments and vendor-reported results.

1. Manufacturing predictive maintenance

1.1 Before-and-after architecture

Cloud-centric “before”

Typical early predictive-maintenance deployments followed this path:

Vibration, acoustic, temperature and current sensors
→ PLC/data-acquisition system
→ plant gateway
→ WAN/Internet
→ cloud data lake and analytics
→ cloud-generated alert
→ plant operator or maintenance system

All or most raw samples were uploaded. This offered inexpensive centralized storage and powerful model training, but created four problems:

1. High-frequency vibration streams consumed substantial uplink capacity.
2. Detection latency included gateway buffering, WAN transit, cloud queues and return-message latency.
3. A WAN or cloud outage suppressed alerts even though the machine and local sensors remained operational.
4. OT data crossed the plant boundary, increasing privacy, intellectual-property and attack-surface concerns.

Edge-distributed “after”

The 2024 pattern is:

Sensors/PLC
→ machine or plant edge gateway:
   • protocol normalization
   • windowing and FFT/feature extraction
   • thresholding and ML inference
   • local alarm and buffering
→ cloud:
   • long-term history
   • cross-plant comparison
   • model training and registry
   • selected features, health scores and anomalous waveform windows
→ updated signed model/container returned to edge

This is not “cloud removal.” It is a division of labor: immediate anomaly detection and fail-safe action occur locally, while computationally expensive training and fleet-level learning remain centralized.

Holcim provides a 2024 production example. C3 AI reports that Holcim runs its Reliability application on resource-constrained, semi-air-gapped plant devices, monitoring thousands of sensors, including those on vertical roller mills. The edge instance retains limited recent live data and performs inference and alerting, while the cloud instance trains models on millions of rows and manages DataOps/MLOps. Local deployment removed the maintenance team’s dependency on central alert availability (https://c3.ai/blog/how-the-c3-ai-platform-helps-holcim-overcome-limitations-of-edge-devices-to-deliver-real-time-ai-powered-predictive-maintenance).

A second real-world example is 3M. Microsoft reports that a plant used Azure SQL Edge and Azure IoT Edge to correlate two production-line streams and run analytics and machine learning locally because plant connectivity was limited and transferring the data was difficult (https://www.microsoft.com/en/customers/story/844496-3m-manufacturing-azure-sql-edge).

1.2 Quantified impact

Latency

For predictive maintenance, a sensible 2024 target is less than 50–100 ms from completion of a sensor window to anomaly classification. Unlike closed-loop motion control, many maintenance forecasts do not require single-digit milliseconds, but rapid detection matters for bearing seizure, overheating and equipment-trip scenarios.

A published 2024 edge-cloud predictive-maintenance framework reported:

• 35% lower latency than cloud-only processing  
• 60% lower bandwidth consumption  
• 28% lower energy consumption

The architecture ran K-nearest-neighbor anomaly detection at the edge and retained LSTM-based failure prediction in the cloud (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39771653/).

The latency relationship is:

Edge latency = Cloud-only latency × (1 − 0.35)

For example, if a cloud round trip and inference took 100 ms:

100 ms × 0.65 = 65 ms at the edge

That example illustrates the reported percentage; the paper’s percentage alone does not establish that every deployment will reach 65 ms.

A vendor-described manufacturing implementation reports local processing below 100 ms and 90% data reduction, but the customer is not independently identified; it should therefore be treated as indicative rather than audited evidence (https://www.ademero.com/ai-resources/case-studies/manufacturing-predictive-maintenance).

Bandwidth

Representative reduction: 60–90%.

At 60% reduction:

1 TB/day raw input × (1 − 0.60) = 0.40 TB/day transmitted  
Daily traffic avoided = 0.60 TB

At 90% reduction:

1 TB/day × (1 − 0.90) = 0.10 TB/day transmitted  
Daily traffic avoided = 0.90 TB

The higher end is plausible when the edge sends FFT features, health scores and exceptions rather than continuous raw waveforms. Some raw windows should still be retained locally or uploaded around anomalous events, because excessive filtering can make later root-cause analysis impossible.

Availability and SLA

The principal improvement is architectural continuity: local inference and alarms remain available when the WAN or central cloud is not. C3 AI says Holcim’s deployment included local persistent storage, self-recovery and operation with limited connectivity, eliminating dependence on central alert availability.

For context, annual downtime implied by common SLAs is:

• 99.9%: 8,760 hours × 0.001 = 8.76 hours/year  
• 99.99%: 8,760 × 0.0001 = 0.876 hour = 52.56 minutes/year  
• 99.999%: 5.256 minutes/year

Moving a critical alert path from a 99.9%-available WAN/cloud dependency to a locally redundant 99.99% edge service would reduce the theoretical unavailability budget by:

8.76 hours − 0.876 hour = 7.884 hours/year, or 90%

This is an illustrative SLA calculation, not a measured Holcim result. Actual end-to-end availability also depends on sensors, power, gateways, local networking and the application itself.

1.3 Trade-offs

Cost

Benefits:

• Lower recurring WAN, cloud-ingestion and storage charges.
• Less production loss because anomalies are recognized locally.
• Existing cloud resources can concentrate on training and historical analysis.

Costs:

• Rugged gateways, local storage, redundant power and sometimes GPUs must be purchased for each plant.
• Hardware refresh and field support become distributed expenses.
• Small deployments may cost more than cloud-only processing if sensor traffic is modest.

Holcim mitigated this by optimizing Kubernetes resource requests, using a fit-for-purpose datastore and deploying only plant-specific models. That saves compute but requires significant engineering.

Security

Benefits:

• Raw production data can remain behind plant firewalls.
• Semi-air-gapped operation reduces continuous exposure to Internet services.
• Only selected features and alerts need leave the site.

Risks:

• Every gateway becomes a privileged OT endpoint.
• Compromised models or containers could suppress warnings or generate false alarms.
• Long-lived edge devices require secure boot, certificate rotation, signed over-the-air updates, role-based access and network segmentation.

Maintainability

Cloud-centric systems offer one centrally patched environment. Edge systems create many software and hardware versions across heterogeneous plants. C3 AI addresses this with containerized deployment, a central model registry and artifact hub, plant-specific model tags, automated inference schedules and retained local logs. Even so, intermittent connectivity complicates observability, patching and rollback.

Bottom line: predictive maintenance gains resilience and avoids moving raw telemetry, but the organization takes on a distributed MLOps and device-management problem.

2. Autonomous mobile robots

2.1 Before-and-after architecture

Cloud-centric or centralized “before”

A centralized robot architecture commonly looked like:

Cameras/LiDAR/odometry
→ Wi-Fi
→ factory server or remote cloud:
   • localization
   • perception
   • path planning
   • fleet coordination
→ commands returned to robot

This could reduce onboard compute cost, but robot operation became sensitive to Wi-Fi roaming, congestion and WAN latency. A dropped handover could stop the robot or force it into a conservative safety state.

Makino’s AMRs illustrate the problem. Its robots previously communicated with a control server over Wi-Fi using protocols including HTTPS and WebRTC. AWS reports that movement between access points produced delayed handovers and unstable communication (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/industries/makino-improves-performance-of-autonomous-mobile-robots-with-aws-wavelength-and-5g-network/).

Edge-distributed “after”

The newer pattern separates hard safety, near-real-time coordination and cloud learning:

On-robot edge:
• emergency stopping and collision avoidance
• sensor fusion and odometry
• minimum safe navigation during disconnection

On-premises/MEC edge:
• compute-intensive vision inference
• shared maps
• multi-robot traffic management
• task dispatch and digital-twin synchronization

Regional cloud:
• model training
• historical optimization
• fleet analytics and software distribution

Makino replaced unstable Wi-Fi connectivity with public 5G and moved its factory server workload to AWS Wavelength near KDDI’s mobile network. AWS reports no communication disconnections while moving across multiple 5G base-station areas and says the public-5G approach cost less than building a private 5G network. The system was launched in under five months.

NAVER’s “Rookie” delivery robots are a more centralized edge-cloud example. Their heavy “brain” functions run in NAVER Cloud over a Samsung private 5G network, allowing centralized updates and smaller, lower-power robots. The private network was selected because Wi-Fi handover was unsuitable and uplink performance was critical (https://www.samsung.com/global/business/networks/insights/blog/0629-samsungs-private-5g-network-5g-autonomous-mobile-robots-in-korea/).

For safety, however, an AMR should not depend entirely on a remote brain: emergency braking and a minimal safe state must remain onboard.

2.2 Quantified impact

Latency

The 2024 3GPP/ETSI service requirements provide the clearest targets:

• Mobile-robot communication: 1–50 ms transfer interval/latency range  
• Video-operated remote control: approximately 10–100 ms  
• Less critical robot communications: approximately 40–500 ms  
• Critical mobile-robot service availability: greater than 99.9999%

These appear in ETSI TS 122 104 V18.3.0, published May 2024 (https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/122100_122199/122104/18.03.00_60/ts_122104v180300p.pdf).

A factory-floor 5G-TSN robot testbed provides measured evidence: 99.9% of 100,000 over-the-air packets had latency bounded at 1 ms, with rare outliers around 2 ms (https://publications.rwth-aachen.de/record/848246/files/848246.pdf). That is network latency, not complete camera-to-command application latency; encoding, inference and control processing must be added.

A 2024 selective-harvesting robot study found that a 5G edge-server design produced more than an 18-fold peak processing speed-up compared with standalone inference on an NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/rob.22384). The result shows why robots offload large perception models, although agricultural harvesting is not identical to an indoor AMR.

Bandwidth

Robots can generate multiple camera feeds and dense LiDAR point clouds. The edge transformation is not necessarily “send less information”; it is “send less raw information.” Onboard or nearby inference can transmit object tracks, occupancy grids, features and exceptions instead of every pixel and point.

A real-world edge-video research result reported an 82.65% communication-cost reduction by selecting task-relevant spatial-temporal information. Treating communication cost as transmitted volume:

100 Mbps raw equivalent × (1 − 0.8265) = 17.35 Mbps

Robotics research also reports up to 11× greater compression of task-relevant sensory representations than competing methods (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10514-023-10093-w). Expressed as reduction:

Reduction = 1 − 1/11 = 0.9091 = 90.9%

Thus, an appropriate planning range is roughly 80–91% reduction when semantic features or selected regions replace continuous raw sensor transmission. This is workload-dependent and should not be applied to safety evidence that must be retained in full fidelity.

Availability and SLA

ETSI’s greater-than-99.9999% target corresponds to less than:

8,760 hours × (1 − 0.999999)
= 0.00876 hour
= 31.536 seconds/year

For comparison:

• 99.9% allows 8.76 hours/year.
• 99.99% allows 52.56 minutes/year.
• 99.9999% allows 31.5 seconds/year.

The nominal unavailability-budget improvement from 99.9% connectivity to six nines is:

8.76 hours ÷ 0.00876 hour = 1,000×

This does not mean a public 5G or edge deployment automatically delivers a six-nines end-to-end robot SLA. The robot, radio, edge server, application and power system all contribute. Makino’s reported absence of handover disconnections is encouraging operational evidence, but AWS did not publish a statistically audited SLA.

Availability also improves through graceful degradation: if the MEC server or backhaul fails, onboard safety logic can stop or navigate the robot to a safe location rather than waiting for the cloud.

2.3 Trade-offs

Cost

Onboard-heavy architecture:

• Higher robot bill of materials, weight, heat and battery draw.
• Less dependence on radio and shared infrastructure.

MEC/private-edge architecture:

• Robots can use smaller computers and share expensive GPUs.
• Central models and maps are easier to update.
• Private 5G spectrum, radios, core networking and redundant MEC servers can be expensive.

Makino selected public 5G plus AWS Wavelength specifically to avoid the higher capital cost of building private 5G. The corresponding trade-off is dependence on carrier coverage, pricing and service boundaries.

NAVER chose the opposite model—a private network—to control uplink capacity, mobility and reliability for hundreds of centrally assisted robots.

Security

Centralized robot perception creates highly sensitive streams: video of workers, plant layouts and operational patterns. Attack consequences can also become physical.

Required controls include:

• Mutual authentication between each robot and edge service.
• Encryption in transit and at rest.
• Network slicing or strict traffic segregation.
• Signed robot software and model artifacts.
• Least-privilege fleet APIs.
• Onboard enforcement of speed, collision and emergency-stop limits, even if the edge sends unsafe commands.

A compromised shared MEC service can affect many robots simultaneously, making centralization a larger correlated-risk domain than isolated onboard computing.

Maintainability

Benefits:

• Shared models can be upgraded once at the edge rather than manually on every robot.
• Fleet-level maps, scheduling and telemetry are easier to coordinate.
• Makino gained remote monitoring and reduced factory-server maintenance.

Costs:

• Engineers must test combinations of robot firmware, ROS middleware, radio software, edge containers and cloud services.
• Wireless coverage and handover performance become part of application maintenance.
• Edge capacity must be admission-controlled so that adding robots does not cause inference queues or unsafe latency spikes.

Bottom line: AMRs benefit from a split architecture—safety and minimal autonomy onboard, shared high-performance perception and coordination at the site/MEC edge, and learning in the cloud.

3. Energy distribution

3.1 Before-and-after architecture

Cloud/control-center-centric “before”

A centralized distribution architecture typically used:

Meters, intelligent electronic devices, line sensors and RTUs
→ utility WAN
→ SCADA/control center or cloud
→ state estimation, fault analysis and switching decision
→ command returned to field equipment

This remains appropriate for system-wide planning and supervision, but central round trips are poorly suited to protection and fault isolation. A WAN or control-center failure can delay action, and continuous high-frequency waveform uploads consume large amounts of bandwidth.

Edge-distributed “after”

The distributed architecture places intelligence in substations, feeder-terminal units and pole-top controllers:

Field sensors/IEDs
→ local feeder or substation edge:
   • protection and interlocking
   • fault classification
   • local state estimation
   • peer-to-peer feeder automation
   • waveform buffering
→ regional/control-center edge:
   • coordination across feeders
   • topology and distributed-energy-resource optimization
→ central cloud:
   • asset analytics
   • forecasting
   • long-term training and regulatory reporting

The most important change is that field devices can act autonomously and then report what they did. 3GPP’s fault-location, isolation and service-restoration model places logic in individual feeder controllers, using peer-to-peer communications without requiring a regional controller or control center. It describes complete fault isolation in about 500 ms and restoration for critical consumers within a few hundred milliseconds (https://www.tech-invite.com/3m22/toc/tinv-3gpp-22-104_k.html).

An implementation study similarly placed GPU-based forecasting, power-flow analysis, local storage and MQTT communication in an existing feeder-terminal unit rather than performing all analysis remotely (https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/14/20/13042).

Iberdrola’s i-DE provides a vendor-backed production example of a hybrid approach. Its SmartPoint platform connects legacy and modern sensors, processes streaming data, analyzes video and alerts operators about substation events using AWS IoT and edge services. The cloud remains valuable for correlation and scalable serverless management (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/industries/iberdrola-reduces-incidents-at-power-distribution-facilities-using-aws-iot-and-edge-services/).

3.2 Quantified impact

Latency

For distributed switching and service restoration, ETSI TS 122 104 specifies:

• Maximum end-to-end latency below 5 ms
• 1 kbit/s in steady state, rising to about 1.5 Mbit/s in a fault
• Communication-service availability of 99.9999%

For high-speed current differential protection, the same specification includes 5, 10 or 15 ms latency classes and transfer intervals of 1–2 ms, depending on the case (https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/122100_122199/122104/18.03.00_60/ts_122104v180300p.pdf).

IEC 61850 guidance reported by Schweitzer Engineering Laboratories requires protection-class messages in under 3 ms 99.99% of the time. Because endpoint processing consumes part of that budget, the network packet-delay-variation allowance can be below 1 ms (https://selinc.com/api/download/102552/).

These figures distinguish communications latency from complete physical restoration:

• Message delivery target: under 3–5 ms.
• Relay logic and breaker operation: additional time.
• Distributed feeder fault isolation: typically around 500 ms.

Local edge control removes the potentially variable control-center/cloud round trip from this chain.

Bandwidth

Substation sensors can produce continuous waveform data at thousands of samples per second. Edge event detection allows the utility to retain raw waveforms locally while sending metadata, disturbance summaries and selected time windows upstream.

One vendor-reported utility deployment states that this changed storage from petabytes of raw waveforms to gigabytes of metadata and events, producing a 99% reduction in bandwidth and storage. It also reports increasing retention from seven days to five years by using local storage priced at $0.003/GB-month rather than $0.023/GB-month in the cloud (https://expanso.io/case-study/power-grid-edge-computing/). Because the utility is not named and the result is vendor-reported, it should be treated as a directional case study, not an industry benchmark.

At 99% reduction:

10 TB/day raw × (1 − 0.99) = 0.1 TB/day transmitted  
Avoided upstream traffic = 9.9 TB/day

The reported unit-storage-price difference is:

$0.023 − $0.003 = $0.020/GB-month saved

Percentage reduction:

($0.020 ÷ $0.023) × 100 = 86.96%

This excludes the capital and maintenance cost of substation storage.

A reasonable planning range is therefore 90–99% reduction for waveform-heavy monitoring, but much less for already compact telemetry such as status bits or slow meter readings.

Availability and SLA

At 99.9999% availability, the theoretical outage budget is 31.5 seconds/year. At the 99.99% level cited for sub-3-ms protection delivery, the budget is 52.56 minutes/year. These percentages describe different service definitions and should not be conflated: packet delivery performance, communications-service availability and complete grid-service availability are not identical.

The larger architectural improvement is survival of a central outage. Peer-to-peer feeder controllers and substation protection can continue fault isolation even if the cloud, control center or WAN is unavailable. The central system loses visibility temporarily, but the protective function remains operational.

For a simplified series dependency:

Cloud-centric availability = local equipment availability × WAN availability × cloud availability

If all three were independently 99.9% available:

0.999³ = 0.997002999 = 99.7003%

An autonomous local edge path depending only on two 99.9% local components would be:

0.999² = 0.998001 = 99.8001%

This simple calculation illustrates why eliminating a series dependency helps, but real utility systems use redundancy and failures are not independent. It is not a measured Iberdrola SLA.

3.3 Trade-offs

Cost

Benefits:

• Reduced telecommunications, cloud-ingestion and central-storage spending.
• Faster isolation can reduce outage duration, equipment damage and regulatory penalties.
• Existing feeder terminals may be upgraded instead of replacing the entire SCADA estate.

Costs:

• Thousands of geographically dispersed substations and feeder devices need compute, storage, environmental hardening, backup power and redundant communications.
• Lifecycle costs can exceed cloud savings if local hardware is overprovisioned.
• Utilities may need parallel legacy and edge systems during long certification and migration periods.

Iberdrola chose serverless cloud components to reduce platform-management effort, illustrating that the economical endpoint is hybrid rather than edge-only.

Security

Benefits:

• Raw customer and waveform data can stay within the substation or utility boundary.
• Protection can operate without accepting inbound cloud commands.
• Segmentation limits some failures to one feeder or substation.

Risks:

• The attack surface expands to many physically accessible sites.
• Compromised peer-to-peer logic could issue malicious switching commands.
• Legacy protocols and long equipment lifetimes complicate patching.
• Edge AI can be affected by poisoned training data or model drift.

Controls should include hardware roots of trust, signed firmware/models, device certificates, allow-listed communications, unidirectional gateways where appropriate, IEC 62443-style segmentation, redundant protection and fail-safe local logic. Safety-critical protection should not rely solely on an opaque ML model.

Maintainability

Distributed edge systems require:

• Remote inventory and configuration management.
• Staged firmware and model deployment with rollback.
• Long-term support across mixed generations of relays, RTUs and gateways.
• Local buffering and observability during communications outages.
• Formal testing whenever topology, protection settings or DER penetration changes.

The advantage is modular fault containment; the disadvantage is version sprawl. Centralized cloud operations are easier to observe, while field-edge operations are more resilient but harder to keep uniform.

Cross-use-case conclusions

1. Edge computing changes the control hierarchy, not merely the compute location.

The cloud remains essential, but it is removed from the hard real-time loop. Local nodes convert raw physical signals into decisions, features and events; regional edges coordinate; clouds learn across sites.

2. Latency targets must match physical consequences.

• Predictive maintenance: generally 50–100 ms is sufficient for anomaly inference, though protective trips can require less.
• AMRs: 1–50 ms for coordination and control; approximately 10–100 ms for remotely assisted vision.
• Distribution protection: under 3–5 ms for critical messages, with complete isolation occurring over hundreds of milliseconds.

3. Bandwidth savings come from semantic reduction.

Sending an anomaly score, object track or fault event instead of raw vibration, video or waveform data yields representative reductions of:

• Predictive maintenance: 60–90%
• Robot perception: approximately 80–91%
• Waveform-heavy grid monitoring: up to 99%

These reductions are not free: retaining too little raw evidence can impede model retraining, incident investigation and regulatory audit.

4. Availability improves by shrinking the dependency chain.

Local processing allows continued operation through WAN and cloud failures. Standards call for six-nines communication availability in critical robot and distribution cases, equal to about 31.5 seconds of annual unavailability. Achieving that end to end requires redundant power, networking, compute and applications—not simply installing an edge gateway.

5. The operating-cost trade is cloud spending versus distributed lifecycle management.

Edge reduces data-transfer and cloud-storage costs but adds rugged hardware, field replacement, certificate management, observability and distributed DevSecOps/MLOps. Public MEC, as in Makino, can reduce private-network capital expense; private 5G, as in NAVER, offers greater control but at higher infrastructure cost.

6. The safest 2024 design is hybrid and fail-safe.

• Manufacturing: local alerting and buffering, cloud training.
• AMRs: onboard safety, site-edge perception/fleet coordination, cloud learning.
• Energy distribution: deterministic relay/feeder logic locally, regional coordination, cloud forecasting and asset analytics.

The core transformation is therefore architectural resilience: industrial systems increasingly use the cloud for global intelligence without allowing cloud distance or availability to determine whether a machine is protected, a robot stops safely or a feeder isolates a fault.

final.content:
# Telehealth design for low-connectivity primary care in Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania

## Executive conclusions

1. **Do not make continuous video the default.** The strongest low-connectivity models separate data capture, specialist review, patient contact, prescribing, and fulfilment into resumable stages. Voice, SMS, USSD, compressed still images, and short diagnostic recordings are more resilient than a single live session.

2. **“Asynchronous” should mean a structured clinical packet, not an unstructured message thread.** High-performing workflows combine a concise history, red flags, current medicines, vital signs, labelled images or recordings, the local provider’s question, and an explicit response deadline. In rural Uganda, nurses captured ECGs and echocardiograms locally, compressed and uploaded them for later cardiologist review, and closed the loop by SMS/WhatsApp; 1,324 patients were managed with a median seven-day consultation turnaround (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0255918).

3. **A local facilitator materially improves completeness and diagnostic usefulness.** Babylon/Babyl Rwanda used USSD booking followed by scheduled nurse callbacks and escalation to senior nurses or general practitioners. mPharma places a nurse in a community pharmacy to prepare the patient and operate remote examination equipment. The Uganda cardiac program similarly relied on trained local nurses. These approaches reduce the burden on patients with limited smartphone proficiency.

4. **Offline-first architecture protects both completion and clinical safety.** Every field, photograph, diagnostic trace, prescription draft, and acknowledgement should be committed locally before upload. Users need visible states such as “saved on this phone,” “waiting to send,” “sent,” “reviewed,” and “action required.” A network interruption must never erase entered information or force the provider to restart a consultation.

5. **Evidence does not support a general claim that remote primary-care diagnosis is always equivalent to in-person care.** Results depend heavily on condition and data quality. Store-and-forward mobile teledermatology achieved 356 matching diagnoses among 391 patients:

   `356 ÷ 391 = 0.9105 = 91.05% agreement`, with Cohen’s κ=0.906  
   (https://medicaljournalssweden.se/actadv/article/download/5605/8499/34034).

   By contrast, rural Kenya’s Mashavu system achieved 78.4% consistency in clinical advice, although agreement on the required patient action—such as referral versus no further care—was 89.2% (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/2150131912461797). A randomized crossover primary-care study in rural India reported 74% diagnostic and 79.8% treatment concordance, illustrating the danger of extrapolating specialty results to all primary care.

6. **The requested vendor comparison needs an important correction.** Available evidence characterizes Zipline primarily as a medical logistics, inventory, and sample-transport system—not as a patient-facing diagnostic or medication-reconciliation application. It should be treated as a fulfilment and logistics layer connected to the telehealth workflow, not as a proven substitute for clinical decision support.

---

## 1. How communication architecture affects consultation quality

### 1.1 Asynchronous communication

Asynchronous store-and-forward care removes the requirement that the patient, local provider, specialist, and network all be available simultaneously. This is particularly valuable on unstable 2G/3G connections.

The useful pattern is:

1. local provider registers the patient and records the clinical question;
2. history, red flags, vital signs, medicines, tests, and media are saved locally;
3. the case is placed in a persistent outbound queue;
4. small structured data upload first, followed by larger media;
5. the remote clinician reviews the packet and either responds or requests specified missing information;
6. the local provider acknowledges and communicates the plan;
7. referral, test, or medicine fulfilment is recorded;
8. unresolved cases remain on a worklist rather than disappearing into a message history.

The Uganda cardiac program demonstrates this separation clearly. A local nurse collected history, examination findings, medications, ECGs, and echocardiograms. DICOM studies were compressed, uploaded through a mobile-data SIM, and reviewed asynchronously in Kampala. Elective cases were announced through closed-loop SMS or WhatsApp; urgent inpatient cases triggered direct communication. A local nurse then communicated the final plan and a local physician issued recommended prescriptions (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0255918).

This model improves quality by allowing:

- deliberate specialist review rather than hurried interpretation during a failing call;
- transmission of objective findings that cannot be conveyed reliably by voice;
- prioritization of urgent cases;
- an auditable record of what was captured, reviewed, and recommended;
- task shifting without leaving the local provider unsupported.

Its principal trade-off is latency. In the Uganda program the median consultation time was seven days. Such a workflow is therefore appropriate only when red-flag logic reliably diverts emergencies to immediate referral or synchronous escalation.

### 1.2 Scheduled voice callbacks

Babyl Rwanda shows a different low-bandwidth strategy: minimize patient-side data requirements rather than attempting a rich smartphone application. Patients dialled `*811#`, selected an appointment, paid through mobile money, received an SMS confirmation, and were called by a triage nurse. The nurse could complete advice, escalate to a senior nurse or GP, or refer the patient to a facility. Prescriptions and laboratory orders were delivered as SMS codes (https://www.babyl.rw/services/; https://www.babyl.rw/).

This is not fully asynchronous clinical care—the callback itself is synchronous—but the workflow is **temporally decoupled**:

- booking does not require a clinician to be online;
- the clinician initiates the call at a scheduled time;
- triage and definitive consultation can occur in separate stages;
- prescriptions and laboratory orders travel through store-and-forward SMS;
- patients do not need mobile data or a smartphone.

The model’s quality advantage is that voice conversation can elicit a fuller history than a patient-completed form, particularly where literacy or smartphone proficiency is limited. In an audit involving 2,532 standardized patient visits for malaria and upper respiratory infection, Babyl’s telephone care was reported to be as good as in-person care for malaria and better for upper respiratory infection. Telephone providers asked more history and symptom questions, used fewer unnecessary medicines and tests, and resisted requested unnecessary antibiotics better than face-to-face providers (https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w34185/w34185.pdf).

That finding is condition-specific. It does not establish equivalence for abdominal emergencies, obstetric complications, severe respiratory disease, neurologic deficits, or other presentations requiring hands-on examination.

### 1.3 Hybrid real-time and store-and-forward examination

mPharma’s mutti Doctor model uses community pharmacies as assisted telehealth sites. An onsite nurse prepares the patient and operates TytoCare equipment for examination of the heart, lungs, skin, ears, throat, abdomen, heart rate, and temperature. The platform supports sharing examination data, cloud storage, and live video examinations (https://www.tytocare.com/news-and-press/african-healthtech-company-mpharma-partners-with-tytocare-to-introduce-comprehensive-telehealth-to-pharmacies/).

This improves remote consultation quality by replacing some of the information lost in an audio-only encounter with nurse-acquired objective findings. More than 8,000 people had been examined across 35 pharmacies in Ghana, Kenya, Uganda, Zambia, and Nigeria by April 2022. A company survey reported that more than 90% of patients at mutti Doctor locations obtained a virtual doctor consultation within ten minutes.

However:

- “within ten minutes” is an access or wait-time measure, not a consultation-completion measure;
- the cited evidence is vendor-reported rather than an independent comparative trial;
- the available source describes cloud sharing and live examination but does **not** establish that mPharma’s implementation can complete the entire encounter offline;
- no published diagnostic-concordance figure for mPharma was found in the gathered evidence.

For a rural deployment, the examination subsystem should therefore be redesigned to record short, validated clips and still images locally and upload them later, rather than assuming continuous video.

---

## 2. Offline-first architecture

### 2.1 Required technical behavior

An offline-first clinical application should provide:

- **Local transaction storage:** Commit each answer immediately to an encrypted on-device database.
- **Autosave by field:** Do not wait for the end of a page or encounter.
- **Resumable encounters:** Reopen at the exact unfinished step after application closure, battery loss, or network interruption.
- **Persistent upload queue:** Retry automatically with exponential backoff without creating duplicate records.
- **Idempotent server operations:** Repeated submission of the same consultation, prescription, or image must not create duplicates.
- **Data-before-media synchronization:** Send demographics, red flags, and clinical text first; upload images, audio, or ultrasound clips afterward.
- **Chunked and resumable media upload:** Restart from the last confirmed chunk rather than from zero.
- **Compression with preservation of diagnostic quality:** Generate a small preview and retain the original locally until the remote reviewer confirms adequacy.
- **Conflict management:** Display conflicting edits rather than silently overwriting them.
- **Clear state labels:** “Draft,” “saved locally,” “queued,” “partly sent,” “submitted,” “reviewed,” “changes requested,” and “closed.”
- **Manual send option:** Providers should be able to defer large uploads until a better signal or lower-cost data window.
- **Multiple communication fallbacks:** Application notification first, then SMS; voice callback for urgent or literacy-sensitive communication.
- **Local reference content:** Red-flag rules, dosing tables, referral criteria, and formulary data must work without connectivity.

The Uganda cardiac service provides concrete evidence that compression and delayed upload can make large diagnostic files usable in a low-bandwidth environment. It used focused imaging protocols, compressed DICOM echocardiograms, automatic cloud upload through a mobile-data SIM, backup equipment, and asynchronous specialist review (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0255918).

### 2.2 Safety rules

Offline-first must not mean “all cases can wait.” The application should perform red-flag evaluation on the device and generate one of three dispositions:

- **Emergency:** stop routine form completion, show immediate stabilization and referral actions, and offer one-tap voice escalation.
- **Urgent:** finish the minimum clinical packet and place it at the front of the synchronization and review queues.
- **Routine:** allow normal store-and-forward processing.

If decision support depends on a server response, it is unsafe under intermittent connectivity. Core triage logic and drug-safety checks should run locally, with version-controlled guideline updates synchronized later. Expert guidance for low-resource clinical decision algorithms emphasizes evidence-based, human-interpretable logic and validation that the software faithfully implements the intended clinical protocol (https://gh.bmj.com/content/5/2/e002067).

---

## 3. Comparison of Babylon/Babyl, mPharma, and Zipline

### Babylon/Babyl Rwanda

**Primary UX strategy**

- feature-phone-compatible USSD registration and booking;
- mobile-money payment;
- SMS confirmation;
- scheduled clinician-initiated voice callback;
- nurse triage followed by senior nurse/GP escalation;
- SMS prescription and laboratory codes;
- referral to a physical facility when remote management is insufficient.

**Connectivity strategy**

Babyl avoids dependence on mobile broadband. USSD, SMS, and ordinary voice work on basic phones and weak networks. The system separates booking, triage, definitive consultation, testing, and prescribing into distinct transactions.

**Store-and-forward diagnostics**

Laboratory orders and results can move through the platform, but the gathered evidence does not demonstrate a mature image-based store-and-forward examination workflow comparable to teledermatology or tele-echocardiography.

**Medication reconciliation**

Babyl provides electronic prescription codes through SMS, but the available sources do not establish a robust patient-facing reconciliation interface showing current medicines, discontinued medicines, duplicates, adherence, and dispensing confirmation.

**Quality evidence**

The strongest comparative evidence among the three vendors is the 2,532-visit standardized-patient audit. Telephone care was comparable to in-person care for malaria and better for upper respiratory infection, with more complete questioning and less unnecessary prescribing (https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w34185/w34185.pdf).

**Main weakness**

Patients and providers have reported process confusion, service delays, device-access problems, and digital-literacy barriers. Providers also expressed concern about diagnostic limits without physical examination (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13041620/).

### mPharma mutti Doctor

**Primary UX strategy**

- community pharmacy as a trusted access point;
- nurse-assisted intake and examination;
- remote doctor consultation;
- integrated prescription review, medicine pickup, or delivery;
- examination hardware that captures heart, lung, ear, throat, skin, abdomen, temperature, and heart-rate findings.

**Connectivity strategy**

The facilitator absorbs most technical complexity. This is advantageous for patients with limited digital skills. Nevertheless, the available evidence does not show a fully offline consultation path; the described platform includes live video and cloud storage.

**Store-and-forward diagnostics**

TytoCare can share captured examination data, making asynchronous review technically plausible. The evidence gathered here does not prove that mPharma routinely uses offline capture and delayed upload under 2G/3G conditions.

**Medication reconciliation**

mPharma has the strongest organizational position for medication reconciliation because the consultation is embedded in a pharmacy network. Its Bloom application is reported to expose patient medication history, drug information, treatment guidance, refill scheduling, and reminders. This claim comes from company-related reporting rather than an independent outcome evaluation, so it should be validated during procurement.

**Performance evidence**

More than 8,000 consultations were reported across 35 pharmacies, and over 90% of visiting patients reportedly reached a virtual physician within ten minutes (https://www.tytocare.com/news-and-press/african-healthtech-company-mpharma-partners-with-tytocare-to-introduce-comprehensive-telehealth-to-pharmacies/). This supports rapid access, not necessarily >90% end-to-end completion or diagnostic equivalence.

**Main weakness**

Hardware, nurse availability, cloud dependence, and potentially large audio/video payloads raise cost and reliability concerns outside staffed pharmacies.

### Zipline

**Primary UX strategy**

Zipline reduces ordering friction for health workers: orders can be placed using WhatsApp, SMS, or phone, without special equipment or extensive data entry. It provides 24/7 logistics support, product-level inventory tracking, and delivery status (https://assets.ctfassets.net/pbn2i2zbvp41/5dpfo3SJfsUZ0Az5fqLA1P/44e71538284dce389d48d3cc05f15142/Zipline-Capabilities-Statement.pdf).

**Connectivity strategy**

Multiple lightweight order channels make the logistics workflow tolerant of limited bandwidth. The company reports delivery within 15–45 minutes from order placement and a 100% on-time, in-full delivery record in its capabilities statement.

**Store-and-forward diagnostics**

Zipline can transport physical test samples to central laboratories, reportedly reducing turnaround from months to days. This complements digital store-and-forward: a provider can submit the electronic case first, dispatch the physical specimen, and link the result later.

**Medication reconciliation**

Zipline tracks products and inventory, not the patient’s verified medication list. It can help answer whether a prescribed medicine is available, dispatched, and delivered, but it does not by itself reconcile what the patient is actually taking.

**Clinical decision support**

The gathered evidence does not substantiate the premise that Zipline offers frontline diagnostic decision tools comparable to Babyl’s triage workflow or mPharma’s examination interface. Its documented role is supply-chain, inventory, sample transport, and fulfilment. A telehealth platform should integrate with Zipline after the clinical decision—for medicine, blood product, vaccine, diagnostic kit, or specimen transport—rather than relying on it for diagnosis.

---

## 4. Interaction patterns associated with completion above 85%

The evidence supports several patterns, but the metrics must not be conflated.

### 4.1 Structured asynchronous specialist packets

The African Asynchronous Consultation for Movement Disorders program reported that all 43 requested consultations were completed as scheduled:

`43 ÷ 43 = 100% completion`.

Local physicians changed evaluation or treatment in response to specialist recommendations 80% of the time. The main problem was uploading and downloading video, reinforcing the need for compressed clips and resumable transfer (https://www.mdsabstracts.org/abstract/asynchronous-telehealth-consultations-for-movement-disorders-in-africa/).

The relevant pattern was not simply “asynchronous messaging”; it was a clinician-to-clinician referral with:

- a known responsible local physician;
- a defined specialist recipient;
- recorded examination media;
- a scheduled completion expectation;
- recommendations returned to someone able to act on them.

The sample is small and specialty-specific, so 100% should not be treated as a general forecast.

### 4.2 Assisted pharmacy consultations

mPharma reported that over 90% of patients reached a remote doctor within ten minutes. The useful interaction pattern is:

- walk-in access;
- a nurse prepares the patient;
- equipment and connectivity are managed by staff;
- doctor availability is pooled centrally;
- prescription fulfilment occurs at the same location.

Again, this is a wait-time/access measure rather than documented end-to-end completion.

### 4.3 Automatic fallback from a failed rich channel to a simple one

A small rural Rwanda telepharmacy feasibility report described 87.4% session completion despite technology failures in 14.7% of sessions, with many failures resolved by callback or switching to SMS. These figures suggest the value of channel fallback, but the source is recent, small, and less authoritative than the peer-reviewed studies above; it should be treated as preliminary rather than procurement-grade evidence.

### 4.4 Agreement above 85% requires condition-appropriate data

Evidence exceeding 85% includes:

- mobile store-and-forward dermatology: 91.05% diagnostic agreement;
- rural Kenya Mashavu: 89.2% agreement on patient action, although only 78.4% consistency in overall clinical advice;
- Babyl Rwanda: standardized-patient evidence of equivalent malaria care and better upper-respiratory-infection care, although the gathered summary does not provide a single diagnostic-agreement percentage.

Thus, the most defensible statement is:

> Completion over 85% is achievable with assigned ownership, structured packets, local facilitation, explicit response deadlines, and low-bandwidth fallback. Diagnostic performance comparable to in-person care is achievable for selected conditions when the remote clinician receives the specific history, test, image, or recording needed for that condition. Neither result is guaranteed for undifferentiated primary care.

---

## 5. Cognitive-load design for providers with limited smartphone proficiency

Network interruptions add cognitive demands to an already difficult clinical task: the provider must remember what was entered, whether it was saved, whether the specialist received it, and what remains undone. The interface should reduce **extraneous cognitive load** while preserving the clinical reasoning that constitutes necessary or intrinsic load.

WHO’s evidence review notes that health workers can perceive digital systems as increasing workload, especially when digital and paper systems run in parallel. Limited digital literacy causes anxiety about errors, and even competent users need repeat training and technical support (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK541898/). Consequently, the platform should embody the following principles.

### 5.1 Recognition rather than recall

- Present common complaints, medicines, units, and dispositions as searchable choices.
- Show the existing medication list for confirmation rather than asking the provider to reconstruct it.
- Display prior vital signs and test results beside the new entry.
- Keep short clinical definitions and image examples available offline.
- Show the next required action on the patient worklist.

### 5.2 Progressive disclosure

Do not display a long comprehensive form at once. Use a short sequence:

1. patient identity;
2. immediate danger signs;
3. chief complaint;
4. complaint-specific history;
5. examination and tests;
6. current medicines and allergies;
7. assessment;
8. disposition and follow-up.

Reveal detailed questions only when clinically relevant. For example, selecting “pregnant,” “child under five,” or “difficulty breathing” should activate the corresponding safety pathway.

### 5.3 One decision per screen

Each screen should have a clear question, a small number of choices, and a large primary action. Avoid dense grids, horizontal scrolling, multiple save buttons, and unexplained icons. Use familiar wording and local language labels, while retaining standard coded values behind the interface.

### 5.4 Externalize progress and network state

A persistent header should show:

- patient identity;
- encounter stage, such as “4 of 7”;
- last saved time;
- offline/online status;
- number of items waiting to upload.

The provider should never need to infer whether pressing “submit” worked. If text was sent but images remain queued, the interface must say exactly that.

### 5.5 Minimize duplicate work

Collect information once and reuse it in the referral, prescription, laboratory request, dispensing screen, and follow-up note. Maintaining parallel paper and digital records increases workload and error risk. If paper is legally required, generate a printable or SMS-compatible summary from the digital encounter.

### 5.6 Safe defaults without automation bias

- Prepopulate normal units, not normal findings.
- Do not preselect “no danger signs.”
- Require explicit confirmation of allergies, pregnancy where relevant, and current medicines.
- Explain why a red flag or drug alert appears.
- Allow clinicians to override recommendations, but require a brief reason for high-risk overrides.
- Keep decision logic human-interpretable and tied to national guidelines.

---

## 6. Image and diagnostic-capture workflow

A poor image wastes bandwidth and creates a second patient visit. Quality assurance should therefore occur **before** upload.

### Recommended sequence

1. **Select examination type:** skin, wound, throat, ear, eye, medication package, rapid-test cassette, ECG, ultrasound, or other.
2. **Show a single visual example:** distance, angle, lighting, and required body landmark.
3. **Capture locally:** never require a live network connection to open the camera.
4. **Perform automatic checks:** blur, darkness, glare, obstruction, orientation, and incomplete framing.
5. **Prompt immediate retake:** use plain language such as “too dark—move closer to the window.”
6. **Collect a minimal set:** for skin, typically an orientation image, a mid-range image, and a close-up with scale; avoid unlimited photographs.
7. **Label at capture time:** body site, left/right, date, symptoms, duration, and whether the image is before or after treatment.
8. **Let the provider review and approve:** show thumbnails and a simple quality indicator.
9. **Upload preview first:** enable rapid triage; send the diagnostic-quality original in resumable chunks.
10. **Retain locally until acknowledged:** delete only after server verification and according to retention policy.
11. **Support “more information required”:** the reviewer should request a specific missing view, measurement, or test rather than rejecting the entire case.

For ECGs or ultrasound clips, use a checklist of required views and mark each as complete. The Uganda cardiac program used focused adult and paediatric echocardiography protocols, backup equipment, image compression, and asynchronous PACS review—an effective model for reducing both capture variability and bandwidth demand (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0255918).

Image quality and clinical context are inseparable. The 91.05% teledermatology agreement was obtained when images were accompanied by medical history collected by a clinician. An image-only inbox is therefore unlikely to reproduce that performance.

---

## 7. Medication reconciliation and fulfilment

Medication reconciliation should be a first-class workflow, not a free-text question near the end of the form.

For each medicine, show:

- generic and local brand name;
- strength and formulation;
- prescribed dose and actual dose taken;
- frequency and duration;
- indication;
- source of medicine;
- last dose;
- adherence or access problem;
- status: continue, change, stop, duplicate, or uncertain.

Support barcode scanning where practical, but always provide photograph and search alternatives. A photograph of the package should be stored locally and linked to the medicine entry.

At sign-off, present one consolidated screen:

- medicines confirmed as currently taken;
- newly prescribed medicines;
- stopped medicines;
- possible duplicates;
- allergies and prior adverse reactions;
- stock or fulfilment status;
- counselling completed;
- follow-up date.

The three compared models contribute different pieces:

- **Babyl:** lightweight SMS prescription codes and insurance-linked redemption.
- **mPharma:** pharmacy staff, medication history, prescription review, pickup or delivery—the best setting for reconciliation and adherence support.
- **Zipline:** availability, batch-level logistics, dispatch, and delivery of medicines or diagnostics, but not verification of what the patient takes.

The recommended architecture is therefore to use the clinical record as the source of the patient medication list, mPharma-like pharmacy workflows for verification and counselling, and Zipline-like logistics for stock and delivery status.

---

## 8. Recommended end-to-end workflow

### At the rural clinic

1. Open or create the patient record offline.
2. Run local danger-sign triage.
3. Capture complaint-specific history, examination, tests, and medication reconciliation.
4. If remote review is needed, generate a structured consultation packet.
5. Save and provide the patient with an SMS or paper reference number.
6. If connectivity permits, upload immediately; otherwise retain in the queue.
7. For urgent cases, use voice escalation while sending the packet in parallel.

### At the remote clinical hub

8. Worklists sort cases by urgency, waiting time, age group, and incomplete data.
9. The clinician reviews structured data before opening large media.
10. The clinician can answer, request one specific missing item, schedule a callback, or refer.
11. Prescriptions run through allergy, interaction, dose, pregnancy, and duplication checks.
12. The plan is digitally signed and sent to the clinic.

### Closing the loop

13. Clinic staff acknowledge receipt.
14. Patient is contacted by voice or SMS.
15. Tests, referral attendance, dispensing, and medicine delivery are recorded.
16. A case closes only when there is a documented disposition—not merely when the remote clinician sends a message.
17. Unacknowledged urgent results and uncollected medicines return automatically to the worklist.

---

## 9. Evaluation targets

The platform should measure separate stages rather than reporting a single ambiguous “completion rate.”

### Operational measures

- intake completion;
- percentage of records recovered successfully after interruption;
- percentage synchronized without manual re-entry;
- median time from capture to successful upload;
- specialist response within the promised time;
- patient successfully reached;
- plan acknowledged by local provider;
- prescription dispensed or referral attended;
- end-to-end closure.

For an 85% target, report the denominator explicitly. For example:

`end-to-end completion = cases with documented disposition ÷ all eligible initiated cases`.

If 892 of 1,000 initiated consultations have a documented communicated disposition:

`892 ÷ 1,000 = 89.2% completion`.

That should not be described as diagnostic accuracy or clinical agreement.

### Quality and safety measures

- agreement with blinded in-person assessment by condition;
- correct case management under Ugandan, Kenyan, and Tanzanian guidelines;
- sensitivity for danger signs;
- appropriate referral;
- antibiotic and antimalarial appropriateness;
- medication discrepancies resolved;
- unusable image rate;
- repeat-capture rate;
- adverse events during delayed review;
- loss to follow-up.

### Human-factors measures

- median taps and time per encounter;
- percentage needing technical assistance;
- form abandonment by screen;
- errors after simulated network loss;
- provider workload and usability scores;
- performance stratified by smartphone proficiency.

---

## Overall recommendation

Build a **facilitated, voice-capable, asynchronous-by-default platform**, not a video-first consumer telemedicine application. Use Babyl’s USSD/SMS/callback pattern for access, mPharma’s nurse-assisted examination and pharmacy linkage for richer diagnostics and medication reconciliation, and Zipline’s lightweight ordering and fulfilment model for physical medicines, tests, and specimens.

The interaction patterns most strongly associated with high completion are assigned ownership, staged and resumable encounters, local facilitation, structured clinical packets, explicit response deadlines, closed-loop acknowledgement, and automatic fallback from data-intensive channels to voice or SMS. Diagnostic performance comparable to in-person care is most plausible when the condition is suitable for remote assessment and the workflow captures the exact objective evidence needed—such as a validated rapid test, high-quality labelled images, ECG, or compressed ultrasound study. It should not be promised across all rural primary-care presentations without condition-specific validation.
