final.content:
Multimodal Grocery Checkout for Blind and Low-Vision Users: Evidence Review and Design Recommendations

Executive summary

The available evidence favors a hybrid design rather than a strictly sequential, voice-only checkout:

- Voice is efficient for broad commands, search, and initial text entry. In a study with eight blind participants, speech input was nearly five times faster than VoiceOver keyboard entry. However, correcting recognition errors was highly burdensome: participants spent an average of 80.3% of their interaction time editing. Speech therefore works best for expressing intent, not as the sole mechanism for inspecting and repairing transaction-critical values (https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/2513383.2513440).
- Touch or gesture input with immediate audio feedback is slower than unconstrained speech for initial entry, but it provides deterministic, user-controlled navigation and correction. GestureCalc’s eight screen-reader users entered characters 40.5% faster than with a conventional accessible touchscreen calculator and completed 52.2% fewer erroneous calculations, despite making more initial gesture mistakes, because the interface made errors easier to detect and correct (https://grail.cs.washington.edu/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/chaudhuri2019gae.pdf).
- Numerical entry is especially vulnerable when feedback is reduced. DigiTaps users entered 0.87 characters per second without per-character audio, but had a 5.63% uncorrected character-error rate; the no-audio condition was faster but less accurate than audio after each input (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2501988.2502056).
- Long, serially spoken cart reviews are a poor fit for 15-plus-item carts. Auditory lists are transient, slow, and place more information in working memory than navigable touch/screen-reader structures. The evidence supports a layered review: first announce totals and exceptions, then let users inspect products by category or item using touch, gestures, or voice commands, with persistent position information and targeted readback.
- Payment authorization should use a distinct, explicit confirmation step that states the amount, payment instrument, delivery destination or slot, and unresolved substitutions or stock changes. Users must be able to review, correct, or reverse the transaction. This follows WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.4 and is also supported by transaction studies in which inaccessible feedback prevented blind participants from completing purchases (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/error-prevention-legal-financial-data.html; https://chorus.scs.carleton.ca/wp-content/papercite-data/pdf/napoli2018-obstacles-soups.pdf).
- There is no located controlled study directly comparing voice-only and hybrid checkout for a 15-plus-item grocery cart, nor a robust published set of modality-specific confidence scores for that exact task. Conclusions about large-cart cognitive load are therefore evidence-based extrapolations from speech input, auditory-list, numerical-entry, screen-reader navigation, and accessible transaction studies—not direct effect estimates.

1. Scope and strength of the evidence

The research base is fragmented. Relevant studies examine:

1. Speech versus VoiceOver keyboard entry for blind users.
2. Targeted touchscreen controls versus target-free gestures with audio.
3. Eyes-free number entry with and without audio confirmation.
4. Auditory menu and list navigation.
5. E-commerce and financial transactions using screen readers.
6. WCAG implementation guidance for errors, status messages, authentication, and transaction confirmation.

Few studies reproduce an end-to-end grocery checkout, and none in the gathered evidence directly randomizes blind or low-vision shoppers between:

- a fully voice-only workflow, and
- a hybrid touch-plus-audio workflow

for product selection, quantity changes, 15-plus-item cart review, and payment authorization.

Consequently, exact differences in grocery-checkout completion rate, numerical error rate, confidence, or NASA-TLX workload cannot responsibly be claimed. The strongest conclusions concern component interactions and failure modes.

2. Sequential voice-only versus hybrid touch-and-audio

2.1 Product finding and selection

Voice-only strengths

Voice can collapse many screen-reader navigation steps into one command, such as “find unsweetened oat milk” or “add the cheapest two-liter semi-skimmed milk.” Speech is particularly advantageous for longer text input. The controlled study of eight blind people found speech nearly five times as fast as the VoiceOver touchscreen keyboard (https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/2513383.2513440).

Blind users also reported greater use of, and satisfaction with, speech input than sighted users in the accompanying survey of 169 blind/low-vision and sighted respondents. This is consistent with speech having a larger relative advantage over nonvisual soft-keyboard entry.

Voice-only weaknesses

The speed benefit can disappear when automatic speech recognition is wrong. In the same study, error correction was frustrating and occupied an average of 80.3% of participants’ time. Later interviews with 12 blind adults similarly identified poor dictation accuracy, noisy environments, and difficulty correcting errors as recurring problems (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3733155.3736593).

For grocery selection, the important risk is not simply transcription accuracy. Product names frequently differ by:

- brand;
- flavor;
- package size;
- count or weight;
- dietary formulation;
- unit price;
- promotional status.

A voice system can recognize the words yet select the wrong entity. A pure conversational sequence also makes comparison difficult because each spoken candidate displaces the previous candidate from working memory.

Hybrid implication

Use voice to form or narrow the query, but expose the results as a persistent, screen-reader-compatible list that can also be explored through touch. Each result should have a stable accessible name that combines the discriminating attributes, for example:

“Brand X oat drink, unsweetened, one liter, £1.80, £1.80 per liter, Add button.”

Research with 19 blind screen-reader users found broad, shallow menu hierarchies faster than narrow, deep ones, with task time correlated with navigation “lostness” (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1016/j.intcom.2010.02.003). Thus, product flows should avoid conversational chains such as category → subcategory → brand → size → flavor when a searchable, filterable, shallow list can expose the same choices.

2.2 Quantity adjustment and numerical entry

Numerical quantities and payment values require a higher standard than ordinary prose because one wrong digit or unintended increment can materially alter the order.

DigiTaps

A longitudinal study of 16 participants found that DigiTaps without audio entered numbers at 0.87 characters per second, with a 5.63% uncorrected character-error rate. Removing per-character audio made entry faster but less accurate than giving audio after every input (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2501988.2502056).

To illustrate the potential cumulative risk, if errors were independent and each digit retained the observed 5.63% error probability, the probability of at least one error would be:

P(error in n digits) = 1 − (1 − 0.0563)^n

- Four digits: 1 − 0.9437^4 = approximately 20.7%
- Six digits: 1 − 0.9437^6 = approximately 29.4%
- Ten digits: 1 − 0.9437^10 = approximately 44.0%

These are not observed transaction failure rates: independence is a simplifying assumption, users may correct mistakes, and the DigiTaps population and task do not exactly reproduce checkout. The calculation nevertheless shows why a seemingly modest character-error rate is unacceptable for unverified quantities, card data, postal codes, or one-time codes.

GestureCalc

GestureCalc combined target-free touch gestures with audio after each digit or operator. Among eight screen-reader users:

- Classic calculator speed: 0.536 characters/second.
- GestureCalc speed: 0.753 characters/second.
- Relative improvement:  
  (0.753 − 0.536) / 0.536 = 40.5%.
- Erroneous calculations were 52.2% lower than with the baseline touchscreen calculator.

Users made more initial mistakes with GestureCalc, but corrected more of them. This distinction is important: the best checkout input is not necessarily the one with the fewest raw slips, but the one producing the fewest undetected or unrecovered errors (https://grail.cs.washington.edu/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/chaudhuri2019gae.pdf).

The interface provided:

- audio after every entered character;
- delete that spoke the deleted character;
- a complete-expression readback command;
- target-free gestures;
- haptic confirmation for long presses.

Participants acknowledged a learning cost but reported confidence that they could become fluent. This was qualitative confidence rather than a standardized numerical confidence score.

BlindSight

BlindSight’s tactile input plus brief auditory confirmation achieved eyes-free error rates below 5% and added about 200 milliseconds per keystroke compared with sighted input. In its final comparison, seven of eight participants preferred or strongly preferred the auditory eyes-free system to the conventional mobile interface. The interface decomposed long output, allowed interruption, and gave short feedback only when requested (https://www.patrickbaudisch.com/publications/2008-Li-CHI08-BlindSight.pdf).

The study did not involve blind grocery shoppers—it addressed eyes-free phone use—so its value is primarily in the interaction principles:

- deterministic tactile input;
- immediate brief confirmation;
- user-controlled pacing;
- interruptible speech;
- decomposition of long sequences;
- direct shortcuts for experienced users.

Recommended quantity pattern

For ordinary quantity changes:

1. Provide separate, screen-reader-labeled Decrease and Increase controls, avoiding drag-only steppers.
2. After every activation, announce the complete resulting state, not merely “increased”:
   “Bananas, quantity 4, estimated weight 800 grams, subtotal £1.76.”
3. Support a direct voice command such as “change bananas to four.”
4. Read back the interpreted product and final value:
   “Bananas changed from 2 to 4.”
5. Provide immediate Undo.
6. If a value is clamped to a limit, explicitly announce both the invalid request and the resulting value:
   “Maximum quantity is 12. Quantity set to 12.”

For unusually large or ambiguous changes, request confirmation:

“You asked for 40 cartons of milk, previously 4. Confirm 40 or say ‘change quantity.’”

Do not require confirmation after every one-item increment; that creates confirmation fatigue and increases time and auditory load.

2.3 Payment and authentication

Voice-only payment introduces privacy and recognition risks. Card numbers, security codes, addresses, totals, and one-time passwords are difficult to enter and verify solely through speech, especially in public or noisy environments. Conversely, conventional touchscreen entry can be slow and error-prone when controls are small or screen-reader labels are incomplete.

WCAG 2.2 adds or reinforces several relevant requirements:

- 3.3.4 Error Prevention for financial transactions: the submission must be reversible, checked with an opportunity to correct, or reviewable and correctable before finalization.
- 3.3.1 Error Identification: identify the item in error and describe the problem in text.
- 3.3.3 Error Suggestion: provide a known correction when possible.
- 4.1.3 Status Messages: expose success, waiting, progress, and error messages so assistive technology can announce them without an unnecessary focus change.
- 3.3.7 Redundant Entry: avoid requiring users to re-enter previously supplied information.
- 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication: provide an authentication path that does not depend on a cognitive-function test such as memorizing or transcribing information without assistance.
- 2.5.7 and 2.5.8: avoid drag-only operation and provide adequate pointer targets.

The complete standard is at https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/. Accessible-authentication guidance specifically identifies remembering passwords and transcribing one-time codes as potentially high cognitive burdens and supports mechanisms such as password managers and paste (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/accessible-authentication-minimum.html).

3. Task completion and error evidence

3.1 Directly reported completion failures

A transactional-web study included 14 participants with visual impairments—seven blind and seven partially sighted—performing tasks involving login, purchase, donation, and security assessment. Two blind participants could not complete an Amazon purchase because an address-reformatting correction was represented visually in red bold text, while the screen reader rendered the original and corrected versions indistinguishably. The problem was not absence of data but absence of accessible contrast between states (https://chorus.scs.carleton.ca/wp-content/papercite-data/pdf/napoli2018-obstacles-soups.pdf).

The same study found:

- error messages for failed logins were buried in page content;
- successful login feedback was insufficient for blind users;
- masked passwords provided no useful confirmation of which key had been pressed;
- zero of six participants exposed to the spoof site identified it as illegitimate.

The phishing result is:

0 / 6 = 0% detection in that condition.

This is a very small sample and should not be treated as a population rate, but it demonstrates that merely making content screen-reader-readable does not ensure transaction confidence or security comprehension.

3.2 Broader mobile accessibility findings

A smartphone-interface evaluation with 56 blind and visually impaired participants reported 100% task effectiveness for its organizational design. Reported satisfaction scores included:

- Blind participants: presentation, 87.62.
- Visually impaired participants: organization and presentation, 89.21 each.

The study concluded that logical organization, reduced redundant information, serialized content, and appropriate presentation improved effectiveness and satisfaction (https://www.techscience.com/iasc/v30n1/43961/html).

These are satisfaction/usability scores, not checkout-specific confidence scores and not a voice-versus-hybrid comparison. They nevertheless support predictable organization and reduced repetition.

A separate payment-app study of 15 visually impaired users found persistent problems with screen-reader compatibility, inconsistent navigation, unclear labels, and non-intuitive controls in Google Pay, PhonePe, and Paytm. One reported failure involved selecting the wrong SIM for UPI verification without a clear error message (http://ijssmr.org/uploads2025/ijssmr08_52.pdf). This reinforces the need for explicit system-state announcements and actionable recovery.

3.3 What the numbers do and do not establish

Supported findings:

- Speech can greatly accelerate initial input.
- Recognition-error correction can consume most interaction time.
- Per-character audio reduces uncorrected numerical errors, though it may slow entry.
- Target-free gestures with audio can improve final numerical outcomes even if they produce more correctable slips.
- Inaccessible error differentiation can reduce transaction completion to failure for individual blind users.
- Structured, predictable interfaces can achieve high effectiveness and satisfaction.

Not supported by the gathered evidence:

- A universal percentage advantage in grocery-checkout completion for hybrid over voice-only.
- A direct 15-item-cart NASA-TLX comparison.
- A standardized confidence-score difference between the two checkout modalities.
- An exact recognition-error rate for grocery quantities or prices.

4. Confirmation strategy

4.1 Match confirmation strength to consequence

Low-consequence, reversible actions

Examples: adding one item, increasing quantity from two to three, applying a filter.

Use:

- immediate concise audio status;
- persistent cart state;
- one-step Undo;
- no blocking confirmation dialog.

Example:

“Added Brand X chopped tomatoes, 400 grams. Cart now 8 items. Undo available.”

W3C’s status-message guidance specifically uses “shopping cart, five items” as an example of a message that should be programmatically exposed to screen readers without moving focus (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages.html).

Medium-risk actions

Examples: removing an item, clearing a cart, changing a quantity by a large amount, accepting a substitution.

Use either:

- explicit confirmation, or
- a reversible action with a clearly announced undo period.

High-consequence actions

Examples: authorizing payment, changing delivery address after review, accepting a materially different total.

Use a distinct review-and-confirm stage. WCAG’s online-retailer example requires displaying items, quantity of each item, shipping address, and payment method so the user can inspect, change, or confirm the order (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/error-prevention-legal-financial-data.html).

4.2 Use selective rather than exhaustive spoken confirmation

For a cart containing 15-plus products, automatically reading every product, quantity, unit price, promotion, and subtotal creates a long serial stream. Instead, the initial payment review should announce:

1. Number of distinct products.
2. Total units if useful.
3. Final payable amount.
4. Delivery or collection time.
5. Payment instrument in privacy-preserving form.
6. Number of substitutions, unavailable items, or quantity limits.
7. Material changes since the last review.

Example:

“Review order. 18 products, 24 total units. Total £73.42 including £3 delivery. Two substitutions and one quantity change need attention. Delivery Tuesday, 6 to 7 p.m. Paying with Visa ending 2048. Say ‘review changes,’ ‘review all items,’ ‘change payment,’ or ‘authorize payment.’”

The user can then request:

- “Review changes only.”
- “Read refrigerated items.”
- “Read items over £5.”
- “Go to item 12.”
- “Repeat total.”
- “Change the second substitution.”

This preserves access to full detail without forcing all details through working memory.

4.3 Make final authorization unmistakable

Avoid a generic “Yes?” because it may refer ambiguously to the last item, the total, or the whole order. The final prompt should bind action and consequence:

“Authorize payment of £73.42 to Grocery Store using Visa ending 2048?”

Accept a narrow set of explicit responses:

- “Authorize payment.”
- Activation of a labeled “Pay £73.42” button.
- An accessible biometric confirmation.

Do not treat conversational fillers such as “yes,” “okay,” or “go on” as payment authorization unless the system has first presented an unambiguous, isolated confirmation state and testing demonstrates that this is safe.

For stronger protection, allow multimodal confirmation: voice for review and a deliberate touch or biometric action for commitment. This separates a potentially fallible recognition channel from the legally and financially consequential act.

5. Error recovery

5.1 Preserve successful work

An error in one field should not clear the cart, address, delivery slot, or payment selection. WCAG 2.2’s redundant-entry requirement and the observed difficulty of nonvisual re-entry both support preserving all valid state.

5.2 Announce identity, problem, and repair

An effective error message contains:

- the affected item or field;
- the rejected value where safe;
- why it is invalid;
- the allowed format or range;
- an immediate correction command.

Example:

“Quantity for apples is 25, above the available maximum of 12. Say ‘set apples to 12,’ enter another quantity, or cancel.”

W3C notes that simply redisplaying a form is insufficient. The item in error and nature of the problem must be described in text; native validation can also be problematic because it may expose only the first error and provide generic messages (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/error-identification.html).

5.3 Keep correction local

After an error:

- move accessibility focus to the erroneous control, or provide a direct “Go to error” action;
- retain the entered value for editing;
- let users replace the complete value in one command;
- provide character- or digit-level navigation for precise repair;
- announce the corrected result;
- return the user to the previous review position.

Speech is particularly weak when correction requires selecting a misrecognized fragment in an undifferentiated transcript. The nearly fivefold input-speed advantage accompanied by 80.3% editing time demonstrates why repair must be a first-class interaction rather than an afterthought.

5.4 Distinguish transaction state from input state

Payment failures require different handling from form-validation errors:

- Decline: announce that payment was not taken, preserve the order, and offer another instrument.
- Network timeout before authorization: state that payment was not submitted.
- Unknown result after submission: do not invite an immediate duplicate payment; announce that status is being checked.
- Success: announce charged amount, merchant, order number, and receipt availability.
- Stock or price change: return to review and require renewed authorization if the total or substituted products changed materially.

All waiting, success, and failure states should be programmatically available as status messages. W3C cautions against interfaces becoming excessively “chatty,” so routine updates should normally use non-interruptive status announcements, reserving assertive alerts or focus-taking dialogs for urgent decisions (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages.html).

6. Cognitive load for carts with 15-plus items

6.1 What is directly known

The gathered evidence does not contain a controlled study in which blind and low-vision participants reviewed a 15-plus-item grocery cart under voice-only and hybrid conditions while NASA-TLX or an equivalent workload scale was recorded. No defensible numerical workload difference can therefore be reported.

Relevant component evidence includes:

- Traditional synthetic speech is slower than visual scanning and places higher demands on short-term memory when users explore lists and tables. A structured auditory list reader produced significantly faster performance and lower reported effort and mental demand than a conventional speech system, although the available summary does not give numerical TLX values (https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/266180.266334).
- BlindSight avoided long auditory blocks by decomposing information, making playback user-initiated and interruptible, and supplying compact non-speech previews (https://www.patrickbaudisch.com/publications/2008-Li-CHI08-BlindSight.pdf).
- GestureCalc’s pilot participants had difficulty remembering complete expressions and frequently requested repetitions. The researchers shortened expressions, presented them in parts, and added complete-expression readback—direct evidence that even relatively short numerical sequences can overload transient auditory memory (https://grail.cs.washington.edu/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/chaudhuri2019gae.pdf).
- Blind people may outperform sighted or low-vision groups on some auditory serial-recall tasks. In one study, 17 blind, 17 visually impaired, and 17 sighted participants recalled eight spoken digits; blind participants had better retention for later positions. This adaptation does not eliminate the usability cost of listening to and comparing 15-plus semantically complex grocery entries (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/17470218241300115).

6.2 Expected modality differences

Sequential voice-only review

Likely workload profile:

- Higher mental demand: users must retain earlier products and quantities while hearing later ones.
- Higher temporal demand: speech is inherently serial and users must wait or interrupt.
- Higher frustration after recognition or navigation errors.
- Higher memory burden when comparing similar products or checking whether an item was omitted.
- Lower physical demand and potentially lower visual demand.
- Good performance for a concise summary or a single known-item query.

Hybrid touch with audio feedback

Likely workload profile:

- Lower working-memory demand because cart structure, position, and item state remain externally represented.
- Better random access: users can move backward, forward, by heading, category, changed item, or error.
- Lower recovery cost because focus can remain on the item being edited.
- Some added physical demand and learning cost for gestures.
- Potentially greater navigation time if controls are small, unlabeled, deeply nested, or require precise targeting.
- Better support for user-controlled pacing and repeated inspection.

The relevant distinction is not “audio versus no audio.” Blind users still receive screen-reader speech in the hybrid condition. The benefit comes from combining audio with persistent structure and deterministic navigation rather than relying on a transient conversation history.

6.3 Recommended workload evaluation

Because direct evidence is absent, the proposed checkout should be tested with blind and low-vision participants using carts of at least 5, 15, and 25 products. Compare:

- sequential voice-only review;
- hybrid touch/screen-reader review;
- layered multimodal review with voice summary plus structured inspection.

Measure:

- completion rate;
- authorization of intentionally seeded wrong totals or quantities;
- corrected and uncorrected errors;
- review time;
- number of repetitions;
- number of backward navigations;
- omission-detection rate;
- NASA-TLX total and mental, temporal, effort, physical, performance, and frustration subscales;
- post-task confidence that product, quantity, total, address, and payment instrument were correct;
- actual-confidence calibration: confidence versus detected correctness.

Confidence should be recorded separately for each decision rather than only as a general usability score. A participant may find voice fast and pleasant yet remain unsure whether the correct product or amount will be charged.

7. Recommended end-to-end interaction

Product selection

- Voice: “Find lactose-free whole milk.”
- App: announce number of results and the active filters.
- Hybrid results: accessible list with product, size, price, unit price, and stock status.
- Selection feedback: “Added Product X, one liter, quantity one, £1.70.”
- Offer Undo without moving focus unnecessarily.

Quantity

- Voice or labeled plus/minus controls.
- Announce the complete new state after each change.
- Read back anomalous or multi-digit values.
- Provide direct replacement and Undo.
- Never silently clamp a quantity.

Cart review

- Begin with product count, unit count, total, delivery charge, and changes requiring attention.
- Organize products under headings such as substitutions, unavailable items, produce, chilled, and pantry.
- Support “next,” “previous,” “repeat,” “go to item,” and “where am I?”
- Maintain position announcements such as “Item 7 of 18.”
- Let users review all items, changes only, or selected categories.

Payment

- Reuse known address and payment data rather than requiring redundant entry.
- Permit password-manager paste, accessible biometrics, and accessible one-time-code retrieval.
- Never require voice as the only payment-input channel.
- Before authorization, state amount, payment instrument, fulfillment details, and unresolved material changes.
- Require an explicit payment action.
- On success, announce the charged amount and order identifier and make the receipt accessible.
- Provide cancellation or amendment where operationally possible.

8. Bottom line

For grocery checkout, voice should be an accelerator, not the sole source of truth. The strongest evidence supports:

- voice for search, intent, and direct commands;
- touch or target-free gestures for deterministic inspection and repair;
- immediate audio feedback after state changes;
- complete-value readback for quantities and payment amounts;
- persistent, shallow, screen-reader-compatible cart structure;
- summaries and exception-first review for large carts;
- explicit, consequence-bound payment confirmation;
- preserved state, local correction, Undo, and accessible status announcements.

Hybrid interaction does not automatically outperform voice-only interaction: poorly labeled controls, precise targeting requirements, hidden focus changes, or verbose live regions can erase its advantages. But when touch supplies persistent structure and audio supplies immediate state confirmation, the combined pattern better addresses the central weaknesses identified across the research: transient auditory memory, speech-recognition repair, numerical-entry errors, inaccessible transaction feedback, and uncertainty about whether a financial action succeeded.

final.content:
NASDAQ INDEPENDENT-DIRECTOR STANDARD

As of October 2026

1. Core definition

NASDAQ Listing Rule 5605(a)(2) defines an “Independent Director” as a person who:

1. is not an executive officer or employee of the listed company; and
2. has no relationship that, in the opinion of the company’s board, would interfere with the exercise of independent judgment in carrying out a director’s responsibilities.

The board must affirmatively determine that the director is independent. Merely avoiding the rule’s express disqualifications is therefore necessary but not always sufficient: the board must also consider any other relationship that could impair independent judgment. Ownership of the company’s shares, standing alone, does not preclude independence. [NASDAQ Rule 5605(a)(2) and IM-5605](https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/nasdaq-5600-series).

For these tests:

- “Executive Officer” means an officer covered by SEC Rule 16a-1(f).
- “Family Member” means the person’s spouse, parents, children, siblings, mothers- and fathers-in-law, sons- and daughters-in-law, brothers- and sisters-in-law, and anyone sharing the person’s home other than a domestic employee.
- References to the “Company” include a parent or subsidiary that the listed company controls and consolidates in its SEC-filed financial statements, but not an entity reported solely as an investment. [NASDAQ interpretive material accompanying Rule 5605](https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/nasdaq-5600-series).

2. Who qualifies

A director qualifies under the general NASDAQ board-independence standard if all of the following are true:

- The director is not currently an executive officer or employee of the company.
- None of the mandatory disqualifications in Rule 5605(a)(2)(A)–(F), discussed below, applies.
- For an investment company, the special “interested person” test in paragraph (G) is satisfied.
- After considering all relevant relationships—including relationships not expressly listed in the rule—the board affirmatively determines that the director can exercise independent judgment.

A substantial shareholder can therefore qualify if share ownership is the only relevant relationship and the board concludes that independence is not impaired. Conversely, someone who passes every numerical “bright-line” test may still be found non-independent because of another material personal, financial, professional, or business relationship. [NASDAQ Rule 5605 and IM-5605](https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/nasdaq-5600-series).

3. Mandatory disqualifications

A. Current or recent employment

A director is not independent if the director:

- is currently employed by the company; or
- was employed by the company at any time during the preceding three years.

This bar concerns the director’s own employment. [Rule 5605(a)(2)(A)](https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/nasdaq-5600-series).

B. Excess compensation from the company

A director is not independent if the director, or a Family Member, accepted more than $120,000 in compensation from the company during any period of 12 consecutive months within the three years preceding the independence determination.

Excluded from this calculation are:

- compensation for service on the board or a board committee;
- compensation paid to a Family Member who is a company employee but not an Executive Officer; and
- benefits under a tax-qualified retirement plan or other non-discretionary compensation.

The quantitative test is:

Disqualification if compensation > $120,000  
during any rolling 12-month period within the preceding three years.

Thus, exactly $120,000 does not trigger this particular bright-line prohibition, although the board must still assess whether the payment impairs independent judgment. Consulting or personal-service payments and indirect compensation can count. [Rule 5605(a)(2)(B) and IM-5605](https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/nasdaq-5600-series).

C. Family relationship with an executive officer

A director is not independent if a Family Member:

- is currently employed by the company as an Executive Officer; or
- was employed by the company as an Executive Officer at any time during the preceding three years.

A Family Member’s employment in a non-executive position is not an automatic disqualification, although it must still be considered by the board. [Rule 5605(a)(2)(C)](https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/nasdaq-5600-series).

D. Material business relationships

A director is not independent if the director or a Family Member is a partner, controlling shareholder, or Executive Officer of an organization to or from which the company made or received payments for property or services, where those payments in the current or any of the preceding three fiscal years exceeded the greater of:

- 5% of the recipient organization’s consolidated gross revenue for that year; or
- $200,000.

The threshold calculation is:

Threshold = greater of (5% × recipient’s consolidated gross revenue) or $200,000.

Examples:

- If recipient revenue is $3 million: 5% × $3 million = $150,000; the applicable threshold is therefore $200,000.
- If recipient revenue is $10 million: 5% × $10 million = $500,000; the applicable threshold is therefore $500,000.

Payments must exceed—not merely equal—the applicable threshold to create the automatic bar. Payments arising solely from investments in the company’s securities and payments under non-discretionary charitable matching programs are excluded. [Rule 5605(a)(2)(D) and IM-5605](https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/nasdaq-5600-series).

The provision focuses on the director’s or Family Member’s leadership, ownership, or partnership relationship with the recipient organization. Even below-threshold dealings must be evaluated under the board’s broader duty to determine whether independent judgment would be impaired.

E. Compensation-committee interlocks

A director is not independent if:

- the director or a Family Member is employed as an Executive Officer of another entity; and
- at any time during the preceding three years, an Executive Officer of the listed company served on that other entity’s compensation committee.

This provision prevents reciprocal executive-compensation oversight relationships. [Rule 5605(a)(2)(E)](https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/nasdaq-5600-series).

F. Relationship with the outside auditor

A director is not independent if the director or a Family Member:

- is a current partner of the company’s outside auditor; or
- was a partner or employee of the outside auditor who worked on the company’s audit at any time during the preceding three years.

[Rule 5605(a)(2)(F)](https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/nasdaq-5600-series).

G. Special rule for investment companies

For an investment company, paragraphs (A)–(F) are replaced by a different test. A director is not independent if the director is an “interested person” of the investment company under Section 2(a)(19) of the Investment Company Act of 1940, other than solely because the individual serves on the board or a board committee. [Rule 5605(a)(2)(G)](https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/nasdaq-5600-series).

4. Additional committee-specific requirements

Qualification as an Independent Director under Rule 5605(a)(2) does not automatically establish eligibility for every committee.

Audit committee

Ordinarily, the audit committee must have at least three directors, each of whom:

- meets the Rule 5605(a)(2) independence definition;
- meets the additional independence requirements of SEC Rule 10A-3(b)(1);
- has not participated in preparing the financial statements of the company or a current subsidiary during the preceding three years; and
- can read and understand fundamental financial statements.

NASDAQ expressly describes the audit-committee requirements as more stringent than the general board-independence standard. [NASDAQ corporate-governance certification form](https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/assets/Corporate%20Governance%20Certification%20Form%20Preview.pdf); [Rule 5605(c)](https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/nasdaq-5600-series).

Compensation committee

Compensation-committee members must be Independent Directors, and the board must additionally consider factors relevant to compensation independence, including the source of the director’s compensation and whether the director is affiliated with the company, a subsidiary, or an affiliate. A fee below the general $120,000 disqualification threshold can still impair compensation-committee independence under the circumstances. [NASDAQ Rule 5605(d)](https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/nasdaq-5600-series).

5. Companies required to have independent directors

General rule

Subject to the exemptions below, companies applying to list or already listed on any NASDAQ market—the Global Select Market, Global Market, or Capital Market—must comply with the Rule 5600 corporate-governance standards. [NASDAQ Listing Rules overview](https://www.nasdaqtrader.com/Content/MarketRegulation/Rulebooks/NASDAQ%20LISTING%20RULES.pdf).

For an ordinary NASDAQ-listed operating company with listed common stock or voting-equivalent equity, the principal requirements are:

- A majority of the full board must consist of Independent Directors.
- Independent Directors must hold regularly scheduled executive sessions at which only independent directors are present.
- The audit committee generally must have at least three members satisfying both NASDAQ and SEC independence standards.
- Executive compensation must be determined or recommended by an independent compensation committee.
- Director nominees generally must be selected or recommended either by a committee composed solely of Independent Directors or by a majority of the Independent Directors acting in executive session.

[Rule 5605(b)–(e)](https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/nasdaq-5600-series).

Newly listed companies—including IPOs, qualifying spin-offs, certain transfers, and companies emerging from bankruptcy—may have phase-in periods rather than being exempt permanently. For example, an IPO company may phase in its audit committee to at least one member on the listing date, at least two within 90 days, and at least three within one year, with the applicable independence requirements phased in under Rule 5615 and SEC Rule 10A-3. [SEC approval order concerning NASDAQ phase-in rules](https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/sro/nasdaq/2024/34-100816.pdf).

6. Exemptions and special categories

The answer to “which companies must have independent directors?” is qualified by Rule 5615. The principal exemptions are as follows.

A. Asset-backed and passive issuers

Asset-backed issuers and passive issuers—such as unit investment trusts organized as trusts or unincorporated associations that lack a conventional board and merely hold or administer securities, collateral, or other assets—are exempt from the majority-independent-board, audit-committee, compensation-committee, and director-nomination requirements. [Rule 5615(a)(1) and IM-5615-1](https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/Nasdaq%205600%20Series).

B. Issuers listing only non-voting preferred, debt, or derivative securities

An issuer whose only NASDAQ-listed securities are non-voting preferred securities, debt securities, or specified derivative securities is exempt from:

- the majority-independent-board requirement;
- the compensation-committee requirement; and
- independent-director oversight of nominations.

It is also exempt from NASDAQ’s audit-committee rule except to the extent SEC Rule 10A-3 applies. If the issuer also lists common stock, voting preferred stock, or an equivalent security, it becomes subject to the full Rule 5600 Series. [Rule 5615(a)(6)](https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/sro/nasdaq/2025/34-102513-ex5.pdf).

C. Controlled companies

A “Controlled Company” is one in which more than 50% of the voting power for electing directors is held by an individual, group, or another company.

A controlled company may elect exemptions from:

- the requirement that a majority of the board be independent;
- the independent compensation-committee requirements; and
- independent-director oversight of nominations.

It is not generally exempt from the independent audit-committee requirements, and it must still hold executive sessions of Independent Directors under Rule 5605(b)(2). A company relying on the controlled-company exemption must make the prescribed disclosure. [Rule 5615(a)(7), reflected in the SEC-approved rule text](https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/sro/nasdaq/2024/34-100208-ex5.pdf).

D. Foreign private issuers

A Foreign Private Issuer may generally follow its home-country corporate-governance practices instead of NASDAQ’s domestic majority-board and committee requirements if it satisfies Rule 5615’s conditions and disclosures. It must nevertheless comply with applicable audit-committee requirements, including the independence requirements derived from SEC Rule 10A-3. If it ceases to qualify as a Foreign Private Issuer, it becomes subject to the relevant domestic-company standards, subject to the applicable transition period. [Rule 5615(a)(3); SEC discussion of the rule](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/08/30/2024-19496/self-regulatory-organizations-the-nasdaq-stock-market-llc-order-granting-approval-of-a-proposed-rule).

E. Cooperatives

Qualifying cooperative associations—such as agricultural cooperatives structured under relevant state and federal tax law and without a publicly traded class of common stock—receive exemptions from certain majority-board, compensation, and nomination requirements. Applicable audit-committee obligations remain relevant. [Rule 5615(a)(2)](https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/Nasdaq%205600%20Series).

F. Limited partnerships

Limited partnerships receive exemptions from the majority-independent-board, independent compensation, and independent nominations requirements because management ordinarily resides with the general partner. Audit-committee requirements generally continue to apply through the governing structure specified by Rule 5615. [Rule 5615(a)(4)](https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/Nasdaq%205600%20Series).

G. Registered management investment companies

Management investment companies, including business development companies, are generally subject to the Rule 5600 Series but registered management investment companies receive exemptions from NASDAQ’s majority-independent-board, compensation-committee, and independent-nomination requirements because they are governed by the Investment Company Act’s separate independence regime. Their audit-committee obligations depend on Rule 5605(c), SEC Rule 10A-3, and any product-specific exemption. [Rule 5615(a)(5)](https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/sro/nasdaq/2019/34-86072-ex5.pdf).

7. Bottom line

An ordinary domestic operating company listing common or voting equity on NASDAQ must have a majority-independent board and independent audit, compensation, and nominating oversight. A director counts as independent only when:

- none of NASDAQ’s employment, compensation, family, business-payment, interlock, or auditor disqualifications applies; and
- the board affirmatively determines that no other relationship would interfere with independent judgment.

Special issuers—particularly controlled companies, foreign private issuers, passive or asset-backed issuers, limited partnerships, cooperatives, investment companies, and issuers listing only debt, non-voting preferred, or derivative securities—may receive partial or complete exemptions. Controlled companies and most other special categories may still need an independent audit committee because SEC Rule 10A-3 operates independently of NASDAQ’s majority-board exemption.

final.content:
CELLULAR SENESCENCE IN AGING: MECHANISTIC CONTROVERSY, HETEROGENEITY, AND TRANSLATIONAL EVIDENCE

Executive assessment

The DNA-damage, mitochondrial, and chromatin-remodeling models are best understood as interacting layers of a temporally evolving senescence program, not as mutually exclusive explanations.

• d’Adda di Fagagna et al. established that dysfunctional telomeres are recognized as persistent DNA lesions, activating checkpoint signaling that initiates and helps maintain proliferative arrest.

• Passos et al. showed that DNA damage can become self-sustaining through a delayed p21–mitochondrial dysfunction–reactive oxygen species (ROS) feedback loop. This makes mitochondrial dysfunction an amplifier and stabilizer of senescence rather than necessarily its original cause.

• Narita et al. explained how arrest becomes resistant to mitogenic reversal: p16–RB signaling and HMGA-dependent senescence-associated heterochromatin foci (SAHF) repress proliferation-associated genes.

Single-cell studies now show that these mechanisms are deployed unevenly across cell types, initiating stresses, tissues, and time. There is no universal transcriptomic “senescent cell,” no marker—including p16INK4a—that is both fully sensitive and specific, and no invariant SASP. The strongest causal evidence that senescent cells promote pathology remains genetic clearance and transplantation/intervention experiments in mice. Human dasatinib-plus-quercetin (D+Q) trials demonstrate feasible senolytic target engagement, but clinical efficacy remains preliminary and heterogeneous.

The apparent paradox—senescence suppresses tumors but contributes to aging—is principally temporal and contextual. Acute, efficiently cleared senescence arrests damaged cells, promotes immune surveillance, and can assist repair. Chronic persistence, especially when immune clearance declines, depletes regenerative capacity and remodels neighboring tissue through inflammatory, fibrotic, and matrix-degrading signals. Baker et al.’s 2011 experiments support this distinction: prevention of p16-high-cell accumulation delayed pathology, while clearance initiated after pathology had developed slowed its subsequent progression. They did not show that senescence is uniformly harmful or that all senescent states should be eliminated.

1. Three mechanistic frameworks

1.1 Persistent DNA-damage response

d’Adda di Fagagna et al. examined replicatively senescent human fibroblasts and found hallmarks of a double-strand-break response: phosphorylated H2AX foci, recruitment of 53BP1, MDC1 and NBS1, activation of CHK1 and CHK2, and direct association of damage-response proteins with uncapped telomeres. Inhibiting checkpoint kinases restored entry into S phase, supporting the interpretation that telomere-initiated senescence is an actively maintained checkpoint rather than passive cellular exhaustion (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature02118).

The model can be summarized as:

telomere uncapping or other persistent lesion
→ ATM/ATR-associated damage signaling
→ p53–p21 and, depending on context, p16–RB activation
→ cell-cycle arrest.

Its principal strengths are mechanistic proximity to a well-defined initiating lesion and direct experimental reversibility of checkpoint-dependent arrest. It readily explains tumor suppression: cells at risk of breakage–fusion–bridge cycles and genomic instability are prevented from proliferating.

Its limitations are equally important. Not all senescence is initiated by telomere attrition, not every senescent cell has the same persistent DNA-damage signature, and a checkpoint alone does not fully explain why arrest becomes “deep,” why the SASP develops after a delay, or why phenotypes remain stable despite changing upstream signals. Furthermore, disabling the checkpoint can restore proliferation without repairing the lesion, potentially converting a degenerative phenotype into genomic instability and cancer.

Telomerase-deficient mice support both sides of this interpretation. Successive generations of mTR/Terc-null mice progressively shorten their initially long murine telomeres. Late-generation animals show shortened lifespan, impaired wound healing and hematopoietic stress responses, infertility and proliferative-organ defects, but not a complete replica of normal aging; spontaneous malignancies can also increase as genomic instability accumulates (https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674(00)80580-2). Thus telomere-induced DDR is sufficient to compromise tissue reserve but is neither synonymous with all organismal aging nor unconditionally tumor suppressive.

1.2 Mitochondrial dysfunction and ROS feedback

Passos et al. did not simply replace the DDR model with a mitochondrial one. Their experiments and modeling connected the two. A DNA-damage or telomere signal induced sustained p21, followed over several days by signaling through GADD45–p38 MAPK–GRB2–TGFBR2–TGF-β. This caused mitochondrial dysfunction and increased ROS. ROS then generated or replenished short-lived DNA-damage foci, maintaining checkpoint signaling and locking cells into “deep” senescence (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1038/msb.2010.5).

The proposed loop is:

initial DDR
→ p53/p21
→ GADD45–p38–TGF-β signaling
→ mitochondrial dysfunction and ROS
→ renewed DNA lesions
→ persistent DDR.

This framework supplies a temporal mechanism missing from the simpler lesion–checkpoint model. Initiation may occur rapidly, whereas mitochondrial reinforcement appears after a delay. It also explains how modest initiating damage can become self-maintaining and why antioxidant or mitochondrial interventions may affect established arrest differently from early checkpoint activation.

For tumor suppression, the loop stabilizes withdrawal from the cell cycle and makes damaged cells difficult to reactivate. For age-related pathology, the same persistent metabolic and oxidative state can damage neighboring structures, maintain inflammatory signaling, and resist physiological resolution.

The qualification is that ROS are context-dependent and difficult to interpret solely as upstream causes. In Passos et al., mitochondrial dysfunction largely followed p21 activation. ROS can therefore be both consequence and cause—a positive-feedback component—not proof that mitochondrial failure is the universal initiating event. Mitochondrial dysfunction-associated senescence can also have a secretory program distinct from canonical inflammatory SASP, further weakening any universal mitochondrial or SASP definition.

1.3 Chromatin remodeling and stable gene repression

Narita et al. focused on the stability of arrest. They found that HMGA1 and HMGA2 accumulate on senescent-cell chromatin and are structural components of SAHF. HMGA proteins cooperate with p16INK4a and RB to repress E2F-regulated proliferation genes. Removing this chromatin support weakened senescence, while co-expression of HDM2 and CDK4 counteracted the antiproliferative effect (https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674%2806%2900913-5).

The framework is:

stress/checkpoint activation
→ p16–CDK4/6–RB engagement
→ HMGA-dependent chromatin reorganization and SAHF
→ stable silencing of E2F/cell-cycle genes.

This is a compelling explanation for durable tumor suppression: mitogenic growth factors cannot easily reactivate a cell whose proliferation program has been heterochromatically insulated. It also explains why senescence can persist after an initiating signal fluctuates.

In aging, however, durable chromatin locking has a cost. Stem and progenitor cells can remain unavailable for regeneration, while altered chromatin can support inflammatory or fibrotic transcriptional programs. The framework therefore separates two features often conflated as “senescence”: stable cell-cycle repression and the active secretory phenotype.

SAHF are not universal. Their occurrence depends on species, cell type and trigger, and senescent cells can maintain arrest without morphologically obvious SAHF. Chromatin remodeling is consequently one stabilization route rather than a required diagnostic criterion.

1.4 Integrated interpretation

The three models address different mechanistic questions:

• DDR: What detects the initiating lesion and begins arrest?

• Mitochondrial feedback: How can initially limited damage become self-maintaining over time?

• Chromatin remodeling: How is proliferative competence durably repressed?

A plausible integrated trajectory is:

damage or oncogenic stress
→ DDR and p53–p21 activation
→ early arrest
→ p16–RB and chromatin stabilization
plus delayed mitochondrial ROS feedback
→ persistent damage signaling, metabolic remodeling and context-specific SASP.

The ordering varies. Oncogene-induced, mitochondrial, developmental, therapy-induced and replicative senescence need not pass through every stage. This variability is now directly supported by single-cell data.

2. Single-cell evidence: senescence is a family of states

Earlier bulk analyses already found that fibroblast strain and tissue of origin explained substantial transcriptomic variation. Hernandez-Segura et al. integrated seven datasets covering six human fibroblast strains, three triggers—replicative, oncogene-induced and ionizing-radiation-induced senescence—and five laboratories. They identified stress-specific as well as shared programs and showed that the phenotype changes with time after induction (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28844647/).

Subsequent single-cell RNA sequencing sharpened this conclusion. Single-cell analysis of human diploid fibroblasts identified subpopulations enriched for arrest, survival or secretory programs. During etoposide-induced senescence, cells diverged into at least two trajectories: one expressed conventional markers such as CDKN2A/p16, whereas another was characterized by long noncoding RNAs and altered splicing. The cell’s proliferative state when injury occurred influenced which trajectory it followed (https://exa.ai/library/publication/62b7zf4p6st).

In vivo muscle studies are particularly informative because they couple molecular classification to function. Single-cell transcriptomics after muscle injury identified senescent fibro-adipogenic progenitors, myogenic cells and other cell types in young and old mice. Cell identity remained detectable, while inflammatory and fibrotic programs were shared across several senescent populations. Transplanting senescent cells delayed regeneration; reducing their abundance or neutralizing the inflammatory secretome through CD36 accelerated regeneration (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-05535-x; accessible manuscript: https://orbilu.uni.lu/bitstream/10993/53341/1/s41586-022-05535-x.pdf).

A broader 2025 analysis assembled 72 mouse and 64 human weighted single-cell signatures—136 signatures in total—and found that cell-type-specific signatures represented in-vivo senescence better than signatures extrapolated from cultured cells (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-57047-7). The quantitative implication is not that there are exactly 136 biological forms of senescence, but that a single unweighted signature is inadequate across species and tissues.

These observations modify all three classical frameworks:

• Persistent DDR is common but not universal at the transcript level.

• Mitochondrial and oxidative programs vary among subpopulations and over time.

• p16/chromatin-dependent stabilization can characterize one trajectory while p21- or other arrest programs dominate another.

They also expose an important measurement problem. CDKN2A RNA is sparse in single-cell datasets, and some p16-high cells—certain macrophages, endothelial cells or pancreatic β cells, for example—need not satisfy functional criteria for senescence. Conversely, some demonstrably senescent cells have little p16. Neither p16, p21, SA-β-gal, DNA-damage foci nor a SASP transcript alone is sufficient; multimarker evidence plus functional arrest is preferable.

3. Mouse genetics and the lifespan comparison

3.1 Why p16 knockout and telomerase deficiency are not mirror-image lifespan tests

A superficial comparison might predict that deleting p16 should prevent senescence and lengthen life, whereas eliminating telomerase should accelerate senescence and shorten life. Mouse genetics does not support this simple one-dimensional model.

Specific p16INK4a-null mice retain p19Arf but have increased immortalization and, in some strains, increased spontaneous or carcinogen-induced cancer, establishing a tumor-suppressive role for p16 (https://www.nature.com/articles/35092592). Another independently generated p16-specific mutant showed no significant increase in spontaneous tumors during the first 17 months, illustrating substantial allele- and background-dependence (https://www.nature.com/articles/35092584). Consequently, there is no robust general finding that constitutive p16 deletion extends normal lifespan. Any improved regenerative capacity is offset by loss of tumor restraint.

A frequently quoted short-survival result involves deletion of the entire Ink4a/Arf locus rather than p16 alone. In that model, 69% of 13 untreated null mice developed tumors by an average age of 29 weeks during 36 weeks of observation (https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674(00)81079-X). Because this removes both p16INK4a and p19Arf, it cannot be treated as a p16-specific lifespan estimate.

Telomerase-null mice present the opposite but equally complicated situation. Early generations can appear relatively normal because laboratory mice begin with very long telomeres. Late generations develop critical shortening, genomic instability, reduced stress tolerance and shortened survival. Thus their phenotype depends on breeding generation and inherited telomere reserve, not merely chronological age (https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674(00)80580-2).

No defensible common “percentage lifespan difference” can be calculated from these studies: they use different genetic backgrounds, alleles, generations and endpoints, and some report tumor-free survival rather than all-cause lifespan. The valid comparative conclusion is qualitative:

• p16 loss can preserve proliferation but raises cancer risk.

• critical telomere shortening activates p53/p21- and sometimes p16-associated checkpoints, reducing regenerative reserve and shortening survival.

• bypassing telomere checkpoints can transiently rescue tissue proliferation but increases chromosomal instability and carcinogenesis.

This trade-off is demonstrated directly by telomere–checkpoint interactions. p53 deletion attenuates some early degenerative effects of telomere dysfunction but cooperates with dysfunctional telomeres to accelerate transformation (https://www.cell.com/fulltext/S0092-8674(00)80762-X). Conversely, in Pot1b-deficient mice with dysfunctional telomeres, p16 deletion increased telomere loss, fusions, ATR-dependent signaling, p53 stabilization and organ impairment rather than rescuing aging phenotypes (https://jci.org/articles/view/69574).

These results favor an integrated model: checkpoints and chromatin arrest are protective at the cellular and oncological level, but excessive or persistent engagement sacrifices tissue regeneration. Telomere damage supplies the lesion; mitochondrial feedback can amplify it; p16–RB/chromatin mechanisms prevent risky re-entry.

4. The temporal question from Baker et al.

Baker et al. engineered INK-ATTAC mice, in which drug-induced dimerization activates apoptosis preferentially in p16INK4a-expressing cells. On a BubR1 progeroid background, lifelong clearance delayed cataract, adipose and skeletal-muscle abnormalities. Crucially, beginning clearance later—after age-associated disorders were already established—attenuated their subsequent progression (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature10600).

This design separates two temporal claims:

1. Initiation/onset: preventing accumulation delays when some pathologies emerge.

2. Maintenance/progression: removing accumulated p16-high cells later can slow worsening even after pathology exists.

The experiment therefore argues against senescence being merely a passive historical scar. At least some continuously present p16-high cells causally maintain tissue dysfunction.

It does not establish that:

• senescent cells initiate every aging phenotype;

• every p16-expressing cell is senescent;

• clearance fully reverses established structural damage;

• benefits in a BubR1 progeroid mouse quantitatively predict normal human aging; or

• continuous clearance is superior to temporally restricted treatment.

The temporal synthesis is that acute senescence can be adaptive if damaged cells arrest, secrete repair or immune-recruiting signals, and are then removed. Pathology arises when production exceeds immune clearance and the state becomes chronic. Lifelong clearance prevents accumulation, whereas late clearance removes an ongoing pathological input but cannot necessarily reconstruct lost tissue.

This also suggests why intermittent senolytic dosing may be preferable to permanent pathway inhibition. Blocking p16 or DDR continuously weakens tumor suppression in every at-risk cell; periodically killing selected persistent senescent cells may preserve initial arrest while limiting late-life accumulation. Current senolytics are not selective enough to guarantee that ideal separation.

5. Human evidence from dasatinib plus quercetin

D+Q is intended to transiently disable senescent-cell anti-apoptotic networks rather than prevent senescence induction. Human trials provide evidence of pharmacological activity but not yet proof of increased lifespan or broad clinical rejuvenation.

5.1 Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

The first open-label IPF pilot enrolled 14 participants receiving dasatinib 100 mg/day plus quercetin 1,250 mg/day for three consecutive days per week over three weeks. Retention was 100%, assessments were completed in 13 of 14 participants, and six-minute walk, gait speed and chair-rise measures improved, while pulmonary function and laboratory indices did not. One serious adverse event occurred, and circulating SASP results were inconclusive (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30616998/).

Because there was no placebo group, practice effects, regression to the mean and selection effects cannot be excluded.

A subsequent randomized pilot assigned 12 IPF participants 1:1 to D+Q or placebo. All 108 scheduled doses and all 60 planned assessments were completed. The D+Q group reported 65 non-serious adverse events versus 22 with placebo:

65 / 22 = 2.95,

or approximately three times as many reported events, although no serious event was judged treatment-related. With only six people per arm, event counts are clustered within individuals and should not be interpreted as a precise threefold risk. Functional and pulmonary outcomes did not differ meaningfully, but the study was explicitly underpowered for efficacy (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/ebiom/article/PIIS2352-3964%2823%2900046-4/fulltext).

5.2 Diabetic kidney disease: biological target engagement

Nine adults with diabetic kidney disease received dasatinib 100 mg plus quercetin 1,000 mg daily for three days. Eleven days later, adipose-tissue p16- and p21-positive cells, SA-β-gal-positive cells, poorly replicating adipocyte progenitors, macrophages and crown-like structures were reduced. Epidermal p16/p21 markers and circulating IL-1α, IL-6, MMP-9 and MMP-12 also fell (https://www.thelancet.com/article/S2352-3964(19)30591-2/fulltext).

This is important proof of target engagement in humans: a short exposure was followed by concordant reductions in several senescence-related measures. It remains an uncontrolled n=9 study and did not establish that the SASP reductions mediated improved kidney function.

5.3 Randomized skeletal-aging trial

A phase 2 randomized study enrolled 60 postmenopausal women. At 20 weeks, the primary bone-resorption endpoint, C-terminal telopeptide, changed by −4.1% with D+Q versus −7.7% in controls. The between-group contrast was:

−4.1% − (−7.7%) = +3.6 percentage points,

which was not beneficial or statistically significant (P=0.611). P1NP, a formation marker, was 16% higher relative to control at weeks 2 and 4 (P=0.020 and 0.024) but not at week 20 (−9%, P=0.149).

Exploratory analysis of women in the highest baseline tertile of T-cell p16 expression found a 34% increase in P1NP, an 11% reduction in resorption at two weeks, and a 2.7% increase in radius bone-mineral density at 20 weeks. These subgroup findings are hypothesis-generating because stratification reduces sample size and increases multiplicity risk. No serious adverse events occurred (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-024-03096-2).

5.4 Cognitive pilot

A 12-person, single-arm study in older adults with mild cognitive impairment and slow gait used six intermittent D+Q cycles. Mean Montreal Cognitive Assessment change was +1.0 point, with a 95% confidence interval of −0.7 to +2.7, so the overall result was not statistically distinguishable from no change. TNF-α changed by −3.0% with a 95% confidence interval of −13.0% to +7.1%. The correlation between TNF-α reduction and cognitive improvement was r=−0.65, P=0.02, but in a small uncontrolled sample correlation cannot establish mediation (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/ebiom/article/PIIS2352-3964(25)00056-8/fulltext).

Overall, human D+Q evidence supports short-term feasibility and some biomarker effects. It does not yet establish disease modification, extension of healthspan, or that killing senescent cells is responsible for every observed change. Dasatinib and quercetin have non-senolytic kinase, immune and metabolic effects, while marker reductions may reflect altered expression or tissue composition as well as cell elimination.

6. Are SASP factors causative or correlative?

6.1 Evidence for causality

Several lines of evidence go beyond correlation:

• SASP components such as IL-6 and IL-8 can reinforce arrest through autocrine signaling, while NF-κB regulates much of the inflammatory secretome. In a lymphoma model, suppressing NF-κB impaired immune recognition, permitted senescence bypass and reduced chemotherapy benefit, demonstrating that secretory signaling can support tumor suppression as well as pathology (https://genesdev.cshlp.org/content/25/20/2125.full).

• In muscle, transplantation of senescent cells delayed regeneration, while reducing senescent-cell burden or neutralizing a CD36-linked inflammatory secretome improved regeneration. That combination of gain- and loss-of-function evidence is stronger than transcriptomic association alone (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-05535-x).

• Baker’s clearance experiment shows that cells bearing a p16-associated senescent phenotype contribute causally to pathology, although it does not isolate secretion from loss of regenerative cells, ROS, immune interactions or other mechanisms.

• The diabetic-kidney D+Q trial found parallel reductions in senescence markers, tissue macrophages and circulating SASP factors, consistent with—but not proving—a senescent-cell-to-inflammation pathway.

6.2 Evidence against a universal “SASP causes aging” formulation

“SASP” is an umbrella term, not a single molecular entity. Its components can be inflammatory, fibrotic, matrix-remodeling, angiogenic, growth-promoting or immunostimulatory. Some reinforce arrest and recruit immune clearance; others promote regeneration or, when chronic, paracrine senescence and tumor progression. A factor can be beneficial early and harmful later.

Single-cell studies show that secretory modules are not obligatorily coupled to p16 or p21 expression. Different senescent populations express different cytokines, and some non-senescent immune or stromal cells produce the same molecules. Consequently, elevated IL-6, TNF-α or an aggregate SASP score may be a marker of tissue inflammation rather than evidence that senescent cells are its source.

Even senolytic studies cannot cleanly distinguish mechanisms: eliminating a cell simultaneously removes its SASP, ROS production, matrix interactions and occupation of a regenerative niche. A beneficial outcome after clearance therefore establishes causality for the targeted cell population more securely than causality for any particular SASP component.

6.3 What recent spatial transcriptomics adds

Spatial transcriptomics addresses a key weakness of dissociative single-cell RNA sequencing: it preserves anatomical neighborhood information.

A 2024 multi-organ spatial atlas of nine tissues from aging male mice identified “senescence-sensitive spots” that co-localized with increased disorganization or tissue entropy and with aggregates of immunoglobulin-expressing cells. IgG accumulated across aged male and female mouse tissues and was also observed in human tissues. Experimental IgG exposure induced pro-senescent states in macrophages and microglia, while reducing IgG mitigated aging phenotypes in male mice (https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674(24)01201-7).

These data imply bidirectional causation rather than a one-way SASP model. Senescent neighborhoods may recruit or alter immune cells, but immune products such as IgG can also drive senescence and tissue dysfunction. Spatial co-localization itself remains correlational; the perturbation experiments supply the causal component.

The scDOT framework integrates lung spatial transcriptomics with single-cell RNA sequencing to infer locations of rare senescent cells, their neighbors and candidate intercellular interactions (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13059-024-03426-0). Such analyses support spatially restricted paracrine signaling, but inferred ligand–receptor communication is not equivalent to demonstrated molecular causation. Current spatial platforms also often contain multiple cells per spot, creating deconvolution uncertainty.

The present consensus is therefore conditional:

• Chronic senescent-cell secretory signaling is causative in some tissues and experimental contexts.

• No universal SASP factor or fixed panel has been shown to be the primary cause of all senescence-associated dysfunction.

• In many human datasets, SASP measurements remain correlative because source cells, timing and exposure are unresolved.

• Spatial transcriptomics strengthens evidence for local senescent niches and reciprocal cell interactions, but intervention or lineage-specific perturbation remains necessary to identify causal factors.

7. Resolving the tumor-suppression/aging paradox

The three frameworks explain complementary aspects of antagonistic pleiotropy.

DDR framework:
• Benefit: arrests telomere-dysfunctional or genotoxically injured cells before mutation propagation.
• Cost: persistent checkpoint signaling removes stem and progenitor cells from productive tissue renewal.
• Failure mode: checkpoint bypass restores proliferation but permits unstable genomes.

Mitochondrial-feedback framework:
• Benefit: converts a potentially reversible early arrest into a robust barrier against malignant re-entry.
• Cost: ROS and metabolic dysfunction maintain damage and inflammatory signaling after the initiating insult.
• Failure mode: chronic feedback spreads dysfunction; indiscriminate antioxidant intervention might also weaken protective arrest or signaling.

Chromatin framework:
• Benefit: stable repression of E2F and other proliferation genes resists oncogenic stimulation.
• Cost: durable epigenetic locking limits regeneration and can coexist with active inflammatory/fibrotic transcription.
• Failure mode: disrupting chromatin arrest may release cells that still contain oncogenic lesions.

SASP:
• Benefit: reinforces arrest, recruits immune surveillance and can coordinate wound repair.
• Cost: if clearance fails, prolonged cytokine, chemokine, protease and matrix signaling creates paracrine senescence, fibrosis and stem-cell inhibition.
• Failure mode: broad SASP suppression can reduce pathology but may also blunt immune clearance or chemotherapy-induced tumor suppression.

The decisive variable is therefore not simply whether senescence occurs, but its timing, cellular identity, persistence, anatomical location and mode of resolution.

Conclusion

The original mechanistic controversy has evolved from competition among single-cause models into a systems-level model of heterogeneous cell states. Telomere or genomic damage can initiate checkpoint arrest; delayed p21-dependent mitochondrial ROS can stabilize and perpetuate it; p16–RB/HMGA chromatin remodeling can make proliferative repression durable. Different senescent cells use these modules to different degrees.

Mouse genetics rejects the idea that simply preventing senescence should extend life. Constitutive p16 loss trades regenerative potential for cancer susceptibility, whereas late-generation telomerase deficiency compromises tissue reserve while also generating genomic instability. Baker et al. provided stronger support for a temporally selective strategy: permit acute tumor-suppressive arrest, but remove selected cells when they persist and become pathological.

Human D+Q studies have crossed the threshold from purely preclinical theory to measurable target engagement, but not to proven geroprotection. The largest cited randomized trial, involving 60 women, missed its primary endpoint, while exploratory benefit was concentrated in participants with high baseline p16 burden. This is consistent with single-cell evidence that treatment response should depend on senescent-cell subtype and burden.

Finally, SASP factors are neither merely incidental biomarkers nor a universal master cause. Specific secretory pathways can be causative, but their effects change with cell type, tissue and time. Recent spatial data reveal senescence as a property of multicellular neighborhoods involving reciprocal stromal, immune and senescent-cell signaling. The most defensible current position is that chronic, spatially organized senescent niches are causal contributors to selected age-related pathologies, while the responsible cells and mediators must be identified—and therapeutically targeted—on a tissue- and stage-specific basis.
