final.content:
# FutureMeds company profile and private-equity assessment

**Information cut-off: 17 November 2025. Currency: GBP unless stated otherwise.**

## 1. Executive assessment

FutureMeds is a fast-growing, founder-led European site-management organisation (“SMO”) that recruits patients and executes clinical trials for pharmaceutical, biotechnology and contract research organisation (“CRO”) customers. Founded in 2019/2020, it had expanded to approximately **27–28 clinical sites across seven European countries** by July 2025, alongside decentralised/hybrid trial capabilities available in **18 countries** (https://fairmountpress.wordpress.com/2025/07/29/futuremeds/; https://www.uk-acc.bdo.global/en-gb/deals/bdo-has-provided-buy-side-cdd-on-the-acquisition-of-futuremeds-by-phoenix-equity-partners).

The latest public statutory accounts available by the cut-off date were for the year ended **31 December 2024**. They show:

- Revenue of **£26.97m**, up **73.1%** from £15.58m in 2023.
- Gross profit of **£11.44m**, a **42.4% gross margin**.
- Reported operating profit of **£3.35m**, a **12.4% operating margin**.
- Estimated statutory EBITDA of approximately **£5.16m**, a **19.1% EBITDA margin**.
- Cash of approximately **£2.64m** and net assets of **£5.87m**.
- Profit before tax of approximately **£1.79m**, but with **£1.58m of interest expense**, indicating meaningful leverage or other interest-bearing obligations.

The company is therefore profitable rather than an early-stage cash-burn business, but its modest cash balance, substantial interest burden and acquisition-led growth require careful scrutiny of net debt, working capital, deferred consideration and post-deal financing.

FutureMeds has already completed a PE transition: HGL Private Capital/Dealspan invested in 2021 and again in 2023, then exited to **Phoenix Equity Partners in July 2025**. HGL subsequently reported a **10.0x money multiple** on its original investment, although the purchase price, enterprise value and valuation multiple were not disclosed (https://scottishbusinessnews.net/private-equity-specialist-hgl-private-capital-announces-successful-exit-from-futuremeds/).

**Overall PE view:** attractive growth-platform characteristics—high organic/M&A growth, positive EBITDA, fragmented addressable market, pan-European footprint and DCT capability—but likely priced accordingly in the 2025 Phoenix transaction. The central underwriting questions are sustainable same-site growth, revenue concentration, quality of EBITDA and leverage after the acquisition.

---

## 2. Company overview

### Business model

FutureMeds provides:

- Patient identification, recruitment and retention.
- Clinical-trial execution through dedicated research sites.
- Site-management services for sponsors and CROs.
- Hybrid and decentralised clinical-trial (“DCT”) services, including home-based trial delivery.
- Access to investigators, healthcare providers and patient communities across Europe.

The company serves major global pharma sponsors and CROs across Phase I–IV trials and multiple therapeutic areas. Its website reported that its investigators had completed more than **2,320 clinical trials**, while its DCT solution had delivered **320+ projects across 120+ indications since 2012** (https://www.futuremeds.com/).

### Footprint and scale

Public descriptions differ slightly depending on timing:

- **27 sites in seven countries** and DCT/hybrid solutions in 18 countries were reported by Fairmount in July 2025 (https://fairmountpress.wordpress.com/2025/07/29/futuremeds/).
- BDO and transaction advisers described **28 clinical sites in seven countries** at the time of the Phoenix transaction (https://www.uk-acc.bdo.global/en-gb/deals/bdo-has-provided-buy-side-cdd-on-the-acquisition-of-futuremeds-by-phoenix-equity-partners; https://www.addleshawgoddard.com/en/news/2025/ag-advises-phoenix-equity-partners-strategic-investment-futuremeds/).
- The company website subsequently displayed **29 strategically located dedicated research sites**, likely including announced or newly commissioned sites (https://www.futuremeds.com/).

Countries identified publicly include Poland, Germany, Spain, Bulgaria, Romania, Ukraine and the UK. The UK operation includes personnel in Birmingham, Glasgow, Liverpool, London, Newcastle and Teesside (https://hglcapital.co.uk/portfolio/futuremeds/).

FutureMeds announced two Romanian sites in Brasov and Galati, expected to become operational in **Q4 2025–Q1 2026**, with oncology, haematology, CNS and metabolic-disease capabilities. Because these sites were not yet fully operational at the cut-off date, the resulting revenue and utilisation should not be assumed in historical performance (https://www.futuremeds.com/post/futuremeds-expands-to-romania-establishing-dedicated-research-sites-in-brasov-and-galati).

### Ownership and management

FutureMeds was founded by:

- Dr Radoslaw Janiak, CEO.
- Marcin Gondek, CFO.
- Paul Chambers, Chair.

The founders remained in leadership following Phoenix’s July 2025 investment (https://fairmountpress.wordpress.com/2025/07/29/futuremeds/).

Companies House records show **Renifer Bidco Limited** becoming a person with significant control on 23 July 2025, consistent with the Phoenix-backed acquisition structure (https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/12521988/filing-history).

---

## 3. Historical financial performance

The following figures come from FutureMeds Ltd’s filed consolidated accounts, as reproduced by company-data services, with the 2024 filing identifiable at Companies House (https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/12521988/filing-history; https://pomanda.com/company/12521988/Futuremeds-Ltd).

### Income statement and margins

| £m except margins | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Revenue | 7.210 | 15.580 | 26.967 |
| Cost of sales | 4.464 | 8.677 | 15.523 |
| Gross profit | 2.746 | 6.903 | 11.443 |
| Gross margin | 38.1% | 44.3% | 42.4% |
| Operating profit/(loss) | (0.122) | 1.952 | 3.347 |
| Operating margin | (1.7%) | 12.5% | 12.4% |
| Depreciation | 0.172 | 1.047 | 1.537 |
| Amortisation | 0.500 | 0.102 | 0.275 |
| Estimated EBITDA | 0.550 | 3.101 | 5.159 |
| Estimated EBITDA margin | 7.6% | 19.9% | 19.1% |
| Interest expense | 0.419 | 0.650 | 1.583 |
| Interest income | 0.080 | 0.024 | 0.026 |
| Profit/(loss) before tax, calculated | (0.461) | 1.326 | 1.790 |

Source figures: https://pomanda.com/company/12521988/Futuremeds-Ltd.  
2024 profit before tax is independently reported as approximately **£1.79m** in the filed-account summary (https://theaccounts.uk/company/12521988/futuremeds-ltd/).

### Explicit calculations

**Revenue growth**

- 2023 growth:  
  \[
  (£15.580m / £7.210m)-1 = 116.1\%
  \]

- 2024 growth:  
  \[
  (£26.967m / £15.580m)-1 = 73.1\%
  \]

- Two-year 2022–2024 CAGR:  
  \[
  (£26.967m / £7.210m)^{1/2}-1 = 93.4\%
  \]

FutureMeds’ Sunday Times ranking reported **96.73% annual sales growth over three years**, placing it **44th** among Britain’s fastest-growing private companies; the small difference from the calculation above likely reflects the ranking’s precise measurement period or underlying data definition (https://www.futuremeds.com/post/futuremeds-named-as-one-of-britain-s-fastest-growing-private-businesses-on-the-sunday-times-100).

**Gross margin**

- 2024:  
  \[
  £11.443m / £26.967m = 42.4\%
  \]

- 2023:  
  \[
  £6.903m / £15.580m = 44.3\%
  \]

- 2022:  
  \[
  £2.746m / £7.210m = 38.1\%
  \]

Gross margin declined about **1.9 percentage points** in 2024 after a large improvement in 2023. Possible causes include site mix, start-up costs, acquisitions and staff investment, but the public accounts do not provide enough segment detail to isolate them.

**EBITDA estimate**

No publicly disclosed management-defined “adjusted EBITDA” was found. Statutory EBITDA can be estimated as operating profit plus depreciation and amortisation:

- 2024:  
  \[
  £3.347m + £1.537m + £0.275m = £5.159m
  \]

- 2023:  
  \[
  £1.952m + £1.047m + £0.102m = £3.101m
  \]

- 2022:  
  \[
  -£0.122m + £0.172m + £0.500m = £0.550m
  \]

These are **unadjusted statutory estimates**, not sponsor-reported adjusted EBITDA. Acquisition costs, site-opening expenses, share-based payments or exceptional items could make a PE-adjusted figure materially different.

### Profitability assessment

Revenue increased by £11.39m in 2024 while EBITDA increased by approximately £2.06m, implying incremental EBITDA conversion of:

\[
£2.058m / £11.387m = 18.1\%
\]

This is healthy but not obviously demonstrating rapid margin expansion. EBITDA margin fell slightly from 19.9% to 19.1%, suggesting that the company was reinvesting in personnel, new sites and integration while growing.

---

## 4. Cash flow, liquidity and burn rate

### Cash position

FutureMeds had approximately:

- **£1.01m cash at 31 December 2022**.
- **£2.64m cash at 31 December 2024**.
- Historical cash balances of **£0.60m in 2020** and **£2.75m in 2021** are also shown in filed-account summaries (https://theaccounts.uk/company/12521988/futuremeds-ltd/).

A reliable 2023 year-end cash figure was not identifiable in the gathered public information.

### Cash flow and burn

The detailed public evidence reviewed does not expose a sufficiently clear complete cash-flow statement to quote audited operating, investing and financing cash flows with confidence. Consequently:

- A precise free-cash-flow figure cannot be stated.
- A monthly burn rate cannot be calculated responsibly.
- The business should not be characterised as a conventional loss-making “cash burner,” because it generated positive operating profit, EBITDA and pre-tax profit in 2023 and 2024.
- Nevertheless, acquisition spending, new-site capex, working-capital movements and debt service could consume considerable cash despite positive EBITDA.

The cash balance of £2.64m represented only:

\[
£2.636m / £26.967m = 9.8\%
\]

of annual revenue, or about **1.2 months of revenue**, so liquidity was not excessive relative to operating scale.

### Working-capital observations

Reported debtor balances increased from approximately **£2.49m in 2022 to £2.68m in 2023 and £4.61m in 2024** (https://pomanda.com/company/12521988/Futuremeds-Ltd). Indicative receivable days for 2024 were:

\[
£4.606m / £26.967m \times 365 = 62.3\text{ days}
\]

This is only an approximation because the disclosed debtor balance may contain non-trade items and should ideally be measured using average trade receivables. It nevertheless points to working-capital intensity: sponsors and CROs may pay after milestones, patient visits or data delivery, while sites must fund staff and facilities continuously.

---

## 5. Debt and capital structure

### Known leverage indicators

The exact 2024 gross debt and net debt were not available in the public evidence gathered. However:

- Interest expense rose from **£0.42m in 2022** to **£0.65m in 2023** and **£1.58m in 2024** (https://pomanda.com/company/12521988/Futuremeds-Ltd).
- 2024 EBITDA interest coverage was approximately:

\[
£5.159m / £1.583m = 3.26x
\]

- 2024 EBIT interest coverage was:

\[
£3.347m / £1.583m = 2.11x
\]

These ratios are serviceable but not conservative for a business exposed to clinical-trial timing and site utilisation.

If, purely illustratively, the £1.58m interest expense reflected an 8%–12% all-in cost of debt, average interest-bearing obligations might be roughly **£13m–£20m**:

\[
£1.583m / 12\% = £13.2m
\]

\[
£1.583m / 8\% = £19.8m
\]

This is **not a reported debt figure**; interest could also include leases, deferred acquisition consideration or shareholder instruments, so the estimate should not be used without diligence.

### Post-Phoenix refinancing

Companies House records show that FutureMeds’ previous charge was satisfied on **31 October 2025**, followed by four new charges created on **3–4 November 2025** (https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/12521988/filing-history). That pattern is consistent with acquisition financing or a post-closing refinancing, but the gathered evidence does not disclose facility size, pricing, covenants or lender exposure.

**PE diligence priority:** obtain the closing funds-flow statement, debt schedule, covenant model, lease liabilities, deferred acquisition consideration and any shareholder loan instruments. The 2024 interest burden and November 2025 security package make leverage one of the most important underwriting issues.

---

## 6. Funding rounds, ownership transactions and valuations

| Date | Investor/event | Publicly known details |
|---|---|---|
| 2020 | Formation/early funding | FutureMeds Ltd incorporated in March 2020; funding amount and valuation not publicly disclosed. |
| September 2021 | Dealspan/HGL investment and refinancing | Dealspan made a strategic investment underpinning a refinancing to support European expansion and growth from six sites toward 12 sites. Amount and valuation were undisclosed (https://www.futuremeds.com/post/dealspan-makes-strategic-investment-in-futuremeds). |
| 2023 | HGL follow-on funding | HGL provided additional capital for management liquidity and further buy-and-build opportunities. Amount and valuation were undisclosed (https://hglcapital.co.uk/portfolio/futuremeds/). |
| July 2025 | Phoenix Equity Partners investment/acquisition | Phoenix became the strategic controlling shareholder; transaction price, equity cheque, enterprise value and multiple were not disclosed (https://phoenix-equity.com/news/phoenix-partners-with-futuremeds/; https://www.futuremeds.com/post/a-strategic-partnership-to-accelerate-access-to-clinical-trials-across-europe-and-beyond). |
| October 2025 disclosure | HGL exit result | HGL reported a **10x money multiple** on its initial 2021 investment after selling to Phoenix. IRR cannot be calculated because investment dates, interim cash flows and proceeds are undisclosed (https://scottishbusinessnews.net/private-equity-specialist-hgl-private-capital-announces-successful-exit-from-futuremeds/). |

No reliable public pre-money or post-money valuation was found for any round. Database claims that FutureMeds raised only hundreds of thousands of dollars are difficult to reconcile with its acquisition programme and should not be treated as comprehensive.

---

## 7. Acquisitions and buy-and-build record

FutureMeds’ expansion has combined greenfield openings and acquisitions.

### emovis

FutureMeds acquired Berlin-based **emovis** in July 2023. emovis brought:

- A dedicated research site.
- A pan-European DCT platform.
- Approximately 12 years of operating history.
- Expected access to 30% more trials through FutureMeds’ network and business-development capabilities.

Purchase price was not disclosed (https://www.futuremeds.com/post/futuremeds-acquires-emovis-marking-a-new-era-in-european-dct-solutions).

### CPS Research

PitchBook’s public profile identifies a 24 August 2023 buyout of **CPS Research**, although transaction value was not publicly visible (https://pitchbook.com/profiles/company/532534-69).

### Overall rollout

The network grew from **six sites in 2021 to approximately 28 locations by 2025**. HGL attributes this expansion to organic investment, buy-and-build activity and acquisition of the decentralised trial service (https://hglcapital.co.uk/portfolio/futuremeds/).

The strategy has proven capable of generating scale, but it creates integration, quality-control and purchase-accounting risks. PE underwriting should separate acquired revenue/EBITDA from same-site organic growth.

---

## 8. Operating KPIs and unit economics

### Publicly disclosed KPIs

- **27–28 sites across seven countries** as of the July 2025 transaction.
- Hybrid/DCT coverage in **18 countries**.
- **29 sites** shown on the company website at a later point in 2025.
- Access to **70m+ patients across Europe**.
- Investigators with experience across **2,320+ clinical trials**.
- DCT solution with **320+ projects across 120+ indications** since 2012.
- **39 CROs and 121 sponsors supported**, according to company marketing materials.
- **1,300+ healthcare-provider partnerships**; other materials referenced more than 1,400 homecare providers.
- “Tens of thousands” of patients enrolled annually, according to HGL’s exit announcement.
- Average employees grew from **287 in 2023 to 397 in 2024** (https://scottishbusinessnews.net/private-equity-specialist-hgl-private-capital-announces-successful-exit-from-futuremeds/).
- No critical findings across the audits and inspections described by FutureMeds for 2024, including two FDA inspections and other regulatory/client audits (https://www.futuremeds.com/post/meeting-clinical-research-industry-demand-and-challenges-head-on).
- FutureMeds became the first private site network admitted to Medpace’s Flagship Site Programme in 2025 (https://www.futuremeds.com/post/futuremeds-joins-medpace-prestigious-flagship-site-programme-as-first-private-site-network).

### Derived productivity metrics

Using 2024 revenue and average employees:

\[
£26.967m / 397 = £67,926\text{ revenue per employee}
\]

Using 2023 revenue and 287 employees:

\[
£15.580m / 287 = £54,286\text{ revenue per employee}
\]

Thus revenue per employee increased approximately:

\[
£67,926 / £54,286 - 1 = 25.1\%
\]

Estimated 2024 EBITDA per employee:

\[
£5.159m / 397 = £12,995
\]

Estimated 2023 EBITDA per employee:

\[
£3.101m / 287 = £10,805
\]

This suggests improving workforce productivity despite rapid hiring.

Using reported 2024 wages of approximately £13.37m:

\[
£13.375m / 397 = £33,689\text{ wages per average employee}
\]

and:

\[
£13.375m / £26.967m = 49.6\%\text{ of revenue}
\]

The wage figure may include wider staff-cost components and country-mix effects, but it confirms that labour utilisation is a critical margin driver (https://theaccounts.uk/company/12521988/futuremeds-ltd/).

### Approximate revenue per site

Applying 2024 revenue to a rough network count of 24–27 sites gives an indicative £1.0m–£1.1m of revenue per site:

\[
£26.967m / 27 = £1.00m
\]

\[
£26.967m / 24 = £1.12m
\]

This is only directional because the site count changed during the year and DCT revenue is not necessarily attributable to physical sites.

### CAC, LTV and site-level economics

No public data were found for:

- Sponsor or CRO customer-acquisition cost.
- Lifetime value or retention by customer cohort.
- Cost per recruited patient.
- Revenue or contribution margin per enrolled patient.
- Site-level EBITDA.
- Site utilisation.
- Trial win rate or feasibility-to-award conversion.
- Backlog, contracted order book or book-to-bill.
- Average revenue per study.
- Same-site growth.
- Investigator productivity.

Traditional software-style CAC/LTV may be less useful for this relationship-driven B2B model than sponsor retention, study-award conversion, backlog, repeat-study revenue and site contribution margin. These should be mandatory diligence requests.

---

## 9. Customers and concentration

FutureMeds says it has supported **39 CROs and 121 sponsors**, indicating a broad relationship universe, and describes partnerships with top-tier CROs, NHS organisations and private hospital groups. It also joined Medpace’s Flagship Site Programme and has relationships with Viamed Salud in Spain (https://www.futuremeds.com/meet-futuremeds; https://www.futuremeds.com/post/meeting-clinical-research-industry-demand-and-challenges-head-on).

However, there is no public disclosure of:

- Top customer revenue.
- Top-five or top-ten customer concentration.
- Sponsor versus CRO revenue mix.
- Customer retention or repeat revenue.
- Therapeutic-area concentration.
- Trial-level concentration.
- Exposure to biotech versus large pharma.
- Revenue concentration by country.

The reported 160 sponsor/CRO relationships should not be equated with 160 material revenue-generating customers. A small number of large studies or CRO master-service relationships could still represent a substantial share of revenue.

**Required diligence:** revenue by ultimate sponsor, intermediary CRO, programme, indication, country and study stage; top-10 concentration over three years; repeat-award rates; backlog cancellation history; and aged receivables by customer.

---

## 10. Market and competitive position

The clinical-trial site market remains highly fragmented. A 2024 industry review estimated more than **80,000 sites globally**, fewer than 10% belonging to broader networks, with the top ten dedicated networks accounting for fewer than 600 sites. It also noted that acquisitions are generally faster routes to profitability than greenfield site openings (https://media.bourne-partners.com/PDFDownloads/Clinical%20Trial%20Sites%20Market%20Update.pdf).

FutureMeds’ differentiators include:

1. One of Europe’s largest independent, fully owned site networks.
2. Cross-border execution with common processes.
3. A mix of Western and Central/Eastern European patient populations.
4. Owned DCT/hybrid capabilities rather than purely physical sites.
5. Relationships with healthcare systems, hospitals and community providers.
6. Broad therapeutic coverage, including increasingly complex areas.
7. Founder and management experience in clinical-site operations.

Competitors include CRO-owned networks and independent platforms such as Accellacare/ICON, IQVIA-linked networks, Synexus-derived operations, Pratia and numerous local sites. CRO vertical integration could both validate the strategic value of networks and create channel conflict.

---

## 11. Financial-strength assessment

### Strengths

- **Exceptional growth:** revenue more than tripled from £7.21m in 2022 to £26.97m in 2024.
- **Established profitability:** estimated EBITDA reached £5.16m with a 19.1% margin in 2024.
- **Positive operating leverage:** operating profit improved from a £0.12m loss in 2022 to £3.35m in 2024.
- **Improving productivity:** revenue per employee increased roughly 25% in 2024.
- **PE validation:** HGL’s reported 10x outcome and Phoenix’s acquisition indicate strong institutional interest.
- **Quality and customer credentials:** no critical findings in cited inspections and entry into Medpace’s flagship programme.
- **Geographic and service diversification:** seven-country site network plus 18-country DCT reach.

### Weaknesses and uncertainties

- **Modest liquidity:** £2.64m cash against nearly £27m revenue.
- **Material interest burden:** £1.58m of 2024 interest expense and only 2.1x EBIT coverage.
- **Unknown net debt:** public evidence does not provide a reliable debt balance, and November 2025 charges indicate a new secured financing package.
- **Limited cash-flow disclosure:** EBITDA-to-cash conversion and acquisition cash requirements cannot be assessed accurately.
- **Gross-margin pressure:** gross margin declined from 44.3% to 42.4% in 2024.
- **Acquisition accounting:** statutory EBITDA may contain integration costs, while sponsor-adjusted EBITDA may add back expenses that recur in a continuing roll-up.
- **No concentration or backlog disclosures:** revenue visibility and downside resilience remain unquantified.

**Conclusion on financial strength:** FutureMeds appears operationally strong and profitable, but only moderately strong from a balance-sheet perspective. Its credit quality cannot be considered robust until net debt, covenant headroom and cash conversion are verified.

---

## 12. Valuation considerations

The July 2025 Phoenix transaction valuation was not disclosed. A reasonable external framework is therefore based on 2024 results and sector benchmarks, not a claim about the actual purchase price.

Industry commentary indicates that mid-market clinical-research site operators often transact around **6x–12x EBITDA**, with larger, differentiated platforms potentially achieving low-teens multiples. Broader pharma-services transactions can command materially higher multiples, while public CRO comparables have been cited around **1.8x revenue** (https://www.objectiveibv.com/resources/life-sciences-tech/valuation-of-clinical-research-sites-what-buyers-look-for-in-a-clinical-research-site-company/).

Applying 8x–12x to FutureMeds’ estimated 2024 statutory EBITDA:

- 8x:
  \[
  £5.159m \times 8 = £41.3m\ EV
  \]

- 10x:
  \[
  £5.159m \times 10 = £51.6m\ EV
  \]

- 12x:
  \[
  £5.159m \times 12 = £61.9m\ EV
  \]

At the cited 1.8x public-CRO revenue benchmark:

\[
£26.967m \times 1.8 = £48.5m\ EV
\]

An indicative **£40m–£65m 2024-performance EV range** is therefore defensible as a broad reference. FutureMeds’ growth and scarcity could support a premium, while leverage, customer concentration, integration risk and small absolute EBITDA could justify a discount. Actual 2025 run-rate EBITDA may also have been higher than 2024 EBITDA, so Phoenix could have underwritten a substantially higher enterprise value.

Any valuation should adjust for:

- Net debt and leases.
- Deferred and contingent acquisition consideration.
- Normalised working capital.
- Greenfield site start-up losses.
- One-off acquisition and transaction costs.
- Sustainable versus one-time trial revenue.
- DCT revenue quality and margin.
- Maintenance versus growth capex.
- Quality-of-earnings adjustments.

---

## 13. Private-equity investment thesis

### Thesis

FutureMeds is a credible European clinical-trial-site consolidation platform with unusually high growth, a demonstrated buy-and-build capability, positive EBITDA and a differentiated combination of owned sites and decentralised trial delivery. The fragmented market gives Phoenix—and potentially a future sponsor or continuation vehicle—scope to compound value through acquisitions, greenfield expansion and higher utilisation of an increasingly standardised network.

The investment is most attractive if diligence confirms that:

1. A material majority of growth is organic or repeatable rather than acquisition-only.
2. Top-customer and top-study concentrations are manageable.
3. 2024 EBITDA converts strongly into operating cash after working capital.
4. Post-transaction leverage remains below approximately 4x–5x sustainable EBITDA with adequate covenant headroom.
5. Site-level contribution margins improve materially after the initial ramp period.
6. DCT services are genuinely differentiated and profitable rather than a low-margin staffing overlay.

### Principal value-creation levers

1. **Increase same-site utilisation.**  
   Centralise feasibility, patient-data analytics and sponsor business development so each existing site wins more trials and recruits more patients without equivalent fixed-cost growth.

2. **Continue disciplined buy-and-build.**  
   Acquire high-quality independent sites in underrepresented European markets and complex therapeutic areas. Integrate them onto common quality, finance, technology and commercial systems.

3. **Scale DCT and hybrid trials.**  
   Cross-sell emovis/FutureMeds-at-home capabilities across the physical-site network, creating wider geographic reach and more defensible sponsor relationships.

4. **Expand into higher-value therapeutic areas.**  
   Build oncology, haematology, CNS, metabolic and Phase I capabilities, where complexity and specialised infrastructure may support higher revenue and margins.

5. **Improve commercial contracting.**  
   Negotiate preferred-provider and master-service agreements with major sponsors and CROs; improve reimbursement for screen failures, inflation, protocol amendments and delayed trial starts.

6. **Professionalise data and operations.**  
   Implement group-wide site-level profitability, investigator utilisation, patient funnel, study start-up, recruitment and working-capital dashboards.

7. **Margin and cash conversion.**  
   Consolidate procurement, facilities, technology and central functions; accelerate billing after patient visits and milestones; reduce receivable days and unbilled revenue.

8. **De-risk revenue.**  
   Diversify by sponsor, CRO, therapeutic area and country while prioritising repeat awards from large pharma and well-capitalised biotech customers.

### Likely exit routes

1. **Strategic sale to a global CRO** seeking captive patient access and European trial-delivery capacity—e.g., an ICON-, IQVIA- or Thermo Fisher/PPD-type buyer.
2. **Sale to a larger global site network** seeking immediate European scale.
3. **Secondary PE buyout** by a larger healthcare or pharma-services fund once EBITDA and geographic scale have increased.
4. **Continuation fund or sponsor-led recapitalisation** if acquisition opportunities remain substantial.
5. **IPO**, possible only at significantly greater scale, profitability and reporting maturity; this is the least likely near-term route.

### Timeline

Given Phoenix’s July 2025 entry, a conventional PE hold implies an exit around **2029–2031**, approximately four to six years post-investment. An earlier 2028–2029 strategic sale is conceivable if growth remains exceptional and European site-network consolidation accelerates. An IPO would more plausibly require a longer horizon.

---

## 14. Top five risks

### 1. Trial, sponsor and customer concentration

A few large clinical programmes can drive site-network revenue. Public data do not disclose top customers, top studies or backlog. Cancellation, delayed enrolment or sponsor funding problems could cause abrupt revenue and utilisation declines.

**Mitigation:** concentration limits, diversified therapeutic areas, minimum-payment provisions, milestone billing, sponsor credit checks and rigorous backlog analytics.

### 2. Leverage, interest coverage and cash conversion

Interest expense reached £1.58m in 2024, EBIT coverage was only 2.1x, and four new charges were registered after the Phoenix transaction. Positive EBITDA may not translate into cash if receivables, unbilled revenue, capex and acquisition consideration consume liquidity.

**Mitigation:** conservative leverage, ample revolver capacity, covenant headroom, cash-conversion incentives and debt amortisation funded by genuine free cash flow.

### 3. Clinical quality, regulatory and patient-safety risk

A serious GCP, data-integrity, privacy or patient-safety failure could lead to study termination, inspection findings, litigation and reputational damage across the entire network. Pan-European operations increase regulatory complexity.

**Mitigation:** independent quality leadership, harmonised SOPs, central monitoring, audit readiness, cybersecurity controls and sufficient professional indemnity insurance.

### 4. M&A integration and greenfield execution

The investment case depends on integrating sites and opening new locations. Inconsistent systems, investigator cultures and local practices can dilute quality and margins. Greenfield sites may remain underutilised longer than expected.

**Mitigation:** standard integration playbook, gated acquisition earn-outs, site-level contribution targets and disciplined closure or restructuring of underperforming locations.

### 5. Labour, investigator and competitive pressure

Clinical research depends on experienced investigators, coordinators and nurses. Wage inflation, investigator departures and competition from CRO-owned networks can constrain capacity and gross margin. CRO vertical integration may also redirect studies toward captive sites.

**Mitigation:** investigator equity or incentive programmes, career development, central recruitment, differentiated patient access and direct sponsor relationships.

---

## 15. Bottom line

FutureMeds is a strong growth asset in an attractive and consolidating segment of outsourced pharmaceutical services. Its 2022–2024 expansion—from £7.2m to £27.0m of revenue and from approximately £0.55m to £5.16m of estimated EBITDA—shows that the model can scale. The network, DCT capability, customer credentials and reported 10x return for the prior investor all support strategic scarcity value.

The principal caveat is that public information is insufficient to validate net debt, free cash flow, customer concentration, backlog and adjusted EBITDA quality. On 2024 figures, an illustrative £40m–£65m enterprise-value range is supportable, but a higher valuation requires confidence in 2025 run-rate earnings and continued rapid growth. For Phoenix, the likely path to an attractive return is to double or triple sustainable EBITDA over four to six years through site utilisation, selective acquisitions, DCT cross-selling and better cash conversion—rather than relying principally on further multiple expansion.

final.content:
Career transition into AI safety research from backend engineering: realistic pathways from Berlin

Executive assessment

For a 28-year-old backend software engineer, the most realistic transition is not to begin by competing for “research scientist” roles that expect a PhD and publications. The strongest route is:

1. Reframe backend experience as research infrastructure, evaluation engineering, agent security, or AI-control engineering.
2. Build one technically credible public AI-safety project while retaining your current job.
3. Use a structured incubator or fellowship to acquire research experience and references.
4. Target research-engineer and evaluation-engineer positions before pure research-scientist positions.

Backend skills are directly relevant to the parts of AI safety that require reproducible experiments, distributed evaluation systems, sandboxed agents, observability, secure model access, CI/CD, and production-quality tooling. Apollo Research, for example, explicitly advertises backend engineering for evaluation libraries and monitoring/control of LLM traffic, valuing AWS, security, LLM-agent, and evaluation experience. Its description emphasizes production-grade pipelines, distributed systems and infrastructure rather than only academic scripting (https://jobs.lever.co/apolloresearch/604b1964-c746-4b6a-bb7b-0ef9b421950a; https://www.apolloresearch.ai/careers).

The main geographic conclusion is:

• Berlin/Germany is a good, low-risk place to begin the transition part-time, but has a relatively small frontier-AI-safety employment market.
• London/Cambridge is currently the strongest European cluster for dedicated frontier-safety research, fellowships and public-sector evaluations.
• Berkeley/San Francisco offers the greatest concentration of frontier laboratories, specialist nonprofits, salaries and compute, but US immigration and the intensity of competition create substantially more transition risk.
• A staged Berlin → European fellowship or London engineering role → optional US move is generally more realistic than applying directly from conventional backend development to a US alignment-research position.

1. Where a backend background fits

The term “AI safety” covers substantially different types of work. Your prospects depend on targeting the areas where software engineering is an asset rather than a substitute for missing research credentials.

Best-fit pathways

A. Evaluation and research-infrastructure engineering

This is likely the highest-probability entry point. Typical work includes:

• Running many model or agent instances in parallel.
• Building reproducible evaluation harnesses.
• Provisioning isolated containers or virtual machines.
• Managing experiment metadata, datasets and model outputs.
• Implementing retry, caching, observability and cost controls.
• Securing access to model APIs and sensitive evaluation results.
• Turning research prototypes into reliable internal platforms.

METR’s current roles illustrate the fit. Its Task Development Engineer position asks for several years of work on complex codebases and experience building difficult, preferably agent-based, evaluations using frameworks such as Inspect. Its Evaluation Execution and application-security roles are similarly engineering-heavy (https://metr.org/careers; https://jobs.lever.co/metr/b4812bf4-c259-406b-8ffa-4a463fff34f7).

Apollo’s backend opening is even more directly aligned: it involves evaluation libraries and systems for monitoring and controlling LLM traffic, with AWS, cybersecurity and LLM-agent experience identified as relevant (https://jobs.lever.co/apolloresearch/604b1964-c746-4b6a-bb7b-0ef9b421950a).

Realism: High after a focused portfolio project; potentially feasible without a PhD.

B. AI-control, monitoring and agent-security engineering

“AI control” asks how potentially unreliable or adversarial models can be monitored and constrained. Backend experience transfers to:

• Permission systems and least-privilege tool access.
• Agent sandboxing and network isolation.
• Audit logs and tamper-resistant monitoring.
• Detection and enforcement services.
• Human approval checkpoints.
• Secure execution of model-generated code.
• Defense against prompt injection, data exfiltration and poisoned artifacts.

Anthropic’s Alignment Science work explicitly includes AI control and alignment stress-testing (https://www.anthropic.com/careers/jobs/4610158008). OpenAI’s frontier-cybersecurity and preparedness work includes prevention, monitoring, detection, enforcement, red-teaming, latency and scalability trade-offs—problems close to production backend and security engineering (https://openai.com/careers/researcher-frontier-cybersecurity-risks-san-francisco/).

Realism: High if you add security fundamentals and hands-on LLM-agent work. Lower if your backend work has been limited to ordinary CRUD applications without systems, cloud or security depth.

C. Empirical research engineering

Here you would implement and run experiments on topics such as:

• Model deception or “scheming.”
• Scalable oversight.
• Interpretability.
• Adversarial robustness.
• Dangerous-capability evaluations.
• Model organisms of misalignment.
• Chain-of-thought monitoring.

This requires stronger Python, statistics and ML competence than infrastructure engineering, but not necessarily a PhD. Anthropic says approximately half of its technical staff entered without prior ML experience and that engineers participate directly in research and paper authorship. It advises engineering candidates to apply as engineers rather than trying to relabel themselves as scientists (https://www.anthropic.com/careers).

Realism: Medium after six to twelve months of ML experimentation and a strong public artifact.

D. Applied safety in regulated or safety-critical domains

Germany has more activity in “trustworthy,” regulated and safety-critical AI than in narrowly defined frontier alignment. DLR’s Institute for AI Safety and Security works on resilient AI engineering, secure data infrastructures, execution environments and mobility applications in Sankt Augustin and Ulm (https://www.dlr.de/en/careers/dlr/institutes-and-facilities/institute-for-ai-safety-and-security). DFKI has work on controllable agentic systems, mechanistic interventions and explicit safety constraints, although the cited senior/postdoctoral position requires an advanced research profile (https://jobs.dfki.de/en/vacancy/senior-researcher-postdoc-m-w-d-x-ai-safety-ethics-and-agentic-systems-618587.html).

Berlin also has an AI-safety research-engineering role at Helsing, though its defense context may or may not match your values (https://helsing.ai/jobs/4334849101). Charité and TU Berlin are developing clinical-AI evaluation work, including funded PhD positions, but that route adds domain specialization and formal academic training (https://cyrusgeyer.github.io/rae/).

Realism: Medium to high for safety engineering; lower for postdoctoral research without a PhD.

E. PhD or research master’s route

A PhD is useful if your intended endpoint is:

• Independent theoretical research.
• Mechanistic interpretability research requiring deep specialization.
• Academic leadership.
• Positions explicitly categorized as research scientist or postdoc.
• Work demanding a publication record at venues such as NeurIPS, ICML or ICLR.

It is not generally necessary for evaluation infrastructure, agent security, platform engineering or many research-engineer roles. A PhD therefore has a large opportunity cost if you have not first tested whether you enjoy open-ended research.

Realism: High as a formal route, but slower—typically several years—and not the default recommendation for someone whose strongest present advantage is engineering execution.

2. Practical entry programmes

Berlin/Germany: part-time bridge

The SAIGE Incubator run by Safe AI Germany is especially suitable for testing the transition without immediately resigning. It offers technical AI safety, technical governance and related tracks, generally requiring 10–20 hours per week for three months, with teams of one to five and expert mentorship. It does not require prior AI-safety knowledge and can be extended for another three months (https://safeaigermany.org/incubator; https://safeaigermany.org/).

This is a lower-financial-risk route, but it should be understood as experience and network building rather than employment. The cited programme information does not indicate a salary.

AI Safety Camp offers remote team research, but its official 2026 information says that it generally has no stipend except for a few projects with matched donations. It also expects project leads to have previous research experience or equivalent programme participation (https://www.aisafety.camp/). It is useful as a portfolio mechanism, not a dependable source of transition funding.

Cambridge: ERA

ERA’s Cambridge fellowship is a ten-week, fully funded programme open to people from varied backgrounds, including technical professionals changing direction. The published package is £10,000 plus visa support, working meals and travel coverage (https://erafellowship.org/fellowship).

Arithmetic:

£10,000 ÷ 10 weeks = £1,000 per week before considering travel and meals.

ERA is attractive for generating a first mentored research output. It is not a guaranteed job pipeline, and the stipend should not be compared directly with a permanent software salary.

Cambridge: Frontier AI Security Residency

For an experienced engineer, the Frontier AI Security Residency may be an unusually good match. It is an eight-week, engineering-heavy programme in AI security and verification, with placements intended to produce work in real organizational environments. It expects many applied-track applicants to have roughly five or more years of industry experience.

Its package includes compensation equivalent to a £34,125 gross annual rate, housing, meals during work, travel, visa support and compute (https://www.securefrontier.ai/residency).

Approximate cash equivalent for eight weeks:

£34,125 × 8 ÷ 52 = approximately £5,250 gross,

plus housing, meals, travel, visa assistance and compute. The non-cash support makes the effective package materially better than the cash figure alone.

London: LASR Labs

LASR Labs is a more research-oriented transition programme. The 2026 programme runs for 13 weeks and offers an £11,000 stipend, food, office space and travel. It reports that 90% of previous alumni subsequently worked in AI safety/security and that half of its spring 2025 papers were accepted to NeurIPS; these are programme-reported figures, not independently audited placement statistics (https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/KBtLzLzrSxzZm4HZK/lasr-labs-summer-2026-applications-are-open).

Arithmetic:

£11,000 ÷ 13 weeks ≈ £846 per week,

plus food, office and travel.

Berkeley or London: MATS

MATS is one of the best-known transition programmes for technical AI safety. It accepts non-US citizens, does not formally require previous AI-safety experience, and offers tracks spanning empirical research, theory, cybersecurity, control, evaluations and governance. The standard package is $1,600 per week, or $19,200 for 12 weeks, with housing, weekday meals, travel, office space and compute (https://www.matsprogram.org/faq; https://www.matsprogram.org/apply).

Check:

$1,600 × 12 weeks = $19,200.

MATS can provide J-1 visas for eligible non-American participants, while London participation is an alternative if a US visa proves difficult. Selected participants may receive six- to twelve-month extensions. It is competitive and commonly involves work tests, coding assessments, interviews or writing samples.

Longer-term MATS residency funding is far larger: the programme advertises $155,000–$285,000 plus benefits and compute for six- to 24-month residencies in London, Berkeley or Washington, DC. However, this is intended for people who can already present a serious independent research agenda rather than complete newcomers (https://matsprogram.org/residency).

3. Europe versus the United States

A. Opportunity concentration

Europe

Europe is not one uniform market:

• Berlin/Germany: a useful community and growing applied-safety ecosystem, but relatively few dedicated frontier-alignment employers.
• London: the main European employment cluster, including the UK AI Security Institute, Apollo Research, frontier-lab offices and several research programmes.
• Cambridge: a strong fellowship and academic ecosystem.
• Other German cities: DLR, DFKI and academic institutes offer safety, robustness and regulated-domain work, though often outside the “catastrophic frontier risk” framing.

The UK AI Security Institute recruits researchers and engineers from varied backgrounds, offers access to pre-release frontier models and substantial compute, and says technical roles can sponsor almost all nationalities (https://www.aisi.gov.uk/careers). It originated with £100 million in initial government funding, alongside a separate £900 million compute investment announced at the time (https://www.gov.uk/government/news/initial-100-million-for-expert-taskforce-to-help-uk-build-and-adopt-next-generation-of-safe-ai). Later UK funding announcements included £240 million for the Institute, although future allocations remain politically contingent (https://www.gov.uk/government/news/55-billion-rd-funding-boost-to-unlock-uk-breakthroughs-from-health-to-clean-energy).

United States

The Bay Area has the deepest concentration of:

• Frontier labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI.
• Evaluation organizations such as METR.
• Independent alignment and security researchers.
• Senior mentors, compute and venture/philanthropic capital.
• Very highly compensated technical positions.

This density creates more opportunities for rapid learning and collaboration, but also means roles are frequently in-person or hybrid and attract global applicants. Moving to the US before establishing a safety-relevant record would be financially and legally riskier than first building that record in Europe.

B. Funding and compensation

Permanent employment

Published US compensation can be dramatically higher:

• Anthropic Alignment Research Engineer/Scientist: $350,000–$500,000 annual salary in the cited listing, with visa sponsorship efforts for successful candidates (https://www.anthropic.com/careers/jobs/4631822008).
• OpenAI Frontier Risk Mitigations: $380,000–$500,000 plus equity in the cited listing, but it expects significant safety and research-engineering experience (https://openai.com/careers/researcher-frontier-risk-mitigations-san-francisco/).
• METR Evaluation Execution: approximately $328,000–$579,000, with the junior/mid-level portion reported as $328,000–$402,000 (https://jobs.lever.co/metr/93baec4d-1e47-40f7-9990-6d7fef12da00).

These figures are exceptional frontier-lab or specialist-nonprofit compensation, not representative US software-engineering averages and certainly not entry guarantees.

European frontier organizations can still pay far above ordinary academic scales:

• Anthropic’s cited London expression-of-interest range is £260,000–£370,000, although the team is primarily centered in San Francisco and London candidates may need occasional US travel (https://www.anthropic.com/careers/jobs/4610158008).
• Apollo’s backend role advertises £100,000–£200,000, with visa sponsorship considered in London and San Francisco (https://jobs.lever.co/apolloresearch/604b1964-c746-4b6a-bb7b-0ef9b421950a).

German public research, PhDs and postdocs will normally be much less lucrative than these frontier-lab examples, although no directly comparable salary figure was available in the gathered sources.

Research funding and compute

Europe has large public funding mechanisms, but much of this funding is broad AI infrastructure rather than dedicated alignment research. Horizon Europe has an indicative €93.5 billion budget for 2021–2027 (https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/funding/funding-opportunities/funding-programmes-and-open-calls/horizon-europe_en). The EU reports €2.6 billion committed to AI Factories and Antennas, with 19 factories being established, and up to €10 billion in EU and national support intended to unlock at least €20 billion of private investment for gigafactories (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-factories; https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/eu-expands-network-ai-factories-strengthening-its-ai-continent-ambition).

The €20 billion private-investment target implies a stated leverage of:

€20 billion private ÷ €10 billion public support = 2:1 private-to-public support,

though these are programme targets, not money specifically available to an individual safety researcher.

The United States has more frontier-lab and philanthropic funding, while public “AI safety” funding is more politically variable. NIST’s FY2025 request included a proposed $47.7 million increase for AI research, standards and testing (https://www.nist.gov/congressional-and-legislative-affairs/fy-2025-presidential-budget-request-summary). The former US AI Safety Institute was subsequently reframed as the Center for AI Standards and Innovation, emphasizing security, testing and voluntary standards (https://www.nist.gov/caisi).

Practical interpretation:

• US advantage: private-lab salaries, compute and proximity to frontier systems.
• European advantage: public-interest institutes, paid transition programmes and broader public research infrastructure.
• Neither region offers automatic funding merely for self-identifying as an independent AI-safety researcher; fellowships and grants are competitive.

C. Visa and mobility considerations

Your citizenship and current German residence title are decisive. Since they were not specified, the relevant cases are:

If you are an EU/EEA citizen

Remaining in Germany or moving within participating EU countries is usually administratively easier than moving to either the UK or US. The UK must nevertheless be treated as a separate immigration jurisdiction.

If you are a non-EU citizen resident in Berlin

Check whether changing employers, becoming a fellow or leaving Germany could affect your existing permit. A German permanent settlement permit allows unrestricted economic activity in Germany, but it does not by itself create an unrestricted right to work in every other country (https://www.berlin.de/einwanderung/en/residence/permanent/).

An EU long-term residence permit, generally available after five years subject to income, language and other conditions, gives improved mobility to most other EU member states, but local permits and sometimes labor-market checks can still apply. Ireland and Denmark are exceptions to the relevant mobility framework (https://www.bamf.de/EN/Themen/MigrationAufenthalt/ZuwandererDrittstaaten/MobilitaetEU/MobilitaetLangfristigerAufenthalt/mobilitaet-langfristigeraufenthalt-node.html; https://www.bamf.de/EN/Themen/MigrationAufenthalt/ZuwandererDrittstaaten/Migrathek/Niederlassen/niederlassen-node.html).

United Kingdom

Likely routes include employer sponsorship or, after building a stronger record, Global Talent. The Global Talent digital-technology route covers developers, engineers, data scientists and AI specialists; it does not require a job offer, minimum salary or language qualification, but generally requires endorsement as a leader or potential leader (https://www.gov.uk/global-talent-digital-technology). The research route may apply to eligible academic jobs, fellowships or grants and can receive fast-track endorsement in some cases (https://www.gov.uk/global-talent-researcher-academic).

For a backend engineer with little public AI research today, employer or fellowship visa support is more realistic than immediately qualifying for Global Talent. Relevant organizations and programmes explicitly offering support include UK AISI, ERA, the Frontier AI Security Residency, MATS London and Apollo.

United States

The main practical routes evidenced here are:

• J-1 for structured programmes: MATS says it arranges J-1 visas for non-American Berkeley participants (https://www.matsprogram.org/faq).
• Employer-sponsored H-1B: ordinary cap-subject H-1Bs require registration and selection. The statutory regular cap is 65,000, with another 20,000 exemptions for holders of advanced US degrees (https://www.uscis.gov/working-in-the-united-states/temporary-workers/h-1b-specialty-occupations/h-1b-cap-season).
• Cap-exempt H-1B in qualifying organizations: METR says it can likely sponsor a cap-exempt H-1B for at least one cited technical role (https://jobs.lever.co/metr/93baec4d-1e47-40f7-9990-6d7fef12da00).
• Frontier-lab sponsorship: Anthropic says it sponsors visas and green cards for eligible roles, though sponsorship cannot succeed for every candidate (https://www.anthropic.com/careers).

Compared with the UK, the standard US employer route can involve more timing uncertainty and employer dependence. A J-1 fellowship is a practical way to enter temporarily, but it should not be assumed to convert automatically into long-term work authorization.

D. Research culture

US/Bay Area culture

The gathered job descriptions indicate a culture characterized by:

• High iteration speed and large-scale empirical experimentation.
• Close integration between engineering and research.
• Access to frontier models and very large compute budgets.
• Greater tolerance for nontraditional credentials when accompanied by exceptional demonstrated work.
• Strong preference for in-person collaboration at many organizations.
• Extremely demanding hiring processes involving code screens, paid work tests, technical interviews and work trials.

Anthropic explicitly says engineers do research and researchers do engineering (https://www.anthropic.com/careers). METR’s hiring process can include code screening, take-home tests, technical assessments and a roughly two-day work trial (https://metr.org/careers).

European culture

Europe contains at least three distinct cultures:

1. UK frontier-safety organizations: relatively similar to Bay Area nonprofits and labs—mission-driven, fast-moving, empirical and increasingly in-person.
2. Government institutes: emphasis on evaluations, national security, policy relevance and public accountability. UK AISI combines researchers, engineers, policy specialists and national-security expertise (https://www.aisi.gov.uk/careers).
3. Continental European academia/public research: typically more structured around grants, degrees, formal roles, regulated applications and multi-institution collaboration. The cited DFKI position, for example, is a 36-month project spanning multiple groups and is aimed at senior researchers or postdocs.

Europe’s comparative strengths are public-interest research, standards, privacy, regulation and safety-critical applications. The US comparative strengths are frontier-model access, capital, compensation and dense networks of empirical alignment researchers. This is a tendency, not a universal rule: London frontier organizations can resemble San Francisco more than they resemble German academia.

4. Recommended transition strategy

Phase 1: first 8–12 weeks, while employed

Choose one narrow technical safety area:

• Agent evaluations and sandboxing.
• Control and monitoring.
• LLM or coding-agent security.
• Reproducible dangerous-capability evaluations.
• Experiment infrastructure for interpretability or behavioral research.

Upgrade the minimum research stack:

• Python and PyTorch.
• Statistical experiment design and uncertainty reporting.
• LLM APIs, local open-weight models and inference tooling.
• Containers, sandboxing and cloud orchestration.
• One evaluation framework, preferably Inspect given its appearance in current role descriptions.
• Core literature in your selected area.

Produce a small but rigorous replication. Avoid a generic chatbot, introductory course certificate or opinion essay; these give weak evidence of research ability.

Phase 2: months 3–6

Build a public project that demonstrates both backend depth and research judgment. A strong example would be:

“An open-source evaluation service that runs coding agents in network-restricted containers, records complete action traces, injects adversarial tasks, measures policy violations and compares several monitoring strategies.”

Useful outputs would include:

• A clear threat model.
• Reproducible code and environment definitions.
• Unit and integration tests.
• An experiment report with baselines and confidence intervals.
• Failure analysis rather than only aggregate scores.
• Cost and throughput measurements.
• A short discussion of what the evaluation does not establish.

Contribute to an existing safety tool or reproduce a published result. A merged contribution or technically serious replication is generally more credible than several superficial personal repositories.

Apply to the next available SAIGE cohort, AI Safety Camp project team, ERA, LASR, MATS and Frontier AI Security Residency according to fit. Do not wait for perfect readiness: these programmes use work samples and tests to assess potential.

Phase 3: months 6–12

Apply in three tiers:

Tier 1 — direct engineering fit

• Backend or platform engineer on a safety-research team.
• Evaluation execution engineer.
• Task development engineer.
• Agent security or application-security engineer.
• Research infrastructure engineer.

Tier 2 — hybrid research-engineering fit

• Empirical research engineer.
• AI-control engineer.
• Evaluation researcher/engineer.
• Red-team or preparedness engineer.

Tier 3 — stretch positions

• Research scientist.
• Independent research fellow.
• Mechanistic-interpretability researcher.
• Roles requiring a strong publication record or several years of direct alignment work.

Give London and UK AISI priority over a direct US move if two offers are otherwise comparable: the European transition is likely to involve less immigration risk, and travel from Berlin is easier. Pursue Berkeley/San Francisco when an employer or fellowship offers explicit visa and relocation support.

5. Decision guidance

Choose a Europe-first route if:

• You want to keep immigration and financial risk low.
• You have not yet completed a research project.
• You value public-interest, regulatory or safety-critical work.
• You want to test the field part-time from Berlin.
• You prefer a fellowship-to-employment transition.
• Maintaining German residence status is important.

Choose a US-first route if:

• You already have unusually strong systems, security or ML credentials.
• You can pass demanding live coding and research work tests.
• You have a public evaluation, agent-security or alignment project.
• A specific organization will sponsor the visa.
• You strongly value frontier-model access and dense in-person networks.
• You accept higher relocation and immigration uncertainty.

Consider a PhD if:

• After completing a mentored project, you find that you prefer formulating and investigating open-ended questions over building systems.
• Your desired roles repeatedly require publications or a doctorate.
• You want a durable academic career rather than the fastest route into applied safety work.

Do not assume a PhD is required merely because the destination contains the word “research.” Current Anthropic, Apollo and METR material demonstrates a substantial engineering route into research teams.

Bottom line

The transition is realistic, but “backend engineer → research scientist” is usually too large a single jump. “Backend engineer → AI evaluation/control/security engineer → research engineer” is much more credible.

The best immediate plan is to remain in Berlin for several months, join a part-time German or remote programme, and ship one rigorous evaluation or agent-security project. Then apply simultaneously to funded European programmes and engineering roles in London, Cambridge and selected German institutes. Treat US fellowships and roles as high-upside applications where visa support is explicit, rather than making an unsupported move to the Bay Area.

The decisive signal will not be your age, formal job title or number of AI-safety courses. It will be whether you can demonstrate that you can turn a safety question into a well-designed, reproducible experiment or production-quality research system.
