final.content:
REGIONAL QUEENSLAND RELOCATION ASSESSMENT

Profile: 52-year-old corporate accountant, Melbourne salary AUD $145,000, planned move within 18 months, retirement target age 60, managed atrial fibrillation, purchase budget up to $550,000 for a three-bedroom home, and desired part-time pay of at least $35/hour.

EXECUTIVE CONCLUSION

Toowoomba offers the best overall balance.

It combines:

- the largest estimated saving across housing, utilities and groceries;
- the deepest and most clearly evidenced market for flexible accounting/bookkeeping work paying at least $35/hour;
- unusually comprehensive regional cardiac services, including local electrophysiologists, arrhythmia ablation, device management and atrial-fibrillation cardioversion; and
- several established suburbs where three-bedroom or modest houses were still around or below $550,000 in 2024, although the citywide three-bedroom median was already slightly above the budget.

Cairns ranks second. It has excellent local electrophysiology and AF-ablation capability and credible $35–$40/hour part-time work, but housing was already at the top of the budget in 2024, groceries are slightly dearer than Melbourne, and subsequent price growth has reduced the number of sub-$550,000 houses.

Bundaberg is the housing-affordability leader, with numerous 2024 suburb medians below $550,000. However, it has the weakest evidenced part-time accounting market and, while local cardiology, cardioversion, coronary care and pacemaker services are available, the evidence does not establish a full local AF electrophysiology/ablation service comparable with Toowoomba or Cairns.

Overall ranking:

1. Toowoomba — best affordability/healthcare/income balance
2. Cairns — best alternative if cardiac capability and tropical lifestyle outweigh cost
3. Bundaberg — best purchase affordability, but weaker employment and advanced rhythm-care security


1. INDICATIVE COST-OF-LIVING DIFFERENTIAL

The estimates below compare only the requested categories: housing, utilities and groceries. They are not complete retirement budgets and exclude transport, insurance, rates, healthcare, maintenance and discretionary spending.

Housing comparison

A consistent city-level rental source reports these average weekly rents:

- Melbourne: $604
- Toowoomba: $520
- Bundaberg: $558
- Cairns: $571

Source: https://nestledger.com.au/cities/

Annual rental differences versus Melbourne are therefore:

- Toowoomba: ($604 − $520) × 52 = $4,368 saving
- Bundaberg: ($604 − $558) × 52 = $2,392 saving
- Cairns: ($604 − $571) × 52 = $1,716 saving

These are broad averages rather than controlled three-bedroom-house medians. As a cross-check, Melbourne’s December 2024 median house rent was $600 per week, close to the $604 city average used above (https://www.rent.com.au/blog/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Rent.com_.au_Rental-Market-Snapshot_December-2024.pdf).

Utilities

For comparability, utilities are defined as basic electricity/heating/cooling/water/garbage, mobile phone and broadband. Crowd-sourced Numbeo observations give:

- Melbourne: $331.94 + $39.82 + $81.10 = $452.86/month
- Toowoomba: $108.44 + $43.59 + $77.00 = $229.03/month
- Bundaberg: $200.69 + $40.00 + $83.33 = $324.02/month
- Cairns: $233.33 + $50.00 + $95.00 = $378.33/month

Sources:

- Melbourne/Cairns comparison: https://www.numbeo.com/cost-of-living/compare_cities.jsp?city1=Melbourne&city2=Cairns&country1=Australia&country2=Australia
- Toowoomba: https://www.numbeo.com/cost-of-living/in/Toowoomba
- Bundaberg: https://www.numbeo.com/cost-of-living/in/Bundaberg

Estimated annual utility savings are:

- Toowoomba: ($452.86 − $229.03) × 12 = $2,686
- Bundaberg: ($452.86 − $324.02) × 12 = $1,546
- Cairns: ($452.86 − $378.33) × 12 = $894

The Toowoomba basic-utilities estimate is especially uncertain: its reported range is very wide, indicating a small or heterogeneous sample. Actual electricity costs will also depend heavily on air conditioning, insulation and solar.

Groceries

Numbeo’s direct Melbourne–Cairns comparison says Cairns groceries are 3.9% more expensive than Melbourne’s. It also reports Toowoomba groceries as 13.7% cheaper than Cairns. Combining those indices:

- Melbourne index = 100
- Cairns = 103.9
- Toowoomba = 103.9 × (1 − 0.137) = 89.7

Thus, the indicated grocery differential is:

- Toowoomba: approximately 10.3% cheaper than Melbourne
- Cairns: approximately 3.9% dearer
- Bundaberg: no robust direct Melbourne index was found

Sources:

- Melbourne–Cairns: https://www.numbeo.com/cost-of-living/compare_cities.jsp?city1=Melbourne&city2=Cairns&country1=Australia&country2=Australia
- Cairns–Toowoomba: https://www.numbeo.com/cost-of-living/compare_cities.jsp?country1=Australia&city1=Cairns&country2=Australia&city2=Toowoomba
- Bundaberg food observations: https://www.numbeo.com/food-prices/in/Bundaberg

A rough matched-staples comparison from the gathered prices suggests Bundaberg may be modestly more expensive than Melbourne—approximately 8%—but this is low-confidence because it is crowd-sourced, based on a small basket and not necessarily collected at the same date.

Illustrative combined cost effect

To turn the grocery percentages into dollars, assume one person currently spends $600 per month, or $7,200 per year, on groceries. This is an illustrative assumption and should be replaced with actual bank-statement spending.

Estimated grocery effect:

- Toowoomba saving: $7,200 × 10.3% = approximately $742
- Bundaberg additional cost at rough +8%: approximately $576
- Cairns additional cost: $7,200 × 3.9% = approximately $281

Combined requested-category differential:

| Location | Housing saving | Utility saving | Grocery effect | Indicative annual saving vs Melbourne |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Toowoomba | $4,368 | $2,686 | +$742 saving | approximately $7,796 |
| Bundaberg | $2,392 | $1,546 | −$576 cost | approximately $3,362 |
| Cairns | $1,716 | $894 | −$281 cost | approximately $2,329 |

Monthly equivalents:

- Toowoomba: approximately $650/month cheaper
- Bundaberg: approximately $280/month cheaper
- Cairns: approximately $194/month cheaper

These figures should be treated as directional rather than precise. Regional rent comparisons depend strongly on suburb and dwelling quality, while utilities and groceries rely partly on crowd-sourced data. Purchase rather than rental housing could produce a much larger long-run saving, but transaction costs, rates, insurance and maintenance need to be added.


2. PART-TIME ACCOUNTING WORK AT $35/HOUR OR MORE

Income benchmark

Nationally, accountants have median hourly earnings of $53 and median full-time weekly earnings of $2,003. Eighty-four per cent work full-time, meaning genuinely part-time professional vacancies form a smaller segment of the occupation (https://www.jobsandskills.gov.au/data/occupation-and-industry-profiles/occupations/2211-accountants).

Your present full-time equivalent hourly salary is approximately:

$145,000 ÷ (52 × 38 hours) = $73.38/hour

Moving to $35/hour would therefore mean accepting approximately:

$35 ÷ $73.38 = 47.7%

of your current base hourly salary.

However, $35/hour is below the national accountant median and should be achievable for an experienced corporate accountant if willing to consider bookkeeping, payroll, finance-officer, management-accounting, BAS/GST or small-practice work.

Illustrative gross part-time income at $35/hour:

- Two 7.6-hour days weekly: 15.2 × $35 × 52 = $27,664/year
- Three days weekly: 22.8 × $35 × 52 = $41,496/year
- Four days weekly: 30.4 × $35 × 52 = $55,328/year

These figures exclude superannuation and assume work is available for all 52 weeks.

Toowoomba: strongest evidence

Recent search results included:

- a permanent part-time administrative/accounts position at $35–$42/hour;
- a part-time finance role at $35–$40/hour;
- an experienced bookkeeper role advertised at a full-time equivalent of $80,000–$90,000;
- flexible part-time accounting work involving BAS, GST and tax returns; and
- a national firm seeking a part-time SMSF accounting officer/bookkeeper for approximately 25–30 hours per week.

Sources:

- https://au.seek.com/part-time-accountant-jobs/in-Toowoomba-&-Darling-Downs-QLD
- https://au.seek.com/undergraduate-accountant-jobs/in-Toowoomba-QLD-4350/part-time
- https://www.uworkin.com/industry/accounting/job/26046605/part-time-accountant
- https://jobs.theshout.com.au/jobview/accounting-officer-bookkeeper-smsf/0811ae19-b1d1-11f1-bc76-0231708ce3cd

Assessment: Good probability of finding $35/hour or better, particularly if your skills include Xero, payroll, management reporting, SMSFs, BAS/GST or tax compliance. Toowoomba’s diversified regional economy and 2024 LGA population of approximately 184,377 support a broader professional-services market than Bundaberg (population source: https://www.qgso.qld.gov.au/issues/3106/population-growth-regional-qld-2023-24.pdf).

Cairns: credible but narrower

Examples included:

- a part-time bookkeeper/weighbridge operator at $40/hour;
- a bookkeeper role at $35/hour;
- a part-time CPA/Xero accountant role designed as potentially suitable for a semi-retired person, though only eight hours per week; and
- part-time hotel-finance/accounts work.

Sources:

- https://au.seek.com/part-time-accountant-jobs/in-Cairns-QLD-4870
- https://au.seek.com/part-time-accounting-jobs/in-Cairns-QLD-4870/part-time
- https://www.jobstralia.com/detail/8/fcb613ffb82354d75eedbc70828d28c4

Assessment: The threshold is achievable, but hours may be fragmented and the role mix is more exposed to tourism, hospitality and small-business bookkeeping. Cairns nevertheless has a sizeable 2024 LGA population of about 178,104, close to Toowoomba’s (https://www.qgso.qld.gov.au/issues/3106/population-growth-regional-qld-2023-24.pdf).

Bundaberg: weakest evidence for part-time availability

Search results showed accounting vacancies, including intermediate and senior positions, and one senior hybrid role at $90,000–$105,000 plus superannuation. However, most visible vacancies were full-time, graduate or taxation/business-services positions; there was little direct evidence of local part-time jobs explicitly paying at least $35/hour.

Sources:

- https://au.seek.com/part-time-accounting-jobs/in-Bundaberg-&-Wide-Bay-Burnett-QLD
- https://au.seek.com/junior-accountant-jobs/in-Bundaberg-QLD-4670
- https://au.seek.com/accounts-jobs/in-Bundaberg-QLD-4670

Assessment: $35/hour is plausible for an experienced accountant, but the risk is finding sufficient and reliably recurring part-time hours rather than the nominal rate itself. Retaining a Melbourne employer remotely, developing a virtual bookkeeping/BAS portfolio, or negotiating a reduced-hours position before moving would materially reduce this risk.

Employment ranking:

1. Toowoomba
2. Cairns
3. Bundaberg


3. CARDIAC CARE WITHIN 90 MINUTES

For managed atrial fibrillation, the relevant distinction is not simply whether a town has a cardiologist. It is whether local services include rhythm specialists, Holter monitoring, echocardiography, cardioversion, electrophysiology, ablation and implanted-device support.

Toowoomba: excellent regional cardiac capability

Toowoomba has multiple locally based cardiologists and electrophysiologists.

Dr Caleb Mengel practises at St Vincent’s Private Hospital Toowoomba and Toowoomba Cardiac Centre. His listed specialty is electrophysiology, including cardiac ablation, pacemakers and defibrillators, and the conditions treated explicitly include atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter (https://hopeforhearts.com.au/specialists/dr-caleb-mengel/).

Care Cardiology offers Holter monitoring, echocardiography, transoesophageal echocardiography and pacemaker/defibrillator checks. Its electrophysiologist provides invasive and non-invasive AF management and performs arrhythmia ablations at Toowoomba Base Hospital (https://www.carecardiology.com.au/about).

St Andrew’s Toowoomba Hospital lists:

- emergency cardiac care;
- ECG and echocardiography;
- electrophysiology;
- angiography and angioplasty;
- electrophysiology studies and ablation;
- pacemaker and defibrillator services; and
- transoesophageal echocardiography and cardioversion for AF.

Source: https://www.sath.org.au/service/cardiology/

Assessment: Strongest overall choice. Routine AF follow-up, diagnostics and significant rhythm interventions are available within the city, comfortably inside 90 minutes.

Cairns: also excellent, including AF ablation

Cairns Hospital has a cardiology service, while Cairns Private Hospital lists a specialist electrophysiologist providing:

- arrhythmia management;
- pacemaker, defibrillator and resynchronisation-device care;
- electrophysiology studies; and
- catheter ablation, explicitly including atrial-fibrillation ablation.

Sources:

- https://www.cairns-hinterland.health.qld.gov.au/services/cardiology/cardiology-cairns-hospital
- https://www.cairnsprivate.com.au/For-GPs/Specialists/cairns-private-hospital/cardiology/108732/dr-corey-smith

Cairns Hospital’s invasive electrophysiology program has operated since 2019. A published audit reported 215 invasive studies, including 62 pulmonary-vein isolations—an AF-ablation procedure—with no mortality and no transfers for cardiac surgery in the reviewed cohort (https://www.heartlungcirc.org/article/S1443-9506(22)00456-5/fulltext).

Assessment: Comparable to Toowoomba for AF-specific rhythm treatment. The main strategic caveat is geographic isolation: if a procedure or complication requires a larger tertiary centre, alternatives are much farther away than they are from Toowoomba.

Bundaberg: good general/interventional cardiology, but less certain electrophysiology depth

Advara HeartCare describes itself as Bundaberg’s sole cardiac service for public and private patients and offers:

- ECG;
- Holter and blood-pressure monitoring;
- echocardiography and stress testing; and
- cardioversion.

Source: https://advaraheartcare.com/locations/base-hospital-bundaberg/

The Friendly Society Private Hospital provides coronary care, a cardiac catheterisation laboratory, angioplasty, pacemaker procedures, rhythm monitoring and management of acute cardiac emergencies (https://thefriendlies.org.au/cardiology-services-bundaberg/). The cath lab is the only facility of its kind in Wide Bay and treats public patients under an arrangement with Queensland Health (https://www.brcnow.bundaberg.qld.gov.au/2023/05/30/cardiac-investigations-unit-upgrade-planned/).

Assessment: Routine managed-AF care, monitoring and cardioversion are available locally. However, the gathered evidence does not show a locally based comprehensive AF electrophysiology and ablation program. Brisbane-based or visiting specialists may be needed for complex rhythm intervention, which would not satisfy a practical 90-minute road-access criterion.

Healthcare ranking:

1. Toowoomba — comprehensive, multiple local options and less geographically isolated
2. Cairns — excellent local AF electrophysiology and ablation
3. Bundaberg — good cardiology but uncertain complex AF-ablation access


4. THREE-BEDROOM PROPERTY TRAJECTORY, 2020–2024

Method

OpenStats reports June 2025 three-bedroom-house medians, one-year changes and five-year compound annual changes. The 2024 and 2020 values can therefore be reconstructed:

2024 estimate = 2025 price ÷ (1 + annual change)

2020 estimate = 2025 price ÷ (1 + five-year CAGR)^5

The resulting estimates are:

| Market/proxy | Derived 2020 median | Derived 2024 median | 2020–24 increase | Under $550,000 in 2024? |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Toowoomba | approximately $329,000 | approximately $560,000 | +$231,000 / +70% | Citywide median: slightly above |
| Bundaberg/Wide Bay proxy | approximately $272,000 | approximately $515,000 | +$243,000 / +89% | Yes |
| Cairns | approximately $338,000 | approximately $545,000 | +$207,000 / +61% | Barely |

Calculations:

Toowoomba:

- 2024 = $634,000 ÷ 1.132 = approximately $560,000
- 2020 = $634,000 ÷ 1.14^5 = approximately $329,000

Source: https://openstats.com.au/dashboards/property-prices/sa4/toowoomba/

Bundaberg/Wide Bay:

- 2024 = $593,000 ÷ 1.151 = approximately $515,000
- 2020 = $593,000 ÷ 1.169^5 = approximately $272,000

Source: https://openstats.com.au/dashboards/property-prices/sa4/wide-bay/

Cairns:

- 2024 = $609,750 ÷ 1.119 = approximately $545,000
- 2020 = $609,750 ÷ 1.125^5 = approximately $338,000

Source: https://openstats.com.au/dashboards/property-prices/sa4/cairns/

These are reconstructed statistical-area medians, not exact annual city medians. Wide Bay is especially imperfect as a Bundaberg proxy because it includes other communities.

Toowoomba under-$550,000 opportunities

Although the reconstructed 2024 three-bedroom median was around $560,000, August 2024 suburb house medians included:

- Rockville: $480,000
- Wilsonton: $502,500
- Harristown: $525,000
- Newtown: $539,500
- North Toowoomba: $545,000
- South Toowoomba: $552,000

Source: https://remaxsuccess.com.au/suburb-profile/how-does-toowoombas-property-market-compare-to-the-rest-of-the-country/

Thus, the $550,000 budget was workable in 2024, but mainly in older or less premium suburbs. Prices had increased sharply: Toowoomba City’s broader house median rose from $330,000 in 2020 (https://remaxsuccess.com.au/2020-property-market-in-toowoomba/) to approximately $595,000 by August 2024.

Bundaberg under-$550,000 opportunities

December 2024 suburb house medians below or around the budget included:

- Bundaberg Central: $428,000
- Walkervale: $443,500
- Bundaberg West: $452,000
- Bundaberg South: $457,000
- Svensson Heights: $475,000
- Bundaberg North: $476,000
- Norville: $478,000
- Avenell Heights: $489,000
- Bundaberg East: $493,000
- Kepnock: $508,000
- Thabeban: $512,000
- Millbank: $525,000

Source: https://firstnationalbundaberg.com.au/blog/how-did-the-bundaberg-property-market-perform-in-2024

Bundaberg’s overall house median was only $295,000 in 2020 (https://www.brcnow.bundaberg.qld.gov.au/2020/12/13/bundaberg-market-report-shows-rising-demand/), confirming a very strong post-2020 rise. Nevertheless, it retained the widest selection below $550,000 at the end of 2024.

Cairns under-$550,000 opportunities

Cairns’ house median was approximately $430,000 in the September 2020 quarter (https://www.realestate.com.au/news/cairns-property-defies-market-predictions-with-median-house-price-increase-of-49-per-cent/). A separate market summary places the 2024 house median at approximately $550,000 (https://fnqbuyersagent.com.au/blog/cairns-median-house-price/), consistent with the reconstructed three-bedroom estimate of approximately $545,000.

This means a $550,000 budget was around the citywide midpoint in 2024 rather than comfortably above it. By June 2025, the reported three-bedroom median had reached $609,750, so continued reliance on a fixed $550,000 ceiling would require targeting outer, older or less sought-after suburbs.

Property-affordability ranking:

1. Bundaberg
2. Toowoomba, because several established suburbs remained around the budget
3. Cairns, where the budget was already at the market median and subsequent growth was strong


5. FINAL RECOMMENDATION

Choose Toowoomba, subject to securing either a suitable property or part-time employment before committing to the move.

Why it is optimal

Affordability: The indicative requested-category saving is approximately $7,800 per year versus Melbourne, substantially ahead of Bundaberg and Cairns. Lower housing and utility costs drive most of the advantage.

Healthcare: It provides local electrophysiology, ablation, cardioversion, Holter monitoring, imaging and implanted-device management. This is the strongest combination for someone with managed AF who wants both routine follow-up and escalation options within 90 minutes.

Income sustainability: Toowoomba has the clearest evidence of several part-time finance and accounting roles at $35–$42/hour. It also has a broader economy and professional-services market than Bundaberg.

Housing: A $550,000 limit is below the current broad market median but was still realistic in suburbs such as Rockville, Wilsonton, Harristown, Newtown and North Toowoomba in 2024. The trade-off is that choice will be narrower than in Bundaberg.

Recommended transition strategy

1. Preserve Melbourne-level income as long as practical. At the current salary, each additional full-time year materially strengthens retirement savings.
2. Ask the current employer about remote or reduced-hours work before moving. A three-day arrangement at even $50/hour would produce $59,280 annually, compared with $41,496 at $35/hour.
3. Broaden the regional search terms beyond “accountant” to management accountant, finance officer, bookkeeper, payroll, BAS, SMSF and commercial analyst.
4. Obtain a referral or transfer plan from the current cardiologist before relocating, including anticoagulation monitoring, medication history and preferred local electrophysiologist.
5. For Toowoomba property searches, prioritise practical access to Toowoomba Base Hospital, St Andrew’s and St Vincent’s rather than choosing solely on purchase price.
6. Have building, flood/stormwater and insurance checks completed before purchase. These costs are excluded from the cost model and can erode regional savings.
7. Do not extrapolate the 2020–24 price trajectory mechanically. All three markets experienced exceptional post-pandemic appreciation, and the reconstructed 2025 data show that a fixed $550,000 ceiling was already becoming restrictive.

If purchasing comfortably below $550,000 is non-negotiable, Bundaberg is the better property choice—but only if a satisfactory cardiology pathway and reliable remote or local income are secured first. If access to dedicated AF ablation is the overriding concern and a smaller house or higher budget is acceptable, Cairns is medically strong. For the stated combination of affordability, healthcare security and semi-retirement income, however, Toowoomba is the most balanced decision.

final.content:
Carbon Pricing in California, the European Union and China, 2020–2024

Executive summary

From 2020 through 2024, the three systems represented distinct carbon-pricing models:

• California operated a declining, economy-wide absolute cap linked with Québec, with a price floor, extensive banking, free allocation for leakage protection and auctions financing climate programs.

• The EU ETS operated the strongest scarcity-based price signal. The Market Stability Reserve (MSR), a tighter Phase 4 cap and expectations surrounding the “Fit for 55” reforms lifted prices from about €24/tCO2 in 2020 to roughly €65–84/tCO2 in 2022–2024. Stationary-source emissions fell to about half their 2005 level by 2024.

• China launched national trading in July 2021 as an output- and emissions-intensity-based system for the power sector. Prices rose steadily but remained much lower than in California or Europe. Because allowances were entirely free and linked to actual output, the system improved plant efficiency but did not impose an absolute emissions cap or generate auction revenue.

Headline comparison:

| Indicator | California | EU ETS | China national ETS |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Approximate allowance price | $17/t in 2020; quarterly average $35.23 in 2024 | €24.36/t in 2020; €64.8/t in 2024 | CNY54.22/t at end-2021; CNY97.49/t at end-2024 |
| Emissions outcome | Statewide emissions fell from 380.4 MtCO2e in 2021 to 346.0 Mt in 2024 | Stationary emissions fell from 1,355 Mt in 2020 to 1,033 Mt in 2024; roughly 50% below 2005 | No official absolute reduction attributed to ETS; first-cycle study estimates 0.86% emissions reduction and 2.46–3.13% intensity reduction |
| 2020–24 public revenue | About $10.20 billion deposited in California’s GGRF over FY2020-21–FY2024-25 | At least €119 billion in 2020 and 2022–24, plus about €14 billion in the first half of 2021 | Zero auction revenue: allowances were 100% free |
| Compliance | 100% for 2018–20; nearly 100% at subsequent events | Generally above 99%; only 31 stationary operators received excess-emissions penalties in 2024 | 99.61% for 2021, 99.88% for 2022 and 99.98% for 2023 |
| COVID response | Auctions continued; demand collapse caused undersubscription, with unsold allowances subject to existing re-offer/retirement rules | No discretionary suspension; the MSR absorbed surplus while banking continued | Initial cycle covered 2019–20 retrospectively; broad banking and limited obligations softened the shock |
| Principal leakage response | Output-based free industrial allocation; carbon obligation on imported electricity | Free allocation to 63 leakage-risk sectors, followed by transitional CBAM reporting from October 2023 | Full free, output-based allocation; no national carbon border adjustment |

A central interpretive limitation is that observed emissions cannot be attributed to carbon pricing alone. Renewable mandates, electricity-sector regulation, fuel prices, COVID restrictions, industrial output and coal or nuclear availability all materially affected emissions. This is particularly important for China, whose national ETS had no fixed absolute cap, and California, where cap-and-trade was explicitly designed as one component of a larger Scoping Plan.

1. Program architecture during 2020–2024

California

California’s program covered electricity generation and imports, large industrial facilities and distributors of transportation and heating fuels. One allowance represented one metric ton of CO2-equivalent. California and Québec held linked quarterly auctions with an annually rising reserve price.

The state distributed allowances through several channels. By 2024, approximately 45% were sold to finance the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, about 37% were freely allocated to electric and natural-gas utilities for ratepayer protection, and approximately 13% were allocated to industrial facilities, primarily to address competitiveness and leakage risks (https://calepa.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/2024-ANNUAL-REPORT-OF-THE-IEMAC.pdf).

California’s cap was therefore absolute, but emissions in an individual year could exceed the year’s newly issued allowance budget through banking of allowances from earlier years. Offsets also provided limited compliance flexibility.

EU ETS

The EU ETS covered electricity and heat generation, energy-intensive industries and intra-European aviation; maritime transport entered in 2024. Approximately 40% of EU emissions fell within its scope. Phase 4 began in 2021 with a steeper declining cap and continued free allocation for trade-exposed industries.

The 2023 revision subsequently established a 62% reduction objective for covered emissions by 2030 relative to 2005, rebased the cap, accelerated annual reductions and added maritime transport. The Commission reported 8,704 stationary installations, 393 aircraft operators and 3,313 shipping companies in scope in 2024 (https://climate.ec.europa.eu/document/download/ff002f5f-12ac-4818-9be7-724a13258bda_en).

China

China’s national ETS began trading on 16 July 2021. During the period studied, it principally regulated power generators and captive power plants. The second compliance cycle included 2,257 entities and approximately 5.1 billion tonnes of annual CO2—more than 40% of national CO2 emissions (https://www.mee.gov.cn/ywdt/xwfb/202407/W020240722528850763859.pdf).

Unlike California and the EU, China used an output-based intensity system. Allowances were calculated from actual electricity or heat output multiplied by technology-specific emissions benchmarks. Thus, an efficient coal plant could earn surplus allowances while absolute sector emissions could still grow if electricity production increased. All allowances were free, and only regulated entities could trade.

2. Allowance-price trajectories

California

CARB’s quarterly joint-auction settlement data show the following simple, unweighted averages:

• 2020: ($17.87 + $16.68 + $16.68 + $16.93) / 4 = $17.04/tCO2e  
• 2021: ($17.80 + $18.80 + $23.30 + $28.26) / 4 = $22.04  
• 2022: ($29.15 + $30.85 + $27.00 + $26.80) / 4 = $28.45  
• 2023: ($27.85 + $30.33 + $35.20 + $38.73) / 4 = $33.03  
• 2024: ($41.76 + $37.02 + $30.24 + $31.91) / 4 = $35.23

The underlying results are published by CARB at https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2020-08/results_summary.pdf.

The path was therefore not monotonic. Prices stayed close to the auction floor during the 2020 lockdown and early 2021, rose sharply as the economy reopened and the post-2020 cap tightened, peaked at $41.76 in February 2024, and then fell to $31.91 by November. Even after that correction, the 2024 quarterly average was:

($35.23 / $17.04 − 1) × 100 = approximately 107% above 2020.

EU ETS

Annual average auction prices were:

• 2020: €24.36/tCO2  
• 2021: €54.15  
• 2022: €80.18  
• 2023: €83.60  
• 2024: €64.80

Sources: EEA technical reports for 2020–22 and the Commission’s market reports for 2023–24 (https://www.eionet.europa.eu/etcs/etc-cm/products/etc-cm-report-2023-07-1/@@download/file/ETC_CM_ETS%20Report_2023_07_2.pdf; https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX%3A52024DC0538).

The 2020 lockdown briefly pushed the EUA price down to €14.60 in March, but it recovered to €30.92 by year-end. The annual average then more than doubled in 2021. Tightened caps, MSR withdrawals, higher gas prices and expectations of stronger climate policy drove the 2022–23 peak.

The 2024 decline was:

(€64.80 − €83.60) / €83.60 = −22.5%.

It reflected weaker industrial demand, lower gas prices, higher renewable generation and additional auction supply, but the price remained approximately 166% above 2020:

(€64.80 / €24.36 − 1) × 100 = 166%.

China

Key market closing prices were:

• First trading day in 2021: approximately CNY48/tCO2  
• 31 December 2021: CNY54.22  
• 29 December 2023: CNY79.42  
• 31 December 2024: CNY97.49

The 2024 price ranged from approximately CNY69 to CNY105.65 and first exceeded CNY100 on 24 April. The year-end increase from 2023 was:

(CNY97.49 / CNY79.42 − 1) × 100 = 22.75%.

Relative to the first trading-day price, the 2024 close had risen 103.1% (https://xcoss.henan.gov.cn/typtfile/20251009/1613827be7d04b2aaa0cfc06b84f458e.pdf).

For 2022–23 together, transaction value divided by volume gives a volume-weighted average:

CNY17.26 billion / 263 million tonnes = CNY65.63/t.

Despite its enormous coverage, China’s price remained far below California and EU levels. Direct currency conversion is imperfect, but the 2024 year-end CNY97.49 price was roughly US$13–14/t, compared with approximately US$32 in California and €65 in Europe.

3. Emissions reductions versus baselines and projections

California

California’s official statewide inventory—not solely cap-and-trade emissions—shows:

• 2021: 380.4 MtCO2e  
• 2022: 371.1 Mt  
• 2023: approximately 360.4 Mt  
• 2024: 346.0 Mt

Sources: CARB inventory reports at https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2024-09/nc-2000_2022_ghg_inventory_trends.pdf and https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/nc-2000_2024_ghg_inventory_trends.pdf.

The 2021–24 reduction was therefore:

380.4 − 346.0 = 34.4 MtCO2e, or 34.4 / 380.4 = 9.0%.

The 2024 decline alone was approximately 14.0 Mt, or 3.9%, from 2023.

California’s AB 32 2020 limit was approximately 1990 emissions, about 431 MtCO2e. Against that statutory baseline, 2024 emissions were approximately:

431 − 346 = 85 MtCO2e lower, or about 19.7% below 1990.

California was already below the 2020 limit in 2014, so the difference cannot be credited to 2020–24 cap-and-trade activity. Nor was the state yet at the statutory 2030 target of 40% below 1990, approximately 259 Mt. At 346 Mt in 2024, the remaining gap was roughly:

346 − 259 = 87 MtCO2e.

CARB has emphasized that cap-and-trade operates alongside regulatory measures and that a reliable “cap-and-trade-only” reduction cannot be isolated. The best separately quantified result is from projects financed with auction proceeds: by the end of 2024, roughly 590,000 California Climate Investments projects were expected to reduce 116.1 MtCO2e over their lifetimes (https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/auction-proceeds/cci_2025ar_factsheet.pdf). These are projected lifetime reductions—not reductions already realized in 2024—and overlap with the state’s broader emissions trajectory.

EU ETS

Verified stationary-installation emissions were:

• 2020: 1,355 MtCO2e, including the UK; 1,253 Mt excluding the UK  
• 2021: 1,337 Mt  
• 2022: 1,313 Mt  
• 2023: 1,095.9 Mt  
• 2024: 1,033.2 Mt

Sources: Commission and EEA reports at https://climate.ec.europa.eu/document/download/5c4c611e-ae32-45d5-bda6-d78360ef52db_en and https://www.eionet.europa.eu/etcs/etc-cm/products/etc-cm-report-2024-09/@@download/file/ETC_CM_2024-09-bis.pdf.

Because the UK left the system, the comparable COVID-to-recovery path should use the 2020 figure excluding the UK:

• 2020–21 rebound: (1,337 − 1,253) / 1,253 = 6.7%  
• 2021–22 decline: approximately 1.8%  
• 2022–23 decline: (1,313 − 1,095.9) / 1,313 = 16.5%  
• 2023–24 decline: approximately 5.8%.

The Commission reported 2023 stationary emissions at 47.6% below 2005. An implied 2005 baseline is:

1,095.9 / (1 − 0.476) = approximately 2,091 MtCO2e.

Using that implied baseline, 2024 stationary emissions were:

1 − 1,033.2 / 2,091 = approximately 50.6% below 2005.

Thus the system had achieved roughly 50% reduction against its baseline by 2024, versus the revised 62% target for 2030. The remaining reduction from the 2024 level to a 38%-of-2005 target was approximately:

Target = 2,091 × 0.38 = 795 Mt;  
Remaining reduction = 1,033 − 795 = approximately 238 MtCO2e.

The sharp 2023–24 decline cannot be attributed solely to allowance prices. Wind and solar expansion, energy efficiency, weak industrial output, lower electricity demand and renewed gas-for-coal switching were major contributors.

China

China has not published an official absolute emissions reduction attributable to the national ETS. This is not simply a data gap: the system’s output-adjusted cap means there is no fixed ex ante absolute baseline comparable to the EU’s 2005 baseline or California’s statutory targets.

MEE reported that by 2023:

• Thermal-generation CO2 intensity was 2.38% below 2018.  
• Overall electricity-generation CO2 intensity was 8.78% below 2018.

These economy-wide power indicators reflect renewable expansion and other policies as well as the ETS (https://www.mee.gov.cn/ywdt/xwfb/202407/W020240722528850763859.pdf).

A plant-level ex post study of the first compliance phase estimated:

• Electricity and heat carbon-intensity reductions of 2.46%–3.13%.  
• An absolute emissions reduction of 0.86%, despite 1.63% production growth.  
• About 57% of abatement from improved energy efficiency and 31% from improved fuel quality.

The study is summarized at https://www.cell.com/cell-reports-sustainability/fulltext/S2949-7906(25)00035-7. Its estimate is more useful for causal assessment than national totals, but it covers the initial phase rather than all of 2020–24.

4. Revenue and allocation

California

CARB’s fiscal-year figures for proceeds deposited in the GGRF were:

• FY2020-21: $1.2969 billion  
• FY2021-22: $2.0295 billion  
• FY2022-23: $2.0026 billion  
• FY2023-24: $2.6650 billion  
• FY2024-25: $2.2007 billion

Total:

1.2969 + 2.0295 + 2.0026 + 2.6650 + 2.2007 = approximately $10.195 billion.

These fiscal years do not exactly match calendar 2020–24, but they are the closest consistent official series (https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2020-09/proceeds_summary.pdf).

Revenue supported high-speed rail, low-carbon transit, affordable housing and sustainable communities, zero-emission vehicles, dairy methane reductions, forest and land programs, energy efficiency and community air-quality measures. State law requires at least 35% of appropriations to benefit disadvantaged or low-income communities and households. In 2024 alone, approximately $1.9 billion was implemented in nearly 12,000 projects, with $1.2 billion benefiting priority populations.

Utilities separately consigned freely allocated allowances to auction and returned their value to customers or used it for approved ratepayer purposes. Thus total auction cash flow exceeded GGRF deposits, but the utility portion should not be described as general state revenue.

EU ETS

Known total auction revenue was:

• 2020: €16.5 billion  
• First half of 2021: approximately €14 billion  
• 2022: approximately €20.1 billion  
• 2023: €43.6 billion  
• 2024: €38.8 billion

The minimum sum using only full-year figures for 2020 and 2022–24 is:

€16.5 + €20.1 + €43.6 + €38.8 = €119.0 billion,

plus approximately €14 billion in the first half of 2021. The complete 2020–24 total was therefore materially above €133 billion, although a consistent full-year 2021 figure is not established by the sources used here.

In 2023, €33 billion went directly to Member States; €30.9 billion was allocated to climate action and energy transformation and €2.1 billion to indirect-cost compensation. In 2024, €24.4 billion went to Member States, while EU-level allocations included:

• Innovation Fund: €2.291 billion  
• Modernisation Fund: €6.271 billion  
• Recovery and Resilience Facility: €5.607 billion  
• EFTA countries and Northern Ireland: approximately €0.25 billion.

These add to approximately €38.8 billion after rounding. The Commission’s allocation data are at https://climate.ec.europa.eu/document/download/ff002f5f-12ac-4818-9be7-724a13258bda_en and https://climate.ec.europa.eu/areas-action/carbon-markets/eu-emissions-trading-system-eu-ets/what-are-ets-revenues-used_en.

Between 2013 and 2022, Member States reported roughly 75% of auction revenue as committed or spent on climate and energy purposes. From 2024 onward, revised rules strengthened climate-related earmarking.

China

China generated no allowance-auction revenue during 2020–24 because allowances were allocated entirely free. Market transaction value is private trading turnover, not government revenue.

Relevant turnover figures were:

• 2022–23: CNY17.26 billion on 263 million tonnes.  
• 2024: CNY18.114 billion on 189 million tonnes.  
• Cumulative through 2024: CNY43.033 billion on 630 million tonnes.

The 2024 turnover figure is reported by the National Center for Climate Change Strategy and International Cooperation at http://www.ncsc.org.cn/xwdt/gnxw/202501/t20250107_1100153.shtml.

Consequently, unlike California and the EU, China’s ETS did not directly finance renewable energy, household compensation or industrial decarbonization programs through auction proceeds.

5. Compliance outcomes

California

California reported 100% compliance for the 2018–20 compliance period: every covered business surrendered the required instruments (https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/news/100-companies-cap-and-trade-program-meet-2020-compliance-obligations).

CARB describes compliance at subsequent annual and multi-year events as nearly 100%. The fourth compliance period covered 2021–23, with annual surrender deadlines in 2022 and 2023 and final surrender in November 2024. California’s result reflects stringent reporting and verification, automatic surrender from compliance accounts and significant financial penalties for shortfalls.

EU ETS

EU ETS compliance was also generally above 99%, although the Commission reports penalties and account-level status rather than one simple annual system-wide percentage.

In 2024, excess-emissions penalties were imposed on 31 stationary operators. Relative to 8,704 stationary installations, that is:

31 / 8,704 × 100 = 0.36%,

meaning approximately 99.64% were not subject to such a penalty. Eleven aircraft operators received excess-emissions penalties, equivalent to:

11 / 393 × 100 = 2.8%.

These ratios are indicators rather than exact surrender-compliance rates because penalties may concern reporting, timing or prior obligations. The underlying figures are in the Commission’s 2024 technical report (https://climate.ec.europa.eu/document/download/ff002f5f-12ac-4818-9be7-724a13258bda_en).

China

Official compliance rates were:

• 2021: 99.61%  
• 2022: 99.88%  
• 2023: 99.98%.

For 2023, entities were required to surrender allowances against approximately 5.244 billion tonnes. The 0.02% unfulfilled share corresponds to roughly:

5.244 billion × 0.0002 = about 1.05 million tonnes,

subject to rounding in the reported compliance percentage.

China’s rates are high, but comparability requires caution. Coal generators’ obligations were capped, gas generators initially faced little or no shortage obligation, and entities received free allowances based on actual output. Compliance was therefore financially less demanding than surrender under a fixed absolute cap.

6. COVID-19 disruption and recovery

California

COVID restrictions sharply reduced transportation fuel use and industrial activity in spring 2020. Secondary-market prices fell below the auction floor and the May 2020 auction sold only a small share of current allowances, producing very little GGRF revenue.

California did not suspend compliance, lower the statutory auction floor or institute a special COVID banking holiday. Instead, existing automatic rules handled excess supply:

• Unsold allowances could be reoffered at later auctions after specified conditions were met.  
• State-owned allowances remaining unsold for more than 24 months moved to the Allowance Price Containment Reserve or were retired.  
• By December 2021, approximately 38.3 million long-unsold state allowances had been retired or transferred to the reserve (https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/cap-and-trade/guidance/guidance_unsold_allowances.pdf).  
• Banking remained unrestricted for covered entities, subject to holding limits.

This avoided a discretionary bailout but preserved a substantial private allowance bank. That bank softened prices during the lockdown and provides future compliance flexibility, while also raising concern that future emissions could exceed future annual cap budgets.

EU ETS

The EU also did not suspend auctions or compliance. The 2020 price fell sharply in March, but recovered before year-end. Verified stationary emissions declined 11.4% in 2020, reflecting both lockdown-related electricity and industrial contraction and pre-existing coal-to-gas and renewable trends.

The MSR was the principal shock absorber. It automatically reduced future auction supply when the total number of allowances in circulation was high. Annual MSR intake was approximately:

• 2021: about 348 million allowances  
• 2022: about 369 million  
• 2023 and 2024: continued substantial withdrawals.

Banking remained allowed; there was no temporary COVID restriction or cancellation of private banked EUAs. From 2021, Phase 4’s tighter cap and the MSR prevented the COVID surplus from recreating the persistent oversupply that had depressed prices after the 2008 financial crisis.

During the later energy crisis and recovery, the EU did not release a large discretionary MSR volume to cap prices. It did, however, increase or front-load auction volumes to help finance the REPowerEU/Recovery and Resilience response. This added supply at the margin, contributing to weaker prices by 2024, while permanent cap reductions and MSR rules preserved long-run scarcity.

China

China’s first national compliance cycle was unusual because trading began in 2021 but covered 2019 and 2020 emissions retrospectively. This incorporated the COVID year into the initial allocation and compliance exercise rather than treating it through a pre-existing market-stability mechanism.

Entities could bank 2019–20 allowances and use them for later compliance. In the 2021–22 cycle, authorities introduced or retained several burden-limiting measures amid weak economic conditions, high coal prices and energy-security concerns:

• A coal generator’s shortage obligation was limited to 20% of verified emissions.  
• Gas-fired generators were protected from net compliance burdens.  
• Entities with a shortage of at least 10% and genuine financial difficulty could borrow 2023 allowances, up to 50% of the shortage.  
• A maximum 5% of obligations could be covered with eligible domestic offsets.  
• The measures helped 202 entities experiencing difficulty comply.

The 2023–24 rules ended temporary borrowing. Banking was also modified to encourage market liquidity: entities could bank a baseline 10,000 tonnes plus 1.5 times their net allowance sales during 2019–24 (https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/news/china-releases-allocation-plan-power-sector-2023-and-2024). These rules addressed hoarding and end-of-cycle price spikes but made China’s bank less unconditional than California’s or the EU’s.

7. Interaction with complementary policies

California

Cap-and-trade was deliberately designed as the “backstop” within a wider policy portfolio rather than the sole emissions driver. Important complementary measures included:

• Renewable Portfolio Standard: 33% renewable retail electricity by 2020, 50% by 2026 and 60% by 2030.  
• SB 100: 100% renewable and zero-carbon retail electricity by 2045 (https://www.cpuc.ca.gov/rps).  
• Low Carbon Fuel Standard, vehicle GHG standards and zero-emission vehicle mandates.  
• Building and appliance efficiency standards.  
• Methane and short-lived climate pollutant regulations.

The interaction is strongest in electricity: renewable mandates reduce fossil generation and allowance demand, lowering allowance prices, while the cap assures that uncovered shortfalls elsewhere cannot cause aggregate covered emissions to exceed the cumulative cap. Auction-funded investment can also accelerate reductions but may reduce allowance demand.

California did not rely on a simple statewide coal-plant phase-out date during 2020–24. Instead, emissions standards, utility procurement rules, renewable requirements and the carbon obligation on imported electricity progressively displaced coal. This matters because much of California’s coal exposure was imported rather than generated in-state.

EU ETS

EU renewable-energy, efficiency and coal policies were central to ETS outcomes:

• Renewable-energy targets and national support systems increased wind and solar generation.  
• National coal phase-outs and plant-closure schedules reduced coal capacity, although dates differed by Member State.  
• The 2021 “Fit for 55” package raised the 2030 economy-wide target to at least 55% below 1990 and tightened the ETS.  
• Energy-efficiency rules, industrial standards and the post-2022 REPowerEU plan reduced fossil-fuel demand.

The carbon price made coal increasingly uneconomic relative to gas and renewables; complementary policies built the generation, grid and efficiency alternatives needed to respond. In 2023, the combination produced a 21% fall in combustion emissions and a 16.5% reduction in total stationary emissions. Because the cap is fixed, renewable mandates can depress EUA demand and prices unless allowance supply is correspondingly reduced—the function increasingly served by tighter cap legislation and the MSR.

China

China’s ETS interacted with a much more administratively managed electricity system. Complementary policies included:

• Renewable portfolio and consumption obligations.  
• National wind and solar expansion targets.  
• Energy-efficiency standards and the retirement or upgrading of inefficient coal units.  
• The “dual-carbon” objectives of peaking CO2 before 2030 and carbon neutrality before 2060.

The division of labor was clear: renewable obligations drove non-fossil generation, while the intensity-based ETS rewarded efficiency improvements within the remaining thermal fleet. IEA modeling found that combining an enhanced ETS with renewable portfolio standards could almost triple power-sector reductions by 2035 relative to renewable standards alone and could reduce electricity emissions to 20% below 2020 by 2035 (https://www.iea.org/reports/enhancing-chinas-ets-for-carbon-neutrality-focus-on-power-sector/executive-summary).

China had no national coal phase-out schedule during 2020–24. Energy-security policy continued to permit coal capacity, so the ETS primarily encouraged lower emissions per unit of coal generation rather than rapid absolute coal retirement. That explains why national and power-sector emissions could rise while carbon intensity improved.

8. Leakage and border adjustment

California

California used two principal anti-leakage instruments:

1. Imported electricity carried a surrender obligation based on reported or default emissions intensity, functioning as a limited border adjustment for electricity.

2. Emissions-intensive, trade-exposed manufacturers received output-based free allocation. Allocation increased with production but used efficiency benchmarks, preserving an incentive to reduce emissions per unit while reducing the incentive to relocate production.

Industrial allocation accounted for approximately 13% of allowance value by 2024. CARB explicitly defines this allocation as protection against production and emissions shifting out of state (https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/our-work/programs/cap-and-trade-program/allowance-allocation/allowance-allocation-industrial).

No authoritative aggregate estimate in the reviewed material identifies how many California plants, jobs or tonnes moved out of state because of cap-and-trade during 2020–24. Consequently, leakage risk can be quantified through the scale of protection, but not as a verified relocation rate. California had no broad carbon border adjustment for cement, steel, refinery products or other industrial goods.

EU ETS

The EU’s 2021–30 carbon-leakage list contained 63 sectors and subsectors representing approximately 94% of industrial ETS emissions. Installations in these sectors were generally eligible for free allocation at 100% of benchmark levels; less exposed sectors received lower shares (https://climate.ec.europa.eu/areas-action/carbon-markets/eu-emissions-trading-system-eu-ets/free-allocation/carbon-leakage_en).

Evidence of actual relocation remained mixed. An ECB study estimated that the ETS reduced EU emissions by approximately 2–2.5 percentage points per year but found some offsetting increases outside the EU and evidence that firms shifted carbon-intensive intermediate production or sourcing abroad (https://www.ecb.europa.eu/pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp2764~3ff8cb597b.en.pdf). It did not establish that a large share of EU heavy industry physically relocated during 2020–24.

The EU nevertheless implemented the period’s most consequential leakage policy: the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism. Its transitional reporting phase began on 1 October 2023 and covered six product groups:

• Cement  
• Iron and steel  
• Aluminium  
• Fertilizers  
• Electricity  
• Hydrogen.

Importers reported embedded emissions during 2023–24 but did not yet purchase CBAM certificates; financial adjustment was scheduled for 2026. Free ETS allocation for corresponding EU producers was therefore not removed during the study period. CBAM made leakage protection progressively border-based, but it could not yet have produced a measured carbon-price payment effect by the end of 2024.

China

China’s output-based, fully free allocation inherently limited competitiveness and relocation pressure. Power prices were also heavily regulated, and electricity is not generally exposed to international trade in the same way as steel or cement. China had no national carbon border adjustment during 2020–24.

The principal leakage concern was therefore domestic rather than international: generation could shift between regulated and less-regulated units, or expanding output could offset intensity improvements. One first-cycle study found intensity at regulated units fell 2.46–3.13%, while comparable non-regulated units’ intensity increased by approximately 7.9–8.3%, suggesting possible operational reshuffling as well as a real treatment effect. This is not proof of industrial relocation, but it illustrates why comprehensive coverage and consistent benchmarks matter.

9. Overall assessment

Environmental effectiveness

The EU ETS produced the clearest absolute reduction relative to a defined baseline: by 2024 stationary emissions were approximately 50% below 2005 and on a trajectory toward the 62% target for 2030. California’s statewide emissions were approximately 20% below 1990 in 2024, but the state still needed roughly another 87 MtCO2e reduction to reach its statutory 2030 target. China’s ETS delivered measurable efficiency improvements but little demonstrated absolute reduction because output growth was accommodated by the allocation formula.

Price strength and resilience

The EU delivered the highest price and strongest scarcity signal. Its MSR successfully absorbed the COVID surplus without suspending the market. California’s price floor prevented a collapse below approximately $17, while automatic treatment of unsold allowances preserved orderly auctions. China avoided instability through free allocation and flexible obligations, but at the cost of a weaker marginal incentive.

Revenue and distribution

California and the EU transformed carbon scarcity into substantial public climate finance. California deposited about $10.2 billion into the GGRF over the five fiscal years most closely corresponding to 2020–24, while the EU generated well over €133 billion over the period based on the available annual and partial-year figures. China generated no public auction proceeds.

Compliance

All three achieved high formal compliance. California reached 100% for 2018–20 and nearly 100% thereafter; EU stationary compliance was above 99%; China rose from 99.61% to 99.98%. These figures do not imply equivalent stringency: China’s free, output-adjusted allocation and capped shortage obligations made compliance materially easier.

Leakage control

California and the EU relied heavily on free allocation. California also priced imported electricity, while the EU added transitional CBAM reporting for six sectors. China largely avoided international leakage pressure through full free allocation and its initial focus on electricity, but that design muted incentives for structural change.

Conclusion

Between 2020 and 2024, the EU ETS evolved into the strongest of the three systems in terms of price, absolute emissions scarcity and border-leakage policy. California combined a moderate but rising carbon price with unusually large, equity-oriented climate investment and an effective price floor, though banking and overlapping regulations made the carbon price’s standalone contribution difficult to isolate. China established the world’s largest market by covered emissions and achieved exceptionally high compliance, but its intensity-based, fully free allocation meant that it functioned principally as an efficiency standard with trading rather than an absolute cap.

COVID demonstrated the importance of automatic stabilizers. California’s auction floor and unsold-allowance rules, and Europe’s MSR, absorbed the shock without emergency suspension. China instead relied on retrospective allocation, broad banking, limited shortage obligations and temporary borrowing. The subsequent recovery showed the trade-off clearly: systems with stronger scarcity controls delivered higher prices and more revenue, while China’s flexible design minimized compliance stress but generated weaker evidence of absolute emissions reductions.

# Comparative MLOps assessment for real-time payment-fraud inference

## Executive conclusion

For 50 million transactions per day across India, Indonesia, and the Philippines, the average arrival rate is:

\[
50{,}000{,}000 / 86{,}400 = 578.7\ \text{transactions/s}
\]

A literal 10× burst is approximately:

\[
578.7 \times 10 = 5{,}787\ \text{transactions/s}
\]

Because consumer-payment traffic is already uneven, capacity should be validated at both approximately 5,800 requests/s and a more conservative 8,000–10,000 requests/s regional aggregate, with one region or availability zone unavailable. A published 50-million-transaction example reported 2,400 TPS sustained, 3,500 TPS short-burst capacity, p95 of 85 ms, and p99 of 150 ms for the complete payment system—not merely inference—illustrating why daily volume alone is an insufficient capacity metric (https://www.staqi.com/blog/scaling-payment-systems-eks).

### Recommended choice

**Use Seldon Core 2 with NVIDIA Triton as the primary serving stack**, provided the startup already intends to operate Kubernetes and can fund a small platform team. It offers the best fit for this particular ensemble:

- Triton’s FIL backend natively supports XGBoost and LightGBM, while its TensorRT, ONNX, PyTorch, and TensorFlow backends can serve the neural component.
- Triton ensembles keep intermediate tensors in-process and support mixed CPU/GPU execution.
- Seldon adds first-class weighted experiments, traffic mirroring, sticky cohorts, model/pipeline abstractions, and integrated asynchronous drift detection.
- Models can be loaded into shared inference servers rather than requiring a completely separate server process for every model, reducing framework sprawl and deployment cold-start exposure.

**KServe with Triton is the strongest alternative** when the organization favors Kubernetes-native, broadly adopted CRDs and Knative/Gateway integration. It has good canary, feature-transformer, inference-graph, and Alibi Detect support, but canary behavior differs by deployment mode, and its Knative/mesh/operator stack is operationally substantial.

**Ray Serve is the best choice when custom Python orchestration dominates**—for example, complex conditional ensembles, graph lookups, shared preprocessing, or rapid experimentation. It is less opinionated about registry, drift, and A/B governance, so those controls must be assembled from MLflow, Feast, Evidently/Alibi, Prometheus, and an external ingress or managed Anyscale service.

**BentoML is the fastest route to a working service and the lowest initial engineering burden.** It is appropriate for a startup that values developer speed over a fully standardized platform. At this scale and regulatory criticality, however, open-source BentoML/Yatai generally requires more custom work for drift monitoring, rollout governance, multi-region operations, and high-density mixed-framework serving. BentoCloud supplies stronger canary and autoscaling features, but introduces a managed-service dependency and potentially material platform charges not included in the infrastructure estimates below.

---

## 1. Workload and architecture assumptions

### Traffic

| Measure | Value |
|---|---:|
| Daily predictions | 50 million |
| Monthly predictions, 30 days | 1.5 billion |
| Average rate | 579 requests/s |
| Literal 10× average burst | 5,787 requests/s |
| Recommended load-test ceiling | 8,000–10,000 requests/s |
| Average per country if evenly distributed | 193 requests/s |
| 10× per-country average | 1,929 requests/s |

The countries will not be evenly distributed, and their peak periods overlap imperfectly. Production sizing should therefore use measured country-level five-minute peaks, not equal allocation.

### Target request path

A practical request path is:

1. Validate payment and identity fields.
2. Fetch online features from a country-local Redis-compatible Feast online store.
3. Run XGBoost and LightGBM—preferably concurrently.
4. Run the neural model, normally on a GPU or ONNX Runtime CPU depending its size.
5. Combine probabilities using a calibrated meta-model or deterministic weighted rule.
6. Apply hard fraud rules and return allow, review, step-up, or block.
7. Asynchronously emit features, predictions, route/model versions, latency, and eventual labels.

Feature retrieval should be separated from GPU inference so slow online-store I/O does not hold GPU capacity. The Ray Feast reference architecture makes this same distinction: preprocessing is I/O-heavy, inference is compute-heavy, and scaling them together wastes CPU, GPU, memory, or all three (https://github.com/ray-project/air-reference-arch/blob/main/ray_serve_feast_tutorial.ipynb).

### Service-level objectives

Reasonable initial goals are:

- **Serving platform plus ensemble, warm cache:** p95 below 30 ms; p99 below 60 ms.
- **Feature lookup plus inference:** p95 below 50 ms; p99 below 100 ms.
- **Full fraud decision path:** p95 below 100 ms; p99 below 150–200 ms.
- **Error rate:** below 0.1%, with deterministic rule fallback if ML is unavailable.
- **No scale-to-zero on the live decision path.**

Razorpay reports that it receives billions of streaming events, has only milliseconds to generate features and predictions, and designed its Flink/Kafka/RocksDB-based “Mitra” platform to generate hundreds of features and predict within 200 ms in a distributed environment (https://razorpay.com/unfiltered/data-science-at-scale-using-apache-flink/). That supports a design in which feature freshness and streaming state are at least as important as the inference server.

---

## 2. Important limitation on latency and cost comparisons

There is no credible, public, controlled benchmark that runs this exact XGBoost–LightGBM–neural ensemble, feature payload, hardware, Kubernetes topology, and 10× burst across all four platforms. Vendor benchmark figures are therefore not directly comparable.

The latency ranges below are **capacity-planning estimates for warm requests**, not claimed vendor measurements. They assume:

- Models are already resident in RAM/GPU memory.
- gRPC or efficient binary V2 inference protocol is used internally.
- Tree models execute concurrently rather than serially.
- Neural inference takes roughly 3–12 ms on the selected accelerator.
- Feature lookup is excluded unless explicitly stated.
- Autoscaling is not allowed to put the live endpoint at zero replicas.
- Each replica operates 10–20% below measured saturation, matching Seldon’s recommendation to retain capacity while new replicas start (https://docs.seldon.ai/seldon-core-2/user-guide/performance-tuning/models/load-testing).

A KServe TorchScript example on a different, single-model workload reported 100 requests/s with p95 6.743 ms and p99 9.286 ms, demonstrating low framework overhead but not the expected latency of this fraud ensemble (https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/0.18/model-serving/predictive-inference/frameworks/triton/torchscript).

---

## 3. Side-by-side assessment

### 3.1 Summary table

## 4. Platform analysis

## 4.1 Seldon Core 2 with Triton Inference Server

### Inference latency and framework compatibility

This pairing has the strongest technical fit for the specified model mix. Triton’s FIL backend supports native XGBoost JSON/UBJSON and LightGBM text models, as well as Treelite checkpoints (https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/triton-inference-server/user-guide/docs/fil_backend/docs/model_support.html). The same server can host the neural model using another backend.

A Triton ensemble is a DAG whose component models can each have dynamic batching. The ensemble scheduler itself is event-driven and described as having minimal overhead; component models are scaled using their own instance groups (https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/triton-inference-server/user-guide/docs/user_guide/ensemble_models.html). That is preferable to serial HTTP calls among three separately containerized services.

Triton can execute on CPU, GPU, or a mixture. NVIDIA’s published pipeline example—not a fraud workload—reported that moving its complete pipeline to GPU reduced latency sixfold and increased throughput from 2,427 to 78,308 samples/s at batch 512 (https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/serving-ml-model-pipelines-on-nvidia-triton-inference-server-with-ensemble-models/). Fraud decisions normally use small batches and strict latency limits, so those absolute gains should not be extrapolated, but the result demonstrates the value of avoiding repeated CPU/GPU transfers.

One caveat is numerical consistency: Triton FIL performs tree inference in single precision, while LightGBM can use double precision. NVIDIA warns this can produce slight output differences (https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/triton-inference-server/user-guide/docs/fil_backend/docs/model_support.html). Threshold-adjacent fraud decisions therefore need offline and shadow validation before migration.

### Burst traffic

Triton dynamic batching can combine stateless requests, with configurable maximum delay, queue size, priority, and timeout (https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/triton-inference-server/user-guide/docs/user_guide/batcher.html). For fraud:

- Use either zero delay or a very small 0.25–1 ms batching window.
- Establish priority classes for payment authorization versus replay or analysis.
- Configure bounded queues and fail fast into rules rather than allowing unbounded latency.
- Keep enough warm capacity for at least the normal peak; do not expect autoscaling alone to absorb an instantaneous 10× attack.

At 5,787 requests/s, if one tuned mixed CPU/GPU replica sustains 400 requests/s below its p99 knee, the arithmetic is:

\[
5{,}787 / 400 = 14.47
\]

Thus at least 15 equivalent replicas are needed globally before N+1 and regional-failure headroom. At a safer 65% utilization:

\[
15 / 0.65 = 23.1
\]

Approximately 23–24 replica-equivalents would be required. The real per-replica number must come from Triton Performance Analyzer using the final feature vector and ensemble.

### A/B testing and rollback

Seldon Core 2 experiments provide weighted traffic splits between models or pipelines, traffic mirroring, and sticky sessions through `x-seldon-route` (https://docs.seldon.ai/seldon-core-2/user-guide/experiment). This is the strongest OSS A/B mechanism among the candidates for fraud because:

- A cohort can remain on one version across repeat transactions.
- A candidate can receive mirrored traffic without controlling the payment decision.
- The complete pipeline—not merely one component—can be compared.
- Rollback can mean setting candidate weight to zero or stopping the experiment, without rebuilding the old model.

Seldon also exposes explicit artifact versions for a model stored in a multi-version Triton repository (https://docs.seldon.ai/seldon-core-2/user-guide/examples/multi-version). During an incident, retain the old artifact and warm replicas until the new version has passed technical and delayed-label checks.

### Feature store and drift

Seldon has no uniquely privileged Feast integration in the evidence reviewed. A lightweight feature-fetch deployment or pipeline step is required. That is a moderate integration cost, especially if maintaining the V2 tensor schema between feature retrieval and Triton.

Drift is stronger: Seldon runs Alibi Detect models like ordinary models, normally on an asynchronous pipeline branch, and publishes alerts through Kafka rather than adding latency to the synchronous output path (https://docs.seldon.ai/seldon-core-2/user-guide/data-science-monitoring/drift).

### Cold starts and operational effort

Seldon can place multiple models on shared Triton/MLServer instances, reducing the need to boot an entire serving pod for every small artifact. Nevertheless, the first deployment must pull images, fetch artifacts, initialize CUDA, allocate GPU memory, and warm kernels. For compact fraud models, a prudent planning range is:

- **Warm shared Triton server, new artifact load:** approximately 2–20 seconds.
- **New pod with cached image:** approximately 10–45 seconds.
- **Uncached image or new GPU node:** approximately 30 seconds to several minutes.

These are planning ranges, not published Seldon measurements. Keep the old and new versions concurrently ready and issue synthetic warm-up requests before shifting traffic.

Initial effort is approximately **8–14 engineer-weeks** for a production-grade, three-country installation, assuming an existing Kubernetes foundation; ongoing effort is roughly **0.75–1.5 platform-engineer equivalents**. The complexity comes from Seldon CRDs, Triton model repositories/configuration, ingress, GPU scheduling, observability, Kafka-based monitoring, and multi-region release controls.

## 4.2 Ray Serve

### Inference latency and model composition

Ray Serve is the most flexible option for expressing the ensemble as Python deployments:

- A feature-fetch actor.
- Parallel XGBoost and LightGBM deployments.
- A GPU neural deployment.
- A lightweight combiner.
- Optional graph, device, or rules services.

Each stage can reserve different CPU/GPU resources and scale independently. This avoids wasting GPU capacity while waiting for Redis. It also permits native framework objects, ONNX Runtime, or calls to Triton.

The trade-off is more Python serialization, actor-routing, and dependency-management exposure than an in-process Triton ensemble. Ray recommends async handlers and dynamic batching, and notes that its default `max_ongoing_requests` is deliberately low—five—to provide backpressure (https://docs.ray.io/en/latest/serve/advanced-guides/performance.html). Untuned defaults are therefore unsuitable for a 5,800-RPS burst.

### Burst traffic

Ray’s autoscaler uses average ongoing requests per replica and adds replicas when queue pressure exceeds the target (https://docs.ray.io/en/latest/serve/autoscaling-guide.html). This is intuitive but reactive: an instantaneous 10× spike first creates queue pressure, then triggers replicas, which still need to load models.

Ray’s advanced guidance recommends setting the maximum queue approximately 20–50% above the target ongoing-request count (https://docs.ray.io/en/latest/serve/advanced-guides/advanced-autoscaling.html). For fraud, combine:

- Nonzero minimum replicas in every country.
- Headroom in the Ray cluster itself, not merely permission to add replicas.
- Aggressive upscale delay and conservative scale-down.
- Small bounded queues.
- Separate replica pools for feature I/O, CPU trees, and GPU neural inference.
- Load shedding and rule-only fallback.

Ray’s own benchmark guidance identifies replica startup latency as a key autoscaling metric because model loading and compilation can make large-model scale-up slow (https://docs.ray.io/en/latest/serve/llm/benchmarks.html). The neural model here should be much smaller than an LLM, but GPU initialization remains material.

### A/B testing and rollback

Open-source Ray Serve does not provide an equally complete, declarative experiment object in the evidence reviewed. A/B testing is usually implemented through:

- A router deployment hashing customer or merchant ID.
- Separate stable and candidate deployment names.
- Shadow calls sent asynchronously.
- An external gateway/service mesh.

This is flexible but puts cohort correctness, metric labels, and fail-safe behavior in application code.

Managed Anyscale performs zero-downtime rollout on separate clusters, gradually shifts traffic, and automatically returns all traffic to the primary version if the candidate fails health checks (https://docs.anyscale.com/services/update). That narrows the rollout gap, but adds managed-service cost and dependency.

Rollback in OSS Ray means redeploying the prior Serve configuration and pinned model/container versions or changing a custom router’s weights. Keep the previous deployments alive during rollout; otherwise rollback is constrained by model reload time.

### Feature store, monitoring, and maintenance

Ray has a reference Feast integration and naturally separates feature I/O from compute-heavy inference (https://github.com/ray-project/air-reference-arch/blob/main/ray_serve_feast_tutorial.ipynb). Integration overhead is therefore relatively low.

Drift is not built into the serving control plane. Use Feast feature-quality monitoring, Evidently, Alibi Detect, or custom jobs. Feast can calculate feature distributions, null rates, percentiles, histograms, baselines, and production-serving-log metrics (https://docs.feast.dev/how-to-guides/feature-monitoring). Prediction and eventual fraud-label monitoring still need a separate pipeline.

Cold-start planning ranges:

- **New actor on an existing warm node:** approximately 5–30 seconds.
- **GPU actor/model initialization:** approximately 15–60 seconds.
- **New cluster node plus image/model:** one to several minutes.

Initial effort is approximately **6–10 engineer-weeks**; ongoing effort **0.5–1.25 engineer equivalents**. Ray reduces Kubernetes custom-resource complexity but adds Ray-cluster lifecycle, Python environment isolation, actor debugging, and custom release/monitoring logic.

## 4.3 KServe on Kubernetes

### Latency and ensemble implementation

KServe can use Triton as the predictor, so its core model execution can be close to Seldon/Triton. An `InferenceGraph` can sequence, switch, or route among services (https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/0.19/model-serving/inferencegraph/image-pipeline). For this ensemble, two patterns are possible:

1. **One Triton ensemble inside one KServe predictor:** lowest network overhead and preferred for the tree/neural combination.
2. **Several InferenceServices connected by an InferenceGraph:** easier independent scaling but introduces service hops, serialization, and more failure points.

The first pattern should have warm latency close to Seldon/Triton; differences will mostly come from ingress, mesh, logging, and deployment topology.

### Burst traffic and cold start

KServe serverless mode can leverage Knative autoscaling and scale-to-zero, but scale-to-zero is inappropriate for payment authorization. Set minimum replicas above zero and maintain pre-provisioned GPU capacity.

KServe’s own TorchScript documentation notes that pulling a Triton image and large model may exceed a default 12-second timeout (https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/0.18/model-serving/predictive-inference/frameworks/triton/torchscript). That provides direct evidence that cold starts can exceed transaction latency budgets by orders of magnitude.

Planning ranges are:

- **Cached pod and small model:** approximately 10–40 seconds.
- **Uncached Triton image/model:** approximately 30–120 seconds.
- **GPU-node provisioning:** potentially several minutes.

Canaries must become Ready and receive warm-up probes before traffic weight increases. For burst resilience, use a warm floor, fast concurrency/RPS autoscaling, spare nodes, pod topology spread, and bounded queues.

### A/B testing and rollback

KServe supports `canaryTrafficPercent`, running the old and new revisions concurrently and routing a configured percentage to the candidate (https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/predictive-inference/rollout-strategies/canary-example). Promotion removes the canary percentage and moves all traffic to the new revision.

A significant constraint is that the documented predictive-inference canary strategy is supported only in serverless deployment mode. KServe ModelMesh improves multi-model density, but its documentation says transformers, explainers, and canary rollouts do not currently fully apply in ModelMesh mode (https://github.com/kserve/modelmesh-serving/blob/main/docs/README.md). That creates an architectural choice between high-density serving and richer rollout features.

Rollback is strong when previous Knative revisions remain available: return traffic to the previous revision or restore its storage URI/spec. Avoid garbage-collecting the prior revision until delayed fraud metrics are available.

### Feature store and drift

KServe documents a Feast transformer that retrieves online features in preprocessing, calls the predictor, and passes the result into postprocessing (https://github.com/kserve/website/blob/main/docs/model-serving/predictive-inference/transformers/feast-feature-store/feast-feature-store.md). This reduces custom scaffolding, but the transformer-to-predictor HTTP call can add latency. For strict p99 targets, use local gRPC, connection pooling, and independent scaling, or enrich the event before it reaches KServe.

KServe integrates Alibi Detect through asynchronous payload logging and Knative processing for drift and outlier detection (https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/predictive-inference/detect/alibi/alibi-detect).

Initial effort is approximately **8–14 engineer-weeks**, with **1–1.75 engineer equivalents** ongoing. The operator, Knative, networking/gateway, cert management, GPU autoscaling, payload logging, and monitoring stack make KServe the most Kubernetes-intensive option.
