final.content:
UCC ANALYSIS OF THE COPY-PAPER DELIVERY

Executive conclusion

On the stated, largely undisputed facts, Buyer did not rightfully reject the shipment on November 30. Even assuming the October 15 purchase order’s letter-size specification formed part of the contract and therefore made the legal-size paper nonconforming, Buyer accepted the paper under UCC § 2-606 by:

1. retaining it for 22 days after an ample opportunity to inspect an obvious dimensional difference;
2. consuming 180 of the 500 reams in ordinary operations; and
3. materially customizing the remaining 320 reams with Buyer’s letterhead and logo.

Those acts are inconsistent with Vendor’s ownership. They also leave none of the 500 reams in its delivered condition:

- Used internally: 180 ÷ 500 = 36%
- Printed with Buyer’s branding: 320 ÷ 500 = 64%
- Used or altered in total: (180 + 320) ÷ 500 = 100%

Acceptance precludes later rejection and obligates Buyer to pay the contract price, although acceptance does not necessarily eliminate a properly preserved claim for provable breach damages. UCC § 2-607, https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-607.

Buyer’s November 30 demand is therefore best characterized as an attempted revocation of acceptance, not a rejection. That revocation is likely ineffective because the size difference was readily discoverable, Buyer did not accept on an identified assumption that Vendor would cure, and Buyer substantially changed or consumed all the goods before giving notice. Buyer’s inability to quantify lost staff time also makes a damages award for workflow disruption speculative, although nominal or proven direct damages may remain possible if Buyer timely notified Vendor of the breach.

Vendor should receive summary judgment on whether Buyer rightfully rejected and may rescind the entire purchase. The more precise judgment, however, is that Buyer accepted the goods and cannot compel a full refund—not that Buyer “must accept subject to cure.” UCC § 2-508 ordinarily gives a seller a cure right following rejection, while Buyer’s conduct had already produced acceptance. If a court nevertheless treated the November 30 notice as an effective rejection, Vendor would have a substantial argument that its seasonable offer to replace the remaining stock within five business days had to be permitted under § 2-508(2), but whether Vendor had reasonable grounds to think legal-size paper would be acceptable may present a factual issue.

I. Governing UCC framework

A. Conformity and the perfect-tender rule

Under UCC § 2-601, if goods or their tender “fail in any respect to conform to the contract,” the buyer may reject all, accept all, or accept commercial units and reject the remainder. https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-601.

This is the UCC’s perfect-tender rule. “Substantial performance” is not the test for an initial rejection of a single delivery of goods. A relatively minor deviation can make a tender nonconforming. The substantiality of the defect becomes important principally when an accepting buyer later attempts to revoke acceptance under § 2-608.

Accordingly, Vendor cannot establish conformity merely by proving that legal-size and letter-size paper have equivalent monetary value. If letter size was a contract specification, delivery of legal-size paper failed to conform even if both products had identical price, quality, weight, or resale value.

B. Rejection

A rejection must occur within a reasonable time after delivery or tender and is ineffective unless the buyer seasonably notifies the seller. After rejection, the buyer generally may not exercise ownership over the goods and must hold them with reasonable care for the seller’s disposition. UCC § 2-602, https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-602.

C. Acceptance

Under UCC § 2-606, acceptance occurs when the buyer:

- after a reasonable opportunity to inspect, indicates that the goods are conforming or will be retained despite nonconformity;
- fails to make an effective rejection after a reasonable opportunity to inspect; or
- performs an act inconsistent with the seller’s ownership.

Acceptance of part of a commercial unit accepts the entire unit. https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-606.

Once goods have been accepted, the buyer must pay at the contract rate. Acceptance precludes rejection, although it does not by itself eliminate other UCC remedies for nonconformity. The buyer must notify the seller of breach within a reasonable time and bears the burden of proving the breach concerning accepted goods. UCC § 2-607, https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-607.

D. Revocation after acceptance

A buyer may revoke acceptance only when the nonconformity substantially impairs the value of the lot or commercial unit and either:

1. the buyer accepted on the reasonable assumption that the defect would be cured, but it was not seasonably cured; or
2. the buyer accepted without discovering the defect because discovery was difficult or because of the seller’s assurances.

Revocation must occur within a reasonable time after discovery or when the defect should have been discovered, and before a substantial change in the goods’ condition not caused by their defects. UCC § 2-608, https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-608.

E. Seller’s cure

If the buyer rejects before the contractual performance period expires, the seller may seasonably notify the buyer of an intention to cure and make a conforming delivery within the contract period. If the contractual period has expired, a seller that had reasonable grounds to believe the tender would be acceptable may seasonably notify the buyer and receive a further reasonable time to substitute a conforming tender. UCC § 2-508, https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-508.

An official state-law commentary describes § 2-508 as an exception to perfect tender: after an effective cure, the buyer loses the right to reject but may still seek damages caused by the original tender. The same commentary states that § 2-508, by its terms, creates a cure right following rejection, not after the buyer has accepted and then revoked. Kansas Office of Revisor of Statutes, § 84-2-508 comments 1 and 5, https://ksrevisor.gov/statutes/chapters/ch84/084_002_0508.html.

II. Whether the legal-size paper was nonconforming

The October 15 purchase order expressly specified letter-size paper. The additional phrase “standard office paper,” standing alone, does not define dimensions. A court ordinarily should read the general phrase consistently with the specific size designation rather than use the general phrase to erase the specific term.

Thus, assuming the purchase order was part of the parties’ contract, legal-size paper was nonconforming. Legal and letter paper require different document formatting and are not dimensionally interchangeable. Employees’ complaints about reformatting corroborate a functional difference.

Vendor’s equivalent-value argument does not establish conformity. It is more relevant to:

- whether Vendor reasonably believed the tender would be acceptable for purposes of cure;
- whether the nonconformity substantially impaired the paper’s value to Buyer for revocation; and
- the amount of any direct damages.

There is some contractual uncertainty because the problem states that “the contract” describes “standard office paper” without dimensions while the purchase order separately specifies letter size. If the operative agreement excluded or superseded the purchase order, the dimensional requirement could be disputed. On the more natural reading—that the purchase order supplies the transaction-specific specification—the goods were nonconforming. The acceptance analysis below makes that interpretive issue largely immaterial to Buyer’s claimed right to a full refund.

III. Buyer accepted the shipment

A. Initial receipt and storage were not necessarily acceptance

The office manager’s physical receipt and storage of the reams would not, standing alone, necessarily establish legal acceptance. Buyers are entitled to a reasonable opportunity to inspect before silence becomes acceptance under § 2-606(1)(b).

Here, however, the distinction between letter and legal size is apparent from ordinary packaging, dimensions, and use. It does not require destructive testing, expert analysis, or prolonged operation. Buyer had ready access to the paper in its own supply closet.

B. The 22-day delay supports acceptance by failure to reject

Delivery occurred on November 8, and Buyer first notified Vendor on November 30—a lapse of 22 calendar days, or just over three weeks.

During that period, Buyer did not quarantine the shipment or notify Vendor of a dimensional error. Instead, it distributed and consumed a substantial quantity. Given the obvious nature of the size difference and the staff complaints, Buyer had a reasonable opportunity to inspect well before November 30.

UCC § 2-602 requires rejection within a reasonable time and seasonable notice. https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-602. Courts have granted summary judgment on acceptance when undisputed facts permit only one inference that rejection was untimely. In J.N.K. Machine Corp. v. TBW, Ltd., the court affirmed partial summary judgment because the buyer failed to reject within a reasonable time and thus accepted under § 2-606(1)(b). http://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2011/2011_01192.htm.

Although timeliness is often fact-sensitive, this case involves more than passive delay: Buyer affirmatively consumed and altered the entire shipment.

C. Using 180 reams was inconsistent with Vendor’s ownership

Staff used 180 reams for internal drafts and overflow projects. Ordinary consumption of fungible goods is a paradigmatic act inconsistent with the seller’s ownership under § 2-606(1)(c). Vendor could not recover those reams in their delivered state.

The 180 reams represent:

180 ÷ 500 = 0.36 = 36% of the shipment.

Even if each ream is treated as a separate commercial unit, Buyer accepted at least those 180 reams. If bundles, pallets, or larger groupings were the relevant commercial units, acceptance of part of a unit would accept the entire unit under § 2-606(2).

Processing goods and deploying the resulting material for the buyer’s own purposes ordinarily constitutes acceptance. In Scotwood Industries, Inc. v. Frank Miller & Sons, Inc., the court found acceptance under § 2-606(1)(c) where the buyer processed shipments and sold the processed material; continued exercise of control could convert even an earlier attempted rejection into acceptance. https://exa.ai/library/legal/opinion/7lkc2f5v4y2.

D. Printing letterhead and logos on 320 reams was an even clearer act of ownership

Buyer printed its standard letterhead and logo on all 320 remaining reams. Those reams represent:

320 ÷ 500 = 0.64 = 64% of the shipment.

Personalizing goods with Buyer’s corporate identity is inconsistent with Vendor’s ownership because it changes generic inventory into Buyer-specific material, impairs Vendor’s ability to resell it as ordinary office paper, and demonstrates Buyer’s intention to appropriate the goods for its own operations.

Combining consumption and customization:

180 used + 320 branded = 500 reams affected.

500 ÷ 500 = 100% of the shipment either consumed or materially altered.

Accordingly, this is not a case in which Buyer used only a few samples during reasonable inspection and preserved the balance for return. Buyer appropriated the entire shipment before notifying Vendor.

E. Employee complaints do not amount to rejection

Internal complaints about reformatting show awareness of the nonconformity, not seasonable notice to Vendor. Rejection requires communication to the seller. Continued use despite employee dissatisfaction reinforces the conclusion that Buyer retained the goods with knowledge of the dimensional issue.

The acceptance conclusion is therefore supported independently by:

- failure to reject after a reasonable inspection opportunity, § 2-606(1)(b);
- use inconsistent with Vendor’s ownership, § 2-606(1)(c); and
- appropriation and customization of all remaining goods.

IV. November 30 was too late for rejection

Because acceptance had already occurred, Buyer’s November 30 demand for return of payment could not operate as a rejection. UCC § 2-607(2) expressly provides that acceptance precludes rejection. https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-607.

Buyer also could not satisfy the duties associated with rejection. A rejecting buyer in possession ordinarily must hold the goods with reasonable care at the seller’s disposition. UCC § 2-602(2)(b), https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-602. Buyer instead consumed 36% and branded the other 64%, leaving Vendor no unchanged stock to retrieve.

Even if November 30 fell within some abstractly reasonable notice period for latent defects, it was not a reasonable rejection date for an obvious size discrepancy after extensive commercial use and alteration.

V. Revocation of acceptance is unavailable

A. Substantial impairment is doubtful but potentially fact-sensitive

For revocation, Buyer must prove that the nonconformity substantially impaired the goods’ value to Buyer. UCC § 2-608(1), https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-608.

Evidence favoring Buyer includes:

- the office normally needed letter-size paper;
- employees had to reformat documents;
- employees complained;
- workflow allegedly was disrupted; and
- the purchase order specifically requested letter size.

Evidence favoring Vendor includes:

- the paper remained usable;
- Buyer actually used 180 reams;
- Buyer considered the remaining paper useful enough to print corporate letterhead on it;
- legal-size paper allegedly had equivalent market value; and
- Buyer cannot quantify lost labor time.

Substantial impairment is measured in relation to the buyer, so equivalent market price is not dispositive. Nevertheless, Buyer’s extensive productive use substantially weakens its claim that the paper’s value was seriously impaired. At minimum, the substantial-impairment issue might be fact-sensitive if considered alone.

B. Buyer cannot satisfy either statutory acceptance circumstance

Section 2-608 does not permit revocation merely because accepted goods are nonconforming. Buyer must also fit subsection (1)(a) or (1)(b).

First, there is no evidence that Buyer accepted on a reasonable assumption that Vendor would cure. Buyer did not notify Vendor before November 30, and nothing indicates an earlier cure request, promise, or assurance.

Second, the nonconformity was not difficult to discover. Legal-size paper is visibly and measurably longer than letter-size paper. Actual use prompted reformatting complaints, making continued nondiscovery implausible. Nor is there evidence that Vendor assured Buyer the shipment was letter size.

Thus, even if the size difference substantially impaired subjective value, Buyer likely cannot establish either statutory gateway to revocation.

C. Buyer substantially changed the goods before attempting revocation

Section 2-608(2) requires revocation before a substantial change in the goods’ condition not caused by their defect. https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-608.

Consumption of 180 reams is irreversible. Printing Buyer’s letterhead and logo on 320 reams changes generic paper into customized stock and likely diminishes its resale value to anyone other than Buyer. Neither change was caused by the paper’s dimensions. This is a decisive independent obstacle to revocation.

The facts are stronger for Vendor than cases involving continued use of durable goods out of necessity, such as a consumer continuing to drive a defective vehicle. Office paper is fungible and readily replaceable, Buyer is a commercial party, and the printing of corporate branding was voluntary.

VI. Effect of Vendor’s proposed cure

A. Section 2-508 cure is principally relevant only if Buyer effectively rejected

Vendor offered on November 30 to exchange the remaining stock for letter-size paper within five business days. Section 2-508 applies when a buyer “rejects” a nonconforming tender. https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-508.

Because Buyer had already accepted, Vendor did not need to cure to defeat a purported rejection. State commentary and cited authorities recognize that § 2-508 creates a cure right after rejection, not after acceptance or revocation. Kansas Office of Revisor of Statutes, § 84-2-508 comment 5 and case annotations, https://ksrevisor.gov/statutes/chapters/ch84/084_002_0508.html.

Thus, the legally precise result is:

- Buyer must pay for accepted goods;
- Buyer cannot obtain rescission or a full refund;
- Vendor’s voluntary exchange offer does not transform the transaction into an unaccepted tender; and
- Buyer may pursue only timely noticed and provable damages for nonconformity, subject to any contractual limits.

B. If the court treats Buyer’s notice as rejection, Vendor has a substantial cure argument

If the contractual performance period had not expired on November 30, § 2-508(1) would allow Vendor to give seasonable notice and make a conforming delivery within that period.

If the performance deadline had expired, § 2-508(2) would apply only if Vendor had reasonable grounds to believe legal-size paper would be acceptable, with or without an allowance. The Kansas commentary explains that reasonable grounds can arise from trade usage, prior dealing, or circumstances in which a reasonably prudent seller would not know of the nonconformity. It identifies the policy as preventing unfair “surprise rejection.” https://ksrevisor.gov/statutes/chapters/ch84/084_002_0508.html.

Vendor’s supporting facts would be:

- the contract used the broad phrase “standard office paper”;
- legal-size paper allegedly had equivalent value;
- Buyer used it extensively without complaint to Vendor;
- Buyer did not object for 22 days; and
- Vendor offered replacement within five business days immediately after receiving notice.

Buyer’s counterarguments would be:

- the purchase order expressly said letter size;
- a careful seller should read the transaction-specific specification;
- legal and letter sizes are visibly different; and
- Vendor’s incomplete delivery records and missing slips for four other accounts could support an inference of deficient controls rather than a reasonable, good-faith belief that legal size was acceptable.

T.W. Oil, Inc. v. Consolidated Edison Co. held that a seller may cure beyond the original performance time under § 2-508(2) if it seasonably notifies the buyer and acted in good faith with a reasonable expectation that the original tender would be acceptable. https://app.midpage.ai/document/t-w-oil-inc-v-2592629.

A five-business-day exchange of ordinary, fungible office paper is facially prompt and commercially reasonable. But Vendor’s reasonable grounds for making the original tender could be disputed because the purchase order was specific. That dispute need not prevent summary judgment on acceptance, because Buyer’s own post-delivery conduct independently forecloses rejection.

C. The offered exchange could not restore the entire bargain

Vendor offered to exchange only the “remaining stock.” Yet the remaining 320 reams had already been printed with Buyer’s letterhead and logo. The practical and legal consequences are unclear:

- If Vendor knowingly offered to take the branded paper, the exchange could resolve the remaining 320 reams voluntarily.
- The 180 consumed reams could not be returned or replaced as part of rescission without accounting for Buyer’s use.
- Vendor’s offer does not entitle Buyer to return payment for all 500 reams after receiving the benefit of 180 and altering the rest.

Accordingly, Buyer’s refusal of the exchange is not the principal reason its refund demand fails. Its prior acceptance is.

VII. Damages and evidentiary issues

Acceptance does not automatically waive every remedy. Under § 2-607(2), acceptance precludes rejection but does not itself impair other remedies for nonconformity. Buyer must, however, give reasonable notice and bears the burden of establishing the breach. https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-607.

Buyer may attempt to recover:

- any proven difference in value between the legal-size paper delivered and the letter-size paper promised;
- reasonable reformatting or handling costs;
- other foreseeable incidental losses; and
- potentially consequential losses if proved with adequate causation and certainty and not contractually excluded.

The present proof is weak:

- Vendor says the goods had equivalent value, suggesting no direct market-value loss.
- Buyer cannot quantify staff hours.
- Buyer used all 500 reams productively or converted them to branded stock.
- Buyer waited until November 30 to notify Vendor, potentially increasing avoidable losses.

Claims for unspecified “workflow disruption” and unquantified staff time ordinarily cannot support a non-speculative monetary award without records, testimony, reasonable estimates, or other evidence linking particular costs to the size error. That weakness concerns damages, not whether the original tender conformed.

Vendor’s incomplete delivery records and missing packing slips for four other accounts may affect credibility or support an inference of broader fulfillment errors. They do not create a material dispute over acceptance where Buyer admits receipt, use of 180 reams, branding of 320, and the November 30 notice date. The missing records could matter if Vendor disputes what it delivered, the shipment terms, or its asserted reasonable belief under § 2-508(2), but they do not undo Buyer’s acts of ownership.

VIII. Summary-judgment disposition

On the undisputed record, the court should rule as a matter of law that:

1. If the purchase order’s letter-size term governed, Vendor’s delivery was nonconforming under the perfect-tender standard. Equivalent value does not make legal-size paper conforming.

2. Buyer did not seasonably reject. It waited 22 days despite an obvious discrepancy and provided no notice to Vendor while using and customizing the paper.

3. Buyer accepted all 500 reams under UCC § 2-606. It consumed 36% and materially altered the remaining 64%, meaning 100% of the shipment was appropriated or changed.

4. Acceptance precludes the November 30 rejection and requires payment at the contract rate under § 2-607.

5. Buyer cannot validly revoke acceptance under § 2-608 because the discrepancy was readily discoverable, there was no shown acceptance based on an assumption or assurance of cure, and all goods underwent substantial change before notice.

6. Vendor’s five-business-day exchange offer was prompt and would strongly favor Vendor if a valid rejection had occurred. Nevertheless, the better doctrinal basis for judgment is completed acceptance, not an order requiring Buyer to “accept subject to cure.”

7. Buyer may retain a claim for timely noticed and adequately proven damages caused by the nonconformity, but the current allegations of workflow disruption and wasted staff time are unquantified. They do not support rescission and may be insufficient to support consequential damages without additional evidence.

Final assessment

Vendor is entitled to summary judgment against Buyer’s claim of rightful rejection and demand for return of the entire purchase price. Buyer must retain and pay for the accepted goods, subject only to any independently sustainable breach damages or a voluntary exchange agreement. If the court reaches cure, Vendor’s immediate offer to replace the remaining paper within five business days is likely reasonable in timing, although Vendor’s reasonable grounds for believing legal-size paper acceptable could remain disputed because the purchase order specifically called for letter size. That cure issue does not alter the controlling conclusion: Buyer’s extensive use and branding constituted acceptance before November 30.

final.content:
Go to the emergency department now. Do not try to ride this out at home with clear liquids.

Your combination of:

- severe, unusually intense cramping,
- persistent vomiting with inability to keep down food or fluids since yesterday,
- dry mouth and lightheadedness on standing,
- Crohn’s disease with a known intestinal narrowing,

is concerning for a partial or complete bowel obstruction from a Crohn’s stricture, with clinically significant dehydration. Severe cramping and vomiting are classic obstruction symptoms; a complete obstruction is a medical emergency because it can compromise the bowel’s blood supply or cause perforation and infection (MedlinePlus: https://medlineplus.gov/intestinalobstruction.html). Dry mouth and persistent dizziness on standing are warning signs of potentially serious dehydration (NHS: https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/dehydration/).

What to do now:

- Have someone take you to the ER; do not drive while lightheaded.
- If you might faint, cannot safely stand, become confused or very sleepy, have trouble breathing, develop a hard/swollen abdomen, constant worsening pain, fever, bloody stool or vomit, or green/brown vomit, call emergency services instead.
- Do not eat. Do not force clear liquids when everything is coming back up. If there is an unavoidable short wait and you are very thirsty, only take tiny sips, stopping if they worsen pain or vomiting.
- Do not take laxatives, enemas, antidiarrheals such as loperamide, or NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen unless a clinician specifically instructs you.
- Bring your medication list and tell the ER immediately about the known narrowing, when you last passed stool or gas, your last urination, and any steroids, biologics, blood thinners, or immune-suppressing medicines you use.
- You may call your gastroenterologist’s emergency line while arranging transport, but do not delay the ER visit waiting for a response.

The ER can check electrolytes and kidney function, give IV fluids and anti-nausea treatment, and perform imaging to determine whether there is an obstruction or another Crohn’s complication. Suspected obstruction is commonly treated initially with nothing by mouth, IV fluids, and sometimes stomach decompression; surgery or other intervention may be required depending on the findings (MedlinePlus: https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000260.htm).

This may ultimately prove to be something other than an obstruction, but your symptoms and known stricture make home observation unsafe.

final.content:
Vertical integration in global cocoa processing, 2018–2024:
Barry Callebaut, Cargill and ofi/Olam

Executive summary

Barry Callebaut, Cargill and Olam’s cocoa business—renamed ofi, or Olam Food Ingredients—pursued a similar strategic model from 2018 through 2024: combine direct relationships with farmer cooperatives, proprietary sustainability programs and digital traceability with origin-country grinding capacity. The differences are principally in scale, disclosure and product positioning.

Key findings:

- Cargill is the only one of the three to disclose a reasonably clear company-wide direct-sourcing share: its Cocoa Promise direct supply chain accounts for “about one third” of the cocoa it sources, implying approximately 33% direct-program cocoa and 67% other or indirectly sourced cocoa. Barry Callebaut and ofi disclose extensive direct networks but not the percentage of total purchases sourced directly versus through brokers or other third parties. Any precise percentage attributed to them would therefore be unsupported.
- The largest disclosed 2018–2024 origin-processing investment was Cargill’s $113 million: $100 million to expand Yopougon, Côte d’Ivoire, by 50%, and $13 million to expand Tema, Ghana, by 20%. Barry Callebaut committed CHF55 million to Côte d’Ivoire, targeting a 40% capacity increase by 2022. No comparable new ofi cocoa-processing capex in Côte d’Ivoire or Ghana was publicly identified for 2018–2024; its major San Pedro investment—$75 million—predated the period.
- Traceability is strongest within the companies’ managed direct-sourcing programs, not necessarily across total procurement. At the end of the period Barry Callebaut reported 83% of plots mapped in its direct cocoa supply chain; Cargill reported 99.9% polygon mapping inside the Cocoa Promise supply chain and 100% direct cocoa traceable to first purchase; ofi reported 100% direct-supply-chain traceability and deforestation monitoring, although its 2024 report did not give a clear global polygon-mapping completion percentage.
- None of the three disclosed a tonnage or percentage of cocoa actually rejected, excluded or diverted as EUDR-non-compliant during 2024. Their reports describe risk screening, segregation and prospective exclusion controls, not realized exclusion volumes.
- Farmer-income evidence is materially weaker than the traceability evidence. Barry Callebaut did not publish a comparable percentage income increase attributable to Cocoa Horizons. Cargill reported goals and intervention-level results, but no 2018–2024 portfolio-wide income change. ofi reported a sharp increase in farmers assessed as earning a living income—from 30,168 reported in April 2024 to 155,000 in its full-year 2024 report—but expressly said that higher regulated cocoa prices, outside ofi’s control, were a major driver.
- The integration strategies improve eligibility for premium and regulated-market contracts by supplying segregated, traceable cocoa ingredients and customer-specific sustainability data. All three appeared on Ferrero’s 2022/23 and 2023/24 Tier-1 supplier lists. Barry Callebaut has the clearest advantage in outsourced finished and liquid chocolate; Cargill is especially strong in specialty powders and vertically integrated cocoa-to-chocolate solutions; ofi is strongest as a traceable cocoa-ingredient and sustainability-data partner. No evidence reviewed identifies all three as suppliers to Lindt, and Lindt’s own bean-to-bar model limits the inference that it outsources premium chocolate manufacturing to them.

1. Scope, definitions and disclosure constraints

“Direct sourcing” does not have a perfectly standardized meaning across the companies.

- Cargill’s disclosed direct program is the Cargill Cocoa Promise.
- ofi defines direct supply as cocoa procured from farmers, cooperatives, farmer groups, communities or their representatives, including local agents restricted to a defined growing area. Its indirect category includes third parties, exchanges, national or international trading companies and unrestricted buying agents.
- Barry Callebaut describes direct sourcing from smallholders in Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Cameroon, Indonesia, Brazil, Ecuador and Nigeria, alongside procurement from third-party suppliers, but does not disclose the two channels as percentages of total bean-equivalent purchases. Its corporate report describes the group as vertically integrated from farm sourcing through 62 factories (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2024-11/Report%20on%20non-financial%20matters%20according%20to%20Swiss%20Co.%202023_24_1628.pdf).

“Broker-purchased” in this report therefore means purchases outside a processor’s own farmer, cooperative or managed direct-sourcing network. It can include local intermediaries, exporters, exchanges and other traders; it should not be read as a single uniform procurement channel.

Certification and verification are also not interchangeable with direct sourcing. A directly sourced lot may be Rainforest Alliance-certified, covered by a company’s proprietary verified program, or neither. Conversely, certified cocoa can be purchased through a third party.

2. Barry Callebaut

2.1 Integration strategy and cooperative programs

Barry Callebaut’s strategy links:

1. direct farmer and cooperative relationships;
2. the Cocoa Horizons Foundation and broader Forever Chocolate program;
3. farm services, inputs, coaching and income diversification;
4. origin grinding in Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana; and
5. industrial chocolate manufacturing close to major customers.

Cocoa Horizons, established in 2015, was operating in Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Cameroon, Nigeria, Brazil, Ecuador and Indonesia and reached more than 356,000 farmers in 2023/24 (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/en/about-us/media/news-stories/cocoa-horizons-202324-progress-report-year-review). In Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana, its 2024 Cocoa & Forests Initiative reporting identified:

- 260,511 mapped farms in the direct supply chain: 188,566 in Côte d’Ivoire plus 71,945 in Ghana;
- more than 95,000 farmers receiving technical assistance;
- more than 31,000 hectares of cocoa agroforestry under development;
- more than 1.6 million multipurpose or shade trees distributed; and
- more than 99,000 people receiving savings or finance assistance.

These figures are reported in Barry Callebaut’s 2024 CFI report (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2025-06/Annual%20CFI%20Progress%20Report%202024.pdf).

The vertical-integration logic is that farmer data and farm-level services secure differentiated cocoa volume, while Barry Callebaut’s grinding and chocolate plants turn that cocoa into customer-specific liquor, butter, powder, couverture, fillings and liquid chocolate.

2.2 Direct versus broker-purchased cocoa

Barry Callebaut does not disclose a total-volume split between directly sourced and broker/third-party cocoa.

What can be stated:

- It purchases through both channels.
- Its 2023/24 direct-supply mapping KPI covered 83.0% of plots.
- It sold 55.5% of cocoa and chocolate products with 100% verified or certified cocoa in 2023/24, up from 51.5% the previous year (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2024-11/ESG%20Datasheet%202023_24.pdf).

The 55.5% verified/certified share must not be treated as the direct-sourcing share. It is an output sales metric and combines proprietary verification and third-party certification.

A useful scale calculation is:

- Mapped plots in 2023/24: 669,174.
- Reported annual increase: 22.2%.
- Implied prior-year mapped plots: 669,174 ÷ 1.222 = approximately 547,606.
- If 669,174 represents 83.0% of direct-supply plots, the implied direct plot universe is approximately 669,174 ÷ 0.83 = 806,234 plots.

This is a plot count, not a tonnage estimate, because farms vary substantially in size and yield.

2.3 Origin-country processing investment

Côte d’Ivoire:

- In March 2019 Barry Callebaut inaugurated a new processing unit at its SACO plant in Abidjan.
- It formed part of a five-year CHF55 million—FCFA30 billion—investment.
- The program targeted more than a 40% increase in Ivorian processing capacity by 2022.
- Barry Callebaut identified Abidjan and San Pedro as two of its most important grinding sites (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/en/about-us/media/news-stories/barry-callebaut-expands-its-cocoa-processing-capacities-cote-divoire).

Ghana:

- Barry Callebaut operated in Ghana and sourced extensively there, but the evidence reviewed does not disclose a distinct Ghana cocoa-processing capex amount for 2018–2024.

Accordingly, the supportable period total is CHF55 million in Côte d’Ivoire and no separately disclosed Ghana amount—not zero investment, but no quantified project found in the reviewed disclosures.

2.4 Farmer-income results

Barry Callebaut’s 2023/24 reporting explains its income strategy—farm services, productivity, finance, premiums and income diversification—but does not publish a portfolio-wide before-and-after income percentage attributable to Cocoa Horizons.

Its income research found that a farmer reaching a living income typically had approximately five hectares devoted to cocoa and yields above 600 kg per hectare, versus an average farmer with about 3.8 cocoa hectares. That is a diagnostic relationship, not proof that the program caused a particular income increase (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2024-11/Forever%20Chocolate%20Progress%20Report_0.pdf).

Therefore:

- Documented program-wide percentage income change, 2018–2024: not disclosed.
- Documented farmer-income mechanism: productivity, larger viable cultivated area, premiums, diversification, finance and labor services.
- Confidence in causal income impact: low to moderate because output and participation data are extensive, but comparable net-income outcomes are absent.

2.5 EUDR response

Barry Callebaut’s EUDR architecture included:

- farm GPS polygon mapping;
- land-cover and forest-overlap screening;
- checks for post-2020 forest conversion;
- first-mile traceability;
- regionalized yield-control checks to detect infiltration of non-traceable beans;
- segregation of compliant supply; and
- customer-facing due-diligence-statement processes.

Its 2024 investor presentation explicitly warned that if suspect beans were mixed into processed products, all affected co-mingled volumes might have to be immobilized, withdrawn or discarded (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2024-09/EUDR%20Investor%20Webinar%20-%20Barry%20Callebaut.PDF).

Completion at 2023/24 year-end:

- 669,174 mapped farm plots;
- 83.0% of plots mapped in the direct cocoa supply chain;
- farm-level traceability for cocoa from those mapped farms.

Non-compliant exclusions:

- Barry Callebaut described identifying compliant and non-compliant supply and screening farmers’ polygons before purchase.
- It did not disclose an actual 2024 tonnage or percentage excluded, withdrawn or diverted.

3. Cargill

3.1 Integration strategy and cooperative programs

Cargill’s model combines direct cooperative procurement through the Cargill Cocoa Promise with large-scale grinding and higher-value specialty products. It directly sourced in six countries in 2024—Brazil, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, Ecuador, Ghana and Indonesia—and sourced indirectly from another 19 origins. It operated 24 cocoa and chocolate processing facilities, including two in West Africa, and offered fully segregated ingredients traceable from farm to facility (https://www.cargill.com/sustainability/doc/1432271059750/2024-impact-report-cocoa.pdf).

The Cocoa Promise supports cooperatives and farmers with:

- agronomic training and coaching;
- cooperative professionalization;
- farm development;
- digital transaction and first-mile traceability;
- child-labor monitoring;
- livelihood diversification; and
- living-income segmentation and modeling.

Its 2024 West African program covered 178 farmer organizations across Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana and Cameroon and approximately 211,000 participating farmers, according to reported impact figures.

3.2 Direct versus broker-purchased cocoa

Cargill states that the Cocoa Promise direct supply chain represents “about one third” of all cocoa sourced.

Thus the most defensible estimate is:

- Direct Cocoa Promise supply: approximately 33⅓%.
- Other/indirect supply: approximately 66⅔%.

Arithmetic:

100% − 33⅓% = 66⅔%.

This is approximate, and the company does not say that every non-Promise tonne is literally purchased from a broker. The remainder includes indirect origins and other procurement routes. Nevertheless, Cargill provides the clearest channel split among the three companies.

Certification and verification:

- Promise Cocoa can carry Rainforest Alliance certification or Cargill’s proprietary Promise Cocoa claims.
- Sustainable cocoa accounted for 54% of cocoa and chocolate volumes sold in 2023/24.
- Again, 54% sustainable sales is not equivalent to the roughly one-third direct-sourcing share.

3.3 Origin-country processing investment

Cargill announced more than $113 million for its West African processing sites in December 2019:

Côte d’Ivoire:

- $100 million at Yopougon.
- Capacity increase: 50%.
- The expansion was completed in 2021.
- Cargill described Yopougon after expansion as Africa’s largest single cocoa-grinding plant.
- A significant share of incremental capacity was assigned to premium dark-brown Gerkens cocoa powder.

Ghana:

- $13 million at Tema.
- Capacity increase: 20%.
- Completed in 2021.
- Annual grind capacity increased to 90,000 tonnes.

Sources: Cargill’s original investment announcement (https://www.cargill.com/2019/cargill-invests-$113-million-in-ivory-coast-and-ghana), Yopougon completion release (https://www.cargill.com/2021/cargill-completes-us$100m-cocoa-processing-expansion), and Tema completion release (https://www.cargill.com/2021/cargill-commissions-us$13-million-cocoa-processing-plant).

Investment allocation:

- Côte d’Ivoire: $100m ÷ $113m = 88.5%.
- Ghana: $13m ÷ $113m = 11.5%.

Cargill separately announced $12.3 million over three years for sustainability and traceability in the two countries. That amount should not be counted as processing-facility capex.

3.4 Farmer-income results

Cargill’s strongest published quantified intervention result in the evidence is a 23% average yield improvement among farmers applying improved crop protection, associated with a $194 net-income increase and a reported 430% return on investment. However, that result predates the core 2018–2024 period and should be treated as historical program evidence, not a period-end outcome (https://www.cargill.com/doc/1432076281572/ccp-full-report.pdf).

For 2024, Cargill reported:

- analysis of more than 90,000 farming households;
- segmentation into three household groups for targeted support;
- a goal that by 2025, 25,000 Côte d’Ivoire households would close or reduce their living-income gap by more than 50%.

The 25,000-household figure is a target, not a measured outcome.

Therefore:

- Documented 2018–2024 portfolio-wide percentage income change: not disclosed.
- Quantified historical intervention evidence: +23% yield and +$194 net income for a crop-protection cohort.
- Current evidence focuses on household segmentation and future gap-closing targets rather than realized average income growth.

This matters because higher yields do not automatically produce higher net income after labor, fertilizer, pesticide and financing costs.

3.5 EUDR response

Cargill began a formal two-phase EUDR project in early 2023:

1. readiness assessment and gap analysis;
2. implementation of an EUDR management system, commodity-specific controls and test runs with authorities and traceability platforms.

Its response includes:

- polygon mapping at farmer level;
- digital First Mile Traceability;
- farm-to-facility segregation;
- deforestation risk assessment;
- government and regulator dry runs;
- inventory controls; and
- due-diligence-statement reference numbers for post-application deliveries.

Cargill characterized this as a “vertical solution,” reflecting its operations from farm procurement through liquor, butter, powder and chocolate production (https://www.cargill.com/food-beverage/emea/news/almost-ready-for-eudr-inside-our-compliance-preparations).

2024 completion indicators:

- 143,554 Cocoa Promise plots polygon-mapped;
- mapping completion: 99.9%;
- implied Promise plot universe: 143,554 ÷ 0.999 ≈ 143,698 plots;
- 100% of cocoa in the direct supply chain traceable to first point of purchase;
- 76.6% of Promise volume delivered through digital First Mile Traceability;
- 54% sustainable cocoa volume sold.

The distinction is important: 99.9% polygon mapping applies to the Promise program, which represents about one third of total sourcing, not necessarily to all indirect cocoa.

Non-compliant exclusions:

- No actual 2024 volume or percentage excluded as EUDR-non-compliant was disclosed.
- Cargill stated that its supply chains would meet the requirements by the application date, but did not quantify rejected farms, tonnes or suppliers.

4. ofi/Olam

4.1 Integration strategy and cooperative programs

ofi’s cocoa integration rests on:

- long-standing direct farmer, cooperative and community procurement;
- Cocoa Compass, launched in 2019;
- the Olam Farmer Information System, or OFIS;
- Track & Trace, linking farm data, purchases, enterprise systems and factories;
- AtSource, a customer-facing sustainability and impact platform;
- origin grinding in Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana; and
- a global cocoa-ingredient portfolio.

The company reported 100% traceability to farm or community and 100% deforestation monitoring in its direct global supply chain by 2020. It also implemented child-labor monitoring across managed sustainability programs. Its direct-system architecture is described at https://www.ofi.com/en-us/news-and-events/press-release/cocoa-compass-targets-for-100-percent-child-labour-and-deforestation-monitoring.

Its environmental activity expanded substantially after the 2018 baseline. By 2024, it reported 9.8 million trees distributed for agroforestry and six active landscape partnerships. It provided livelihood support to 320,000 farmer households in 2024 (https://downloads.ctfassets.net/yzlb24ni1fxz/37uF0nYZ3aF62YUDaFrJ6K/dba5dd3dd8b302279fb64d4a12134ff7/ofi_Cocoa_Compass_Report_2024.pdf).

4.2 Direct versus broker-purchased cocoa

ofi clearly defines and tracks its direct supply chain, but does not disclose what percentage of total cocoa volume is direct versus indirect.

Supported conclusions:

- Direct chain: 100% traceable to farm or community and covered by deforestation monitoring.
- Indirect chain: acknowledged as including third-party suppliers, exchanges, companies and unrestricted local agents.
- Total-volume percentage split: not disclosed.

ofi’s sustainability claims therefore cannot be converted into a direct-sourcing percentage. “100% direct-chain traceability” means every tonne classified as direct is traceable; it does not mean 100% of total purchases are direct.

4.3 Origin-country processing investment

Côte d’Ivoire:

- ofi/Olam operates a major cocoa plant at San Pedro.
- The facility had 75,000 tonnes of annual grind capacity and represented an overall investment of $75 million.
- It was commissioned in 2014 and inaugurated in 2015, outside the requested 2018–2024 investment window (https://www.olamgroup.com/news/all-news/press-release/ouattara-olam-cocoa-processing-facility-cote-divoire.html).

Ghana:

- Olam’s Kumasi cocoa facility was established in 2009 and processes Ghanaian beans into cocoa mass.
- No new 2018–2024 cocoa-processing capex amount for Ghana was identified in the reviewed disclosures.

Period conclusion:

- New disclosed cocoa-processing capex in Côte d’Ivoire or Ghana, 2018–2024: none identified.
- This does not imply no maintenance or incremental investment. It means ofi did not disclose a comparable major project amount in the evidence reviewed.
- ofi entered the period with an already established origin-processing footprint, unlike Cargill and Barry Callebaut, which announced major expansions during the period.

4.4 Farmer-income results

In April 2024 ofi reported 30,168 farmers in its supply chain earning a living income (https://www.ofi.com/en-us/news-and-events/press-release/ofi-cocoa-shares-how-transparency-and-traceability-are-driving-sustainability-impact-for-food-and-beverage-sector).

Its full-year 2024 Cocoa Compass report subsequently stated:

- 155,000 farmers earning a living income;
- 320,000 farmer households receiving livelihood support;
- the 155,000 result exceeded its 2030 target of 150,000;
- higher cocoa prices were a major cause, alongside livelihood support and income diversification.

Quantitative change between the two published figures:

- Absolute increase: 155,000 − 30,168 = 124,832 farmers.
- Percentage increase: 124,832 ÷ 30,168 × 100 ≈ 413.8%.
- 155,000 as a share of the 320,000 households receiving livelihood support: 155,000 ÷ 320,000 × 100 ≈ 48.4%.

These calculations should be interpreted cautiously:

- The April and full-year numbers may not have identical measurement dates, samples or methodological coverage.
- “Farmers earning a living income” is a threshold count, not the percentage increase in average household income.
- ofi itself says the increase was influenced largely by rising cocoa prices outside its control. It cannot be attributed solely to Cocoa Compass interventions.

Broader West African evidence also cautions against assuming steady program-led gains. An Oxfam study of Ghanaian cocoa households estimated that participating farmers’ net income fell 16.38% between 2019/20 and 2021/22, with larger declines for women, reflecting rising costs and production challenges. That result is sectoral and not attributable specifically to ofi, but demonstrates why nominal farmgate-price or yield gains cannot substitute for net-income measurement.

4.5 EUDR response

ofi entered EUDR implementation with the most mature claim of complete traceability across its direct chain. Its principal tools are:

- OFIS for farmer registration, farm data, training and purchasing records;
- GPS polygons for mapped farms;
- Track & Trace for linking farms, purchase transactions, enterprise systems and processing plants;
- AtSource for sharing environmental and social data with customers;
- Google Earth Engine, Global Forest Watch and historical satellite analysis for deforestation risk;
- supplier-code obligations; and
- data transfer readiness for the EU’s TRACES system.

Its 2023 Cocoa Compass report said Track & Trace was being enhanced for EUDR and could connect individually mapped farms to the factory (https://downloads.ctfassets.net/yzlb24ni1fxz/59dP6xwmGeJLdC7ziQ3ImL/677b6dd2042d6301873f9e59a3ed614e/Cocoa_Compass_Impact_Report_2023_FINAL.pdf).

Completion indicators:

- 100% direct-supply-chain traceability to farm or community since 2020;
- 100% direct-chain deforestation monitoring;
- more than 90% of farmer groups in sustainability programs polygon-mapped by 2022;
- continued polygon-mapping progress in 2024.

However, the 2024 report did not disclose a single comparable global farm-polygon completion percentage. Traceability to community or farmer group is not always identical to EUDR-compliant polygon traceability for every farm larger than the applicable threshold.

Non-compliant exclusions:

- No 2024 tonnage or percentage excluded as non-compliant was disclosed.
- ofi described supplier expectations, assessments and controls, but not realized rejected or diverted volume.

5. Comparative EUDR assessment

5.1 Regulatory timing

The regulation entered into force on June 29, 2023 and was originally scheduled to apply to large operators and traders on December 30, 2024. In December 2024 the EU formally postponed application by one year, to December 30, 2025 for large operators and traders and June 30, 2026 for micro and small enterprises (https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2024/12/18/eu-deforestation-law-council-formally-adopts-its-one-year-postponement/).

Thus, “effective 2024” describes the deadline for which the companies prepared during most of the period, but not the final legal application date.

The core requirements relevant to cocoa are:

- exact production geolocation;
- proof of no post-December 2020 deforestation;
- legal production under origin-country law;
- risk assessment and mitigation;
- segregation or data-preserving identity through processing; and
- submission of a due-diligence statement.

5.2 Side-by-side comparison

Barry Callebaut
- Direct/indirect split: not disclosed.
- Direct plots mapped: 83.0%.
- Mapped plots: 669,174.
- Main system: farm polygons, forest overlays, yield controls, first-mile audits and due-diligence statements.
- Strength: integration from mapped origin supply through industrial chocolate.
- Residual weakness: 17% of direct plots not mapped at the reported date, plus undisclosed third-party exposure.
- Non-compliant volume excluded: not disclosed.

Cargill
- Direct Cocoa Promise share: about one third of total sourcing.
- Promise plots mapped: 99.9%.
- Direct supply traceable to first purchase: 100%.
- Digitally first-mile-traced Promise volume: 76.6%.
- Main system: First Mile Traceability, polygon mapping, segregation and a group-wide EUDR management platform.
- Strength: near-complete mapping within the managed direct program.
- Residual weakness: roughly two thirds of sourcing is outside the disclosed Promise share, and indirect-chain farm-level metrics are not reported comparably.
- Non-compliant volume excluded: not disclosed.

ofi
- Direct/indirect split: not disclosed.
- Direct traceability and deforestation monitoring: 100%.
- Polygon mapping: more than 90% of farmer groups in sustainability programs by 2022; no clear 2024 global farm percentage.
- Main system: OFIS, Track & Trace, AtSource and satellite risk screening.
- Strength: long-established digital origin data and customer-facing sustainability analytics.
- Residual weakness: community/group traceability and deforestation monitoring do not by themselves prove polygon completeness for every farm; indirect exposure is unquantified.
- Non-compliant volume excluded: not disclosed.

5.3 Overall ranking

No simple ranking is definitive because denominators differ.

- Highest disclosed direct-program polygon completion: Cargill at 99.9%.
- Broadest mature claim across the direct chain: ofi at 100% traceability and deforestation monitoring.
- Largest absolute mapped-plot database reported for 2023/24: Barry Callebaut at 669,174.
- Clearest total sourcing-channel disclosure: Cargill, with about one third in its direct Promise supply chain.
- Clearest disclosure of operational consequences of contamination: Barry Callebaut, which explicitly described immobilization, withdrawal or disposal of mixed products.

All three remain exposed where cocoa is obtained outside managed direct networks. Industry-level evidence illustrates the problem: Reuters reported that 83% of directly sourced cocoa in Ghana and 82% in Côte d’Ivoire was traceable to plot, but only around 35% of Côte d’Ivoire’s exports were directly sourced from cooperatives in 2022 (https://www.reuters.com/markets/commodities/cocoa-traceability-rates-fail-improve-eu-deforestation-law-looms-2024-10-01/). Consequently, an impressive direct-program mapping percentage does not establish equivalent coverage of total national or corporate supply.

6. Competitive effects in premium chocolate and confectionery contracts

6.1 Barry Callebaut

Barry Callebaut is best positioned for contracts requiring finished or semi-finished premium chocolate rather than only cocoa ingredients.

Advantages include:

- the largest end-to-end chocolate-manufacturing footprint among the three;
- customer-specific recipes, liquid chocolate, fillings, decorations and couverture;
- origin traceability connected to downstream chocolate factories;
- Cocoa Horizons premiums and verified sustainability claims;
- ability to absorb or operate customer chocolate facilities; and
- established long-term outsourcing relationships.

Its strategic agreement with Mondelēz included acquisition and integration of Mondelēz’s Halle, Belgium chocolate facility and a long-term additional supply of 30,000 tonnes of liquid chocolate per year (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/en/group/media/news-stories/barry-callebaut-extend-strategic-supply-partnership-mondelez-international). Although the agreement predates 2018, it demonstrates the outsourcing model strengthened by subsequent origin integration.

Competitive constraint: Barry Callebaut’s 83% direct-plot mapping rate was below Cargill’s reported Promise mapping percentage, and only 55.5% of products sold contained fully verified or certified cocoa in 2023/24. Customers requiring complete segregation may therefore need dedicated contract streams rather than relying on the company-wide average.

6.2 Cargill

Cargill’s strongest differentiation is between farm supply and specialized cocoa ingredients:

- Africa’s largest single grinding facility after the Yopougon expansion;
- premium dark-brown Gerkens powders;
- a 90,000-tonne Tema plant;
- segregated farm-to-facility options;
- near-complete mapping in Cocoa Promise; and
- cocoa-to-chocolate technical and innovation capacity.

Cargill also signed a formal partnership to support Mondelēz’s Cocoa Life program, aligning Cocoa Promise activities with Mondelēz’s sustainable-sourcing objectives. This makes Cargill attractive where customers want a processor to execute their own branded sustainability program rather than substitute a supplier brand for it.

Competitive constraint: Cocoa Promise covers only about one third of Cargill’s sourcing. Premium customers seeking EUDR-ready, fully segregated or certified inputs may have to contract specifically for Promise Cocoa, reducing fungibility and potentially increasing premiums.

6.3 ofi/Olam

ofi’s strongest differentiator is transparent cocoa ingredients and customer-accessible sustainability information:

- 100% traceability and deforestation monitoring in the direct chain;
- OFIS, Track & Trace and AtSource;
- farm-income modeling;
- extensive farmer and agroforestry programs;
- existing processing in major origins; and
- capacity to co-design customer sustainability projects.

ofi and Mondelēz announced a 2021 collaboration to create a large sustainable commercial cocoa farm in Indonesia, combining Cocoa Compass with Mondelēz Cocoa Life (https://ir.mondelezinternational.com/news-releases/news-release-details/mondelez-international-and-olam-food-ingredients-announce). Though outside West Africa, the partnership demonstrates ofi’s position as a strategic agricultural and traceability partner, not just a commodity processor.

Competitive constraint: ofi is less prominent than Barry Callebaut in outsourced finished premium chocolate manufacturing, and its lack of a disclosed direct-versus-indirect volume split makes total-company EUDR readiness harder for customers to evaluate.

6.4 Ferrero

Ferrero’s published Tier-1 supplier lists provide direct evidence that all three compete successfully for major confectionery business:

- Barry Callebaut;
- Cargill; and
- ofi/Olam

all appear in Ferrero’s 2022/23 list (https://www.ferrero.com/int/sites/ferrero_int/files/2024-06/cocoa-supplier-list-22-23.pdf) and the 2023/24 list (https://www.ferrero.com/uk/sites/ferrero_uk/files/2025-07/cocoa-suppliers-list-23-24.pdf).

This confirms supplier status but not contract volumes, margins, specific brands or whether the supplied product is beans, liquor, butter, powder or finished chocolate.

Ferrero’s annual publication of suppliers and farmer groups favors processors that can:

- segregate farmer-group volume;
- provide geolocation and deforestation data;
- align certification with Ferrero’s sourcing standards; and
- document premiums and remediation.

The three processors’ investments therefore protect access to Ferrero tenders, but the available evidence does not establish that one won share from another.

6.5 Mondelēz

All three have documented strategic relationships with Mondelēz:

- Barry Callebaut: long-term liquid-chocolate supply and plant integration.
- Cargill: Cocoa Promise alignment with Cocoa Life in West Africa.
- ofi: Cocoa Compass/Cocoa Life collaboration and a joint sustainable-farming project.

Barry Callebaut has the clearest manufacturing-outsourcing advantage. Cargill and ofi are especially credible as ingredient and origin-program implementation partners.

6.6 Lindt & Sprüngli

The reviewed evidence does not identify Barry Callebaut, Cargill or ofi by name as Lindt suppliers. Lindt reports that it is one of the relatively few chocolate manufacturers producing its own cocoa mass from beans, giving it “bean-to-bar” control (https://reports.lindt-spruengli.com/sustainability-report-2024/strategy-and-governance/strategy/our-business-model-and-value-chain.html).

Implications:

- Lindt may purchase beans and selected ingredients rather than outsource core chocolate manufacturing to the same extent as some competitors.
- Processor integration remains relevant for butter, powder, specialty ingredients, logistics or supplementary supply, but no specific contract should be inferred.
- Traceability systems can still improve a processor’s eligibility as a Lindt supplier because Lindt evaluates cocoa suppliers against responsible-sourcing requirements. The evidence does not permit a market-share or contract-volume conclusion.

7. Strategic conclusions

1. Direct sourcing is becoming regulatory infrastructure, not merely corporate social responsibility.

Farmer registration, cooperative relationships, polygons and digital purchase records now determine whether cocoa can enter high-value European supply chains. Direct networks reduce data and contamination risk and can command an “EUDR-ready” premium.

2. Origin processing creates both efficiency and contamination risk.

Grinding near the farms lowers logistics costs, captures more origin-country value and gives processors tighter quality control. But once beans are mixed into liquor, butter or powder, one suspect lot can compromise a much larger processed batch. Barry Callebaut’s warning about immobilizing or discarding co-mingled products captures this operational risk.

3. Cargill made the largest disclosed period capex commitment.

Comparable 2018–2024 project amounts are:

- Cargill: $113 million—$100 million Côte d’Ivoire and $13 million Ghana.
- Barry Callebaut: CHF55 million in Côte d’Ivoire; no quantified Ghana project identified.
- ofi: no comparable new period project disclosed; its $75 million San Pedro facility predates the period.

Currency differences prevent a precise combined ranking without historical exchange-rate assumptions, but Cargill’s disclosed investment is clearly larger than Barry Callebaut’s CHF55 million project under normal 2019 exchange rates.

4. Traceability claims need denominator discipline.

- Cargill’s 99.9% applies to Cocoa Promise, about one third of total sourcing.
- Barry Callebaut’s 83% applies to direct-supply plots.
- ofi’s 100% applies to direct-chain traceability and monitoring, not necessarily polygon completion across total procurement.

None supports a claim of 100% EUDR-ready total cocoa volume at the end of 2024.

5. Farmer-income claims are not comparable and are not yet robust enough to rank the companies.

- Barry Callebaut: no quantified program-wide income change.
- Cargill: no current portfolio-wide change; historical cohort evidence of +$194 net income and a 23% yield gain.
- ofi: 155,000 farmers above a living-income threshold in 2024, but much of the increase was price-driven.

The proper conclusion is not that ofi necessarily delivered the greatest causal income improvement, but that it disclosed the largest living-income threshold count.

6. Premium-contract positioning follows product specialization.

- Barry Callebaut: strongest for outsourced liquid and finished premium chocolate, innovation and customer factory integration.
- Cargill: strongest for specialty cocoa powders, large-scale grinding and vertically integrated segregated ingredients.
- ofi: strongest for traceable cocoa ingredients, farm data and customer-specific sustainability analytics.

7. EUDR readiness is likely to increase concentration.

Large customers such as Ferrero and Mondelēz need auditable farm data and reliable segregated volume. The cost of mapping, satellite monitoring, digital transaction capture, separate storage and due diligence favors processors with large direct networks and origin plants. That strengthens the top three relative to smaller brokers, even though their indirect procurement remains the least transparent part of their own supply chains.

Final assessment

Across 2018–2024, Cargill undertook the most aggressive disclosed physical expansion in Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana and provided the clearest direct-versus-indirect sourcing estimate. Barry Callebaut maintained the strongest downstream integration into premium and outsourced chocolate manufacturing and assembled the largest disclosed mapped-plot database. ofi developed the most mature integrated farm-data and customer sustainability platform and reported the largest living-income threshold count, but disclosed less about its total direct-sourcing share and new period processing capex.

All three are materially better positioned for EUDR-sensitive and premium confectionery contracts than processors dependent on anonymous brokered cocoa. Nevertheless, none provided all the information needed for a complete comparison: Barry Callebaut and ofi withheld total direct-sourcing percentages; all three lacked comparable net farmer-income changes; and none disclosed actual 2024 non-compliant cocoa exclusion volumes. Those disclosure gaps should be treated as substantive uncertainty, not as evidence that the undisclosed exposure was zero.

Detail each company's percentage of direct-sourced versus broker-purchased cocoa, capital expenditures on origin-country processing facilities in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana, and documented farmer income changes under their respective programs. Assess how these strategies affect their competitive positioning in premium chocolate manufacturing contracts with companies like Lindt, Ferrero, and Mondelēz.
