WHOLE-HOME HVAC COMPARISON FOR A 2,400-SQ-FT PHOENIX HOME

Executive conclusion

1. The three named products are not directly equivalent:
   - Carrier Infinity 26, model 24VNA6, is a cooling-only air conditioner, not a heat pump.
   - Lennox SL28XCV is also a cooling-only air conditioner.
   - Mitsubishi Hyper-Heat H2i is a reversible heat pump.

   Consequently, the Carrier Infinity 26 and Lennox SL28XCV have no HSPF2 rating. A valid all-heat-pump comparison would substitute Carrier’s Infinity 24/25VNA4 and Lennox’s SL25XPV for the two cooling-only products.

2. For Phoenix’s principal requirement—reliable cooling above 115°F—the Carrier has the strongest documented high-ambient operating envelope. Carrier specifies full-power operation to 125°F, while the Lennox is reported to have a 120°F ceiling and Mitsubishi’s published P-Series cooling range ends at 115°F. The available 115°F capacity-retention figures for Carrier and Lennox come from an HVAC contractor’s field experience, not a controlled independent laboratory test. No defensible third-party 115°F capacity curve was found for the Mitsubishi H2i combination.

3. Under the screening assumptions stated below, Carrier delivers the lowest 15-year cost per effective cooling ton at 115°F:
   - Carrier: approximately $7,800 per retained ton over 15 years.
   - Lennox: approximately $8,500 per retained ton.
   - Mitsubishi 42,000-Btu/h H2i: at least approximately $12,100 per rated ton, with its capacity above 115°F unverified.

4. The Lennox has the lowest modeled seasonal cooling-energy cost because of its higher SEER2, but its higher assumed installed price, slightly greater reported high-temperature derating, and narrower operating margin offset that advantage.

5. The Mitsubishi H2i is the best cold-weather heater, but that is of limited economic value in Phoenix. Its 42,000-Btu/h ducted pairing is likely too small for many 2,400-square-foot Phoenix houses unless a Manual J calculation shows a design load no greater than about 3.5 tons. H2i’s cold-climate hardware does not confer a demonstrated advantage in 115°F–120°F cooling.

Recommended choice: Carrier’s corresponding Infinity heat pump, not the cooling-only Infinity 26, provided an AHRI-listed exact match and a Manual J/S/D design confirm capacity. If choosing strictly among the exact named products and retaining another heat source, the Infinity 26 is the strongest extreme-desert cooling choice.

1. Ratings and product-equivalence problem

Published ratings are “up to” figures and depend on the exact outdoor unit, indoor coil or air handler, blower, and sometimes furnace. SRP requires qualifying equipment to be listed in the AHRI Verified Directory and requires the invoice to identify all components and the AHRI reference number (https://www.srpnet.com/energy-savings-rebates/home/rebates/air-conditioner).

| Product | Actual equipment type | Relevant large-system rating | HSPF2 | Important qualification |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Carrier Infinity 26 / 24VNA6 | Cooling-only AC | Up to 24 SEER2; up to 16 EER2 | Not applicable | Carrier identifies it as an air conditioner; capacity range 2–5 nominal tons (https://www.carrier.com/residential/en/us/products/air-conditioners/24VNA6/) |
| Lennox SL28XCV-060 | Cooling-only AC | Up to 25.8 SEER2 for the 5-ton unit | Not applicable | Requires an iComfort-enabled variable-speed indoor unit; R-410A (https://www.lennoxpros.com/sl28xcv-060-air-conditioner-5-ton/p/19U53) |
| Mitsubishi PVA-A42AA7 + PUZ-HA42NKA1 H2i | Ducted heat pump | 15.4 SEER2; 9.3 HSPF2; 42,000 Btu/h rated cooling | 9.3 | 3.5 nominal tons, not a 5-ton equivalent (https://www.acwholesalers.com/manuals/2b9934eb2f59ab622ae24f2cc413a2f0.pdf) |

AHRI verification caveat

The gathered documentation supports the ratings above as manufacturer or distributor-published ratings based on AHRI test conditions, but it does not establish one specific active AHRI certificate number for each proposed whole system. AHRI certification attaches to the complete matchup, not just the condenser model. Before contract signing, the contractor should supply a current AHRI certificate showing:

- Outdoor model.
- Indoor air handler or coil model.
- Furnace model, if applicable.
- Cooling capacity at 95°F.
- SEER2 and EER2.
- Heating capacity and HSPF2 for an actual heat pump.
- Active model status.

Do not accept an “up to 24” or “up to 25.8” sales claim in place of the certificate for the actual 4- or 5-ton combination.

Appropriate heat-pump substitutes

For a true whole-home heat-pump comparison:

- Carrier Infinity 24 / 25VNA4: up to 23 SEER2 and 10.5 HSPF2 according to Carrier (https://www.carrier.com/residential/en/us/products/heat-pumps/25VNA4/).
- Lennox SL25XPV: up to 23 SEER2 and 10.3 HSPF2 across the product line, although the listed 5-ton version is only up to 20.4 SEER2 and 9.0 HSPF2 (https://www.lennox.com/residential/products/heating-cooling/heat-pumps/SL25XPV; https://www.lennoxpros.com/sl25xpv-060-heat-pump-dlsc-5-ton-variable-capacity-230v/p/19U28).

Those heat-pump ratings should be used in final bids, rather than assigning an HSPF2 to either cooling-only model.

2. Performance at 115°F and above

Carrier Infinity 26

Carrier’s product announcement states that the Infinity 26 can provide high-ambient cooling at full power up to 125°F (https://www.achrnews.com/articles/152182-new-carrier-infinity-26-air-conditioner-and-infinity-24-heat-pump-with-greenspeed-intelligence).

An HVAC contractor serving a similar desert climate estimates 85%–90% capacity retention at 115°F. Its midpoint is:

5.0 rated tons × 87.5% = 4.375 effective tons at 115°F.

Source: https://www.thecoolingco.com/blog/carrier-infinity-vs-lennox-signature/

This is useful field evidence but not an independent laboratory test. It should be treated as an approximate design range, not an AHRI-certified 115°F result.

Lennox SL28XCV

The same desert contractor reports:

- Maximum ambient rating: approximately 120°F.
- Capacity retention at 115°F: approximately 82%–87%.

Using the midpoint:

5.0 rated tons × 84.5% = 4.225 effective tons at 115°F.

Source: https://www.thecoolingco.com/blog/lennox-sl28xcv-review-las-vegas/

The Lennox should therefore cool at 115°F if correctly sized, but it operates closer to its reported upper-temperature limit than the Carrier. Again, the retention figure is contractor field experience, not a published independent laboratory curve.

Mitsubishi Hyper-Heat H2i

Mitsubishi’s current P-Series literature gives a cooling operating range of 14°F–115°F (https://hvacdirect.com/media/pdf/Mitsubishi_M-_and_P-Series_Catalog_Sept-25.pdf). For the older 42,000-Btu/h PVA/PUZ H2i combination:

- Rated cooling: 42,000 Btu/h at 95°F.
- Rated input: 3,960 W.
- EER at the older test point: 10.6.
- SEER2: 15.4.
- HSPF2: 9.3.

Source: https://www.meiersupply.com/customer/docs/skudocs/Document_Links/Vendors/106835%20-%20Mitsubishi/Submittals/PVA/M_SUBMITTAL_PVA-A42AA7_PUZ-HA42NKA1_en.pdf

No reliable 115°F capacity-retention percentage was found for this exact combination. More importantly, 115°F is the published edge of the product’s cooling envelope. Phoenix has exceeded 115°F, so this is a material design concern. A Mitsubishi proposal should include the manufacturer’s expanded cooling table at 115°F and written confirmation of operation at the project’s selected outdoor design temperature.

Bottom line on extreme heat

| Product | Reported upper cooling ambient | Estimated capacity at 115°F | Confidence |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Carrier Infinity 26, 5 ton | 125°F | 4.25–4.50 tons | Moderate; operating limit is documented, capacity retention is contractor field data |
| Lennox SL28XCV, 5 ton | 120°F | 4.10–4.35 tons | Moderate-to-low; contractor field data |
| Mitsubishi H2i 42k | 115°F | Unknown; no more than 3.5 rated tons before derating | Low; no 115°F capacity curve found |

The Carrier has the best available evidence for extreme desert operation.

3. Noise and property-line compliance

Published outdoor sound

- Carrier advertises operation as low as 51 dB (https://www.achrnews.com/articles/152182-new-carrier-infinity-26-air-conditioner-and-infinity-24-heat-pump-with-greenspeed-intelligence).
- Lennox lists sound levels as low as 56 dBA for the SL28XCV (https://www.lennoxpros.com/sl28xcv-060-air-conditioner-5-ton/p/19U53).
- Mitsubishi literature describes PUZ outdoor-unit sound around 40 dB for selected conditions/models, but that is not necessarily the full-speed rating of the proposed 42,000-Btu/h unit (https://cdn.agilitycms.com/mesca/mem-202519_r-454b-p-series_catalogue_lr_10.16.25.pdf).

“as low as” is not the correct value for evaluating a 115°F property-line condition. At extreme temperature the compressor and fan will approach maximum speed, where sound is higher.

Municipal-code issue

The available Phoenix code source prohibits “unreasonably loud, disturbing and unnecessary noise” but does not establish the simple residential HVAC property-line limit of 65 dBA assumed in the question (https://phoenix.municipal.codes/CC/23-14). The search result containing an explicit 65-dBA nighttime figure was for Page, Arizona, not Phoenix, and should not be applied to this property.

Nevertheless, using 65 dBA as the homeowner’s design criterion is prudent.

Property-line determination

Equipment sound ratings are not automatically equivalent to sound pressure at the lot line. Distance, reflective walls, corners, ground surface, screening, and multiple condensers matter. A rough free-field calculation is:

Reduction = 20 log10(r₂/r₁).

For example, if a unit produced 65 dBA at 3 feet, at 15 feet the theoretical free-field level would be:

20 log10(15/3) = 20 log10(5) = 14.0 dB reduction,

so approximately:

65 − 14 = 51 dBA at the property line.

A unit between two masonry walls can be several decibels louder than this simple estimate.

Recommendation:

- Require maximum-speed sound data, not minimum-speed marketing numbers.
- Keep the condenser at least 10–15 feet from the nearest property line where feasible.
- Avoid corners and placement directly between parallel masonry walls.
- Use vibration isolators and a solid, level pad.
- Include a post-installation nighttime measurement at the property line while forcing maximum cooling.

All three can probably meet a 65-dBA lot-line design target with appropriate siting, but none can be certified compliant solely from its “as low as” product rating.

4. Electrical-service compatibility

A 200-amp, 120/240-volt service will usually support one 4- or 5-ton inverter system, but service size alone is insufficient. NEC service/load calculations must include electric water heating, cooking, pool equipment, EV charging, solar/battery equipment, and any resistance backup heat.

Lennox SL28XCV-060

Published electrical data:

- 208/230 V, single phase.
- Minimum circuit ampacity: 29.5 A.
- Maximum overcurrent protection: 50 A.
- Compressor input: 21.5 A.
- Outdoor fan: 2.6 A.

Source: https://tech.lennoxintl.com/C03e7o14l/VIu12Ch2uV/100012.pdf

This is normally compatible with a 200-amp service and a dedicated 50-amp branch circuit. It does not include electric heating because the SL28XCV is cooling-only.

Carrier Infinity 26

The 5-ton unit is a 208/230-V variable-speed condenser, but the gathered evidence does not provide a sufficiently clear MCA/MOCP value for the exact proposed match. The contractor must place the nameplate MCA and MOCP in the bid and verify breaker and conductor size. As a cooling-only unit, it also requires a separate heating source.

Mitsubishi H2i

The 42,000-Btu/h combination uses 208/230-V, single-phase power. Mitsubishi documentation indicates a roughly 30-amp outdoor breaker recommendation for the combination, although the final circuit must follow the specific unit nameplate and installation manual. The indoor air handler also needs its specified power/control connection.

Backup heat is the potential electrical constraint. For illustration:

- 10 kW strip heat: 10,000 W ÷ 240 V = 41.7 A before required sizing allowances.
- 15 kW: 62.5 A.
- 20 kW: 83.3 A.

Phoenix usually needs much less supplemental heat than a cold climate, and Mitsubishi H2i may need none if correctly sized. Nonetheless, adding large resistance strips, an EV charger, and pool equipment could make a 200-amp load calculation fail.

Electrical conclusion: all three outdoor systems are likely compatible with 200 amps, but the whole-home heat-pump configuration must be checked with backup heat included. A service upgrade should not be assumed necessary.

5. Ductwork and controls

A 2,400-square-foot Phoenix house cannot be sized by floor area alone. A room-by-room ACCA Manual J calculation is essential because insulation, windows, orientation, air leakage, attic ducts, and renovation improvements can move the design load by more than a ton.

Carrier

Expected requirements:

- Matched Carrier variable-speed air handler or approved coil/furnace combination.
- Infinity communicating control.
- Verification that ducts can carry roughly 1,600 CFM for a 4-ton design or about 2,000 CFM for 5 tons without excessive static pressure.
- Return-air resizing is common if the present return is undersized.
- Refrigerant-line verification; replacement is preferable if existing lines are contaminated, damaged, incorrectly sized, or formerly used with incompatible oil/refrigerant.
- Duct sealing and insulation, especially for attic ducts.

Carrier supports long refrigerant-line applications, but line size, lift and equivalent length must follow the application guide.

Lennox

The SL28XCV can only be matched with an iComfort-enabled variable-speed furnace or air handler (https://www.lennoxpros.com/sl28xcv-060-air-conditioner-5-ton/p/19U53). Therefore, this is not normally an outdoor-unit-only retrofit.

The 5-ton unit uses:

- 3/8-inch liquid line.
- 1-1/8-inch suction line.

Existing smaller suction piping may have to be replaced. Lennox warns that a line previously exposed to mineral oil must be properly flushed and that contamination can reduce heat transfer or clog the expansion device (https://tech.lennoxintl.com/C03e7o14l/VIu12Ch2uV/100012.pdf).

Mitsubishi

The PVA-A42AA7 air handler provides approximately 1,040–1,485 CFM and can be configured for external static pressure up to approximately 0.8 inch water column (https://www.meiersupply.com/customer/docs/skudocs/Document_Links/Vendors/106835%20-%20Mitsubishi/Submittals/PVA/M_SUBMITTAL_PVA-A42AA7_PUZ-HA42NKA1_en.pdf).

Advantages:

- Better static-pressure capability than many mini-split-style ducted units.
- Multi-position air-handler format is suitable for central-duct retrofits.
- Lower required airflow than a conventional 5-ton system.

Risks:

- Its 42,000-Btu/h cooling capacity may be insufficient for the house.
- Existing ducts designed for 5 tons may need balancing because the Mitsubishi’s maximum airflow is closer to a conventional 3.5–4-ton airflow.
- Mitsubishi controls and sensors should be used; thermostat-interface choices can sacrifice some modulation or diagnostics.
- If multiple indoor zones are proposed instead of one PVA air handler, the ductwork scope and cost become fundamentally different.

Minimum duct scope for any option

The contract should include:

- Manual J load calculation.
- Manual S equipment selection using expanded 115°F performance.
- Static-pressure measurement before and after installation.
- Total external static target consistent with the air handler.
- Room-by-room airflow schedule.
- Return-air sizing.
- Leakage testing and sealing.
- At least R-8 insulation for attic ducts where applicable.
- Commissioned airflow and refrigerant charge.

6. Reliability and projected failure rates

No credible, brand-specific HVAC-technician survey providing 15-year failure percentages for these exact inverter models was found. Claims that one model has a precise projected compressor or board failure rate would therefore overstate the evidence.

The strongest available broad evidence is Consumer Reports’ owner survey:

- 13,753 heat pumps installed between 2009 and 2025.
- Approximately 29% broke or stopped working by the end of year eight.
- The survey covers entire brands and many product generations, not these exact models.

Source: https://www.consumerreports.org/appliances/heat-pumps/most-and-least-reliable-heat-pumps-a2741062924/

If, only as a screening exercise, that 29% eight-year incidence is converted to a constant annual hazard, the implied 15-year chance of at least one such event is:

P₁₅ = 1 − (1 − 0.29)^(15/8)

P₁₅ = 1 − 0.71^1.875

P₁₅ ≈ 1 − 0.526 = 47.4%.

This is not a probability of total system replacement. It represents at least one breakdown or loss of proper operation and should not be assigned equally to every brand or installation.

Older Consumer Reports central-AC survey material rated:

- Mitsubishi: 5/5 predicted reliability, based largely on ductless products.
- Carrier: 4/5.
- Lennox: 4/5.

The survey covered 18,172 systems installed between 2007 and 2022 (https://reliablehvachelp.com/wp-content/uploads/Central-Air-Conditioning-Reliability-Consumer-Reports.pdf). Mitsubishi’s result should not be treated as proof that a centrally ducted PVA/PUZ H2i system will outperform the others in Phoenix.

Practical reliability distinctions

Carrier:
- Broad dealer network and mature communicating platform.
- Exposure to inverter-board, ECM and proprietary-control repair costs.
- Best high-ambient margin of the three, potentially reducing operation near protective limits.

Lennox:
- Similar inverter/control complexity.
- Proprietary iComfort ecosystem and model-specific parts availability can increase downtime.
- Narrower reported ambient margin than Carrier.

Mitsubishi:
- Strong general reputation for inverter systems.
- Installation quality, refrigerant piping and control configuration are critical.
- Fewer contractors may have deep experience with large ducted P-Series systems than with conventional Carrier/Lennox equipment.
- Published 115°F cooling ceiling is a Phoenix-specific operational concern unrelated to cold-weather reliability.

7. SRP rebate

SRP Cool Cash currently offers the following for qualifying equipment of at least 15.2 SEER2:

- Single-stage: $75 per ton.
- Multi-stage: $150 per ton.
- Variable-capacity heat pump or AC: $225 per ton.
- Inverter-driven mini-split: $225 per ton.

Source: https://www.srpnet.com/energy-savings-rebates/home/rebates/air-conditioner

Applicable screening rebates:

- 5-ton Carrier: 5 × $225 = $1,125.
- 5-ton Lennox: 5 × $225 = $1,125.
- 3.5-ton Mitsubishi: 3.5 × $225 = $787.50.

Conditions include:

- Permanent SRP residential customer.
- Arizona-licensed installer.
- Qualifying installation before April 30, 2027.
- AHRI-listed system.
- Application and paid invoice with exact AHRI reference.
- Replacement of the required indoor and outdoor equipment.

The rebate is not guaranteed until SRP confirms the exact AHRI matchup.

8. Fifteen-year total cost of ownership

Method and assumptions

Because no three local, like-for-like contractor bids were supplied, this is a screening model, not a quotation.

Installed-price assumptions:
- Carrier 5-ton premium variable system: $18,000.
- Lennox 5-ton premium variable system: $20,000.
- Mitsubishi 42,000-Btu/h ducted H2i: $20,000.

Phoenix market evidence places complete variable-speed systems around $16,000–$22,000 (https://www.championair.com/ac-replacement-cost-phoenix). A Phoenix Lennox SL28 five-ton package has been advertised at approximately $27,835 with a furnace and premium installation scope, illustrating the potential upper end (https://reeis.com/products/lennox-sl28-5-ton-ac-with-furnace). Duct repairs or replacement can add roughly $1,500–$4,000.

Energy assumptions:
- Annual equivalent cooling load: 60,000 Btu/h × 2,141 equivalent full-load hours.
- Initial electricity price: $0.1204/kWh, corresponding to an SRP standard summer figure shown in its plan comparison (https://www.srpnet.com/price-plans/residential-electric/compare-plans).
- Electricity escalation: 2.5% annually.
- Fifteen-year undiscounted escalation multiplier:

Σ from year 0 to 14 of 1.025^year = approximately 17.29.

- Heating-energy differences are excluded because two named products are not heat pumps and no existing heating-fuel information was provided.
- Maintenance plan: $249/year, based on a Phoenix provider’s two-visit plan (https://www.azenergyefficienthome.com/services/hvac-maintenance-phoenix-arizona/).
- Fifteen-year maintenance: $249 × 15 = $3,735.
- Repair reserves are scenario assumptions, not measured brand failure rates:
  - Carrier: $2,500.
  - Lennox: $3,000.
  - Mitsubishi: $2,000.

Annual cooling electricity

Annual delivered cooling load:

60,000 × 2,141 = 128,460,000 Btu.

Carrier at 24 SEER2:

128,460,000 ÷ 24 Btu/Wh = 5,352,500 Wh  
= 5,353 kWh/year.

Lennox at 25.8 SEER2:

128,460,000 ÷ 25.8 = 4,979,070 Wh  
= 4,979 kWh/year.

Mitsubishi at 15.4 SEER2:

128,460,000 ÷ 15.4 = 8,341,558 Wh  
= 8,342 kWh/year.

This Mitsubishi figure assumes it can meet the same annual load. It does not establish that the 3.5-ton unit can meet the peak load.

Fifteen-year electricity cost

Cost = annual kWh × $0.1204 × 17.29.

- Carrier: 5,353 × 0.1204 × 17.29 ≈ $11,140.
- Lennox: 4,979 × 0.1204 × 17.29 ≈ $10,365.
- Mitsubishi: 8,342 × 0.1204 × 17.29 ≈ $17,360.

Screening TCO

| Component | Carrier | Lennox | Mitsubishi H2i |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Assumed installed cost | $18,000 | $20,000 | $20,000 |
| Less SRP rebate | −$1,125 | −$1,125 | −$788 |
| Net initial cost | $16,875 | $18,875 | $19,212 |
| 15-year cooling electricity | $11,140 | $10,365 | $17,360 |
| 15-year maintenance | $3,735 | $3,735 | $3,735 |
| Repair reserve | $2,500 | $3,000 | $2,000 |
| Indicative 15-year TCO | $34,250 | $35,975 | $42,307 |

Important uncertainty

A reasonable change in contractor price can reverse the Carrier-versus-Lennox TCO result. For example, Lennox saves only about:

$11,140 − $10,365 = $775

in modeled 15-year cooling electricity. If the Lennox bid is more than approximately $775 above the Carrier bid after rebates and equivalent scope, its efficiency advantage does not recover the price difference under these assumptions.

The Mitsubishi result is more decisively disadvantaged because its ducted H2i efficiency is lower and the evaluated unit has only 42,000 Btu/h of rated cooling.

9. Cost per cooling ton in extreme desert conditions

For this report, “cost per cooling ton” means 15-year TCO divided by estimated cooling capacity retained at 115°F.

Carrier midpoint capacity:

5 × 87.5% = 4.375 tons.

TCO per effective ton:

$34,250 ÷ 4.375 = approximately $7,829 per effective 115°F ton.

Lennox midpoint capacity:

5 × 84.5% = 4.225 tons.

TCO per effective ton:

$35,975 ÷ 4.225 = approximately $8,515 per effective 115°F ton.

Mitsubishi best case, assuming no derating at its 115°F operating limit:

$42,307 ÷ 3.5 = approximately $12,088 per rated ton.

Because Mitsubishi’s actual 115°F capacity is unknown and likely below or at its 95°F rating, $12,088 is a best-case lower bound. At 85% retention, for example:

3.5 × 85% = 2.975 effective tons,

$42,307 ÷ 2.975 = approximately $14,221 per effective ton.

Result: Carrier has the lowest modeled 15-year cost per effective cooling ton in extreme desert conditions. Lennox has the lowest seasonal electricity consumption, but not the lowest overall cost per retained peak ton under the central assumptions.

10. Final procurement recommendation

Preferred specification

Obtain bids for:

1. Carrier Infinity 24 heat pump/Greenspeed system in the Manual-J-selected size.
2. Lennox SL25XPV heat pump in the same delivered-capacity class.
3. Mitsubishi P-Series H2i only if Mitsubishi supplies expanded cooling data at 115°F–120°F and the Manual J load fits its available capacity.

For each bid require:

- Current AHRI certificate for the complete combination.
- Manual J at an appropriate Phoenix summer design temperature.
- Manual S using expanded high-ambient capacity, not nominal tonnage.
- SEER2, EER2 and HSPF2 for the exact match.
- Capacity and input watts at 115°F, preferably 120°F.
- Maximum cooling ambient.
- Maximum-speed outdoor sound data.
- MCA, MOCP, breaker and conductor requirements.
- Size of any electric backup heater.
- Service-load calculation for the existing 200-amp panel.
- Duct static-pressure and airflow report.
- Written duct and refrigerant-line scope.
- Ten-year parts/compressor warranty terms and labor-warranty price.
- Guaranteed emergency response time during extreme heat.
- SRP rebate paperwork and exact AHRI reference number.

Decision

- Best extreme-desert value: Carrier, specifically the corresponding Infinity heat pump rather than the cooling-only Infinity 26.
- Best seasonal cooling efficiency: Lennox SL28XCV, but it is not a heat pump and offers less documented high-ambient margin.
- Best cold-climate heating: Mitsubishi H2i, but Phoenix does not need its principal advantage, and the evaluated 42,000-Btu/h model has the weakest peak-cooling fit and highest modeled TCO.
- Best overall for this renovation: Carrier if its net installed bid is within roughly $1,000–$2,000 of Lennox and the exact system retains enough capacity at the Manual J design condition. If Lennox is materially cheaper on an equivalent heat-pump configuration and provides satisfactory 115°F expanded data, it could become the lower-TCO choice.

final.content:
PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL AND REMOTE-WORK ARRANGEMENT: JORDAN HAYES

Executive conclusion

Assuming Texas law governs, Hayes is unlikely to obtain summary judgment enforcing indefinite full-time remote work. The company has the stronger argument for summary judgment, particularly as to reliance occurring after Hayes signed the May 1 offer letter.

The principal defects are:

1. The May 1 writing expressly says “hybrid schedule per company policy,” which is inconsistent with an unconditional full-remote arrangement.
2. Its conspicuous integration clause expressly supersedes prior verbal representations.
3. Hayes signed the document before entering the Texas lease on May 15, making reliance on the superseded April statement difficult to characterize as reasonable.
4. The June email came after the relevant relocation commitments and was sent by a manager who, according to HR records, lacked authority to modify standard terms.
5. Texas appellate authority is particularly restrictive toward affirmative promissory-estoppel claims in at-will employment.
6. Equity ordinarily protects reliance rather than creating an indefinite employment benefit inconsistent with the governing writing.

Hayes nevertheless has enough evidence to dispute whether a concrete promise was actually made and whether the company knowingly accepted full-remote performance through June. Those points might allow him to resist summary judgment on a narrowly framed reliance-damages theory if he proves that the $40,000 loss was incurred before May 1, or was irrevocably set in motion before then, and that the manager was acting with company authority during negotiations. They are much less likely to support an order compelling permanent full-remote work.

I. Governing law and summary-judgment framework

Because the employment was in Austin and the disputed performance concerns a Texas workplace, Texas law is the natural assumption. The conclusion could change if the offer letter contains a different choice-of-law provision, which the facts do not disclose.

Texas states the traditional promissory-estoppel elements as:

1. a promise;
2. foreseeability to the promisor that the promisee would rely;
3. substantial detrimental reliance; and
4. under the Restatement formulation adopted in Texas, enforcement must be necessary to avoid injustice.

Wheeler v. White recognized relief where a promisee acts to his detriment in reasonable reliance on an otherwise unenforceable promise and quoted Restatement § 90: the promise must be one the promisor should reasonably expect to induce “action or forbearance of a definite and substantial character,” and enforcement must be necessary to avoid injustice (https://law.justia.com/cases/texas/supreme-court/1965/a-10598-0.html).

On summary judgment, Texas courts view evidence and reasonable inferences in favor of the nonmovant. Judgment is appropriate only when no genuine issue of material fact exists and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. BPX Operating Co. v. Strickhausen summarizes that standard (https://law.justia.com/cases/texas/supreme-court/2021/19-0567.html).

That distinction matters:

- Hayes’s own motion for summary judgment should fail if authority, reliance, timing, or ratification remains genuinely disputed.
- The company’s motion is stronger, but its success may depend on whether Hayes seeks permanent enforcement or only losses traceable to pre-May 1 reliance.

II. Clear and definite promise

A. Evidence favoring Hayes

“Full remote work” is reasonably concrete as to frequency: it naturally means no regular office-attendance requirement. It is substantially more definite than vague assurances of flexibility, favorable treatment, or continued employment.

The June email is important corroboration. Although it postdates the offer letter, it is documentary evidence from the alleged speaker confirming that an April promise was made. The absence of a contemporaneous April record therefore affects weight and credibility but does not mean there is literally no evidence of the promise.

The circumstances also support foreseeability. The manager allegedly made the representation “to convince Hayes to relocate from Seattle to Austin.” If that evidence is accepted, the manager knew the promise was directed toward a major change of position rather than casual workplace planning.

Texas’s foundational estoppel decision emphasizes promises designed to influence the promisee’s conduct and conduct that the promisor knew had to occur before performance could begin. Wheeler, 398 S.W.2d at 96–97 (https://law.justia.com/cases/texas/supreme-court/1965/a-10598-0.html).

B. Evidence favoring the company

The promise is incomplete in important respects. Nothing establishes:

- a duration for full-remote status;
- whether the company could later change the arrangement;
- whether it was subject to general policy;
- whether occasional attendance could be required;
- whether it survived a management or policy change; or
- whether it was intended to alter an at-will employment relationship.

Texas requires definite employment commitments. In Montgomery County Hospital District v. Brown, the Texas Supreme Court held that oral employment assurances do not alter at-will status without a “definite, stated intention” to do so. General assurances that an employee would remain employed while performing satisfactorily were too indefinite (https://exa.ai/library/legal/opinion/xr39kv6rtt6; see also https://openjurist.org/965/sw2d/501/montgomery-county-hospital-district-v-brown).

The present promise is clearer about work location than Brown’s statements were about job security. But Hayes is not merely asking the court to find that zero office days were initially contemplated; he is asking it to enforce that arrangement against a later policy. Without evidence concerning duration or immunity from future policy changes, a court could find no sufficiently definite promise of permanent full-remote work.

C. Effect of the written offer

The May 1 offer says “hybrid schedule per company policy.” “Hybrid” ordinarily means a combination of remote and in-office work, not full remote. Thus, the written term does not merely omit an agreed number of remote days; it affirmatively points away from zero office attendance and incorporates company policy.

The offer’s bold integration clause is still more direct: “This agreement supersedes all prior verbal representations.” The alleged April promise falls squarely within “prior verbal representations.”

Texas distinguishes a standard merger clause from an explicit disclaimer of reliance. In Italian Cowboy Partners v. Prudential, the Texas Supreme Court held that a standard merger clause, standing alone, does not necessarily disclaim reliance for fraudulent-inducement purposes (https://law.justia.com/cases/texas/supreme-court/2011/2001694.html). Likewise, IBM v. Lufkin Industries explains that merger and reliance-disclaimer language are analytically distinct; the contract there both replaced prior communications and separately disclaimed reliance (https://law.justia.com/cases/texas/supreme-court/2019/17-0666.html).

Hayes’s clause does not literally say, “Hayes has not relied on any outside representation.” He can therefore argue that it is a merger clause, not an unequivocal waiver of reliance. Even so, it expressly supersedes the precise category of statement on which he relies, and the operative schedule term says “hybrid,” not “remote.” Those features make post-signing reliance materially less reasonable than reliance in a case involving only silence or a generic “entire agreement” provision.

D. Finding on this factor

There is evidence of a clear initial promise of zero regular office days. But there is not conclusive evidence of an irrevocable or indefinite right to full remote work. The May 1 writing superseded the April statement and substituted a policy-governed hybrid term. Accordingly:

- Hayes cannot establish the clear-promise factor conclusively for purposes of his own summary-judgment motion.
- The company has a strong argument that no enforceable promise of permanent full-remote work survived May 1.

III. Reasonable and foreseeable reliance

A. Foreseeability

Foreseeability strongly favors Hayes if the factfinder credits his account. A manager who promises full-remote work specifically to induce a Seattle-to-Austin relocation should expect the candidate to incur housing and moving consequences.

The $40,000 home-sale loss and Texas lease are the kinds of concrete transactions relocation discussions foreseeably induce. This case is therefore distinguishable from vague expectations of future business.

B. Timing of reliance

The timing substantially weakens Hayes’s position.

Known dates:

- May 1: Hayes received and signed the offer containing the hybrid-policy term and integration clause.
- May 15: Hayes signed the Texas lease.
- July 1: the three-office-days policy took effect.
- July 8: Hayes refused compliance.

The lease was signed 14 calendar days after the written offer:

May 15 − May 1 = 14 days.

Thus, when Hayes entered the lease, he had already agreed that the written offer superseded prior verbal representations and that his schedule was hybrid “per company policy.” Reliance on the April statement after May 1 was therefore reliance in the face of contrary written language.

The timing of the Seattle sale is not supplied. That omission is potentially dispositive:

- If the sale closed, or Hayes became irrevocably bound to sell, before May 1, the integration clause cannot retroactively make that already-completed reliance factually nonexistent. It would still bear on the available remedy, but the reliance occurred before the contradictory writing.
- If Hayes sold after May 1, the company can argue that the written offer made continued reliance on the April statement unreasonable as a matter of law.
- If the sale process began before May 1 but closed afterward, the relevant questions include when Hayes accepted a binding sale contract, whether he retained cancellation rights, and what portion of the $40,000 loss was avoidable after reading the offer.

C. Texas employment precedents

Texas employment cases are divided or restrictive concerning promissory estoppel.

Roberts v. Geosource Drilling Services allowed a prospective employee’s estoppel theory to survive summary judgment where the employer knew the applicant would leave existing employment, the employee signed employment documents, and the employer withdrew before work began. The court treated leaving the prior job in foreseeable reliance as potentially actionable (https://www.leagle.com/decision/1988805757sw2d481799).

But Patterson v. Leal rejected an affirmative promissory-estoppel claim based only on oral representations of indefinite at-will employment (https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/tx-court-of-appeals/1020724.html). Lotito v. Knife River likewise held in the Waco appellate district that promissory estoppel is defensive rather than an independent basis for affirmative relief in employment cases (https://cases.justia.com/texas/tenth-court-of-appeals/10-11-00216-cv.pdf?ts=1396146780).

Those cases are not perfectly aligned with Hayes’s claim. Hayes challenges a work-location term, not a promise of a fixed employment duration. Nevertheless, they demonstrate that Texas courts are reluctant to use promissory estoppel to circumvent written at-will employment terms.

D. Effect of written approvals for comparators

The two contemporaneously hired engineers who received written remote approvals cut both ways.

For Hayes, they show:

- full-remote arrangements were available;
- the alleged promise was operationally plausible rather than impossible;
- enforcing remote work would not necessarily create a benefit unknown to the company; and
- the company knew how important remote status was to recruits.

For the company, they show:

- a formal approval process existed;
- remote exceptions were documented in writing;
- Hayes’s absence of comparable written approval should have alerted him that his status was different; and
- the offer’s hybrid language was meaningful rather than boilerplate that everyone ignored.

On reasonable reliance, the second inference is probably stronger. A candidate who receives “hybrid per company policy,” while peers receive express written remote approval, has reason to seek correction before selling a home or signing a lease.

E. Finding on this factor

Foreseeability favors Hayes. Reasonableness does not, especially for actions taken after May 1. Hayes’s strongest possible reliance is a binding, documented commitment made before he signed the superseding offer. The May 15 lease is unlikely to qualify as reasonable reliance on the April oral statement.

IV. Substantial detriment

A. Quantitative assessment

The asserted realized loss is $40,000. That is facially substantial; it is not a nominal inconvenience or speculative future loss.

The office requirement is three days per week. Assuming a conventional five-day workweek:

3 required office days ÷ 5 workdays = 60% in-office.

That leaves at most:

2 remote days ÷ 5 workdays = 40% remote.

The difference between the alleged promise and the July policy is therefore:

- promised arrangement: 0 regular office days;
- new policy: 3 regular office days;
- change: 3 additional office days per week, or 60 percentage points of a five-day workweek.

The lease also constitutes a legal and financial commitment, although its monetary burden cannot be quantified without the rent, duration, deposit, early-termination terms, and mitigation evidence.

B. Causation problems

Hayes must connect the detriment to the remote-work promise, not merely to accepting employment or relocating.

There is an apparent factual tension: a promise of full remote work ordinarily reduces the need to relocate, yet the manager allegedly used it to convince Hayes to relocate from Seattle to Austin. Hayes would need to explain why full remote status induced an Austin move—for example, because the company required Texas residency but promised no routine office attendance, or because Hayes would not have relocated if he also had to commute three days weekly.

The $40,000 home-sale loss may also have resulted from market conditions or Hayes’s decision to accept the Austin job generally rather than the remote term specifically. Relevant evidence would include:

- the Seattle sale contract and closing date;
- the home’s basis and objective market value;
- competing offers;
- communications showing that Hayes conditioned relocation on remote work;
- whether Hayes would have moved for the job on a hybrid basis; and
- whether the lease was necessary notwithstanding full-remote status.

C. Finding on this factor

The amount is sufficiently substantial if causally attributable to the promise. But substantiality alone does not establish reasonable reliance, authority, or entitlement to the requested remedy. The missing timing and causation evidence prevents summary judgment for Hayes.

V. Authority, ratification, and the June email

A. Actual authority

HR records show that the manager lacked authority to modify standard terms. If undisputed and properly authenticated, that defeats actual authority.

The June email proves at most that the manager repeated or confirmed the promise. It does not itself prove that the company authorized the manager to create an exception. Moreover, it came after the May 15 lease, so it cannot have induced that transaction.

B. Apparent authority

Under Gaines v. Kelly, apparent authority must arise from the principal’s conduct, not merely from the purported agent’s statements. It exists when the principal knowingly permits the agent to appear authorized or, through lack of ordinary care, clothes the agent with indicia of authority. The third party must also act as a reasonably prudent person using diligence to ascertain authority. Gaines further stresses that authority to facilitate a transaction does not necessarily include authority to alter terms or commit the principal (http://docs.texasappellate.com/scotx/op/05-1092/2007-08-24.medina.pdf).

Applied here:

- The hiring manager’s role in negotiations may create some appearance of authority to discuss work conditions.
- But the manager’s own assurances cannot alone establish apparent authority.
- The company’s written offer is direct principal conduct and places the schedule under company policy.
- The written approvals issued to two other engineers show that exceptions normally required formal documentation.
- Hayes’s signed integration clause further undermines an inference that the manager could orally override the standard offer.

On the present facts, apparent authority is weak and probably insufficient as a matter of law unless Hayes can identify company conduct—apart from the manager’s own words—holding the manager out as authorized to approve permanent remote exceptions.

C. Ratification by remote work through June

Hayes worked fully remotely through June without objection. That supplies a possible ratification, waiver, or course-of-performance argument, but it is not conclusive.

The period is limited. May and June contain 61 calendar days in total:

31 days in May + 30 days in June = 61 days.

The actual number of working days would be lower, and the record does not specify Hayes’s start date. More importantly:

- the July policy did not take effect until July 1;
- full-remote performance before July may have complied with then-existing policy;
- no evidence shows that HR or an authorized executive knew of the manager’s special promise;
- ratification generally requires knowledge of the material facts; and
- one or two months of tolerated remote work does not necessarily demonstrate an intent to grant a permanent exception from future policy.

Texas describes ratification as adoption or confirmation, with knowledge of all material facts, of an earlier act that was not originally binding. BPX Operating Co. v. Strickhausen (https://law.justia.com/cases/texas/supreme-court/2021/19-0567.html). Without evidence that an authorized corporate decisionmaker knew both of the promise and the manager’s lack of authority, ratification cannot be established conclusively.

D. Finding on authority

The current record favors the company. Hayes cannot obtain summary judgment because actual authority is negated by HR records and apparent authority or ratification would require additional principal-side evidence. The company may obtain summary judgment if Hayes cannot produce evidence that an authorized corporate actor knew of and adopted the exception.

VI. Injustice without enforcement

A. Arguments for Hayes

Hayes made an unusually large housing sacrifice in response to a recruiting representation. If the manager deliberately used full remote work to secure acceptance and relocation, allowing the company immediately to invoke a contrary policy could appear inequitable.

The June confirmation, initial acceptance of full-remote performance, and written remote approvals for peers reinforce the argument that the promise was genuine and operationally feasible. Hayes can also argue that money may not fully compensate him for continuing commuting burdens or loss of control over where he works.

B. Arguments for the company

The injustice inquiry asks whether enforcement is necessary, not merely whether Hayes was disappointed. Several alternatives weaken the necessity of permanently enforcing remote work:

- reliance damages for any proven, reasonable pre-May 1 loss;
- lease-mitigation damages;
- rescission or negotiated separation;
- prospective compliance with the policy while preserving a damages claim; or
- a limited transition period rather than a perpetual exception.

Wheeler explains that promissory estoppel does not simply create the contract the parties failed to make; it prevents insistence on strict legal rights where doing so would be unjust (https://law.justia.com/cases/texas/supreme-court/1965/a-10598-0.html). That equitable principle generally supports compensation for foreseeable reliance, not automatic benefit-of-the-bargain enforcement of an undefined-duration employment arrangement.

The company also gave Hayes the written governing term before the May 15 lease. Enforcing the prior oral term would effectively delete “hybrid schedule per company policy” and the integration clause. Equity is unlikely to rewrite the signed offer where Hayes had an opportunity to request the same written approval his peers received.

C. Scope and duration problem

Even if some relief is warranted, “enforce the remote work arrangement” lacks an endpoint. Possible durations include:

- until Hayes resigns or is terminated;
- until the next policy amendment;
- for a reasonable relocation transition;
- for a specific but unstated period; or
- indefinitely.

A court cannot readily enforce a promise whose duration and termination conditions were never established. Permanent specific enforcement would also sit uneasily with at-will employment: if the company could lawfully terminate Hayes, ordering it to preserve one working condition indefinitely would offer limited practical protection.

D. Finding on injustice

A factfinder could regard uncompensated pre-May 1 reliance as unjust. But permanent full-remote enforcement is not shown to be the only way to avoid that injustice. Reliance damages, if properly proved, are the more natural equitable remedy.

VII. Likely summary-judgment disposition

A. Hayes’s motion to enforce full remote work

Hayes should not receive summary judgment. At minimum, genuine disputes remain over:

- the promise’s duration and immunity from later policy;
- when the Seattle sale became binding;
- whether remote status, rather than the job generally, caused the loss;
- the manager’s authority;
- corporate knowledge and ratification; and
- whether permanent enforcement is necessary to avoid injustice.

Several points affirmatively favor the company as a matter of law: the superseding integration clause, the conflicting hybrid-policy term, and the manager’s documented lack of actual authority.

B. Company’s motion against permanent enforcement

The company is likely entitled to summary judgment against a claim for an indefinite judicially enforced right to full remote work. The best grounds are:

1. no sufficiently definite promise concerning duration or future policy changes;
2. the April representation was superseded by the May 1 writing;
3. post-May 1 reliance was not reasonable in light of the signed terms;
4. no evidence that the manager had authority to override the offer;
5. no conclusive ratification by an authorized actor; and
6. permanent enforcement is not necessary where narrower reliance relief could address any injustice.

Texas’s restrictive employment-estoppel decisions provide an additional, though jurisdiction-dependent, basis. Lotito treats promissory estoppel as defensive only in employment cases, while Patterson rejects reliance on purely oral promises of indefinite employment. Roberts is more favorable to an employee but involved repudiation before employment began after the employee left an existing job, not an attempt to override a signed offer governing ongoing employment.

C. Possible surviving claim

A narrow claim for reliance damages may survive if Hayes produces evidence that:

- before May 1 he sold the Seattle home or became irrevocably obligated to do so;
- the manager knew that action would follow from the full-remote assurance;
- company conduct gave the manager apparent authority over remote-work approvals;
- the $40,000 loss is documented and was caused by the promise; and
- Hayes could not reasonably avoid or mitigate that loss after receiving the written offer.

If the home-sale commitment occurred after May 1, the company’s summary-judgment position becomes substantially stronger. The May 15 lease, standing alone, is unlikely to sustain the claim because it was executed two weeks after Hayes accepted the superseding written terms.

Final determination

Hayes probably cannot enforce full remote work on summary judgment. The April statement and June confirmation create evidence that a promise was made, and the alleged $40,000 loss is plainly substantial. But the decisive weaknesses are reasonable reliance, authority, definiteness, and remedy.

The most likely result under Texas law is:

- summary judgment denied to Hayes on permanent full-remote enforcement;
- summary judgment likely granted to the company against an indefinite remote-work entitlement; and
- possible survival of a limited reliance-damages claim only if Hayes proves a binding pre-May 1 housing detriment and company-side facts supporting authority or ratification.

The unknown date and contractual status of the Seattle sale is the largest factual uncertainty. If it occurred before May 1, Hayes has a materially stronger equitable damages claim. If it occurred after May 1, both the home loss and the May 15 lease were incurred after written notice that his schedule was hybrid and policy-governed, making detrimental reliance on the April oral promise unreasonable as a matter of law.

final.content:
COMPARATIVE REPORT: JOHN DEERE 9RX 540 VS. CASE IH STEIGER 540 QUADTRAC
Regina-area, Saskatchewan; 200-acre canola/wheat operation

EXECUTIVE CONCLUSION

For the stated soil, guidance fleet and dealer geography, the Case IH Steiger 540 Quadtrac is the better fit—provided the tractor will actually be used intensively for custom work or additional rented land. It should deliver slightly lower fuel cost per hectare, easier integration with the existing Trimble RTK system, and potentially faster local field support through Young’s Equipment in Regina. Its long-established oscillating Quadtrac undercarriage is also a modest uptime advantage on sticky clay-loam.

The advantage is not large enough to make either tractor economically rational for only 200 owned acres. A 540-hp four-track tractor costing roughly C$850,000–C$950,000 would be drastically underutilized. If it performs one tillage pass and one seeding pass annually, only about 162 hectare-passes are worked per year. Fixed ownership cost would dominate fuel and track differences, producing an estimated ten-year tractor-only cost above C$600 per hectare-pass. Custom hiring, leasing during peak periods, or a much smaller 300–400 hp tractor is economically preferable.

If “180+ operational days” means substantial custom work and approximately 600 engine hours per year, the modeled ten-year result is:

• Case IH Steiger 540 Quadtrac: approximately C$1.93 million after estimated CCA tax benefit, or C$28/ha worked.
• John Deere 9RX 540: approximately C$2.04 million after estimated CCA tax benefit, or C$29.5/ha worked.
• Modeled Case advantage: approximately C$1.5/ha, or about C$100,000 over ten years.

These figures exclude implements, operator labour and financing-specific tax effects. Dealer quotes for both tractors, replacement belts and guaranteed service response are essential before purchase.

1. OPERATING-SCALE ISSUE

Two hundred acres equals:

200 acres × 0.404686 = 80.94 hectares.

With one seeding and one heavy-tillage pass annually:

80.94 ha × 2 passes = 161.9 hectare-passes/year
161.9 × 10 years = 1,619 hectare-passes over ten years.

Either tractor can cover 200 acres in approximately one long day per operation with a large implement. Consequently, “180+ operational days annually” cannot describe work on the owned 200 acres alone. It presumably means custom farming, rented land, transport, scraper work or other non-crop use.

Hours and hectares worked—not calendar days—determine belt life, fuel consumption and cost per hectare. The conclusions therefore distinguish:

1. A 200-acre own-farm case; and
2. A high-utilization case of 600 hours per year, consistent with meaningful custom or expanded-acreage work.

2. MACHINE CAPABILITY

John Deere 9RX 540

The 9RX has a 13.6-litre JD14 engine rated at 540 hp and 594 maximum hp, an e18 18-speed powershift transmission, standard four-track drive, and a base weight of 24,639–25,546 kg depending on undercarriage. Standard track width is 762 mm/30 inches, with 18-, 24- and 36-inch alternatives. Deere offers Camso 3500 and heavy-duty 6500 belts, up to 416 L/min hydraulic output, a 1,514-litre fuel tank and 120-litre DEF tank. Engine oil and hydraulic/transmission intervals are 500 and 1,500 hours respectively (https://www.deere.ca/en/tractors/4wd-track-tractors/9rx-540/).

Case IH Steiger 540 Quadtrac

The Case is also a 540-hp-class articulated four-track tractor, using an FPT 12.9-litre engine. A Nebraska-tested earlier Steiger 540 Quadtrac used a 16-speed powershift. Current AFS Connect machines can be configured with PowerDrive or CVXDrive depending on market and specification. Case describes the Quadtrac as four individually driven, positive-drive oscillating tracks designed to maintain ground contact and flotation (https://www.caseih.com/en-ca/canada/products/tractors/steiger-series).

Representative published specifications for the earlier 540 include approximately 1,173 litres of fuel and an unballasted weight around 23,900 kg, although current-machine specification must be confirmed in the purchase quote.

Practical capacity

Both tractors can comfortably pull large air drills and primary-tillage implements. Deere has the larger published fuel tank and therefore the longer potential refuelling interval. Both offer hydraulic capacities sufficient for large air seeders if ordered with their high-flow packages.

3. FIELD SPEED AND FUEL EFFICIENCY

Important speed qualification

Twelve to fifteen mph is not a normal sustained speed for heavy primary tillage or air seeding on Saskatchewan clay-loam:

• Heavy tillage is normally limited by draft, residue flow and finish quality, often around 5–8 mph.
• Air seeding is commonly around 4.5–6.5 mph, depending on opener, soil moisture and desired seed placement.
• At 12–15 mph, opener bounce, poor depth control, rock impact and undercarriage shock become concerns.
• Deere’s Nebraska test gearing shows the 9RX 540 reaching only 10.75 mph by 14th gear; the upper gears are principally transport/light-load ratios, not full-draft working gears (https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=4491&context=tractormuseumlit).

Consequently, a fuel-per-acre estimate at 12–15 mph is meaningful only if implement width and draft are specified. Higher speed increases theoretical acres per hour, but a tractor may have to pull a narrower or shallower implement to maintain that speed.

Independent fuel evidence

The newer John Deere Nebraska Test 2310 reported, at rated-speed drawbar load:

• Drawbar power: 406.93 hp
• Fuel efficiency: 15.89 hp-h/US gal
• Calculated fuel rate: 406.93 ÷ 15.89 = 25.61 US gal/h
• Metric rate: 25.61 × 3.785 = 96.9 L/h

The same report gives a drawbar-operation fuel-mass range of 77.9–84.1 kg/h, approximately 92–100 L/h depending on load and fuel density (https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=4491&context=tractormuseumlit).

Nebraska Test 2188 for the earlier Steiger 540 Quadtrac reported:

• Rated PTO output: 480.46 hp at 26.21 US gal/h
• Maximum PTO output: 541.99 hp at 27.81 US gal/h
• Rated fuel efficiency: 18.33 hp-h/gal
• Maximum fuel efficiency: 19.49 hp-h/gal

Thus:

26.21 × 3.785 = 99.2 L/h at rated PTO load
27.81 × 3.785 = 105.3 L/h at maximum PTO power

These are PTO rather than directly comparable drawbar observations, so they should not be interpreted as proving that one tractor uses a precise percentage less in field work (https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=3656&context=tractormuseumlit).

Case’s earlier Steiger platform also recorded 16.59 drawbar hp-h/gal at maximum power and 15.82 hp-h/gal at 75% pull in Nebraska Test 2096, indicating strong drawbar efficiency for its generation (https://ocj.com/2015/04/case-ih-steigertractors-break-drawbar-fuel-efficiency-records-in-nebraska-test-results/).

Fuel per acre at 12–15 mph

Theoretical field capacity is:

Acres/hour = width in feet × speed in mph × 0.1212 × field efficiency.

At 80% field efficiency:

40-foot implement at 12 mph:
40 × 12 × 0.1212 × 0.80 = 46.54 ac/h

40-foot implement at 15 mph:
40 × 15 × 0.1212 × 0.80 = 58.18 ac/h

60-foot implement at 12 mph:
60 × 12 × 0.1212 × 0.80 = 69.81 ac/h

60-foot implement at 15 mph:
60 × 15 × 0.1212 × 0.80 = 87.26 ac/h

Using 97–100 L/h:

| Width and speed | Capacity | Deere at 97 L/h | Case at 100 L/h |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 40 ft, 12 mph | 46.5 ac/h | 2.08 L/ac | 2.15 L/ac |
| 40 ft, 15 mph | 58.2 ac/h | 1.67 L/ac | 1.72 L/ac |
| 60 ft, 12 mph | 69.8 ac/h | 1.39 L/ac | 1.43 L/ac |
| 60 ft, 15 mph | 87.3 ac/h | 1.11 L/ac | 1.15 L/ac |

These are theoretical full-width figures and should not be used as a purchase guarantee. They omit turning, overlap, filling, headlands, partial engine loading, hydraulic-fan demand and field variability.

More realistic Saskatchewan examples

Heavy tillage, 40 feet, 6 mph, 75% field efficiency:

40 × 6 × 0.1212 × 0.75 = 21.82 ac/h

At 97–100 L/h:

Deere: 97 ÷ 21.82 = 4.45 L/ac = 11.0 L/ha
Case: 100 ÷ 21.82 = 4.58 L/ac = 11.3 L/ha

Seeding, 60 feet, 5.5 mph, 75% efficiency:

60 × 5.5 × 0.1212 × 0.75 = 30.0 ac/h

Deere: 97 ÷ 30.0 = 3.23 L/ac = 7.98 L/ha
Case: 100 ÷ 30.0 = 3.33 L/ac = 8.23 L/ha

In actual reduced-load operation, the Steiger’s engine and transmission may run below the quoted maximum fuel rate. Its historical drawbar results suggest a possible 2–4% Case fuel advantage at equivalent work, but the available tests are from different model years and test points. A properly controlled dealer demonstration with the same implement is needed to establish a credible Regina-area difference.

Fuel verdict: effectively a tie within normal field variability, with a slight probable advantage to Case under sustained drawbar load and a range/refuelling advantage to Deere because of its 1,514-litre tank.

4. TRACK PERFORMANCE AND DURABILITY ON CLAY-LOAM

Soil interaction

Four independent tracks distribute load better than a two-track crawler and reduce power hop compared with a high-horsepower wheeled tractor. Both machines are suitable for clay-loam and intermittent wet conditions.

A recent comparison using 760 mm belts reported almost identical footprints—about 5.7 m² for Quadtrac and 5.8 m² for 9RX. On sandy test soil, measured slip was 4.0% for Quadtrac and 4.6% for 9RX. That is not a Saskatchewan clay-loam test and involved different horsepower models, but it supports the conclusion that the traction difference is small (https://www.profi.co.uk/test-centre/high-horsepower-tracked-tractors-in-comparison-part-1-the-three-musketeers/).

John Deere

Advantages:

• Camso 6500 belts use reinforced drive-lug technology.
• Deere explicitly lists Camso 3500 and 6500 belts for the 9RX.
• The 6500 is identified as suitable for hard-packed clay, sticky/wet ground and gumbo, and is designed for aggressive heavy-draft applications (https://www.dandjfarmsupply.com/index.php?main_page=product_info&products_id=804).
• The 9RX’s belt and undercarriage options are well suited to heavy tillage.

Risks:

• High draft plus sharp articulated turns can stress drive lugs and increase berming.
• High-speed road travel creates belt heat.
• Deere’s four-track agricultural population is younger than the Quadtrac platform, so there is less long-duration fleet history.

Case IH

Advantages:

• Quadtrac has more than 25 years of commercial track-system development.
• Each positive-drive track oscillates independently, helping maintain contact over field irregularities (https://www.caseih.com/en-ca/canada/products/tractors/steiger-series).
• The platform has a very large Western Canadian installed base, improving technician familiarity and used/aftermarket parts availability.
• Young’s specifically advertises Quadtrac inspection capability.

Risks:

• More bogie wheels, seals and undercarriage components create multiple inspection points.
• Mud packed around rollers and idlers can accelerate seal and bearing wear.
• Belt heat and lug damage remain risks during long road travel.

Expected life

A replacement-track source reports a Camso agricultural warranty of four years/2,000 hours for 9RX belts. The same supplier reports that some Soucy Quadtrac replacements carry five-year/3,000-hour warranty coverage (https://www.ntstiresupply.com/ptk-shared/the-top-replacement-tracks-for-your-john-deere-9rx; https://www.ntstiresupply.com/ptk-shared/the-top-tracks-for-your-case-ih-quadtrac).

Warranty is not expected life, but it gives a useful risk boundary:

• At 600 h/year, 2,000 hours occurs in 3.3 years and 3,000 hours in 5 years.
• At 1,440 h/year—180 days × 8 h/day—2,000 hours occurs in only 1.4 years.
• A ten-year, 600 h/year ownership period is 6,000 hours, making at least one complete belt replacement plausible and two possible.
• At 1,440 h/year, the machine reaches 14,400 hours in ten years; multiple belt sets and major undercarriage rebuilding would be expected.

Clay-loam itself is less abrasive than sandy or gravelly soil, but sticky wet clay can pack around rollers. Belt life will depend more on road percentage, alignment, tension, turning practice and loading than on the difference between these two tractors.

Track verdict: slight Case advantage for long-proven undercarriage experience and replacement-belt choice; no evidence supports a large life difference. Deere’s Camso 6500 is fully suitable for the stated soil.

5. TRIMBLE RTK AND TELEMATICS

Case IH

The Steiger is the stronger fit with an existing Trimble fleet. Trimble offers an Autopilot installation specifically for AccuGuide-ready Case IH tractors, including Steiger Tier 4B 370, 420, 470, 500, 540, 580 and 620. The kit integrates into vehicle hydraulics and includes CNH hybrid cabling and NAV-900/CAN support (https://vantagenortheast.com/autopilot----accuguide-ready-case-ih---intellisteer-ready-new-holland-vehicles-w/-gfx-750---xcn-1050-displays/).

The NAV-900 supports RTK-capable multi-constellation positioning, two CAN ports and guidance-ready J1939 integration. Trimble says it can normally be installed with a compatible GFX display and autoguidance in approximately half a day (https://ag.ptxtrimble.com/hubfs/PTx%20Datasheets/022503-2051_PTx%20Trimble_NAV-900_DS_USL_0724_LR%20-%20SEC.pdf?hsLang=en).

Case’s current telematics platform provides lifetime connectivity and access through FieldOps, with third-party sharing of machine, field and agronomic information (https://www.caseih.com/en-ca/canada/products/tractors/steiger-series).

John Deere

The 9RX comes with an integrated StarFire receiver, G5 Plus display, AutoTrac, JDLink, wireless data transfer, Remote Display Access, Expert Alerts and Service ADVISOR Remote. Deere’s integrated system is arguably the more complete single-brand telematics package (https://www.deere.ca/en/tractors/4wd-track-tractors/9rx-540/).

However, retaining Trimble RTK can require a separate display, receiver, steering interface or unlock. That duplicates hardware already included in the Deere purchase and may not expose every Deere automation feature to the Trimble display. Deere’s most advanced functions—AutoPath, Turn Automation, implement guidance and Machine Sync—are optimized around its own G5/StarFire ecosystem.

Telematics verdict:

• Best native machine diagnostics and tightly integrated OEM automation: Deere.
• Best fit with the farm’s existing Trimble RTK corrections, displays, AB lines and operator training: Case.
• For this operation, Case wins unless the farm intends to migrate the entire precision-ag fleet to Deere Operations Center and StarFire.

6. DEALER COVERAGE AND SERVICE RESPONSE WITHIN 100 KM OF REGINA

Case IH

Young’s Equipment has a Regina branch at 4000 East Victoria Avenue/Highway 1 East, telephone 306-565-2405, with an after-hours parts number. It describes itself as Saskatchewan’s largest Case IH dealer and operates nine locations, including Regina, Moose Jaw, Weyburn, Windthorst, Davidson, Raymore, Watrous, Chamberlain and Assiniboia (https://www.youngs.ca/; https://www.youngs.ca/service/case-ih-inpection-program).

Young’s reports:

• More than C$22 million in parts inventory;
• More than 260 employees;
• Approximately 60 hours of annual training per service technician;
• Dedicated Quadtrac inspection capability (https://www.youngs.ca/about).

That combination is a material uptime advantage for a tractor based near Regina.

John Deere

Brandt has Regina headquarters and a substantial John Deere presence, including parts support and 24/7 live-operator coverage, but its Regina listing is also associated heavily with John Deere construction and forestry. The available evidence does not clearly establish that the Regina branch dispatches agricultural 9RX field technicians on the same basis as a full-line rural Deere agriculture store (https://www.brandt.ca/Divisions/Tractor/Branch-Locator; https://www.brandt.ca/Divisions/Tractor/Contact-Us).

Pattison Agriculture’s full-line Deere branch at Balcarres is approximately at the outer edge of the requested 100 km radius, depending on farm location. It advertises after-hours service until 10 p.m. daily and provides a dedicated service number (https://www.pattisonag.com/map-hours-directions-tractors-tillages-excavators-dealership--balcarres-sk).

Response-time limitation

Neither manufacturer nor local dealer publishes a binding technician-arrival time. It would be unsupported to claim a specific two-, four- or eight-hour response. Before purchase, request a written seasonal service-level agreement covering:

• Telephone response within 30 minutes;
• Remote diagnostic connection within one hour;
• Field technician dispatch target;
• Maximum technician travel charge;
• Priority during seeding;
• Loaner tractor or rental-credit terms;
• Stocking of bogie seals, rollers, tension components, DEF sensors and critical hydraulic/electronic parts.

Dealer verdict: Case has the clearer local agricultural-service advantage because Young’s is physically in Regina, explicitly supports Quadtracs and has a dense southern Saskatchewan branch network.

7. TEN-YEAR OWNERSHIP-COST MODEL

Assumptions

Because current transaction prices, track quotations and service contracts were not available, this is a decision model rather than a dealer quote.

High-use case:

• 10 years;
• 600 hours/year, or 6,000 total hours;
• Deere acquisition: C$943,000, anchored to a Saskatchewan listing for a 2024 9RX 540 with 357 hours (https://www.agdealer.com/detail/1354974/2024-john-deere-9rx-540);
• Case acquisition: assumed C$850,000 pending quote;
• Salvage value: 33% of acquisition price;
• Opportunity/financing cost: 5% on average invested capital;
• Insurance and housing: 1% of acquisition cost annually;
• Repairs and maintenance: 2.6% of purchase price annually, including a provision for worn parts and undercarriage work;
• Diesel: C$1.40/L;
• Deere field fuel: 97 L/h;
• Case field fuel: 100 L/h in the conservative base case;
• Trimble adaptation/duplication allowance: C$20,000 Deere and C$10,000 Case;
• Operator, implements, DEF and GST excluded;
• PST assumed exempt for qualifying primary-farm machinery. Saskatchewan guidance states that qualifying farm implements, machinery and repairs used directly in primary farming may be purchased PST-exempt (https://publications.saskatchewan.ca/api/v1/products/7947/formats/11441/download).

Deere calculation

Depreciation:
C$943,000 − (33% × C$943,000)
= C$943,000 − C$311,190
= C$631,810

Financing/opportunity cost:
[(C$943,000 + C$311,190) ÷ 2] × 5% × 10
= C$313,548

Insurance/housing:
C$943,000 × 1% × 10 = C$94,300

Repairs/maintenance:
C$943,000 × 2.6% × 10 = C$245,180

Fuel:
97 L/h × 6,000 h × C$1.40/L = C$814,800

Trimble allowance:
C$20,000

Pre-tax ten-year economic cost:
C$631,810 + C$313,548 + C$94,300 + C$245,180 + C$814,800 + C$20,000
= C$2,119,638

Case calculation

Depreciation:
C$850,000 − (33% × C$850,000)
= C$850,000 − C$280,500
= C$569,500

Financing/opportunity cost:
[(C$850,000 + C$280,500) ÷ 2] × 5% × 10
= C$282,625

Insurance/housing:
C$850,000 × 1% × 10 = C$85,000

Repairs/maintenance:
C$850,000 × 2.6% × 10 = C$221,000

Fuel:
100 L/h × 6,000 h × C$1.40/L = C$840,000

Trimble allowance:
C$10,000

Pre-tax ten-year economic cost:
C$569,500 + C$282,625 + C$85,000 + C$221,000 + C$840,000 + C$10,000
= C$2,008,125

The Case is approximately C$111,500 less before CCA tax effects. If Case achieves a 2% field-fuel advantage rather than consuming 100 L/h, its ten-year advantage increases by approximately:

2 L/h × 6,000 h × C$1.40 = C$16,800.

8. SASKATCHEWAN CCA IMPLICATIONS

A farm tractor is generally Class 10 property with a 30% declining-balance CCA rate (https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/forms-publications/publications/rc4060/rc4060-13.html).

The reinstated Accelerated Investment Incentive was proposed for eligible assets acquired and available for use from 2025 through 2029. For property normally subject to the half-year rule, the enhanced first-year deduction is three times the normal first-year allowance. For a 30% Class 10 asset:

Normal first year:
30% × 50% = 15%

Accelerated first year:
15% × 3 = 45%

The federal description is at https://budget.canada.ca/update-miseajour/2024/report-rapport/tm-mf-en.html.

Illustrative ten-year deductions per C$1 of capital cost are:

Year 1: 0.4500
Year 2: 0.1650
Year 3: 0.1155
Year 4: 0.08085
Year 5: 0.05660
Year 6: 0.03962
Year 7: 0.02773
Year 8: 0.01941
Year 9: 0.01359
Year 10: 0.00951

Total nominal CCA over ten years:
0.9783 per C$1, before disposition and possible recapture.

At a 5% discount rate, the approximate present value of those deductions is 0.866 per C$1. Therefore:

At the 10% combined Saskatchewan small-business rate:
CCA tax-shield NPV ≈ 0.866 × 10% = 8.66% of basis.

At the 27% general corporate rate:
CCA tax-shield NPV ≈ 0.866 × 27% = 23.38% of basis.

Saskatchewan’s combined 2026 rate is approximately 10% on qualifying income up to C$500,000, 16% between C$500,000 and C$600,000, and 27% at the general rate. The provincial small-business limit is C$600,000 (https://www.saskatchewan.ca/business/taxes-licensing-and-reporting/provincial-taxes-policies-and-bulletins/corporation-income-tax).

At a 10% marginal rate:

Deere tax shield:
C$943,000 × 8.66% = approximately C$81,700

Case tax shield:
C$850,000 × 8.66% = approximately C$73,600

After estimated CCA benefit:

Deere: C$2,119,638 − C$81,700 = C$2,037,938
Case: C$2,008,125 − C$73,600 = C$1,934,525

CCA does not change the ranking: the more expensive tractor produces a larger deduction but still requires more capital.

Any proposed post-September 2026 immediate-expensing measure should not be assumed until eligibility, enactment and available-for-use timing are confirmed with the farm’s accountant. Even a 100% first-year deduction changes cash-flow timing rather than the machine’s underlying economic cost. Disposition can also create CCA recapture.

9. COST PER HECTARE WORKED

High-use case

Assume half the hours are seeding at approximately 14.1 ha/h and half are heavy tillage at approximately 8.8 ha/h:

Average productivity:
(14.1 + 8.8) ÷ 2 = 11.45 ha/h

Ten-year hectares worked:
11.45 ha/h × 6,000 h = 68,700 ha

After-tax tractor-only cost:

Deere:
C$2,037,938 ÷ 68,700 = C$29.66/ha

Case:
C$1,934,525 ÷ 68,700 = C$28.16/ha

Case advantage:
C$1.50/ha, approximately 5%.

Own 200-acre case

Ten-year work is only 1,619 hectare-passes. Even if low utilization reduces fuel and repairs, fixed depreciation and capital cost remain close to C$1 million.

A simplified low-use fixed-cost floor for Deere is:

Depreciation C$631,810
+ capital cost C$313,548
+ insurance C$94,300
= C$1,039,658 before fuel, repairs and Trimble.

C$1,039,658 ÷ 1,619 ha = C$642/ha-pass.

Case:

C$569,500 + C$282,625 + C$85,000
= C$937,125

C$937,125 ÷ 1,619 = C$579/ha-pass.

Actual all-in cost would be higher. This confirms that neither tractor is financially justified by 200 acres.

10. UPTIME ASSESSMENT

Factors favouring Deere:

• Larger fuel tank and potentially longer work period between refuelling;
• JDLink, Expert Alerts, Remote Display Access and Service ADVISOR Remote;
• 500-hour engine-oil and 1,500-hour hydraulic intervals;
• Simplified JD14 aftertreatment without a diesel particulate filter;
• Heavy-duty Camso 6500 belt option.

Factors favouring Case:

• Regina-based full-line agricultural dealer with after-hours parts;
• Explicit local Quadtrac inspection experience;
• Dense Young’s branch network;
• Long-established Quadtrac undercarriage and large Western Canadian fleet;
• Easier Trimble Autopilot/NAV-900 integration;
• Broader replacement-belt choices, including reported 3,000-hour Soucy warranty options.

On balance, Case should deliver superior practical uptime for this particular farm—not because the 9RX is inherently unreliable, but because local agricultural dealer depth and Trimble compatibility reduce the most likely sources of seasonal delay.

FINAL RECOMMENDATION

1. If the tractor will serve only the 200 owned acres, buy neither. Use a custom operator, rent a tractor for peak periods, or select a substantially smaller machine. The potential Case saving of roughly C$1–C$2/ha under high utilization is immaterial compared with the hundreds of dollars per hectare caused by underutilizing a C$850,000–C$950,000 tractor.

2. If the operation genuinely expects approximately 600 or more hours per year through custom farming or acreage expansion, select the Case IH Steiger 540 Quadtrac, subject to:
   • A delivered price at least C$50,000–C$75,000 below the comparable Deere;
   • Written Trimble NAV-900/GFX compatibility confirmation;
   • A Young’s seasonal service-response agreement;
   • Full-set belt and bogie-rebuild quotations;
   • A same-implement field demonstration measuring litres/hectare, slip and hectares/hour.

3. Specify 30- or 36-inch general-ag/heavy-duty belts, high-flow hydraulics appropriate to the air seeder, and telematics access for dealer remote diagnostics. Minimize loaded road travel and sharp headland turns to protect belts.

4. Do not base the purchase case on 12–15 mph field operation. Budget at approximately 5–8 mph for tillage and 4.5–6.5 mph for seeding. Under those realistic conditions, implement width, field efficiency and operator practice will affect fuel per hectare more than the small efficiency difference between these tractors.

Overall ranking for this operation:

• Uptime: Case IH, modest advantage.
• Trimble integration: Case IH, clear advantage.
• Clay-loam track suitability: both strong; Case slight lifecycle advantage.
• Fuel efficiency per hectare: near tie, with a possible small Case advantage under equal drawbar work.
• Refuelling range and integrated OEM diagnostics: John Deere advantage.
• Ten-year cost per hectare at high utilization: Case IH lower by approximately 5%.
• Economics on only 200 acres: neither tractor is justified.

Which delivers superior uptime and lower cost per hectare worked given our soil conditions and operational intensity?
